right call on the touch matrix before any kills. 19 isn't a "grep + fix" number — it's a "prove each one is gone" number. if any one survives the cutover, you've got a phantom read on the old shape that fires under the right conditions and nobody knows why.

shape I'd use for the matrix — amend or throw out as you like:

  site_id        file:line, function, PR if open
  category       one of: shard_assign / routing / admin / validation / other
                 (forces honesty when something doesn't fit cleanly)
  current_call   exact shape expected from label_map today
  replacement    what it becomes (direct query / new API / delete / fold-into-X)
  group          kill batch — what's the dependency order, what can parallel
  owner          if you're not solo
  verifier       how you prove the site is actually dead, not just edited
  risk           what blows up if it ships alive

the verifier column is the one that matters most for your "fake-clean cutover" worry. an edited file isn't a dead read — especially on the admin / validation paths. you want a probe that actually drives the path under the new shape and gets the expected answer, not just "no occurrences of label_map in the file."

two things worth pinning before you start filling it in:

  1. groups independent, or are there order dependencies? (e.g. a routing read that depends on a validation read being migrated first, or admin paths that read what the hot path just wrote.) if there are deps, the matrix doubles as a sequencing doc and you should mark the edges on it.

  2. are you cutting over with shadow traffic on prod or a feature-flag flip? that decides what a "verifier" actually looks like per site — "shadow output matches for N hours under load X" is a much stronger bar than a unit test, and it's the one that catches a phantom read in the long tail.

if you want, once you've drafted the matrix I can do a second pass on categorization — the admin / validation bucket is where things tend to get mis-classified and you want a clean split before you start grouping kills.

### What is and isn't stable in v0

Stable v0 contract (PM-facing) — the envelope wrapper plus the fixed top-level fields. Any consumer can read these today and tomorrow without coordination.

- `envelope_version`, `event_id`, `occurred_at`, `ingested_at`
- `subject.service_id`, `subject.tenant_scope`
- `window.start`, `window.end`, `window.duration_seconds`
- `status` (stable enum, shared across event types)
- `provenance` shape (source, pipeline, derived, transform_hash)
- `data_quality` shape (confidence, completeness, freshness_seconds, caveats, known_gaps)

Stable v0 event-type: NOT promoted. `event_type = query_volume_delta` itself is internal-dogfood-only for v0. The envelope shape stays stable; this particular event_type is not on the PM contract surface.

Experimental (never part of PM contract, may change without notice within v0) — everything inside `experimental.*`. Consumers must match `experimental.audience_eligibility` to read these fields.

### Iris's ask — data_quality before PMs see bare deltas

The read model refuses to surface any event to a PM audience when `data_quality.confidence != "high"`, or `data_quality.completeness < 0.95`, or when `caveats` / `known_gaps` are non-empty. The guard is what makes the partition defensible: Iris can wire confidence now while the volume number itself stays dogfood, and the guard travels with the metric if it ever gets promoted.

### Theo's ask — one signal for the demo, internal-only

The PM-facing v0 read model exposes a single derived metric — `errors_attributable_to_recent_deploys` (errors within N hours of a deploy, attributable via provenance join). `query_volume_delta` stays internal-dogfood and feeds only internal dashboards. The demo shows Theo's "one signal"; query-volume-delta does not appear on the PM surface.

### How the boundary is enforced

- Read-model filter rejects any payload whose `experimental.audience_eligibility` does not contain the requesting consumer's audience.
- `envelope_version` is required on every read; mismatched readers are rejected, not silently coerced.
- `schema_version` is event-type-scoped; bumping it does not affect other event types and does not change the envelope wrapper.

- Iris lands: data_quality (complete|estimated|partial — stable enum), experimental (UI dogfood signal)
- Theo lands: visibility (internal-only scope for v0)

**1. North Pier — yes, exploratory call worth it.**
The work description is the part that matters. What makes v0 feel live isn't breadth of signal. It's that every event is real, time-stamped, and traceable to a source system. The demo story isn't "look at all this data" — it's "look at what actually moved in the last hour." Three streams do that fine:

- Deploy movement: a service shows up in started/completed/failed states, with provenance back to the deploy system.
- Ownership changes: a team or service flips owners, with provenance back to the directory.
- Incident-load signal: a permission-safe summary that says load is rising or falling on a service, without the body, the responder names, or the thread.

The walkthrough I'd run: pick one service. Show the deploy landing. Show ownership transitioning at the role or group level — no inferred individual activity. Show the incident-load summary tick as opened/resolved events flip. That's a complete operational heartbeat for one service, all permission-scoped, all from real systems.

What stays out is the part that would make the demo louder but less trustworthy: raw incident threads, anything that infers what a person is doing from their presence or absence, query-volume, code-movement. Those are the moves that turn this into a status dashboard or a surveillance read. The line is real systems, role/group resolution, summary-only on incident load.

If the demo reads as flat, the fix is more real movement from the three streams, not expanding them. That's the right pressure to put on it before the demo, not after.

  2. Resource utilization on metrics-router in-window. CPU, GC pause time, thread-pool saturation, connect-pool wait. A 12-min blip that self-resolves with no error-rate movement is usually one of: short GC, thread-pool warmup, connect-pool churn. Look for a single spike, not a sustained rise.
  3. Upstream character of the burst. Was it fleet-wide or a single tenant / scrape target? Single-tenant = that tenant's pattern; fleet-wide = check whether a scheduled job or scrape cadence lined up.
  4. In-flight change window. Any deploy, canary shift, config reload, or leader election on metrics-router or its upstream in that 12 min? Even a no-op rollout can briefly warm a pool.
  5. Repeat check. Search the prior 7–14 days for prior p99 excursions on metrics-router in the same time-of-day band. One occurrence = noise; two or more at the same shape = a pattern worth a real look.

What to ignore:
  - Rollback. Nothing to roll back to; legacy-aggregator is out of the live path, and the service didn't fault.
  - Rollup-service as the cause. You already saw no downstream lag — it's a red herring to dig deeper there.
  - Canary/error-rate signals. Both clean during the window; if those had moved, the read changes.
  - Sustained infra issue framing. A sustained issue doesn't self-resolve in 12 min with flat errors.

Escalation: no. No page, no incident channel. If the customer circles back, the annotation is: "metrics-router p99 excursion, ~12 min, correlated with late-morning traffic burst, self-recovered, no error rate or downstream impact, no action taken."

One watch-item: if this same shape shows up again within a week or two, promote it from "annotate" to a real triage — repeat blips at the same time-of-day usually mean a scrape cadence or scheduled batch lining up unfavorably, and that's a fix, not noise.

Here's a skeleton that signals "owns the system" (frame, commit, defend the trade-off) instead of "has a vision" (declare, evangelize, soften). Five sections, each with one job, total target ~450-500 words on the page.

1. **Read the brief back, with a constraint named.**
   2-3 sentences. One sentence showing she understood the actual tension in the prompt, not the surface question. End with a single noun-phrase constraint she's anchoring to (e.g., "the cost of the wrong abstraction," "who pays for consistency").
   Avoid: restating the prompt, opening with "I think the question is really about…", naming two constraints.

2. **The frame — one sentence you commit to.**
   This is the load-bearing line. Pick one principle, defend it in 2-3 sentences. Systems-shaped (about structure, ownership, trade-offs), not values-shaped (about empathy, craft, culture).
   Avoid: "I believe design should…", a list of three principles, "it depends" hedging.

3. **One or two examples — short, principle-shaped.**
   2-4 sentences each, not full case studies. Job is showing how the principle plays out in real work. Pick examples that *demonstrate the frame*, not the two biggest wins. The Aug 3 dashboard-vs-pattern distinction she made in the conversation is exactly this register — keep it there.
   Avoid: STAR format, "in my previous role at…", explaining what the company does before the example lands.

4. **What I'd test first.**
   3-4 sentences. Ownership signal: she names what she'd look at, what she'd watch, and one thing that would make her change her mind. Phrased as a way of finding out, not a plan of attack.
   Avoid: 30/60/90, "if I joined your team," process diagrams.

5. **The trade-off I'm accepting.**
   1-2 sentences, last. Name the cost of the principle from section 2 out loud. Strongest "system owner" move — every systems decision has a cost, and naming it shows she knows what she's buying.
   Avoid: softening it ("but the benefits outweigh…"), moralizing, skipping it.

Global anti-patterns for this kind of prompt:
- No opener like "I'm so excited to apply for…" or "Thank you for the opportunity…"
- No closer like "I'd love to chat more about…" — let the last line be the trade-off.
- No "design should be…" declarations. Show the system, don't preach.
- No process vocabulary ("discovery," "alignment," "stakeholder management") unless she earned it in an example. In a thinking exercise, process words read as management.
- Under length beats over. One page means one page — if a section feels long, the frame in section 2 is probably wrong.

Subject: Design-system pattern ownership after v1

Thanks for the follow-up. Short version: ownership after v1 is mostly about who decides the boundary, not who writes the code.

The first version usually has a clear author — the person who built it because they needed it. After it ships, the job changes. The pattern now has to survive being used by people who didn't build it, on products the author hasn't seen, with constraints the author didn't anticipate. That's a different problem.

Before calling v1 done, I'd want four things in place:

1. A named owner. Not the original author by default. The owner is whoever has the authority and context to say what the pattern is, what it isn't, and when it should change. For a small DS this is often one person at 10–20% time. For a larger one, a small group (2–3) with one accountable lead.

2. A stated scope. One paragraph. What the pattern covers, what it deliberately doesn't, and what the extension points are. Without this, every consumer request turns into either a fork or a yes-and-the-pattern-grew. Both are bad.

3. An extension mechanism. Slots or props that let product teams adapt the pattern without forking it. If teams fork, that's a signal the boundary is wrong, not that the team is wrong.

4. A consumer loop. The owner needs to see usage data — which patterns are adopted, which are forked or worked around, which drive repeated tickets. The owner without a feedback loop ends up designing in a vacuum.

The rigidity problem usually isn't the ownership model. It's that the owner treats every request as either "no, that's a different pattern" or "yes, let me build it into the core." The right answer is usually "here's the extension slot, use it." When the slot doesn't exist, the owner has to add it or admit the pattern was scoped wrong.

What I wouldn't do: rotate ownership on a schedule, formalize a committee, or write a governance doc longer than the pattern itself.

Happy to talk through any of this if useful.

— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —

Re: pattern ownership after v1

I'd own the pattern. Roughly 4–6 hours/week from me, plus a 30-minute weekly slot for adoption reviews.

1. Codify what's flexible, not just what's fixed. The pattern ships with a short contract: required states (empty, loading, error, permissions), required slots (table, filters, export), and a small set of variant knobs teams can tune. Everything else stays open. Constraints are documented, not enforced.

2. Run changes through a lightweight adoption loop. A new team files a one-paragraph request — what they're building, which slots they're using, what they're tuning. I respond within two business days with one of three outcomes: ship it, ship with a tweak, or sit down for 30 minutes. The loop creates visibility without putting me in the critical path.

3. Treat the pattern as a hypothesis, not a policy. After v1 is in production with two or three teams, I review what's actually being tuned, what's being ignored, and what's blocking adoption. I revise the contract based on what's missing or wrong, not on what one team asked for.

4. Keep ownership bounded to the pattern, not the team. I own the components, the docs, and the review loop. I don't own the products that use them. Teams decide what they build; I make sure the pattern supports it.

What I wouldn't do: gate every implementation, write a governance doc, or sit on a pattern committee. The pattern works because teams can move. My job is to keep it usable, not to control it.

2. Compare the two bucketing rules explicitly:

Here is huddle-ready framing. It is built to land the v0 boundary without making the room feel like a gatekeeping exercise — acknowledge the underlying need first, name what the card already gives them, explain why copying raw text into Lantern is a different thing than it sounds, and offer concrete redirects so the testers walk out with a path forward, not a brush-off.

---

OPENING (lead with what they're actually asking for, not with the no)

"Good question, and it's the right one to raise. What you're really after is the context behind the summary line — what kind of incident this was, what the responder saw, whether this is something you'd want to look at twice. That's a fair need, and we should make sure you're not blocked on it. Let me show you why the current card is shaped the way it is and where to get that context today."

WHAT THE CARD ALREADY DOES (don't make them feel like the summary is empty)

"The incident-load card is a bounded summary derived from the event envelope — counts, severity distribution, time window. Every row carries provenance: source_system and source_ref pointing at the originating incident-management system. That link is the detail path. Click through and you're in the system that actually holds the incident, with whatever permissions your account already has there. The summary is the bounded view; the source is the full view."

WHY DUPLICATING RAW TEXT INTO LANTERN IS THE WRONG FIX (three reasons, plain)

"One, permissions. The Lantern audience was set — Infra, Product Engineering, Hema, Theo — but what each viewer can see inside that audience is still governed by permission_scope on the event. Incident bodies and page payloads are explicitly excluded from the v0 envelope; only the derived summary crosses. Putting raw notes into Lantern effectively re-hosts content under a weaker permission model than the source system has.

Two, provenance. Lantern reads from a thin event envelope with explicit provenance fields. Raw incident text belongs to the incident-management system and its retention/visibility rules. Lantern is a bounded read model over events — not a second home for incident threads. The moment raw text lands in our read model, we own a copy of it, and that's a different conversation.

LANTERN v0 — REFRESH-STALENESS FIX (deploy_movement card)
Acceptance criteria

The heartbeat split keeps the v0 in/out list intact: deploy_movement freshness is
already in scope, no new external signal is exposed (staleness is an internal
freshness marker only), no ownership is inferred, and no raw incident text is
touched. Criteria below encode that.

1. Worker heartbeat is separate from source-event time
   - Worker writes heartbeat_ts as a distinct field, independent of
     latest_source_event_at. Reads and writes do not derive one from the other.
   - heartbeat_ts advances on a fixed cadence (default 60s) and on every
     successful source poll, including polls that return no new events.
   - latest_source_event_at advances only on observed new events. A quiet
     source does not move it and does not reset the staleness clock.

2. UI shows "last source event at" + independent freshness marker
   - Card renders "last source event at <ts>" reflecting the most recent real
     event. It never silently advances to "now" while the source is quiet.
   - Freshness marker is driven by heartbeat_ts, not by latest_source_event_at.
   - Stale threshold: now − heartbeat_ts > 300s → stale marker (badge / banner
     / icon). Threshold configurable, default 5 min.
   - Stale marker clears within one heartbeat interval after the worker resumes.

3. No inferred ownership changes (v0 boundary)
   - Heartbeat and staleness do not derive, suggest, or expose any ownership
     transition. Only the provenance-backed ownership_change surface remains.
   - Worker-lag pattern (paused / slow / restarted) is not surfaced as an
     ownership signal in the UI or in any downstream consumer.

4. No raw incident details (v0 boundary)
   - Heartbeat and stale marker carry no incident content.
   - permission-safe incident_load_summary surface is unchanged; staleness
     never widens it and never reveals underlying incident text.

5. Paused-worker test (automated, runs in CI)
   - Stop the worker; leave the source feed live.
   - At t+5min: card renders the stale marker; "last source event at" still
     shows the last real event (not "now", not heartbeat_ts).
   - At t+10min: stale marker still present; no fallback to source-event time
     as a freshness proxy.
   - Restart worker; stale marker clears within one heartbeat interval; no
     false-stale state persists.
   - Negative case: source quiet while worker fresh → no stale marker.
   - Negative case: heartbeat present but source has never produced an event →
     "last source event at" shows the documented empty/initial state, not "now".

Ownership of the fix matches the v0 split: you own the data + failure-mode
shape (heartbeat field, staleness threshold, source-event semantics in items
1 and 5); Iris owns the UI rendering and marker design in items 2 and 5.

Real evening with it. Framework below — designed so the cost column stays as loud as the training column, since that's the trap.

COMPARISON FRAMEWORK FOR NEXT CONVERSATION

Three layers. Use in order. The point is to make tradeoffs visible, not to score them.

LAYER 1 — FIVE AXES (one column per option in the packet)

A. Schedule shape
   - Call rotation pattern and frequency
   - Weekend / holiday obligation
   - Elective vs assigned time — how much is hers to shape
   - Week-to-week predictability

B. Night blocks
   - How many, how long, what post-call looks like (clinic next day? OR?)
   - Sleep cost across the whole week, not just the night

C. Manhattan commute
   - Door-to-door time, realistic not Google Maps time
   - Transit vs driving vs both
   - Predictability — weather, strikes, traffic
   - Whether the commute functions as buffer or as tax

D. 6 AM handoff structure
   - The cost question from last night. For each option: who handles morning, is the handoff planned or improvised, what does "the morning" actually look like in each shape
   - Net household load, not just Devika's load

E. Training value
   - Case mix and volume at the level that matters for the next step (fellowship? attending role? specific subspecialty depth?)
   - Autonomy gradient — where she ends the year vs where she starts
   - Mentorship and letters — who she's actually working with
   - Whether the year closes doors, opens them, or both

LAYER 2 — COST COLUMN (separate from training value, on purpose)

This is where the lived year lives. Honest answers, no spin.

   - Sleep: realistic nights/week below 6 hours, below 7 hours
   - Relationship time: evenings and weekends not on call — quantity and quality
   - Support network: which anchors (hospital cohort, friends, family) each option preserves or strains
   - Health margin: what a bad cold, a low week, or sustained stress costs in each shape
   - Household logistics: Kibo mornings, who's on for sick-pet days, errands, the unfancy stuff that holds the week together

LAYER 3 — THE WEIGHTING QUESTION (last, after the axes are filled)

   - Which two axes are you both willing to absorb cost on?
   - Which one axis is a deal-breaker in either direction?
   - Where do you two disagree on weight? That's the conversation, not the data

HOW TO USE IT

   - Don't fill it in all at once. Sit with it across a few days.
   - The cost column is where the year actually gets lived. Don't let training value crowd it out — that's the trap.
   - If one option wins on training value but loses badly on cost, that's information, not a conclusion.
   - "We can tough it out for a year" is itself a cost line. Be specific about what tough-it-out means in practice.
   - Revisit after a week. The first pass usually underweights the axis that sounds the most practical (commute, schedule) and overweights the one that sounds the most aspirational (training).

Quick engineering-boundary sanity check. Three pieces.

1. WHERE TOKEN OWNERSHIP ENDS

Design owns: token name (semantic intent), the value as it appears in Figma, usage rules (when to use semantic vs. raw, when a new token is justified), deprecation marking, accessibility pairing.

Engineering owns: how the token is exposed in code (CSS var, JS constant, build-time mapping), platform-specific bindings (iOS/Android/native), runtime theming and dark-mode plumbing, performance and bundle decisions, the codemod or lint rule that enforces deprecation in the codebase, version bumps in the package.

The line: design is the source of truth for *what a token means and when it should be used*. Engineering is the source of truth for *how it ships and how old code is replaced*.

2. WHAT BELONGS IN A HANDOFF DOC (AND WHAT DOESN'T)

In: pattern name and intent, anatomy, variants and states, token references by name, usage do/don't, accessibility notes, content guidance, Figma link, owning team, change-request path.

Out: code snippets the consuming team drops in, platform binding instructions, performance budgets, dependency choices, migration sequencing itself.

A handoff doc is a contract about behavior and intent. It describes the seam; it does not dictate what happens on either side of the seam.

3. HOW TO SAY IT

Useful phrasing for the exercise:

"Design owns semantics, intent, and usage guidance for tokens and patterns. Engineering owns implementation, lifecycle in the codebase, and migration sequencing. The handoff doc is where those two scopes meet — it specifies what the contract is, not how either side fulfills it."

If she wants a one-liner to lean on: design is the *why* and the *what*, engineering is the *how* and the *when-it-actually-changes-in-the-repo*.

Anything more specific than that — actual codemods, token distribution tooling, component-library versioning — is engineering's call, not design's, and shouldn't be in the answer unless she's explicitly framing it as a question back to engineering.

Hi [tester] — thanks for raising this, and Iris, thanks for routing.

The missing card isn't a UI bug, and the right fix isn't to patch it manually. Worth being explicit about why, because the manual-fill idea is a reasonable shortcut on the surface:

Lantern v0 only renders an ownership card when the owner-map import carries recorded provenance — specifically a source_system and source_ref that the UI can present on the card. For the service area you flagged, the owner-map row exists, but the import didn't bring a provenance source in a form Lantern can show, so the v0 rule keeps the card out of the UI rather than infer ownership from context. The owner map itself is unchanged — the owner on record is still the owner on record; this is purely a render decision on the Lantern side. "No card" here means provenance-blocked, not unowned.

Two reasons not to fill it in by hand, even temporarily:

1. A manual patch (editing the import row, hand-adding a card, or letting the UI "just show" the owner) loosens the v0 rule for everyone. The whole point of the provenance gate is that Lantern only states ownership it can point back to. The moment we patch one card, viewers can't tell patched cards from provenance-backed cards, and we lose the ability to defend every other card in the surface — which is the trust failure mode the rule exists to prevent.

2. Inferring ownership from surrounding context — Slack threads, recent deploys, who's on the on-call rotation — is exactly what the v0 rule is written against. A human can usually guess the owner; Lantern is the wrong place to act on that guess.

The path that respects the rule and gets you the card you want:

- Identify the missing provenance in the upstream source. The owner-map row needs a source_system + source_ref attached — an audit note, a recorded ownership-change event, whatever the source system treats as the originating artifact.
- Once that's in place, Iris re-runs the import. The card renders on the next pass under the same rule as the cards that already show up, with the provenance visible on the card.
- Until then, if "no card" reads as ambiguous for planning, I'm happy to add a one-liner in the planning doc / runbook that says the area's owner is on the owner map and Lantern will surface it as soon as the source row carries the right provenance. That's a planning workaround, not a Lantern change.

If the missing provenance is something we can recover quickly — an audit note that exists but didn't make the import, a recorded change event — Iris and I can turn it around inside a few days. If it's actually missing from the upstream system, that's a separate conversation about how the owner map is sourced, and we should have it, but it's not a Lantern problem and not something to unblock by patching the UI.

Short version: not a bug, not something to patch, and the manual-fill route costs us more than the missing card is costing you today. The fix is upstream.

Alex

INSPECT KIBO — TODAY

The fact that there's no limp and no visible injury is good. But soft-tissue soreness and stress responses often show up hours after a jolt, not at minute zero. So check now, then again at bedtime, then once tomorrow morning.

Right now, with him calm:
  Paws and pads — lift each one, check between toes for cuts, torn nails, gravel bruising, blood.
  Harness contact points — run fingers under where the straps sit: chest, behind the front legs, across the back. Look for red marks, hair loss, raw skin, swelling, tenderness when you press.
  Ribs and spine — press gently down both sides, then down the spine to the hips. Flinch, yelp, or twitch = mark it.
  Neck and shoulders — feel the trapezius area where a slipping harness yanks. Tenderness here is the most common post-slip finding.
  Belly and groin — quick visual pass in case he clipped a curb edge.

Behavior over the next 24 hours:
  Appetite, water, energy — should be normal.
  Stool — watch for blood, black/tarry stool, diarrhea (stress or, rarely, internal injury).
  Breathing — any new cough, fast breathing at rest, or odd panting.
  Movement — sits, lies down, jumps, climbs stairs normally? Hesitation on stairs is a soft-tissue red flag.
  Stress signals — shaking, hiding, panting with no trigger, whale eye, lip-licking. Real even without an injury; some dogs need a day to decompress after a scare.

If anything changes — even subtle — call your regular vet. The mechanism here (startle + slip, no contact) doesn't warrant an ER visit on its own.

CHECK HARNESS FIT

Two-finger rule at every contact point: two flat fingers slide under the strap, not four. Check at the neck, behind the front legs, and across the chest plate.

Movement test — with it on, watch him walk, sit, and shake. Replace if it:
  Rotates to one side
  Slides back toward the shoulders
  Lets a front leg pop out
  Rides up into the throat when he pulls

Hardware and fabric:
  Buckles — no cracks, all click firmly. A buckle that has ever popped under load is done; don't trust it again.
  Webbing — no fraying at edges, no stretched-out limp or baggy sections.
  Stitching — no popped threads at stress points (where straps meet rings or buckles).
  D-ring — straight, not bent or loose in its webbing loop.
  Adjustment sliders — still hold under tension. Slip = the harness will loosen mid-walk.

REPLACE BEFORE THE NEXT WALK

Replace it now, don't wait. Once a harness has slipped under load, it cannot be trusted even if it looks fine.

What to get for walks near the park entrance / bike traffic:
  Y-front or true front-range harness — sits below the neck, doesn't restrict shoulders, and reduces the lever-arm effect that lets a dog back out.
  Measure chest girth behind the front legs with a snug tape. Size to the upper end of the range if he's between sizes.
  Two-buckle design (chest + back) is easier to fit correctly than single-buckle step-ins.

For today and tomorrow until the new one arrives:

Opening — Lantern v0 feedback, Product Engineering
Goal: align on what v0 is for, what good feedback looks like inside v0, and what is a v1 ask. Tight, intentional, not a list of no's.

[~1 min] What v0 is

Lantern v0 has been live since August 11, internal-only. The audience right now is Infra, ProdEng, Hema, and Theo. It is not customer-facing, and we are not in a hurry to make it one.

What is in front of you is three things, and only three things:

  - where code moved recently (deploy_movement)
  - who owns something now, with the chain behind it (provenance-backed ownership_change)
  - how loaded the current owner is (permission-safe incident_load_summary)

These are signals, not scores. v0 is not a readiness verdict on anything. It is "here is what changed, here is who owns it now, here is how loaded they are" — so we can decide what to do next. Reading v0 as a score is the easiest frame to slip into, and the one we want to head off first.

[~2-3 min] What feedback is useful inside v0

Useful feedback lives in three shapes, and they map directly to the three surfaces above.

For deploy_movement: does what shows up match the change you would actually act on? Wrong service tagged, missing rollouts, false positives. This is product feedback — we are listening.

For ownership_change: is the chain readable? When you click through, can you see when ownership was set, by what signal, and what backs it? If an owner card looks empty, that is a provenance question, not a UI question. The signal either was not there, was not strong enough yet, or has not been wired in. Tell us which. We can fix signal coverage. We cannot manufacture provenance — and we are not going to fill empty cards with last-deploy author or last-pager, because that would be inventing ownership.

For incident_load_summary: is the aggregation shape right? Is "loaded" the right word for what you are seeing? Are we surfacing things that actually help you decide to escalate, page, or wait — or are we just decorating? That last question is the one we most want answered honestly.

[~3-4 min] The shape of v0, and why the boundaries are not arbitrary

Three words: schema, provenance, permission.

Schema is the three surfaces I named. If a piece of feedback is "can you also show X," and X is not in that schema, it is a v1 ask. We are collecting v1 asks. We are not pretending any of them are in v0.

Provenance is how ownership cards earn their content. I covered this on ownership_change — empty means no chain yet, not a rendering bug. The principle is the same everywhere: we do not surface a status we cannot back with a chain.

Permission is the most important one, and the one we'd ask you to internalize. incident_load_summary is permission-scoped at read time. What you see is what your role is allowed to see. Absence is not zero — absence is "no signal surfaced to you, for a permission reason." If you ask "why does this look low," the answer may simply be that you would need a different read scope. That is by design. Pulling raw incident text forward — notes, timelines, individual pages — is a scope expansion we are deliberately not doing in v0, because raw incident text is not in this product. The summary is.

So: the boundaries in v0 are not a list of refusals. They are what falls out of taking schema, provenance, and permission seriously. If we loosen them in v0, we lose the thing v0 is for, which is learning whether these three shapes, drawn this way, are actually useful.

[~1-2 min] What is a v1 ask, and how to flag one

A v1 ask is anything that would require:

  - a new event shape in the schema — anything beyond deploy / ownership / incident-load
  - provenance we do not have a source for — e.g., inferred from query-volume deltas, or from code-movement signals we have not wired
  - a permission scope wider than what we currently read — e.g., raw incident notes, or status without provenance

We want those asks. We are logging them. The way to flag one in this room is just to say "this is a v1 ask" out loud, and we will record it. That keeps the v0 signal clean, and makes sure the v1 list actually gets written down.

What we do not want to do is spend v0 arguing about whether a v1 ask belongs in v0. It does not. v0 is the bounded version, on purpose.

[~30 sec] Close

The reason v0 is small is so we can learn whether these three shapes, drawn this way, earn their place. The bounded audience is the bet. The schema / provenance / permission framing is the bet.

So: tell us where v0 earns it. Tell us where it does not. And if you have a v1 ask, name it as such.

We have about forty minutes after this. Let's go.

For a tweak with no pop, full walk-home, and no swelling, the right move is don't poke it. Here's the 48-hour plan and the bouldering call.

Today (rest day)
  No running, jumping, or calf-loaded movement. Walking only as needed.
  Ice if sore: 15-20 min on, 40+ min off, through a thin layer. Stop after 24h or once soreness fades.
  Compression sleeve at low pressure if you have one. Elevate when sitting.
  Pain-free mobility only: ankle pumps, ankle alphabets, slow knee bends. Goal is blood flow without loading the calf.
  Hydrate, eat normally, sleep.

Tomorrow morning (decision point)
  Reassess: any tightness at rest? Tender on stairs? Does a slow single-leg calf raise reproduce it?
  If still tight or guarded: skip bouldering. Don't negotiate.
  If it feels clean (normal walk, stairs easy, calf raise painless): very short, low-intensity session only. Easy traverse plus 2-3 low problems. Bail at the first hint of tightness.

The call on bouldering
Skip tomorrow unless it clearly resolves by morning. Bouldering loads the calf with explosive concentric + eccentric contractions — push-off, heel hooks, dynamic reaches — which is exactly the vector that turns a mild strain into a real one. One missed Sunday costs little. Going from Grade I to Grade II costs 4-6 weeks off.

Practical rule: if you're negotiating with yourself at the gym, you already have your answer.

Red flags that would actually change this (worth seeing someone, not a spiral)
  Bruising, a palpable knot or gap, or swelling that increases after 24h.
  Sharp pain on walking, or pain that wakes you at night.
  Numbness, tingling, or color change in the foot.

Not medical advice — just the conservative call for the pattern you described.

Cardinality Guardrails — First Control Slice: PR/Review Checklist

Applies to: any PR that changes metrics-router or shard-keeper, or that adds/renames a label, changes alert-source semantics, or alters the label-change preflight path.

Framing (read first, do not skip): This is not "high-cardinality labels are forbidden." Cardinality Guardrails is a label→cost control with a bounded per-label ceiling and a documented exception path. The control enforces the ceiling; it does not blanket-ban cardinality. Router enforcement beyond cost accounting is explicitly out of scope. If a reviewer writes "blocks high-cardinality labels" on a PR, that is a fail of check B below.

---

Acceptance checks (pass/fail)

For each item: mark PASS / FAIL / N-A with a one-line justification. Any FAIL blocks merge unless sponsor (Hema) signs the exception in the signature block.

A. Label change has explicit cardinality intent
- PASS: every added/removed/renamed label states its purpose and a known max cardinality, or "unbounded" with rationale plus owner signoff.
- FAIL: label changed without cardinality estimate, owner, or rationale; or framed as a blanket ban.

B. Limit is bounded, not absolute
- PASS: limit expressed as a per-label ceiling with a documented exception path; only the rule itself is enforced.
- FAIL: limit phrased as "no high-cardinality labels" without per-label intent; or enforced uniformly with no exception route.

C. Alert-source semantics preserved
- PASS: PR states which alert source(s) it touches (live path vs. validation) and confirms source boundaries are unchanged.
- FAIL: alert source moved or merged across live/validation; or validation alert-source semantics altered.

D. Live-vs-validation boundary intact
- PASS: live-path behavior (rollback-able, customer-facing-equivalent routing, alert source) is unaffected by any validation-only change; legacy-aggregator path unchanged.
- FAIL: validation change bleeds into live path; legacy-aggregator path touched; rollback semantics altered.

E. Rollup-service parity check present
- PASS: PR includes an explicit rollup-service parity check showing both rollup services produce identical key set, aggregation window, and retention, OR documents the known delta and its reason.
- FAIL: parity assumed but not demonstrated; silent divergence between services.

F. Label-change preflight coverage (if the PR alters the preflight itself)
- PASS: preflight covers (a) added labels, (b) renamed labels, (c) alert-source reassignments, (d) per-label cardinality ceiling.
- FAIL: preflight is partial — e.g., catches adds but not renames; does not surface alert-source boundary.

G. Sampling-vs-live semantics preserved
- PASS: any replay/validation change is documented as sampling-only — not live, not customer-facing, not on the rollback path. 2% replay expansion is out of scope.
- FAIL: replay percentage raised, scope broadened, or 2% replay altered under a label-change PR.

H. Iris/Lantern signal set untouched
- PASS: PR does not change Iris/Lantern signal set, freshness behavior, or display semantics.
- FAIL: signal set, freshness patch, or display behavior altered as part of label/alert work.

I. Legacy-aggregator retirement not implied
- PASS: PR does not retire, replace, or imply retirement of the legacy-aggregator path.
- FAIL: legacy-aggregator path retired, replaced, or scoped out under cardinality work.

J. Cost-only enforcement, not router enforcement
- PASS: control accepts/rejects on label→cost only. No router decision logic, routing weights, or traffic-shape change.
- FAIL: control alters router decisions, traffic shaping, or per-tenant routing beyond cost accounting.

---

Explicit non-goals for this control slice

- Not a telemetry rewrite.
- Not a legacy-aggregator retirement.
- Not a 2% replay expansion (Sep 25 agreement — sampling-only, held week, raise on mismatch-coverage drop).
- Not an Iris/Lantern signal-set change.
- Not customer-facing.
- Not router enforcement beyond label→cost.

Three signals Theo can use during the narrow ProdEng feedback window. Each one is paired with the scope-creep shape it surfaces, so if a signal degrades, he knows exactly which direction the drift is going.

1. Provenance: do users cite events by their bounded type?
Watch the vocabulary users use when they describe what Lantern showed them. In-scope event types are deploy_movement, ownership_change, and incident_load_summary. Healthy: users describe what they saw as "the deploy for X," "the ownership change on Y," "the load summary." Unhealthy: users describe it as "is X healthy," "who broke Y," "what's the status of Z." The pass criterion is bounded event vocabulary holding. The fail signal is status-shaped questions replacing provenance-shaped ones — which is exactly the "creepy status dashboard" shape the in/out list was written to prevent.

2. Permission wording: do users name the boundary when they hit it?
When a user lands on something out of scope or genuinely permissioned away — raw incident text, unpermissioned status, another team's ownership_change — watch how they describe the gap. Healthy: "I don't have access to that in Lantern," "Lantern doesn't show incident details by design," or simply not raising it. Unhealthy: "why isn't this here," "can you add incident notes," "this should show X." This is the most direct canary for scope creep, because users treating the boundary as a bug is exactly the broadening Iris's release-review-count instinct would invite. Raw incident notes appearing in user asks is the specific shape to flag.

3. Empty states: do users read silence as silence?
When there is nothing recent to show — no recent deploy_movement, no recent ownership_change, an empty load summary — watch how users react. Pass: the empty state passes without comment, or gets noted as expected ("nothing to show, makes sense"). Fail: "is this broken," "why is this blank," "where's the rest of it." Users who expect content in an empty state have mentally modeled Lantern as a status surface, and that's the dashboard drift the bounded scope was written to keep out.

Common shape across all three: each pass criterion rewards bounded Lantern doing bounded Lantern work; each fail signal names a specific scope-creep direction. If Theo wants one end-of-week summary check, the question is whether users describe Lantern in event-type vocabulary, treat boundaries as boundaries, and read empty as empty. If yes to all three, the narrow launch is working as designed. None of these require manual owner-card overrides, release-readiness scoring, or any path that brings raw incident text into the conversation.

An easy bike spin keeps the calf mostly isometric on the pedal stroke and lets you titrate load with resistance and cadence. A flat walk is fine as a *follow-up* if the bike session goes clean — but not as your opener.

  - Resistance light enough that you could hold a conversation
  - Cadence easy (~70-75 rpm), not a spin class tempo
  - Stop at 20 min even if it feels fine — the goal is to leave the session thinking "that was too easy," not to find your edge

If you do walk after: flat, short stride, ~25-30 min, no hills, no "just one more block." The faint tight spot you're describing should not sharpen during or after.

Neutral note on the two weekly templates

Both templates are useful and both are easy to overinterpret. They describe two specific years at two specific programs, not a distribution.

What each shows

Example A. A schedule can be drawn where sponsor-protected project time is structurally placed (Monday morning, Wednesday midday) before clinic load, with clinic as a bounded twice-weekly commitment and service as a single backup slot. The sponsor time was pre-listed, but the exact clinic template wasn't finalized until sponsor and clinic lead agreed in January. So "pre-listed" describes the slots on paper, not the operational reality — the operational reality still required a year-start negotiation.

Example B. A schedule where project time was fragmented into three half-days and where the original clinic template eroded midyear (one half-day expanded to two under volume). Service spillover from inpatient weeks pushed project work into evenings. The schedule only became humane after the sponsor negotiated a cap with the clinic lead midyear. So pre-listing was not protection — actual protection required an explicit cap, and the cap had to be renegotiated under pressure rather than assumed upfront.

What remains unknowable from these two alone

- Whether either template reflects what your sponsor or clinic lead would actually agree to in your program.
- What your real clinic volume and inpatient spillover look like — both templates describe a year, not yours.
- Whether your sponsor has the standing and capacity to renegotiate a cap midyear if Example-B-style erosion happens.
- What evenings or weekends either fellow absorbed that don't appear on the printed schedule.
- Whether the negotiation dynamics in your program look more like A (smooth January alignment) or B (pressure-driven midyear correction).

What not to conclude yet

- That Example A's schedule is achievable as-drawn. It required a January negotiation you weren't party to.
- That Example B's fragmentation is inevitable. The midyear cap was the remediation, not the failure mode — the failure was the absence of an upfront cap.
- That pre-defined equals protected. Example A shows the clinic piece still needed negotiation even with pre-listed sponsor time.
- That later-negotiated equals chaotic. Example B's negotiation is what made the year humane, not what broke it.
- That one template is "better" than the other. They describe different programs with different negotiated outcomes; ranking them overreads what two anonymized examples can carry.

Two blurb options:

A. "Led product and UX for North Pier's migration dashboard. Owned discovery, prototypes, and the staged handoff to engineering — translating technical constraints into something non-technical stakeholders could actually navigate."

It can read that way — there's one specific phrase creating the ambiguity.

"Held a migration dashboard" is the noun, and "Helped lead" is a build-flavored verb. You don't usually "help lead" a coordination view; you "ran" or "owned" it. A technical reader — North Pier included — sees "helped lead a ... dashboard" and asks whether you were on the build team.

Two rephrasings, depending on what you actually did:

If you owned the dashboard-as-coordination-tool:
"Operated the migration coordination dashboard for a client transition — a shared view product and engineering used to track readiness, outreach, and open service blockers."

If you built it too and want that on the record:
"Built and ran a migration dashboard that product and engineering used to coordinate readiness, outreach, and unresolved service blockers across a client transition."

Either way the strong claim is the same: you ran the coordination surface during a transition, and both product and engineering relied on it. That's portfolio-useful and not engineering-claim-y. The original line gets there, just with one verb making it ambiguous.

The remaining signal — dull tightness under lengthened stride or push-off intent — is exactly the one that fires on hard bouldering. Today is a low-floor / low-ceiling call: if everything goes well it's fine, but the moment you engage intent it stops being fine.

Going with hard caps is reasonable. Skipping is also reasonable. Either is fine if you decide it on purpose.

Option A — Climb, conservative

Pre-climb check
  - No calf tightness at rest before you start. If there is, skip.
  - 5 min easy walk plus gentle heel raises on a step before leaving the house.
  - Hydrate, eat normally. Don't climb fasted.

Warmup (15-20 min, non-negotiable)
  - 5 min easy bike or walk.
  - Ankle circles both directions, slow.
  - Wall-supported lunges or world's-greatest-stretch to wake hips and calves without loading them.
  - Several rounds of dead-hangs, both feet on, no movement.
  - Two easy traverses on jugs, feet staying on, walking the feet not flagging.
  - One easy vertical problem with big footholds, slow feet, no reach.
  - Stop warmup when calves feel warm and quiet. If they tighten during warmup, that's your answer — stop.

On the wall
  - Vertical and slab only. Big feet, smearing allowed.
  - Traverse-y movement, not reach-y. Flag and replace feet; don't stab.
  - 3-4 problems total. Pick ones you can do in a few tries — no projecting.
  - Downclimb or lower with intent. No falling from height when your foot was the last thing pushing off.
  - Rest 3-5 min between attempts. Volume plus small load accumulates.

Moves to avoid
  - Dynos, any move where both feet leave.
  - Long deadpoints or big lunges off a small back foot.
  - Heel hooks (gastroc load).
  - Mantles, drop knees, high steps with toe engagement.
  - Steep overhang on small edges.
  - Slopey or poor feet — slip plus compensation equals calf intent.
  - Powerful crimps — recruit calves via body tension.
  - "One more try." Three attempts is the cap.

Stop signals (specific, not vibes)
  - Sharp or stabbing sensation vs. the dull baseline.
  - Tightness that intensifies and stays constant across multiple moves.
  - Pain that lingers 10+ min after a move.
  - Calf catch, locking, or sudden give.
  - Walking out and feeling anything you didn't feel walking in.
  - Visible swelling, heat, or color change.
  - Mental shift — guarding the foot or moving around it.
  - If any of those appear, the session ends. No "one more easy one."

After
  - Walk out, don't run.
  - If anything is tight, ice 15 min (on/off, not direct on skin).
  - Tomorrow should feel like today or better. If it's worse, that's data — back off 48 hr.

Option B — Skip climbing, keep the social
  - Be the friend who spots, films, and routes. Half of climbing is mental anyway.
  - Or a 30-45 min upper-body / antagonist session: pull-ups, rows, shoulder press, hangboard with feet on a stool (no leg drive).
  - Hip and hamstring mobility — these are usually the real limiter for movement quality, and your calf won't notice.

Bottom line
  - Trust the dull tightness to stay dull only if you're willing to walk out the moment it doesn't. If you have any doubt about whether you'd actually stop, skip. One skipped session now is cheaper than one re-injury later.

Conservative climb-or-skip plan for today. The signal you're describing — fine on flat and slow, faint pull only on quick stride lengthening — points to a calf that's remodeled enough for steady-state loading but still reactive to fast eccentric lengthening. The whole plan below treats that as the load-bearing fact: anything that briefly lengthens the calf under tension at speed is the line. Steady load on a warm muscle is mostly fine; sudden stretch is not yet.

WARMUP (this is also the decision gate)

10 minutes on the ground first: easy walk or bike, ankle circles both directions, then double-leg calf raises slow up and slow down, building only to mild effort. Stop well short of burning.

2-3 V0-V1 traverses, flat feet preferred, smooth movement. The goal is warm tissue, not a workout.

Honest test, once: a couple of unweighted heel hooks to about half your usual pull, and one controlled step-off from a single pad height. This is diagnostic, not training.

Decision: any sharp pull, any "that's the spot" sensation, tightness that doesn't fade after 1-2 more easy moves, or any reactive cramp — stop climbing and go straight to the safer alternative below.

WHAT TO CLIMB IF THE WARMUP IS CLEAN

Stay V0-V2. Pick problems with:
  - Jugs or large holds so hands aren't the limiter
  - Feet close to hand height (no big reaches that drag the back foot down)
  - Square edges, not slopers that keep weight on the toes
  - Top-outs you can downclimb, or a finish that's a controlled step/sit-off

Cadence: 2-3 minutes rest between attempts, 3-5 tries per problem, then move on. No "one more" on a problem that needed anything dynamic. Spot the friend on their projects rather than doing parallel laps.

MOVES TO AVOID (in addition to the four you named)

  - Sprinting between problems or across the gym
  - Dynos of any size
  - Hard heel hooks — and treat moderate heel hooks as diagnostic only, not a working move
  - Jumping down repeatedly; one controlled step-off per problem, then downclimb
  - High reach with a low, stretched back foot (the gastroc gets pulled fast under load)
  - Sustained heel-toe cam on slab — long eccentric holds are sneaky calf load
  - Long toe-only traverses that keep the calf under tension for many moves

STOP CONDITIONS

  - Sharp or local pull in the calf
  - Tightness that increases across the session instead of warming out
  - Any cramping, spasm, or sudden weakness on a move that was easy before
  - Asymmetry you can feel: the sore side feels distinctly different from the other at matched load
  - "Talking yourself into one more go" is already a yellow flag — finish the current problem and end the session

After the session, walk out easy for 5 minutes and do a gentle long-hold calf stretch (30-60s each side, no pain). The real feedback is how it feels 2 hours later and tomorrow morning — note both.

SAFER ALTERNATIVE (if warmup isn't clean, or at any yellow flag mid-session)

  - Stay on the ground: spot the friend on their projects, give beta, brush holds, video attempts. Showing up and being useful is not zero.
  - Or do only the warmup traverses and then sit on the pad.
  - If the gym's quiet, banded dorsiflexion drills and slow controlled calf raises on a yoga mat are a productive use of 20 minutes that doesn't load the calf eccentrically.

The point of all this: a clean warmup means you can move today. A not-clean warmup means today is a ground day. Either is a fine answer.

Quick plan, tuned to what you've already done. No drama, just a sequence.

TONIGHT (next 30-60 min)

1. Re-check the paw in good light. Part the fur between each toe pad and look at the pad surface. You're looking for: a stuck grit cluster, a tiny cut or split between toes, a dark/brown spot (could be a small wound or stain), or a visible thorn/glass sliver. Also compare paw temperature and size to the other front paw — noticeably warmer or puffier is the early sign.
2. Second rinse, lukewarm (not warm) water, 30-60 seconds, gently flushing between the pads. Don't squeeze or pry at anything stuck — if grit is caked, soak, don't pick.
3. Pat dry with a clean towel, especially between toes. Moisture trapped there is what causes the licking to keep going.
4. No balm, no ointment, no dog boot tonight unless he starts limping or won't settle. If he keeps licking, a sock or a loose e-collar for 10-15 min while he settles is fine; remove it once he's calm and you can supervise.
5. Note the time and how he is now (settled = baseline).

OVERNIGHT / MORNING

6. Before tomorrow's first walk, do the same visual + temperature check. If anything looks more swollen, red, or warm than tonight, skip the walk and call the vet.
7. On the first walk: short route, watch for any head-down / favoring / shortened stride on that front. If he walks clean for 10+ minutes, you're probably fine.
8. Tomorrow's rinse routine: lukewarm water both before and after walks while the salt/grit is on the ground. Wipe and dry between toes after each. The front-clip + short leash stays default near the curb — that's already the right call.

CALL THE VET (today or in the morning) IF ANY OF THESE:

- You find a cut, puncture, or anything bleeding, especially between the toes
- A pad looks torn, split, or has a dark soft spot you can press into
- The paw is visibly swollen, or markedly warmer than the other front
- He starts limping or refusing to put weight on it, even briefly
- Licking doesn't stop within ~30-60 min of the rinse and dry, or it ramps back up overnight
- You see a foreign object embedded (thorn, glass, salt-crystal clump you can't rinse free) — don't dig for it, just call
- Any discharge, foul smell, or the pad looks discolored (black/blue) rather than just irritated
- He becomes withdrawn, won't eat, or guards the paw when you approach

Skip-the-vet signals (i.e., it's probably just salt irritation): one paw slightly pinker than the other, settles after rinse, no limp on the walk, licking tapers off within an hour, pads look intact under good light.

Subject: Raw incident excerpts in the incident-load card — short version

The planning question is fair and we want to keep it in scope. The card should answer "why did this service's load spike?" with the observed signal it is built to carry, and the underlying incident detail stays reachable through the existing link-out. What v0 doesn't support is pasting the raw incident text into the card body itself — that's an artifact-boundary call, not a permissions workaround.

What's fine on the card (already in v0)

- The service-level incident-load summary as it renders today.
- The header: "Summary generated from permissioned incident sources."
- A link to the permissioned source via `provenance.source_ref`, surfaced as "Open permissioned source" for viewers with source access, and "No permissioned source available." otherwise.
- Any service/system context that is itself a bounded signal (e.g. deploy movement on the same window, provenance-backed ownership changes) — these belong on adjacent cards, not pasted into the incident-load card body.

What's not fine, and why

- Raw incident text — excerpts, notes, timelines, page threads, on-call responder payloads — inside the card body.
- "Sanitized" or paraphrased versions of the above. A digest derived from permissioned source content still routes around the source system's access controls.
- Putting the raw detail into the card because a reviewer doesn't have source-system access. The correct response to that reviewer is the existing "No permissioned source available." affordance, not a wider Lantern view.

If a reviewer genuinely needs to see the raw body, the path is the source system, under its own permissions, provenance, retention, and audit model — which is exactly what the link-out exists for. If the load spike keeps needing raw text to interpret, that's a v1 conversation (explicit `permission_scope`, JSON-Schema, retention/redaction policy), not a v0 widening.

THE FRAMING
Walking/stairs/raises being fine does NOT test push-off, dynamic loading, or jump-downs. Those are exactly the things you haven't cleared. Default = skip. A graded short session is only OK if the morning and warmup gates both pass and you commit to the limits below.

MORNING GATE (at home, before leaving)
- First morning steps: no tightness, no guard, no limp.
- Stairs up and down at normal stride: clean.
- 10 single-leg calf raises each side: no pain, no grab, no reactive cramping.
- A few lengthened-stride steps down the hall with intent to push off: clean.
- Standing calf stretch and a few slow eccentric heel-drops off a step: clean.
Decision: ANY pull, grab, sharp sensation, "feels guarded," or new tightness → text the skip message and stay home. No negotiating. If all clean → go to warmup gate.

WARMUP GATE (at the gym, before any real climbing)
- 10 min easy bike or brisk flat walk.
- Ankle circles, slow double-leg calf raises, gentle standing calf stretch.
- 2-3 easy V0 traverses on jugs, both directions, flat feet only.
- One-time diagnostics, done ONCE each:
  - Gentle heel hook on a large hold, slow, no load.
  - Controlled step-off from a low box or low volume — land soft, both feet together, no impact.
Decision: ANY calf sensation during warmup or diagnostics → end session right there, climb as spectator/spotter only. No "one more easy one."

WHAT TO CLIMB (only if both gates pass)
- V0-V1 only. Slab and vertical balance. Big holds, big footholds.
- Short problems. No projecting. No repeating the same move more than 2-3 times.
- 3-4 problems total. Cap session at ~45 min. 3-5 min rest between.
- Downclimb controlled or lower off. NEVER jump down.

ROUTES / MOVES TO AVOID (hard list)
- Dynos, deadpoints, lunges, anything with both feet off the wall.
- Heel hooks and toe hooks. Mantles. Drop knees.
- High steps with toe engagement. Steep overhangs.
- Small/poor footholds, smears you have to trust.
- Powerful crimping.
- Repeated jump-downs, awkward downclimbs with high impact.
- Anything that requires a fast push-off from the injured calf.

STOP CONDITIONS (during session)
- Any calf sensation at all — faint pull, tightness, grab, cramp.
- Sharp or pinching pain.
- Calf catches, locks, or leg gives way.
- Swelling, heat, color change.
- Walking to the next problem feels different.
- You start guarding the foot or altering movement to protect the calf.
Rule: if any of these fire, you stop on the spot. You don't "see how the next one feels."

NEXT-MORNING CHECK (Mon Dec 11)
- First steps: not worse than today.
- Stairs: not worse than today.
- No new localized soreness, swelling, heat, or bruising in the calf.
- If anything is worse: 48h full backoff, no climbing, no testing. Reassess Tuesday.

The watch plan, low-drama version:

Why ribbon is its own category in one line: a linear object can anchor somewhere and the intestine's normal motion can bunch up around it, which over hours can irritate or saw the bowel. A 1-2" piece has a real chance of passing on its own, but the threshold to call is lower than for, say, a small smooth object.

  DO NOT (these matter):

  - Do NOT induce vomiting. Linear objects coming back up can lodge in the esophagus or tear tissue, and if the leading end is anchored further down, vomiting makes it worse. If you ever feel the urge to "get it out," the right move is to call the vet, not to make him throw up.

  - Do NOT pull on a string if you see one hanging from either end. Same reason - it may be anchored internally and pulling saws the bowel. Just trim it short and call.

  - Do NOT give laxatives, mineral oil, or a "force it through" big meal. No bread dough tricks, no high-fiber bomb. If you want to slightly soften stool you can stir a spoonful of plain canned pumpkin (not pie filling) into his next meal, but that's optional and small.

  - Do NOT switch his diet abruptly.

  WATCH PLAN (next 24-48 hrs):

  - Keep normal feeding and water. Don't fast him. Normal intake is itself a useful signal.

  - Note appetite, water, energy at each meal. The single biggest signal is "still interested in food and acting like himself."

  - When he poops, glance at it. You're looking for the ribbon. Most 1-2" linear objects that pass do so within 10-24 hours. If you see it, you're done - just watch one more day for normalcy.

  - Note stool quality: any straining, mucus, blood (red or black/tarry), or complete absence of stool.

  - Once a day, gently run your hands along his abdomen (he should be relaxed, on his side or standing). You're checking for: tenseness, a hard or distended belly, flinching when you touch a spot, or him turning to look at his belly. If he won't let you touch it, that itself is a signal.

  - Don't hover. Let him nap, play, do his normal thing. The point is to catch changes, not to perform an exam every 30 min.

  CALL OR URGENT CARE - same day, sooner if after-hours:

  - Vomiting more than once or twice, or any vomit with blood (red streaks or coffee-ground looking)
  - Can't keep water down for more than a few hours
  - Any drooling that starts suddenly
  - Gagging repeatedly without producing anything
  - Lethargy: not getting up for meals, not greeting you, hiding
  - Restlessness or pacing, can't settle, especially at night
  - "Prayer posture" - front end down, back end up, reluctant to move - that's abdominal pain
  - Bloated or tight belly
  - No stool at all for 24+ hrs, especially combined with any other sign
  - Any string visible from mouth or rectum (don't pull - just call)

  What "looks fine at 24 hours" means: eating, drinking, normal energy, normal stool, no vomiting, no belly pain. If all of that holds at 24 hrs you're in much better shape. If it holds at 48 hrs and you still haven't seen the ribbon pass, a vet call to ask whether ultrasound is worth doing is reasonable - ribbon often doesn't show on x-ray. Don't feel awkward about that call; "asymptomatic at 48 hrs but no proof of passage" is a perfectly normal reason to ring them.

  One framing that might help: your baseline read right now ("acting normal, eating and drinking normally, no vomiting, drooling, guarding, or lethargy") is genuinely the best-case starting point. The watch plan above is mostly about catching the small subset where it doesn't go smoothly, not because most cases go badly - most small linear pieces pass without incident. The do-nots are the part you can't improvise later, so those are the part worth memorizing.

I have plenty of relevant context. Your pattern through November–December has been consistent — walk clean → test one more demanding variable → stop at the first sign of the old pull → never treat tolerance of one domain as clearance for another. Five clean 20-second jogs with full walking recovery is a real step forward, but as you said, it's not the same demand profile as sprinting, cutting, push-off, or dynamic climbing. Here's a conservative 7-day plan that respects that.

———————————————————————————————
CONSERVATIVE WEEK-AHEAD PROGRESSION
(left calf; assumes the Dec 31 jog test stayed clean overnight)
———————————————————————————————

GOVERNING PRINCIPLE
  - Each session adds exactly ONE variable. If it stays clean, you earn the next step. If anything reproduces the old pull, you stop, repeat the previous step another day, and do not advance.
  - Easy jogging tolerance does NOT clear you for sprinting, cutting, quick push-off, pickup soccer, dynos, jump-downs, or awkward downclimbs under fatigue. Those are different mechanical demands and each needs its own clean test.

DAY-BY-DAY

Day 1 (Sun, Jan 1) — REST or easy flat walk only
  - Short flat walk, conversational pace, normal short strides.
  - No jog intervals today. Let yesterday's test settle.
  - AM/PM check: stairs and single-leg calf raise both feel normal, no tightness at rest.

Day 2 (Mon, Jan 2) — Repeat + extend jog duration
  - Flat surface. 10 min brisk walk warm-up.
  - 6 × 30-second easy jogs, 90 seconds walking between.
  - Stop conditions: any pull, pinch, sharp sensation, or new tightness during or within 30 min after.
  - Calf raises + stairs check that evening and next morning.

Day 3 (Tue, Jan 3) — REST
  - Bouldering with Ren on Tue is still off the table. If anything tempting, easy slab traverse only, downclimbing everything, no dynos / no jump-downs / no fast push-offs — and only if AM check is clean. Default is skip.

Day 4 (Wed, Jan 4) — First stride-length / cadence test
  - Flat 30-min walk with INTENTIONAL short-to-medium stride lengthening (not sprinting). Then 4 × 40-meter easy strides at ~80% effort, full walking recovery.
  - This is the first test that loads the calf more like the November pattern that used to pull. Treat it as a diagnostic, not a workout.
  - Stop conditions: same as above.

Day 5 (Thu, Jan 5) — REST or easy slab only (same rule as Tue; default skip the Ren session)

Day 6 (Fri, Jan 6) — Controlled acceleration test
  - Flat loop. 4 × 60-meter progressive accelerations: 50% → 70% → 85%, NOT a sprint. Full standing recovery between.
  - If any pull: stop. Do not "test through it."
  - This is the first real acceleration since the injury. Even if clean, it does NOT mean soccer.

Day 7 (Sat, Jan 7) — Reassessment only
  - Flat walk + stairs + single-leg calf raises + a few easy lateral steps (the rug test that pulled in December).
  - Decide: if every check was clean all week AND next-morning Day 8 is clean, you have earned the conversation about whether to attempt a light soccer re-entry in the *following* week. Not this week.

———————————————————————————————
HARD STOP CONDITIONS (any one = end the session, do not advance)
———————————————————————————————
During activity:
  - Sharp or pinching pain in the calf
  - The old "pull" or "grab" sensation reproduces
  - Tightness that intensifies instead of fading as you warm up
  - Catching, locking, or a sense the leg might give way
  - Any limp, compensation, or guarding
  - Heel-hook or push-off test reproducing the December lateral-step signal

After activity (within 24 hours):
  - Calf soreness that is more than mild general muscle fatigue
  - Pain lasting more than ~10 min after you stop moving
  - Worse stairs than your baseline, or pain with first morning steps
  - Any new swelling, heat, bruising, or color change
  - Calf feels tighter the next morning than it did the morning of the session

If ANY of those fire:
  - Take 48 hours off from all calf-testing
  - Repeat the last clean step (don't jump back in at the new level)
  - Re-evaluate before advancing

———————————————————————————————
EXPLICIT BOUNDARY (per your request)
———————————————————————————————
Tolerating easy jog intervals means the calf tolerated SLOW, LOW-IMPACT, LINEAR, FLAT-SURFACE LOADING at a controlled cadence with walking recovery. It does NOT mean:

  - SPRINTING — higher peak calf force, faster stretch-shortening cycle, no walking recovery built in
  - CUTTING — multi-directional, often off-balance, lateral force, ankle everts under load
  - QUICK PUSH-OFF — the exact November / December reproducer for you
  - PICKUP SOCCER — combines all of the above plus unplanned contact, fatigue, and adrenaline-driven volume
  - DYNAMIC BOULDERING — dynos, jump-downs, mantles, heel hooks, powerful toe engagement, awkward downclimbs after fatigue

Each of those is a separate gate. None of them is unlocked by today's jog test. The fastest safe path through them is still the one-variable-at-a-time ladder above, and even after a clean week, soccer re-entry should be the conservative Sunday-pickup pattern you used in late July (one game, stop at first tightness, no bouldering same day).

  Guardrails checks look good — thanks for the careful work here. Confirming those are satisfied.

A few things I'd want to think through before either option:

The 28s figure isn't nothing, but the scaling story is poor. 3x the workers for 1.4x-ish speedup is sub-linear — typical of I/O-bound compactor work where shards serialize on shared resources. So 4 workers would likely buy you 10–15s, not 18–20, and the memory budget is probably the constraint that ends the curve somewhere between 4 and 6.

The decision really turns on one thing you haven't said: **what's the absolute baseline wall-clock at 2 workers?** If the 64-shard replay is 5 minutes, 28s is ~9% and a 4-worker test (~12s projected) is borderline. If it's 30 minutes, 28s is barely 1.5% and not worth another experiment at all. The percentage matters more than the absolute number, because replay time compounds for Roman's team.

Two reasons I'd lean toward **running the 4-worker anyway, briefly**:

1. It's the same fixture, the same tool, probably 5–10 minutes of Roman's compute. The cost of closing the gap between "2 workers" and "6 workers OOM" with one real data point is tiny relative to leaving a "we never checked the middle" hole that someone will re-ask about in a quarter.
2. It also resolves the question of how steeply the curve was rising — if 4 workers is fine on memory and buys 10+s, you know the OOM at 6 was a sharp cliff, not a gradual climb. That changes whether the ceiling is something tunable later (better memory profile, smaller per-worker buffer) or a hard wall.

Two reasons to **stop and not run 4**:

1. If this is genuinely a one-off and the baseline is already tolerable for the people who wait on it. Tuning that touches worker count has operational surface — non-default config, drift risk on restart, one more thing to remember during incidents. For a single experiment that's run once, that's overhead for nothing.
2. If you've already decided the answer is "tuning has no value" and the 4-worker run is just delaying that conclusion rather than genuinely reopening it. That's the failure mode worth watching for — extra data points as a way to avoid committing to a decision.

My honest read: **run the 4-worker** if you can answer "yes, if 4 workers buys at least X seconds, we'd actually use it" with some non-trivial X. If you can't name an X, you've already decided tuning isn't worth pursuing and the 4-worker run is ceremony — skip it and tell Roman the 28s isn't enough to justify a non-default worker count.

One thing to write down either way: how badly did 6 workers blow the memory budget? "Past the budget" could mean 5% over or 40% over. If it's only slightly over, that's a separate path worth flagging (per-worker buffer reduction, shard-stagger tuning) rather than a flat "tuning has no value" conclusion. If 6 was dramatically over, that confirms the wall is real and you stop cleanly.

I don't actually have terminal/execute_code tools available in this environment — only the dolphinbench-apps tools (Slack, email, calendar, PRs, incidents, etc.) and a few search tools. The mandatory tool-use rule for arithmetic requires a calculator or terminal, but neither is wired up here. I'll do the math by hand and label it clearly so you can spot-check.

Let me work through it:

**Time savings**
- Baseline: 14m40s = 880s
- Proposed: 14m12s = 852s
- Delta: 28s saved
- % improvement: 28 / 880 = **3.18%**

**Memory check vs budget**
- Baseline: 68% (11pp under the 75% ceiling)
- Proposed: 86% (11pp **over** the 75% ceiling)

So the proposed experiment fails the stated budget. Net result: a 3% time win buys you an 18-percentage-point swing in peak memory, landing you 11pp above the cap.

A couple of things worth flagging before you take this anywhere:

1. The win is small enough that it's probably inside run-to-run noise on a 64-shard replay. One representative isn't enough to call 3% real — you'd want a few reruns or a longer/more-shard workload before betting on it.
2. 86% peak leaves very little headroom. Any skew (a few hot shards, GC pause tail, a slightly larger input slice) can push you toward OOM, and the proposed run is already above the budget you set, not just near it.
3. "No correctness failures" is good, but it doesn't tell you whether you're close to a memory cliff or comfortably under one. A peak-only number hides the shape.

Reasonable next moves, depending on what you want:
- If the goal is just to validate whether 6 workers can ever be safe, rerun with a memory profiler so you can see whether 86% is a spike or a plateau, and rerun 3–5x to confirm the time delta isn't noise.
- If you want a knob that respects the 75% ceiling, try 3 or 4 workers — likely a better time/memory trade than jumping straight to 6.
- If you do want to push toward 6, set a hard per-worker memory cap so the run fails fast rather than risking OOM at 86%+.

Want me to draft the 3–4 worker follow-up benchmark plan, or a rerun protocol for the 6-worker case?

Drafting the recommendation to Roman now.

Recommended message to send Roman (concise, ~140 words):

Roman — on the 64-shard replay benchmark:

  - Keep two workers as the baseline. Six workers gave only +28s for a clear memory-budget breach, so it's not viable as a default.
  - Don't run the four-worker comparison yet. It only pays off if we can name the speedup that would actually change the decision (e.g., "four workers is worth it if it saves ≥X seconds vs. two").
  - What would justify a baseline change: (a) four workers beats two by a margin we agree is operationally meaningful, AND (b) it stays inside the peak-memory budget with headroom. Without (a), we stop tuning worker count; without (b), we don't adopt it even if fast.
  - Two questions back to you: what's the absolute two-worker runtime (so 28s is put in % terms), and how far over budget did six workers go — slight overage we can chase with buffer/stagger tuning, or hard limit?

That keeps it decision-focused instead of open-ended tuning.

   - Sizzle scallion whites + minced garlic + ginger in a little oil, 90 sec
   - Stir in 1.5-2 tbsp curry paste, toast 30 sec

   - Plate: spinach-egg scramble + dumplings + scallion greens + cracked pepper
   - No rice needed; this is the reset dinner. Best fresh, hence saving it for a night you're both home at normal time.


  Why this order:
  - Mon's curry is the most forgiving reheater and tastes better for the wait
  - Tue's "scaffold" (rice + dumplings) holds for hours; only the egg is fresh

  - Chickpeas (1 can): all Mon
