INSPECTION SEQUENCE — pre-power, Kibo-safe

Context: 1/4" rigid plywood bolted through existing accordion-panel holes, captured between locked sash and frame, foam perimeter seal, AC unplugged, dog excluded from room. Run phases in order. Unit stays unplugged until Phase 4. Any STOP means halt and remediate before continuing.

PHASE 1 — VISUAL (unit off, sash locked)

1.1 Sharp edges
- Drag a thin paper towel or cotton cloth along every exposed plywood face: top, the two sides facing the sash, and the bottom toward the sill.
- Run a finger (then a thumbnail) along the same edges — anything that snags cloth or catches a nail is a cut risk for a muzzle or paw pad.
- Check the foam-to-plywood seam: foam must not stand proud of wood at any point. A dog tooth can catch a proud edge and tear foam free.
- Look for exposed bolt threads, washers, or nut edges on the room side.
  STOP: snagging, splinters, foam proud of wood, exposed fastener edges on the room side.

1.2 Sash restraint
- Confirm the sash lock is fully engaged (visual: lock foot or pivot fully seated).
- Confirm the sash cannot be pushed up more than ~1/16" anywhere along its run with firm palm pressure.
- Note: the plywood is now load-sharing with the sash lock against outward AC weight. If the lock ever fails, the plywood + bolts are the only thing between the AC and the yard. Treat lock integrity as critical.
  STOP: any visible daylight at sash/filler interface, any vertical sash play, lock not fully seated, any bolt on the plywood loose.

1.3 Foam perimeter compression
- Foam should be visibly compressed ~30–50% of free height all the way around.
- No daylight between foam and frame, foam and sash, foam and plywood.
- No foam bowing inward into the room (means over-compressed or plywood bowed).
  STOP: any light gap, uncompressed foam anywhere, foam bulging into the room, plywood visibly bowed.

1.4 Exterior gap seal
- From outside (or with a helper outside and a flashlight inside): scan all four sides of the filler for daylight.
- Top corners are the usual leak points where sash meets frame.
- Accordion panels should still meet the filler flush — no daylight at the panel/filler seam.
  STOP: any visible light from inside, panel not flush to filler, daylight at any top corner, daylight along the sill-side bottom.

1.5 Cord clearance
- Cord exits the AC housing and reaches the outlet without crossing the sash line, the filler, or any plywood edge.
- Cord is not pinched between sash and frame, filler and frame, or in any accordion fold.
- Cord is not in contact with the AC housing (heat + abrasion over time).
- Outlet rating matches the AC nameplate (typically 125 V / 15 A or 20 A dedicated; no extension cord, no power strip, no shared circuit with another large load).
  STOP: any pinch point, cord crossing sash, cord touching AC housing, outlet rating below nameplate, any adapter in line.

PHASE 2 — MECHANICAL (still unplugged)

2.1 Plywood retention
- From inside, firm upward hand pressure at the center and at each end of the plywood. Should feel fully captured — no lift, no give, no rattle.
- Lateral hand pressure at the same points — should be solid, no shift.
  STOP: any lift, any rattle, any give. Re-check bolt torque and foam shimming before continuing.

2.2 Sash restraint push test
- Firm upward palm pressure on the sash from inside, at center and both ends.
- Sash should not move. Lock should hold with no audible click or slip.
  STOP: any upward movement, any sound of lock disengaging, any visible flex in the lock hardware.

2.3 Panel movement check — OPTIONAL, skip if uncertain
- Briefly unlock the sash to test that the accordion panels still fold/unfold smoothly with the plywood attached.
- Have a second person support the AC from inside (hands under the front lip, lifting straight up) for the entire duration this sash is unlocked. The bracket alone is not a substitute for a hand on the unit during this test.
- The plywood must NOT bind on the frame or sill during sash travel.
- Re-lock sash immediately and re-verify the lock before releasing the AC.
  STOP: binding, cracking, panels not extending fully, plywood scraping, sash notably harder to move than before the filler was added. If in doubt, skip this test — the panel geometry is preserved by bolting through existing holes, so skipping is low risk.

2.4 Bracket engagement (no-load verification)
- From inside, both hands under the AC's bottom front edge, lift straight up ~1/4". Unit should rise and settle back solidly into the bracket with no fore-aft shift.
- The bracket should NOT flex audibly or visibly.
- Do NOT pull the AC toward you. Do NOT push it outward. Do NOT stand, sit, or lean weight on the unit.
  STOP: bracket flex, AC shifting in or out of the bracket, any sound of the bracket or its fasteners moving, AC not settling flush when released.

PHASE 3 — PET-SAFETY (Kibo still excluded)

3.1 Foam bite risk
- Any foam exposed at a height Kibo could reach (standing on floor, on a chair, on a bed pushed to the window) must be fully concealed behind the sash/frame OR replaced with a hard, non-chewable edge cap.
- Sweep the sill and floor for loose foam scraps.
  STOP: any reachable foam, any foam scraps on floor or sill.

3.2 Cord bite risk
- Re-check cord from dog's height: no segment below ~3 ft in a dog-accessible spot, no loops that can be tugged.
- If the cord crosses any path the dog could reach, route behind a piece of furniture the dog cannot get behind, or use a hard cord cover.
- Confirm zero tension on the cord if Kibo pulls — failure point should be the outlet (releasing the plug), not the AC housing.
  STOP: any cord segment in dog-reach, any cord that would tension the AC if pulled, any chewable cord cover.

3.3 Condensation management
- AC condensate should drip outside, not onto the sill or floor inside.
- If the model has an internal drain pan, route the drain outside or to a sealed container Kibo cannot drink from.
  STOP: any visible drip path inside, any puddle risk, drain pan accessible to dog.

3.4 Sash-from-outside check
- Confirm the window cannot be opened or the sash lifted from outside. A standard interior sash lock usually prevents this, but verify by pushing up on the sash from outside while the lock is engaged.
  STOP: any external release, any gap large enough for a paw or muzzle.

PHASE 4 — FIRST POWER (Kibo still excluded from the room)

4.1 Plug in, unit OFF
- Plug in. Listen and smell for 30 seconds at the outlet and at the plug. Touch the plug face — should be ambient temperature.
  STOP: any buzzing, clicking, or arcing at outlet or plug; warm or hot plug; scorch smell. Unplug immediately, check outlet wiring and circuit rating.

4.2 Fan-only test
- Run fan-only (no compressor) for 5 minutes.
- Listen for: panel rattle, plywood buzz, sash vibration, anything suggesting the filler is now in contact with a moving or oscillating surface.
- Hand flat on the plywood — should be still, no vibration transmitted.
  STOP: any rattle, any vibration in the filler, any new noise from the window assembly.

4.3 Low-cool test
- Switch to low cool for 10–15 minutes.
- Re-check exterior seal from inside: condensation may reveal micro-gaps as dark streaks on the frame or sash.
- Listen for smooth compressor cycling.
  STOP: any new noise, water streaks inside on frame/sash, any panel movement, ice forming on the interior line set.

4.4 Sustained run before granting access
- After 30 minutes of stable operation, leave the room Kibo-free for one full cooling cycle (typically 1–2 hours).
- One last walk-around: sill dry, floor under unit dry, cord routing unchanged, no new sounds, panel still.
- Only then consider allowing Kibo back into the room, with a normal-supervision level of watchfulness the first few cycles.
  STOP: any drip, any cord heating, any panel movement, any change in operational sound, any new smell.

MASTER STOP CONDITIONS (any one of these halts the sequence)
- Sharp edge that snags cloth or skin.
- Visible daylight at the filler perimeter.
- Sash movement of any kind under hand pressure.
- Plywood lift, rattle, or horizontal play.
- Loose bolt anywhere on the filler.
- Panel binding, cracking, or incomplete extension.
- Bracket flex or AC shift.
- Reachable foam or cord within dog-reach.
- Unusual sound, smell, heat, or drip at first power.
- Condensation path leading inside or onto any surface the dog can lick.

Two things worth restating because they're easy to forget when you're focused on the inspection itself:

1. The sash lock is now the single point that keeps the AC from falling if the bracket is ever disturbed (someone leaning on the window, a hard gust, AC vibration loosening a bolt over time). Re-check it at the start of every cooling season and after any windstorm.

2. Keep the unit unplugged whenever the room is unoccupied with Kibo home alone, until you've run a full week of normal-use cycles with no issues. That gives you time to catch a slow leak, a cord that warms under sustained load, or a panel that creeps.

Flushing order, drinking guidance, appliance reset, and the report-to-management threshold — based on what you're describing (cloudy cold that cleared in 2 min, faint yellow hot that hasn't cleared at 30 sec, no sediment/smell/advisory).

================================================================
1. FLUSHING ORDER
================================================================

Prep before you start:
- Remove the aerator from the kitchen cold and bathroom hot/cold taps (counterclockwise by hand, or with tape-wrapped pliers if stuck; keep the rubber washer). The aerator clogs first and chokes flow, which makes flushing look worse than it is. Put aerators in a cup so nothing falls down the drain.
- Open each fixture fully (handle all the way to hot/cold, not partway).

Then run in this order, cold side first, then hot side:

  A. Kitchen cold tap, full bore, 5-15 min — until no cloudiness or tint.
  B. Bathroom cold tap (sink, then shower/tub if separate), full bore, 5-10 min each.
  C. Toilets — flush 3-5 times each. Don't worry about the tank.
  D. (Optional) Laundry cold tap if you have one, 5 min.
  E. Water heater — only if hot water stays heavily discolored after step F. This is
     usually the building's job (drain valve at the bottom of the heater, hose to a
     floor drain, 5-10 min until clear, then close and let it refill). If you're in
     an apartment and not sure you have access, skip this and report — see section 4.
  F. Hot taps, full hot, full bore: kitchen hot first (shares the line your dishwasher
     uses), then bathroom hot. Run each 10-20 min until clear. The heater and its
     piping hold a lot of stagnant water, so hot takes longer than cold.

After each tap runs clear, reassemble aerators. Run each tap once more for 30 sec
to flush any debris that came loose when you unscrewed the aerator.

What you're seeing is normal disturbance (air + mobilized iron/scale) after a
depressurization event. Two minutes for the cold to clear is exactly what
air-induced cloudiness looks like. The yellow hot after 30 sec is not yet a
problem — just keep flushing.

================================================================
2. WHEN THE WATER IS SUITABLE FOR DRINKING / COOKING
================================================================

General rules:
- Use only the COLD tap for drinking and cooking. Heat it on the stove or in a kettle
  if you want hot water. Hot tap water is a standing recommendation to avoid
  regardless — water heaters and hot lines leach metals more readily, and the
  heater environment isn't suitable for direct consumption.
- After any fixture has been idle 6+ hours (overnight, after work), run the cold tap
  1-2 minutes before drawing drinking/cooking water. This is the "first-draw flush"
  and is standard practice in older buildings.
- Visually clear + no smell + no off-taste = drinkable, given no advisory from
  management or your utility. Iron discoloration at the level you're describing
  is an aesthetic issue (secondary MCL 0.3 mg/L), not a toxicity issue — but don't
  drink it until it's clear, both for palatability and because discoloration means
  other particulates are also in suspension.

If management/your utility issues a boil-water advisory at any point:
- Follow it strictly. Rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes at elevations above
  6,500 ft), or use bottled water, for drinking, brushing teeth, washing produce,
  and any food prep where water isn't boiled for several minutes.
- They will tell you when it's lifted (usually after negative test results,
  24-48 hours). Don't lift it yourself.

Status check for your current state:
- Kitchen cold: cleared in 2 min → ready to drink (still do the overnight first-draw
  flush going forward).
- Bathroom hot: yellow at 30 sec → not yet. Keep flushing per step F. Don't drink
  from the hot tap regardless of clearance.

================================================================
3. APPLIANCE RETURN-TO-SERVICE CRITERIA
================================================================

Wait until both kitchen hot and cold run visibly clear at the sink for several
minutes straight. Sediment in the supply line will clog appliance inlet filters
and, worse, leave grit on dishes or rust stains on laundry.

Dishwasher:
  1. Confirm kitchen hot runs clear at the tap.
  2. If you can reach the dishwasher's hot supply connection (under the sink or
     behind the unit), there's usually a small mesh inlet screen at the hose
     fitting — clean it if you can.
  3. Run an EMPTY cycle on the hottest/longest setting with detergent (or a
     dishwasher cleaner like Affresh). This flushes the internal sump, spray arm,
     and drain line.
  4. After the empty cycle, inspect the bottom filter (most dishwashers have a
     removable cylindrical filter at the floor of the tub — twist out, rinse,
     reinstall).
  5. Run a real load. Check dishes for grit before unloading. If grit appears,
     run another empty cycle and recheck the filter.
  Ready for normal use after: empty cycle runs clean + no grit on a test load.

Washing machine:
  1. Flush the hot and cold supply taps behind the washer (usually quarter-turn
     valves) into a bucket, 5-10 min each, until clear.
  2. Disconnect the hoses from the taps. There's a small cylindrical mesh screen
     inside each hose fitting — pull it out with needle-nose pliers, rinse, reinstall.
     This is the most common failure point after a disturbance event; skipping this
     step is why washers run slow or don't fill after a main break.
  3. Run an EMPTY hot cycle with a washer-cleaning tablet or 1 cup white vinegar
     poured into the detergent dispenser. Wipe the rubber door gasket after.
  4. Avoid whites on the first real load if you saw any yellow tint — iron residue
     can leave rust spots on white fabrics. Use the extra-rinse option if you have it.
  Ready for normal use after: hose screens cleaned + empty cycle done + first test
  load shows no staining.

================================================================
4. WHEN TO REPORT TO MANAGEMENT
================================================================

Continue flushing and don't escalate yet if: clear trend within ~15-30 min of full-bore
flushing, no smell, no leaks, no sediment particles, pressure is normal.

Report to management (today, the same email/thread you're already on if there's an
active thread about the shutdown) if any of the following:

  - Yellow/brown tint persists in any fixture beyond ~30 min of full-bore flushing,
    OR hot water stays discolored long after cold has cleared (this usually means
    sediment stirred up in the water heater — their responsibility to flush).
  - Visible particles or sediment in the water.
  - Any unusual smell: sewage, sulfur / rotten egg, chlorine overwhelming, fuel/oil,
    chemical/solvent.
  - Any leak anywhere — under sinks, behind appliances, around the water heater,
    or the T&P relief valve discharging (dripping is normal; a steady stream is not).
  - Pressure drops after initial restoration, or persistently low pressure at any
    one fixture vs. the others.
  - Discoloration that returns after clearing (e.g., first-draw yellow every morning).
  - Any management advisory that doesn't match what you observe, or no advisory at
    all when one would be expected for the work they did.
  - Any gastrointestinal or other health symptoms in you or a household member that
    could plausibly be water-related within the next few days.

Suggested phrasing if you need to write it up:

  "Following the scheduled shutdown today, the kitchen cold ran cloudy for ~2 min
  then cleared, and the bathroom hot has a faint yellow tint after 30+ sec of
  full-bore flushing. I'm continuing to flush. Please confirm whether a flush of
  the building water heater is planned as part of the restoration, and let me
  know if a boil-water advisory applies or if the work performed warrants one.
  Dishwasher and washing machine remain out of service pending clear water at
  the relevant supply taps."

================================================================
BOTTOM LINE FOR RIGHT NOW
================================================================

- Kitchen cold: usable now for drinking (keep doing the overnight 1-2 min first-draw
  flush going forward). Don't drink from the hot tap regardless.
- Bathroom hot: keep flushing full-bore, expect 10-20 min. If it's not visibly
  clearing by then, that's the threshold to message management about a heater
  flush.
- Don't run the dishwasher or washing machine yet. Even with clear water at the
  tap, the inlet screens on those appliances catch sediment that bypasses the
  aerator, so flush + clean screens + empty cycle first.
- No advisory + clearing trend + no smell/sediment/leak = you're in the normal
  post-restoration window. If anything in section 4 shows up, report immediately
  rather than waiting it out.

I have enough to do the review. Two distinct sets of facts matter:

1. The first team's failure (May 14): the schema-2-vs-schema-3 mismatch. The published baseline is still 0.8.4 with schema 2 outputs.
2. The workflow constraints Anya already committed to: isolated candidate directory only, atomic promotion, all-or-nothing, schema-validation before drift comparison, no manual override, no partial publication.

The proposed sequence is conceptually right, but there are five concrete partial-publication / misleading-comparison risks the second team should patch before rerunning. Let me lay them out for Alex.

---

**Review of Anya's isolated-branch sequence — risks before the second team reruns**

The framing is correct: this has to be one coordinated 2→3 transition, not a series of single-pin bumps in shared CI, and 0.8.4 must stay published the whole time. The five risks below are about where the proposed wording still lets the second team either quietly publish a partial result, or pass the matrix on evidence weaker than it claims.

**Risk 1 — Step 2 doesn't actually pin the shared CI generator**
"Pin the consumer and shared CI generator together at 0.9.0" is the right *intent*, but the original failure mode was exactly that shared CI silently resolved a different version than the consumer. The second team needs to state the *exact* version (e.g. `0.9.0` exact, not `^0.9.0` or `~0.9.0`) and the pin must be recorded in CI's own lockfile, not just the consumer's. Otherwise a future shared-CI bump reintroduces the May-14 drift. The earlier session explicitly requires an exact pin on the latest minor plus a recorded CI lockfile entry; step 2 should call that out, not just say "together at 0.9.0."

**Risk 2 — Steps 3 and 4 need a precondition gate, not just generation**
Step 3 generates into something; step 4 compares to fixtures and runs 20x for byte stability. The missing piece is the **precondition gate** between steps 2 and 3: CI must assert (a) the pinned generator accepts the canonical source's `schema_version: 3` and (b) the consumer lockfile's pinned `@northpier/tokens` version is a known-compatible pair with the pinned generator. Without that, a generator that silently downgrades or a tokens version that lacks schema 3 can produce a clean 20x run that is internally consistent but cross-component incompatible — and that *is* how the first team got burned. The precondition check should fail loudly with all three numbers named (generator, tokens, schema_version).

**Risk 3 — Step 4 is the misleading-comparison trap**
"Compare all targets to semantic fixtures and repeat generation 20 times for byte stability" looks like two checks but it's really one check performed twice. A semantic-fixture match plus byte-stable repeat tells you the generator is *deterministic against its own inputs*. It does **not** tell you the schema-3 outputs semantically match the schema-2 fixtures they are meant to replace — fixtures were authored against schema 2, and a schema bump can produce semantically equivalent but structurally different output (renamed keys, regrouped namespaces, new required tokens, dropped legacy tokens). The second team needs to either:
  - carry forward a schema-2-to-schema-3 semantic mapping that asserts token-by-token equivalence at the *value* level (not just structural match), and
  - run schema-validation against the canonical package's structural contract *before* the byte-stability check, per the established rule that schema validation must precede drift comparison.

  Otherwise "matches semantic fixtures" can pass on a matrix that has quietly changed semantics.

**Risk 4 — Steps 5 and 6 are positive controls; they don't replace a clean baseline run**
The intentional CSS-edit drift test and the schema-validation-failure no-publish test are good — they're the positive controls that proved the harness can *fail*. But the matrix hasn't actually passed yet at that point. Step 6 ends with "require zero publication," which is correct, but step 7 ("keep 0.8.4 published until the complete matrix passes") implies the matrix passes when 5 and 6 also pass. That's misleading. The order should be:
  - clean matrix pass (steps 3–4 with the precondition gate and the schema-2-to-schema-3 semantic mapping from risk 3)
  - *then* positive controls (steps 5 and 6)
  - *then* one more clean matrix pass to confirm the harness wasn't perturbed by the control injections
  - *then* atomic promotion, with 0.8.4 still published and identical

  Skipping the post-control clean pass means a control injection could have left the candidate location in a state the team mistakes for a real pass.

**Risk 5 — Step 7 needs the atomic-promotion mechanism spelled out, not just the intent**
"Keep 0.8.4 outputs published until the complete matrix passes" is the right outcome but doesn't enforce the mechanism. The established rules require:
  - generators write *only* to an isolated candidate location (never the published path),
  - a single atomic promotion (rename / swap) after both generators succeed and all drift checks pass,
  - on any failure (schema, generator, timeout, crash, drift) the candidate is discarded and 0.8.4 is left byte-identical and available for rollback,
  - no manual promotion, no `--force`, no out-of-band bypass, and every publish reruns both generators + drift check even when the canonical package is unchanged.

  If the second team implements step 7 as "don't publish until green," they can still accidentally publish from a different branch or by a different path. The sequence should explicitly say *what* the atomic step is and *what* is disallowed, otherwise the workflow constraint isn't enforced — just hoped for.

---

**Suggested tightening before rerun** (small, additive — doesn't change the sequence's shape):

  - 2: state exact version (`0.9.0`, not `^0.9.0`) and require CI's own lockfile to record it.
  - between 2 and 3: add a precondition gate that asserts generator ↔ tokens ↔ schema_version are a known-compatible triple, with a failure message naming all three.
  - 4: split into (a) schema-validation against the canonical contract, then (b) semantic comparison against a schema-2-to-schema-3 mapped fixture, then (c) the 20x byte-stability repeat. Document the mapping or the semantic equivalence is unproven.
  - 5 and 6: keep, but only run after a clean pass. Add a final clean pass after the controls.
  - 7: spell out the atomic promotion (single swap from isolated candidate → published) and explicitly disallow manual promotion, force flags, and bypass routes.

Net: the seven steps are the right shape and the fail-closed intent is right, but as written they leave room for (a) silent shared-CI pin drift, (b) a fixture match that doesn't actually prove schema-2→schema-3 semantic equivalence, and (c) a "passed" matrix that hasn't been confirmed clean after the positive-control injections. Tighten those five points and the second team's rerun will produce evidence the studio can actually trust.

I haven't sent anything to Anya or touched the pilot's shared CI — this is review-only, no side effects. If you want, I can draft the tightened sequence as a short pre-rerun checklist for the second team, or open a runbook entry capturing the five risks as guardrails for any future schema bump.

A plan for two: cumin-roasted sweet potato and crispy chickpeas over rice, with bright lemon-tahini sauce, last-minute wilted kale, and a cool yogurt dollop. Warm but not heavy. Almost everything is staged by 8:55 and holds; the kale and the final plate happen only after the text.

CONCEPT
- Rice and the roasting tray carry the warmth and do the long cook.
- Kale is wilted in the last 2-3 minutes, so it stays vivid green instead of going dull.
- Sauce and yogurt are made early so flavors settle; yogurt on top at service keeps the bowl from feeling heavy.

PHASE 1 — 8:30 to ~8:55 (active work, then it holds)

8:30  Oven to 425°F. Start 1 cup white rice (1 cup rice to 1.5 cups water, salted, lid on). If you're using brown rice, start at 8:15 instead — it needs ~45 min.

8:32  Peel and cube the 2 sweet potatoes into 3/4-inch pieces. Drain the chickpeas and PAT THEM DRY thoroughly — wet chickpeas steam, they don't crisp. Toss both on a sheet pan with 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp cumin, 3 cloves garlic minced, 1/2 tsp salt, pepper. Spread in a single layer; if it's crowded, split to two pans.

8:35  Pan into the oven. Timer 22 min, stir once at the halfway mark.

8:38  Make the sauce: whisk 3 tbsp tahini, juice of the half lemon, 1 small grated garlic clove, 3-4 tbsp warm water, pinch of salt. It should coat a spoon, not run. Set aside at room temp.

8:45  Stem the kale, tear into bite-sized pieces, wash and dry it really well (wet kale = sad wilt). Put it in a bowl, cover with a damp towel, leave on the counter. This is your hold-station.

8:50-ish  Rice is done. Keep the lid on, leave it on the (off) burner. Sweet potatoes and chickpeas are nearly there. Sauce ready, kale staged.

HOLD POINT
From ~8:55 until she texts, you do nothing. Oven off, tray inside (residual heat keeps it warm 20+ min); rice covered; sauce and yogurt waiting; kale at room temp under the towel. This is the part that keeps it from feeling like a job.

You have ~15-20 minutes from text to door. Five minutes of actual work.

Minute 0-1   If the tray has been sitting under 15 min, leave it. If longer, oven back on at 350°F for 90 seconds to rewarm, then pull.

Minute 1-4   Wilt the kale. Large skillet, 1 tbsp olive oil, 1 thinly sliced garlic clove, medium-high heat ~30 seconds until fragrant. Add kale in batches with a pinch of salt. Toss until just wilted and bright green — 2 to 2.5 minutes total. Off heat, a tiny squeeze of lemon over the top.

Minute 4-6   Plate. Scoop of rice, sweet potato + chickpeas, then the kale pushed to one side so it doesn't bleed color into everything. Drizzle tahini sauce generously. Spoon a dollop of yogurt on top. Crack of pepper, tiny pinch of cumin to finish.

- Not heavy: rice is the base, not the bulk; lemon, tahini, and yogurt keep it bright; kale is a small mound, not a pile.

PR #229 isn't fetchable from this session — it isn't in the open list, and the get_pr endpoint returns NOT_FOUND. Rather than fabricate observations about a PR I can't actually read, I'll stop trying to look it up and review the pseudocode the user posted directly against the runbook and the prior 413 incident pattern. The user gave me a concrete code sketch; the review is on the sketch, not on the diff.

Here is my review, grounded in the runbook above (v2.19.4 randomized Retry-After is production behavior — must not regress; alex = final approver on cross-service releases) and the 413 closure pattern (decoded body, not wire).

## Verdict: do not accept as-is. Three blockers, two follow-ups.

### Blocker 1 — Permit leak on tenant-permit cancellation (the one you flagged)

The current shape is:

```
global.acquire(ctx)
if err := tenant.acquire(ctx); err != nil {
    return canceled(err)   // global permit never released
}
defer tenant.release()
defer global.release()
```

If `tenant.acquire(ctx)` errors (deadline, cancel, timeout), we return without releasing the global permit. The defer stack is registered *after* the failing call, so it never runs on this path. Under load, this slowly drains the global pool until the service stops accepting decompressed bodies altogether — silent DoS via permit starvation, with no error budget signal.

Fixes (any one is sufficient; I'd take both):

- Reorder so the global defer is registered immediately after `global.acquire`, and only the *tenant* acquire is unprotected:
  ```
  global.acquire(ctx)
  defer global.release()
  if err := tenant.acquire(ctx); err != nil { return canceled(err) }
  defer tenant.release()
  ```
- Or, more defensively, use an `errgroup`-style guard / named return so every return path releases what was acquired.

The first form is what I'd push for: matches Go convention and is the smallest diff.

### Blocker 2 — Allocation before limit check

```
for chunk := range decoder {
    output = append(output, chunk...)
    decompressed += len(chunk)
    if decompressed > bodyLimit {
        return bodyTooLarge()
    }
}
```

The buffer is extended *before* the limit is checked. `append` may grow the backing array past the limit, and on the first offending chunk we've already committed a write that exceeds `bodyLimit`. Two issues:

1. We allocate up to `bodyLimit + maxChunkSize` per request before returning. With a malicious client and a chunky zstd/gzip stream, that's a per-request amplification of `maxChunkSize` beyond the advertised cap. The runbook doesn't say "this is fine" — the prior 413 closure explicitly anchored the limit on *decoded* bytes, and a per-request overshoot of one chunk defeats the cap.
2. The check happens after the write, so the bodyTooLarge response is honest about the *total* but the buffer is already over budget and has to be GC'd, not reused.

Fix: check the prospective total *before* the append:

```
for chunk := range decoder {
    decompressed += len(chunk)
    if decompressed > bodyLimit {
        return bodyTooLarge()
    }
    output = append(output, chunk...)
}
```

Or, better still: if the decoder exposes a reader interface, wrap it in a `LimitReader(decompressed)` at the bodyLimit so the decoder itself stops producing — then the check is structural, not a post-hoc guard.

### Blocker 3 — The "Retry-After" line at the bottom contradicts the function

The sketch says:

> Overflow before permit acquisition returns HTTP 429 with the existing randomized Retry-After value.

But the `bodyTooLarge()` branch above the limit returns *after* permit acquisition — meaning on the actual overflow path (the one that matters in practice), the request goes through `defer tenant.release(); defer global.release()` cleanly and presumably returns 413. The 429 + randomized Retry-After comment doesn't apply to the code as shown; it appears to be a copy-paste from the v2.19.4 cutover note in the runbook.

This needs to be reconciled. Either:

- The PR introduces a *new* 429 path for overflow (then say so and confirm the Retry-After is 1–3s randomized — the v2.19.4 behavior — not something new), and document why overflow is 429 instead of 413, or
- Overflow remains 413 and the comment is wrong and should be removed.

The runbook is explicit that v2.19.4's randomized 1–3s `Retry-After` is the production behavior of 429 and must not regress, but it also doesn't authorize *expanding* 429 onto a code path that was previously 413 without a note in the cutover playbook. I'd want a one-line justification: "we route this to 429 because overflow is retryable after the client compresses; 413 implies the body is permanently rejected" — or push back to 413 with `Connection: close` and call it a day. Don't ship with a comment that just asserts the existing behavior.

### Follow-up 4 — Cancellation semantics on `decoder` itself

The loop reads `for chunk := range decoder`. If the request context is canceled *while* the decoder is mid-chunk, we return mid-iteration with both permits held (that's fine after Blocker 1), but we also leak whatever buffered state the decoder holds. For zstd that's bounded; for gzip+brotli it isn't always. Worth a regression test that:

- cancels the context between two chunks,
- asserts both permits are released (global pool counter returns to baseline),
- asserts no goroutine is left blocked in the decoder.

### Follow-up 5 — Minimum regression tests

Before acceptance, I want to see at minimum:

1. **Permit release on tenant-permit failure** — global pool size returns to baseline after `tenant.acquire` returns `context.Canceled`. (Catches Blocker 1.)
2. **Limit is enforced before allocation** — a stream that produces a single chunk larger than `bodyLimit` returns 413 without growing `output` past `bodyLimit`. Use a fake decoder that emits one chunk of `bodyLimit + 1`; assert `len(output) <= bodyLimit` after the call returns. (Catches Blocker 2.)
3. **Limit is enforced across many small chunks** — the running total never exceeds `bodyLimit` at any point. Assert with a chunked decoder.
4. **Decoder context cancel** — both permits released, decoder goroutine exits. (Catches Follow-up 4.)
5. **Retry-After on overflow** — if 429, header is in [1s, 3s] and not zero. If 413, this test doesn't apply and the comment is removed. (Catches Blocker 3.)
6. **Happy path** — stream within limit, both permits released, no allocation overshoot.

Tests 1–4 are non-negotiable. Test 5 forces a decision on Blocker 3 instead of letting it ship by accident. Test 6 is sanity.

### Other notes

- The `canceled(err)` helper name is fine but I'd want it confirmed to map `context.Canceled` / `context.DeadlineExceeded` to the right HTTP status (499 vs 408 vs 504). Not in scope for this PR's stated review, but flag it.
- `defer tenant.release(); defer global.release()` order matters: defers run LIFO, so tenant releases first, then global. That's correct (release the inner lock before the outer), but it's also the *opposite* of the natural reading order, which is how the Blocker 1 bug shipped in the first place. A short comment ("defer LIFO: tenant, then global") on the defers would have prevented this.
- Per the runbook, I'm the final approver on cross-service releases; the implementation, telemetry, and release train stay with the owner. This review is scoped to the four axes you listed — permit ordering/cleanup, allocation-before-limit, cancellation, and minimum regression tests — not to telemetry, SLOs, or the cutover plan.

### Recommended next step

Ask the author to land Blockers 1 and 2 in the same PR (small, mechanical), resolve Blocker 3 explicitly (delete the comment *or* justify 429), and add tests 1–4. Re-review once those land. I'll sign off when the test diff is in front of me.

Reader safety — sound in pattern, conditional on two things I can't verify from the snippet.

The shape is RCU: a reader holds an epoch from Enter to Exit; the writer's Swap + Retire defers freeing old until all reader epochs entered before the swap have drained. As long as (a) Enter is paired with Exit on every path including panic, (b) the swap of active is an atomic pointer swap and not a struct mutation in place, and (c) Lookup and Match do not capture or stash references that outlive the guard, an in-flight reader cannot observe a freed or partially freed generation. The pattern itself reads correctly.

Two things I would still want confirmed out of band:
  - that gen.Lookup returns a matcher owned by that generation, not a shared/global one whose lifetime is independent of the gen,
  - that the epoch tracker's quiescent-state detection and retire path are correct (no missed wakeups, no skew between Enter/Exit accounting and the drainer).

Neither is visible in the snippet; the snippet only shows the API contract, and the contract is the right one.

Retention — yes, failed reloads still retain candidate generations indefinitely. The rejection did not fix this. It is the actual bug.

The failure branch as written:

  generationRegistry[candidate.ID] = candidate.Matchers   // publish first
  if err := Validate(candidate); err != nil {
      candidate = nil                                     // local pointer dropped
      return err                                          // registry entry NOT removed
  }

After candidate = nil there is no Go reference to the local, but generationRegistry[candidate.ID] still pins candidate.Matchers (and through it whatever the compiled matchers retain — automata, AST nodes, captured config). Candidate was never swapped into active, so it never goes through epochs.Retire, so it never enters the drain-and-free path. The only thing that could remove the entry is something else writing to generationRegistry at the same ID.

Whether this leaks permanently or only until the next reload at the same ID depends on the ID scheme, which the snippet doesn't show:
  - if candidate.ID is unique per attempt (UUID, monotonic counter), every failed reload leaks one generation permanently. Slow but real.
  - if candidate.ID is content-derived and can repeat, the leak is bounded by the gap between a failed validation and the next successful reload at the same ID, but it is still observable and still wrong.

A second, separate problem on the same lines: the registry is published before validation. Anything that reads generationRegistry (diagnostics, introspection, another hot path) during the window between the insert and the Validate result will see an unvalidated generation. The snippet doesn't show registry readers, but a process-wide map that gets pre-validation writes is a hazard on its own — even if no current reader exists, the invariant "registry contents are validated" is no longer enforceable.

Minimum fix:
  - on the failure path, delete(generationRegistry, candidate.ID) before returning err.

Defensible fix (preferred):
  - build candidate off-registry, run Validate, and only insert into generationRegistry after Validate returns nil. The active swap can still happen immediately after the registry insert. This closes both the leak and the unvalidated-read window, and keeps the registry's invariant ("entries here are validated") true by construction.

Either is small. The second is the one I'd push for, because the registry's existence implies something reads from it, and "writes happen before validation" is the kind of invariant that erodes the next time someone touches this code.

**Cross-service invariant review — rollup-service 14:05–14:10 undercount**

Scope reminder: Cyrus's team owns rollup-service operationally; you asked me only for the contract read and the gating assertions, not the watermark/log forensics or the fix itself. Memory confirms that boundary — Roman/Cyrus own threshold and watermark tuning; I'm looking at invariants and the assertion set a fix should satisfy.

Numbers as you handed them:
- Window 14:05–14:10; lateness allowance 90s
- First complete mark: 14:10:31 (31s after window end)
- 312 late records arrived, latest at 14:11:18 (78s after window end — comfortably inside the 90s allowance)
- Initial published count 38,721; corrected 39,033 on next compaction pass
- Undercount = 312, which matches the late-record count exactly

**1. Does the completion rule violate the stated lateness contract?**

No — not as described. The completion rule, as it fired here, is consistent with a contract of the form: "a window may be marked complete once the configured lateness allowance has elapsed without new accepted-point activity." Evidence that fits that contract:

- The 90s allowance had fully elapsed before completion fired (31s mark is later than 90s would suggest only if there was no incoming traffic in the first 59s; the salient fact is that all 312 late records arrived at 78s ≤ 90s, inside the budget).
- All 312 late records were still inside the 90s window when they arrived. None arrived after the allowance.
- The corrected count (39,033) equals the initial count (38,721) plus the 312 late records — i.e., the data was retained and incorporated on the next compaction. Nothing was dropped.
- Upstream accepted-point count is stable and upstream commit latency is normal, so the undercount is not a producer-side hole that the completion rule would be hiding.

So the rule did exactly what the contract says: it finalized at 14:10:31 based on a watermark that, under normal upstream behavior, had nothing more to wait for inside the 90s budget. The 312 records that *did* arrive under budget were captured and applied by the next compaction pass — which is the documented recovery path, not a violation.

The thing worth flagging — and this is the only thing I think is contract-adjacent rather than purely operational — is that "completion" here means "durable commit of the current best count," not "definitive." A reader who treats the 14:10:31 mark as a freeze will be wrong by 312 / 39,033 ≈ 0.8% until the next compaction lands. That's not a contract violation, but it *is* an invariant worth naming explicitly so nobody downstream treats T+31s as a final number.

**2. What assertions should gate a fix**

I don't know yet whether there will be a fix — the operational correction worked and the contract held. But if a code change is proposed, these are the assertions that should gate it, framed at the cross-service invariant level rather than the implementation level. They fall into three groups.

*A. The contract itself (must not weaken)*
- The 90s lateness allowance must remain the published window-completion budget. Any change is a contract change and should be treated like one — Cyrus's team proposes, cross-service review on the producer/consumer seam, with explicit re-statement of the allowance.
- "Window complete" continues to mean "durable aggregate commit at the current watermark after the allowance has elapsed," not "no more records will ever be added." Recovery via the next compaction pass is part of the contract; a fix must not silently turn recovery into in-window correction.
- Idempotency invariant preserved: identical inputs produce a byte-identical rollup, and the next compaction's corrected 39,033 must be derivable deterministically from (window, source-event set, config version, dedup keys). Last-completed-attempt-wins on reads. A fix that makes the corrected value depend on which compaction pass touched it is a regression.

*B. The signal set that proves the fix works (not just today, but on the next similar event)*
- Late-record counters by arrival skew: a histogram of (record_arrival_time − window_end_seconds) for the 90s window, so we can see whether the 312-at-78s pattern is a one-off or a recurring tail near the allowance boundary.
- Watermark finalize timestamps verified against a same-region peer — i.e., two independent finalizers should agree on the finalization time within a small skew.
- raw_write_accept vs. batch_reject for the affected tenant around 14:05–14:10: confirm upstream really was clean and the 312 records were legitimate late-but-in-budget arrivals, not retries of something upstream had rejected.
- For the affected hours, recompute/aggregate-replay entries showing the corrected value path. If those entries aren't present, the recovery story is incomplete regardless of how the math works out.
- Acceptance band: the corrected-vs-initial delta on similar windows should be ≪ 0.8% in steady state. A fix that reduces the size of the tail without changing the *shape* of the late-arrival distribution is more convincing than one that just narrows the window.

*C. Things the fix must not break (the cross-service blast-radius checks)*

Eggs verde with quick cabbage slaw — one skillet, ~25 min.

The trick is keeping cabbage out of the pan. Dress it raw so it stays crunchy and sharp, and warm the beans in salsa verde as the "sauce" the eggs cook in. Same skillet, but cabbage and eggs never meet.

Start two things at once.

Slaw (10 min hands-off):
- 2 cups shredded cabbage (about 1/3 of the head, sliced thin)
- 3 scallions, whites minced, greens sliced thin and kept separate
- Juice of 1 lime (or 1 tbsp vinegar), 1/2 tsp salt, pepper, a glug of olive oil
- Toss, leave on the counter. It'll wilt just enough to bend, not cook.

Skillet (10 min):
- 8 eggs beaten with a pinch of salt
- Drain the black beans, then warm them in the same skillet with the salsa verde (about 1/2 cup; use most of the jar) over medium heat, mashing a bit so it thickens, ~4 min
- Pour eggs in, stir gently until just set, ~3 min. Pull off heat — they'll keep cooking on the plate.

Meanwhile warm the tortillas directly over a gas burner (30 sec/side) or stacked in a low oven.

Plate: eggs and beans on tortillas, slaw on top or alongside so it stays crunchy, sliced avocado, reserved scallion greens, a handful of grated cheddar.

Why it works: cabbage dresses, not cooks — keeps the snap you asked for. Beans in salsa verde do double duty as sauce and protein, so the eggs stay loose rather than binding everything into a hash. One pan, 25 minutes, and nothing gets soggy.

Drink: a cortado while it rests.

SUMMARY: The combination most likely tripped the GFCI via cumulative leakage current pushed over its ~4-6 mA ground-fault threshold while the circuit was also under heavy load. With your described observations (no smell, no heat, no damage, both appliances run fine solo, reset holds), there is no immediate hazard, but do not run both on that outlet again until you isolate the cause.

============================================================
IMMEDIATE GUIDANCE
============================================================
- Leave both appliances unplugged at that outlet for now. You have already done this; keep it that way.
- The reset holding with nothing plugged in is a good sign, not a clearance to resume. Do not assume it is fixed.
- Use a different kitchen outlet for breakfast needs today. If only one outlet is convenient, run one appliance at a time in it.
- Locate the breaker panel and identify the breaker labeled "kitchen" or "counter." Verify it is ON (not partially tripped). A breaker that has tripped often sits in a middle position; push it fully OFF, then ON to be sure.
- Note the time of the trip and what was running. If the GFCI trips again later (even with nothing plugged in), record that and treat it as a professional-help trigger (below).

============================================================
LOW-RISK CHECKS YOU CAN DO
============================================================
- Visual inspection (appliance cords, plugs, outlet face):
  - Plugs: bent or loose prongs, discoloration, melting, black soot.
  - Cords: cracking, fraying at the strain relief, kinks, pet/heat damage.
  - Outlet face: any brown/yellow discoloration around the slots, any plastic that looks warped or shiny.
- GFCI self-test: press TEST on the GFCI; it should click and stop powering the outlet. Press RESET; power should return. Do this once, then leave it in the RESET position. If TEST does not trip the GFCI, or RESET will not latch, the GFCI itself is suspect and needs replacement.
- Appliance isolation, one at a time, on the same GFCI outlet:
  - Run only the kettle through a full boil. If it does not trip, run only the toaster oven through a full cycle. If either trips the GFCI alone, that appliance has a real ground fault and should be retired or serviced; the other one is fine.
  - Important: full boil and full toaster cycle means several minutes, not just 5 seconds. Some leakage only shows up when heating elements get hot or wet (kettles especially).
- Cross-check on a known-good outlet: run the same two appliances, one at a time, on a different kitchen outlet that is on a different circuit (use a lamp or another small device to confirm which outlets share a circuit). If both work fine elsewhere, the GFCI receptacle or its circuit is suspect, not the appliances.
- Check the kettle for water on the outside, around the base, or in the cord connection. Dry everything thoroughly before any further test. A damp kettle base is a common culprit.
- Check the toaster oven plug and the kettle plug for warmth right after a solo run (touch the plastic plug body, not the prongs). Any warmth = that appliance has high resistance at the plug and should be replaced or have the cord serviced.

============================================================
WHAT NOT TO TEST OR DO
============================================================
- Do NOT run both appliances on that outlet again to "see if it still happens." That is the failure mode; repeating it does not diagnose anything and risks a real ground fault developing under load.
- Do NOT use an extension cord, power strip, or outlet splitter to run either of these appliances. Code prohibits it for fixed cooking/heating appliances, and a worn cord can itself cause a ground fault the GFCI will then catch.
- Do NOT bypass the GFCI (cheater plug, adapter, swapping in a non-GFCI receptacle, taping the TEST button). The GFCI is the only thing standing between a fault and a person; removing it converts a nuisance trip into a shock hazard.
- Do NOT open the kettle or toaster oven. Heating elements, thermal fuses, and stored energy in controls are not user-serviceable, and you will void any recall protection.
- Do NOT keep resetting the GFCI repeatedly if it re-trips. Each re-trip under the same load is a sign the cause is ongoing.
- Do NOT assume the GFCI reset means everything is fine. The GFCI tripped for a reason; you have not yet ruled out a developing fault in an appliance or in the wiring behind the outlet.

============================================================
SIGNS THAT REQUIRE LEAVING THE CIRCUIT OFF AND CALLING MAINTENANCE OR AN ELECTRICIAN
============================================================
If you observe any of the following, stop using the outlet entirely, leave the GFCI in the RESET (off) or tripped position, and contact building maintenance (if you rent) or a licensed electrician (if you own):

- GFCI trips with NOTHING plugged in. This points to wiring, not appliances.
- GFCI will not reset (RESET button will not stay in, or clicks but immediately releases).
- GFCI TEST button does not cause the outlet to lose power. The protection itself is dead.
- Any warmth at the outlet face, even slight, with or without load.
- Any discoloration, scorch marks, melting, or a smell from the outlet (ozone, plastic, fishy).
- Buzzing, crackling, popping, or sizzling from the outlet or from either appliance.
- Visible sparking when you plug or unplug either appliance.
- Tingling sensation when you touch an appliance, its cord, or the outlet face.
- Tripping of any other GFCI or breaker in the apartment when you use that outlet.
- Repeated tripping with a single, known-good appliance plugged into that outlet.
- A breaker in the panel trips together with (or instead of) the GFCI.
- Water reaching the outlet, or the outlet feeling damp.

============================================================
IS THIS CONSISTENT WITH AN OVERLOAD?
============================================================
Partially, with an important caveat:

- A typical kettle draws about 1,200-1,500 W (~10-12.5 A). A typical toaster oven draws about 1,200-1,500 W (~10-12.5 A). Run together on a 15 A circuit, total draw of ~20-25 A clearly exceeds the circuit's capacity (a 15 A branch is rated for ~1,800 W total, 1,440 W continuous). On a 20 A kitchen small-appliance circuit, ~20-25 A is at or above the breaker's trip curve and would eventually trip the breaker.
- That part matches overload.
- But what tripped was the GFCI, not the breaker. A standard GFCI receptacle does not include overcurrent protection; it trips on ground-fault current above roughly 4-6 mA, or on cumulative appliance leakage that sums past that threshold. So if the breaker did not trip and only the GFCI did, the most likely explanations are:
  1. Cumulative leakage from both appliances summing above the GFCI threshold (each appliance has small inherent leakage through its filters and capacitive coupling; two together can exceed 5 mA).
  2. A marginal ground fault in one appliance that becomes visible only under load or heat (kettles with moisture in the base, toaster ovens with degraded insulation around the element).
  3. A worn or overly sensitive GFCI that trips at lower current than spec.
- Net: the trip is consistent with "the circuit was overloaded AND a GFCI interpreted the combination as a fault." It is not a classic breaker-style overload, but the simultaneous use was well outside good practice for one receptacle regardless of cause.

============================================================
PRACTICAL GOING-FORWARD RULE
============================================================
On kitchen counter receptacles, treat the two small-appliance branch circuits as shared capacity: run one high-draw heating appliance (kettle, toaster oven, coffee maker, microwave, Instant Pot, air fryer, hot plate) per receptacle at a time. If your kitchen has two separate counter receptacles on different circuits, you can run a kettle on one and a toaster oven on the other simultaneously.

If you rent, report the trip to building maintenance now even if it seems resolved, so the GFCI and circuit are logged and the landlord can verify the receptacle is in good shape.

Summary

Diagnosis: Real packaging nondeterminism, not a drift-check flaw. Three vectors are visible/latent — entry-order sort differs across platforms (Linux css/ios/android/json vs macOS json/css/ios/android), per-entry mtimes leak from host filesystem (single UTC timestamp on Linux vs five distinct local values on macOS), and uid/gid/extra-fields almost certainly differ too but weren't in your evidence. This is the same failure family as the 2024-04-30 Android JSON map-traversal-order incident: a nondeterministic serialization step leaking into a hashable artifact. The drift check correctly blocked and fail-closed held — nothing was published. The May 25 evidence (20/20 byte-identical) only covered file bodies, not the wrapping archive, which is why this slipped.

Remediation, both halves required before CI reruns:

Half A (canonical packaging, build/CI owner — do not touch canonical source or generator pin): sort entries by canonical path ascending byte-wise; clamp every mtime to one fixed UTC value anchored to canonical version_published_at (or a CI build epoch constant); force uid=0/gid=0; pin mode 0644 explicitly; strip extra fields; pin compression algorithm and level; exclude directory entries/symlinks unless required. Do not trust Python `zipfile` or CLI `zip` defaults.

Half B (two-gate comparison, build/CI owner): Gate 1 = archive_sha256 over canonical archive bytes (Wes 2024-03-05 contract). Gate 2 = semantic comparator (schema-validate structure, then semantic compare ignoring key order/whitespace/formatting, flagging missing/renamed/type/metadata/alias/precision/alpha changes). Failure routing must not collapse: hash-only mismatch = packaging nondeterminism, build owner; semantic mismatch = real drift, canonical-token owner (Anya side); both = real drift + packaging bug, both fixes land before next rerun. Hash mismatches must not be papered over with regenerate-with-flag or side-channel publish.

Acceptance tests before CI rerun: (1) 20/20 byte-stable Linux, (2) 20/20 byte-stable macOS, (3) cross-platform byte-identical, (4) extracted content hashes + mode 0644 match on both platforms, (5) byte-edit positive control — both gates block, (6) mtime-only positive control — Gate 1 fails with correct "packaging nondeterminism" classification, Gate 2 passes. Test 6 is the one that distinguishes packaging bugs from drift bugs in CI output; if it doesn't classify correctly, your CI is collapsing two failure modes.

Status framing for any draft: this is one identified packaging nondeterminism source with a remediation path and six acceptance tests. Workflow is under remediation, not adopted, until tests 1–6 all pass on both platforms. The April 27 overclaim pattern still applies.

Two teaspoons on the sill after a humid first long cycle on a 5-day-old install is most likely condensate that exceeded the unit's self-evaporating capacity for an hour or two — normal-ish for the first humid run on a fresh install, but worth confirming before you keep using it. Nothing you've described (dry cord/plug, no smell, no sound, no wall water, immobile sash) is a red flag on its own.

The plan below keeps the unit unpowered and the bracket untouched the whole way through.

PRE-INSPECTION PREP (already mostly done)
- Unit OFF and UNPLUGGED — keep it that way until step 9.
- Wipe the existing ~2 tsp off the sill now with a dry cloth. Mark the spot mentally so you can tell whether new water appears later vs. residual.
- Door to the room closed or Kibo supervised for the whole inspection — pet can't reach the cord or the unit, but keep it that way until power is back.

INSPECTION ORDER — do these in sequence, stop on any stop condition

1. Exterior-side view (no leaning out, no opening sash further)
   Stand inside and look through the window glass at the outdoor shroud/louvers. You're checking that the outdoor coil area isn't packed with leaves/debris from the install and that the outer cabinet is intact.
   STOP if: visible damage, packed debris, or the outer shroud looks unseated — call installer/Devika, don't run.

2. Sash and side-filler seals (visual + finger-touch only)
   Confirm the rigid side fillers are flush top-to-bottom, the foam sash seal is continuous, and no daylight shows at the seams. The sash restraints being immobile is good — you're just verifying the seal, not the lock.
   STOP if: any daylight gap or compressed/missing foam strip — water intrusion is then possible, not just condensate. Don't resume until the seal is restored (installer).

3. Tilt/pitch (eyeball only, don't touch the bracket)
   Look at the unit from the side: it should drop ~1/4" to 1/2" toward the OUTSIDE over its depth. Place a small level or your phone level app on the top of the cabinet without shifting the unit. Condensate has to run to the outdoor-side pan; if the unit is level or tipped indoors, condensate pools on the indoor side and overflows onto your sill.
   STOP if: level or tipped the wrong way, or visibly different from the install checks — that's a bracket/geometry conversation with the installer, not a user fix. Don't try to shim or re-level yourself.

4. Indoor grille and filter (no tools needed)
   Open the indoor front grille. Slide the filter out. Hold it up to light: if you can't see much light through it, it's restrictive and that's raising condensate volume. Rinse under cool water, shake, set aside to dry fully (30–60 min). While the filter is out, look at the evaporator coil behind it.
   STOP if: visible ICE anywhere on the evaporator coil — do not restart, do not chip the ice. Let it thaw naturally for several hours with the unit off and the room ventilated. Restart only after a full thaw AND the cause is addressed (ice on a 5-day-old unit points to low refrigerant or severely restricted airflow — service call, not DIY).

5. Drain pan and drain port (look only, don't open)
   With the filter out and a flashlight, look down into the bottom of the indoor cabinet. You're checking whether the pan is empty/lightly damp vs. holding standing water, and whether you can see a small rubber drain plug/cap on the indoor-side bottom (often front corner).
   STOP if: the pan is holding visible standing water — DO NOT pull the drain plug. You're explicitly not drilling a drain hole, and pulling the plug indoors just dumps water where you don't want it. Let it wick/evaporate with the unit off and the grille open, or absorb with a towel. If the pan was full enough to overflow, that's a clog or pitch problem — service call.

6. Indoor humidity sources (no tools)
   Note whether the AC was running while someone cooked, showered, or dried laundry, or whether outdoor humidity was unusually high. Self-evaporating units have a hard ceiling on how fast they can re-evaporate condensate; on the first very humid day after install they often exceed it for the first cycle or two and then catch up.

7. Cord, plug, and receptacle (dry-touch only)
   Confirm the plug prongs, the cord jacket where it enters the unit, and the wall receptacle faceplate are dry and cool. No discoloration, no warmth.
   STOP if: any warmth, discoloration, or smell at the plug/receptacle — that's an electrical issue, not a condensate issue. Don't restart; the receptacle or circuit needs a look.

8. Dry-wait period
   Leave the unit off, grille open if possible, room ventilated for 1–2 hours. Re-check the sill and the wall beneath the unit. If the original 2 tsp was from a one-time overflow, nothing new appears. If new water appears with the unit completely off and unplugged, it's seal/bracket/rainwater intrusion, not condensate — don't restart.
   STOP if: any new water appears with the unit off — installer.

9. Pre-restart checklist — all of these must be true:
   [ ] Filter clean and fully dry
   [ ] No ice anywhere on the coil
   [ ] No standing water visible in the indoor pan
   [ ] Sash and side-filler seals continuous, no daylight
   [ ] Pitch confirmed toward outside
   [ ] Plug/receptacle/cord dry and cool
   [ ] Sill and wall dry after the wait period
   [ ] No smell at the unit when you briefly plug it in before turning it on

10. Restart and monitor
    Plug in, set fan to High (not Auto), set thermostat a couple of degrees higher than room temp so the compressor doesn't immediately slam on. After 5 minutes, no unusual sound/smell → set to normal. Check the sill at 30 min and 60 min. A few drops on the OUTDOOR side from the condenser shroud is normal; anything new on the indoor sill in the first hour of a restart means the underlying issue isn't resolved.

WHAT YOU EXPLICITLY WILL NOT DO (re-affirming your constraints)
- No drilling a drain hole.
- No loosening, shimming, or repositioning the bracket or the unit.
- No pulling the indoor drain plug.
- No scraping ice off the coil.

ESCALATE TO DEVIKA / INSTALLER IF
- Ice on the evaporator coil
- Pitch is wrong
- Visible seal gap or daylight at the filler/sash
- Pan was visibly holding water
- New water appears with the unit completely off
- Any smell, warmth, or sound at restart

If everything in step 9 is green and the first restart hour stays dry indoors, you're fine to keep using it; some light condensate on the outdoor side is normal. If the indoor sill gets wet again on a non-extreme-humidity day, that's the same checklist repeating and it's time to loop Devika in rather than keep wiping.

================================================================
CROSS-SERVICE INVARIANT BEING PROTECTED
================================================================

  (a)  A rollup window for W does not become eligible for completion
       until the SLOWEST assigned partition has honored the 90s
       lateness allowance. min() across assigned partitions, not max,
       not mean, not "any one" — this is the bug.

  (b)  The committed output values and the committed checkpoint for
       a given (window, compaction_id) are observed atomically by
       every reader. No reader ever sees a "completed" window whose
       values and checkpoint disagree, or vice versa.

  (c)  Records arriving after first-pass commit do not mutate that
       committed output. They flow into a correction pass that
       produces a NEW compaction_id. Downstream consumers
       (Cardinality, Lantern) must be able to distinguish first-pass
       from correction-pass by compaction_id, monotonically.

================================================================
AMBIGUITIES TO RESOLVE BEFORE APPROVAL
================================================================

  These don't fail the tests below, but they will bite someone:

  1.  min() over an empty assigned_partitions set (partition all
       unassigned mid-evaluation, transient). Define: defer + retry
       vs. error. Must not silently "complete" via min() == +inf.

  2.  Snapshot consistency between "reload checkpoint" and "reload
       assigned partition watermarks". If they are two reads, the
       second can race the first. Either read both under one
       consistent snapshot, or re-evaluate eligibility after the
       second read.

  3.  Correction pass trigger — not stated in the patch. Timer-based,
       watermark-advance-based, or event-based? How is starvation
       bounded (e.g., a partition whose watermark never advances
       past end+90s+N)?

  4.  compaction_id generation scheme — worker-local UUID? Monotonic
       per (worker, window)? Cross-worker collision policy? This is
       the load-bearing key for atomicity, so it needs to be pinned.

  5.  Is the 90s value the same constant the watermark producer
       (ingest-edge side) honors? If the producer has a tighter
       lateness config, the rollup's 90s allowance is moot upstream.
       Confirm single source of truth.

================================================================
FOCUSED TESTS — MUST PASS BEFORE APPROVAL
================================================================

BOUNDARY (eligibility evaluation at the 90s seam)

  B1.  Last assigned-partition record at window.end + 89s -> NOT
       eligible. Window stays open.

  B2.  Last assigned-partition record at window.end + 90s -> eligible
       (>= is the documented boundary; verify inclusive).

  B3.  Last assigned-partition record at window.end + 91s -> eligible.

  B4.  Empty window — no records on any partition but all assigned
       watermarks past end + 90s (heartbeat-driven) -> completes
       with empty/null values; output row + checkpoint both written.

  B5.  THE ORIGINAL BUG. 9 of 10 assigned partitions have watermark
       well past end + 90s; ONE partition is at end + 30s -> window
       must NOT complete. Effective watermark is min, not max.

  B6.  Producer-side late record arrives at end + 95s AFTER first-
       pass commit -> correction pass produces a new compaction_id;
       first-pass output row is byte-identical before and after.

  B7.  No assigned partitions at evaluation time -> explicit defer
       or error; never silent completion.

PARTITION-SKEW (slowest partition drives completion)

  P1.  Hot partition lags 5 min behind the other 9 -> window stays
       open for the full 5 min lag. Completion time = lag + 90s, not
       completion time of the fast 9.

  P2.  Cold partition (zero records, heartbeat-driven watermark) ->
       window completes when that cold partition's heartbeat crosses
       end + 90s. Verify heartbeat semantics are honored, not just
       data-record watermark.

  P3.  Straggler partition stuck indefinitely (e.g., network
       partition, slow consumer) -> NO false completion. Alert
       surfaced on watermark_skew metric; window remains open.

  P4.  Persistent late-arrival partition: every window receives a
       record at end + N (N > 90s) for several consecutive windows
       -> first-pass output stable per window; correction pass emits
       monotonically increasing compaction_ids; no first-pass
       mutation.

REBALANCE (handoff mid-evaluation)

  R1.  Worker A mid-evaluation on W, partitions reassigned to B
       before any commit -> B reloads (no checkpoint exists) +
       current watermarks; evaluates fresh. A's draft state must
       not leak into B's commit.

  R2.  Worker A already committed (output, checkpoint,
       compaction_id=X) for W -> reassignment to B -> B reloads
       sees X; any subsequent late records produce correction
       compaction_id=Y where Y != X. X is preserved verbatim.

  R3.  Partial reassignment: 4 of 10 partitions move to B, 6 stay
       on A -> B's eligibility uses min over its 4 partitions (not
       over the original 10); checkpoint reload reflects committed
       state regardless of the subset held.

  R4.  Split-brain: A and B both evaluate W concurrently during the
       rebalance window. The atomic transaction allows exactly one
       commit per (window, compaction_id). The loser detects the
       winner via read-after-write or unique-constraint violation;
       no competing compaction_id is produced. compaction_conflict
       counter increments.

  R5.  Reassignment DURING a correction pass -> new worker reloads
       the prior committed checkpoint (first-pass X), evaluates
       correction eligibility against the NEW assigned-partition
       set; does not regress first-pass.

RECOVERY (crash + idempotency)

  RC1. Worker crash after eligibility computed, before commit ->
       no commit recorded; replacement re-evaluates from scratch;
       no half-decided state.

  RC2. Worker crash mid-transaction (between output write and
       checkpoint write) -> atomicity guarantee: both exist or
       neither exists. No partial state where output exists without
       checkpoint.

  RC3. Worker crash immediately AFTER successful commit ->
       replacement reloads, sees committed state, does not
       re-complete first-pass.

  RC4. Worker restart with in-memory watermark cache lost ->
       authoritative watermark store is re-read; no eligibility
       decision based on cached/stale watermark.

  RC5. Commit succeeded but ack lost to caller; retry submitted ->
       idempotent: existing (window, compaction_id) detected; no
       duplicate output rows, no duplicate checkpoint.

  RC6. Worker restart holding a persisted checkpoint but with a
       stale view of which partitions it owns -> reconcile current
       assignment from authoritative source BEFORE evaluating
       eligibility; do not trust the cached assignment map.

DUPLICATE-COMPACTION (atomicity + ordering)

  D1.  Two concurrent transactions with the SAME (window,
       compaction_id) -> second rejected (unique constraint or
       no-op detection); output table has exactly one row per
       (window, compaction_id).

  D2.  Two concurrent transactions with DIFFERENT compaction_ids
       for the same window (e.g., first-pass vs. correction racing,
       or two correction passes) -> exactly one wins per (window,
       compaction_id); the loser surfaces as a compaction-conflict
       alert. No silent overwrite of the winner's row.

  D3.  Idempotent retry of an already-committed completion (same
       compaction_id resubmitted) -> no duplicate output rows, no
       duplicate checkpoint row, no spurious downstream notification.

  D4.  Correction pass for window W produces compaction_id=Y after
       first-pass X. Both persist. Downstream readers can observe
       both with compaction_id ordering; default read returns the
       max compaction_id. First-pass X is queryable as historical
       truth for audit/replay.

  D5.  Stale first-pass X surfaces after correction Y is already
       committed (delayed retry, queue replay, late-arriving
       producer retry) -> Y remains authoritative; system does not
       regress to X. compaction_conflict counter increments.

  D6.  compaction_id uniqueness across workers -> two workers
       cannot mint the same id; collisions detectable at write time,
       not by downstream reconciliation.

================================================================
TELEMETRY NEEDED FOR APPROVAL VISIBILITY
================================================================

  These are read-only signals I'll check before signing the release.
  Cyrus's team owns the implementation; I just need them emitted
  and dashboarded:

  - watermark_skew_across_partitions (per window evaluation;
    p_max - p_min)
  - completion_lag_seconds (window.end + 90s -> actual commit ts)
  - reassignment_during_evaluation_count
  - compaction_conflict_count (increments on D2/D5 path)
  - correction_pass_compaction_ids_emitted_per_window
  - empty_window_completion_count (B4 path; should be non-zero in
    steady state, alerts if it spikes)

================================================================
SUMMARY
================================================================

YES — ordinary use can resume. Your diagnostic clears the obvious interior-condensate causes:

  - Tilt is outward and within spec (quarter-inch sits at the conservative end of the typical 1/4"–1/2" range, so gravity is helping condensate toward the drain slot, not against it).
  - The drain slot is clear of debris, and the 45-minute cooling test produced normal exterior drip afterward — that confirms the path is open under real condensate load, not just a visual inspection.
  - No mechanical or electrical symptoms during 75 minutes of operation.
  - The unit is ~6 days post-install; a single paint flake from the drain slot is within expected first-week cure/shedding and is not itself a fault, but recurrence would be.

MONITORING — first 48 hours, then ongoing during humid stretches:

  1. Visual check of the interior cabinet base, sill, and wall under the unit after each cooling cycle for the first 2 days. Dry = baseline established.
  2. Confirm exterior drip continues for roughly 10–15 minutes after the compressor cycles off. That post-cycle drip is the pan draining as the coils thaw, and a steady exterior drip during/after a run is a healthy sign.
  3. Listen for new sounds: gurgling, sloshing, dripping from inside the chassis, or a high-pitched hiss. Any of these warrant a stop.
  4. Verify supply air stays cool and the airflow stays strong. Reduced airflow with warm air = evaporator icing; when ice melts, it dumps a sudden pulse of water.
  5. After the first heavy rain or wind event, recheck both interior and exterior for any change in behavior.
  6. Note any musty or mildew odor from the unit's interior side. A clean dry pan doesn't smell; a persistent odor usually means biological growth in standing water, which is a different problem from drain flow.

ESCALATION — stop use, unplug, and arrange service if any of these occur:

  A. ANY interior moisture: drip, streak, puddle, damp sill, wet insulation around the sleeve, or water on the floor under the unit. Even a one-time event — interior water is not normal operation for a properly tilted window unit.
  B. Exterior drip stops while interior symptoms appear simultaneously. That's a blockage past the slot (pan port, internal trough, or condensate path inside the chassis).
  C. Visible frost or ice on the indoor coil or supply grille, or a sudden drip pulse after a cycle that previously ran clean.
  D. New vibration, panel movement, hot plug, or breaker trip.
  E. Musty smell persisting after a dry-out day with fan-only running.
  F. Repeated paint flakes from the drain slot — more than one per week indicates a coating failure on the drain pan rather than one-time settling.

ONE OPTIONAL CONFIDENCE TEST, only if you want extra assurance before relying on it overnight:

  Pour roughly 1/4 cup of clean water slowly into the interior drain trough (usually accessible behind/under the filter, where the indoor coil drains). It should exit through the exterior drain slot within a few seconds. Pour no faster than the slot can carry, and keep water away from any electricals or the control board. If it backs up or appears indoors, that's a hard stop regardless of any prior test result.

SAFETY: if you lay a towel or tray under the unit during the monitoring window, weight or tuck it so it can't be pulled into the chassis. The 5/22 install arrangement (door open, Kibo can't reach screen/edges) still keeps the cat out of the unit itself, but a loose towel would be a new vector.
