Decision: yes, pause only the queue-cap canary. Do not roll back bounded decompression.

Rationale:
  - Defect is a contract violation isolated to the early-return path: 37/37 queue-cap 429s missing Retry-After, while every decompression 429 carries the standard 1/2/3s randomized value. Behavior on the happy path is clean (active work stays under per-pod and per-tenant limits, cancellations fully drain queued work, no accepted-point drops, no pod restarts). Nothing here suggests a capacity or correctness bug — this is a header-emission oversight on a new code path, which is exactly what a canary is for.
  - Bounded decompression is a different code path with clean evidence. Coupling its rollback to the queue-cap defect would erase a separate, working mitigation and broaden blast radius for no gain.

Patch (minimal, contract-preserving):
  - Centralize 429 Retry-After emission. Both the decompression-pressure path and the queue-cap early-return path must call the same helper that draws from the established randomized 1/2/3s distribution. No second implementation, no value drift.
  - On the early-return path, set Retry-After before the response is written; do not return early until the header is attached. Treat missing Retry-After on any 429 as a build-time invariant.
  - Add a counter metric queue_cap_rejections_total{tenant_id, retry_after_bucket="1|2|3"} and emit a structured log line with reason="queue_cap_reached" so future regressions are caught by alert rather than by spot-checking headers.
  - No change to admission semantics: still reject before acceptance, still drain queued work on cancel.

Regression tests (must pass before re-canary):
  1. Unit: any 429 produced by the queue-cap early-return path MUST contain a Retry-After header whose parsed value is in {1, 2, 3} seconds. Property-style: feed the path 10k over-cap requests, assert zero missing-header and value ∈ {1,2,3} for all.
  2. Distribution: chi-square over the 10k samples confirms the 1/2/3 distribution matches the decompression path within tolerance — closes the "helper reuse" loop.
  3. Header-schema parity: a contract test enumerates every header on a 429 from each path and asserts set equality. Catches accidental field drift (e.g. one path adding Retry-After while another adds something new).
  4. Integration under sustained over-cap load: no accepted point dropped, no queued work left behind on cancel, no pod restart, active concurrency stays under configured per-pod and per-tenant limits, every 429 carries Retry-After.
  5. SDK round-trip: a client receiving a queue-cap 429 retries within the advertised window and is admitted on second attempt once load subsides; a client on the default SDK behavior (Retry-After unaware) still backs off via the 429 status. This protects both contract-aware and default consumers.

Roll-forward protocol, consistent with the 6/5 and 6/14 patterns:
  - Patch + the five tests land together. No separate ship.
  - Resume canary at 1 pod / 45m. Abort conditions, zero-tolerance: any 429 missing Retry-After; p99 drift >20% vs. pre-canary baseline; heap >+10% on the canary pod; any dirty cancellation; any accepted-point drop.
  - Bump past the failure point (1 → 2 → full) on clean windows only, per the soak convention. Mid-week, no Friday push.
  - Owner keeps impl/telemetry/release per the Feb 27 framework; my sign-off here is on the cross-service invariant (429 contract parity) and the canary gates, not on the implementation details.

Out of scope for this change: investigating whether 429 Retry-After should be made mandatory at the SDK layer. That is a separate, owner-driven decision and should not gate this fix.

Assessment (and the tests I'll gate on before approval):

Decision: Do not accept the 310 ms. The serving path must fail closed at the moment of lease loss, not on the next 500 ms poll.

Why the owner's framing is wrong

- "Below one polling period" is the wrong metric. The polling period is the defect, not a justification. Any window in which a non-leased process returns authoritative-looking routing snapshots is exactly the split-brain fencing exists to prevent; on the write side this is already enforced, on the read side it isn't.
- Read snapshots drive client decisions (pinning, caches, handed-back addresses). "No writes occurred" is not the test — routing reads are a read-side mirror of authority, and 310 ms × N clients × N requests is real client exposure.
- This is the third premature-close pattern from this owner in staging: March 18 declared failover done at process readiness (real convergence at 96 s), and the same owner previously minimized a follower-read gap. The framing "the gap is small, so accept it" is the pattern, not the math.
- Per the Feb 23/27 lane: the cross-service invariant is "the process serving routing snapshots must hold a valid lease at the moment of read." That invariant is mine to gate. How to enforce it (sync check on read, lease-watch callback with cache invalidation, monotonic epoch watermark) is the owner's call — but the invariant itself is non-negotiable.

Minimum serving-gate shape (owner implements, I gate)

- Lease validity evaluated on the read path synchronously, OR a lease-watch callback that invalidates local serving state inside the propagation budget (target: < 50 ms; hard ceiling: sub-poll-interval, not poll-interval-plus-epsilon).
- Monotonic epoch watermark: if a newer epoch has been observed anywhere (gossip, control plane, or local watcher), refuse to serve the cached snapshot.
- A missed watch event must self-fail-closed; "last-known-good" is not a serving mode once the lease is gone.

Focused failover tests (must pass before approval)

A. Functional failover
1. Lease revoked mid-snapshot: serving must stop within the propagation budget (target ≤ 50 ms) of lease-loss observation. Measure p99 time-from-lease-loss-to-serving-stop.
2. Lease renewed, then lost: confirm the cache-invalidation path actually runs and is not skipped on a fast renew-then-revoke.
3. Reacquisition: serving resumes only after a fresh acquisition + new epoch, never on lease-validity alone.
4. Partition then revoke: when connectivity returns after a revocation, the old holder must not serve; it must revalidate before reopening the gate.
5. Lease TTL shorter than poll period (adversarial): poll-based gates must fail or be inadmissible.

B. Concurrency races
6. Read in flight at the instant of revocation: snapshot must not reach the client. Either pre-send epoch check or client-side epoch rejection.
7. Two replicas each holding what they believe is a valid lease during a flap (e.g., chronyd step): the loser must be rejected by epoch/fencing on the very next read.
8. Snapshot in local cache when lease epoch bumps: cached snapshot is invalidated before serving; served snapshots carry epoch and are rejected if stale.
9. Lease-watch channel full / event missed: replica must self-fail-closed, not continue serving last-known-good.
10. Replacement acquires at t = 8.4 s: for any window t > 8.4 s, the old holder returns zero snapshots. Assert zero on a counter, not on a rate.

C. Telemetry required to gate approval
- p99 time-from-lease-loss-to-serving-stop, per replica.
- Counter: snapshots_served_after_lease_loss (must be 0 across the drill matrix).
- Counter: lease_watch_events_missed / lease_watch_channel_full (signals poll-budget deficiency).
- Per-replica lease-epoch histogram.
- Stale-owner messages logged for two full renewal intervals (mirrors the existing rb_1789241064338 exit check).

D. Exit conditions for "failover drill passed"
- Lease convergence: one owner per partition, monotonic lease epochs, no stale-owner messages for two full renewal intervals (existing bar from rb_1789241064338).
- AND serving-stop convergence: zero snapshots served after lease loss across the full drill matrix above, on N runs (propose N = 50 with mixed timings).

What I will and won't sign off on

- I will sign off when the invariant ("serve only with a valid, current-epoch lease at read time") is demonstrated by the counters above across the drill matrix, and the runbook entry for this gate is updated to require serving-stop convergence — not just lease convergence — as an exit condition.
- I will not sign off on "310 ms is acceptable because it is sub-poll." That is the change I am blocking.
- Owner retains implementation choice (sync read-path check vs push callback vs epoch watermark), telemetry, and release sequencing. My lane is the invariant and the drill gate; not the code shape.

  3. Put a shallow pan or baking sheet under the heaviest drip. Much easier than chasing droplets, and it buys you time between towel swaps.
  4. Do NOT open the window. Wind-driven rain on a broken seal gets worse fast.
  5. Do NOT touch the window AC controls, plug, or cord during the storm. Lightning + window-mounted metal + line-voltage is not the moment.
  6. After the rain stops, leave a dry towel pressed against the area and recheck in 30 minutes. That is when the trailing "rain that already found a path" shows up.
  7. Don't caulk or seal anything from the inside while water is active. Trapping it inside the wall frame makes the next failure worse.

Low-risk observations that help maintenance (do these while it's happening, all from the ground):

  - Time the leak started, when it pulsed, when it stopped.
  - Exact location of the bead: top-left, top-center, top-right of the frame. Whether it tracks along the head jamb (horizontal) or drops from one spot.
  - Whether flow is steady or pulses with wind gusts.
  - Window orientation (which compass wall) and roughly how hard the wind is hitting that face.
  - Once rain eases, look at the exterior from the ground: any visible gap, missing or cracked caulk, or dark staining on siding/trim directly above the window. Pay particular attention to the AC sleeve edge — caulk separation there is a common culprit, and the AC install was only about a month ago. If exterior work of any kind happened around that window recently, flag it.
  - Are there gutters above this window? Present? Clear? Overflowing?
  - Phone photos: one wide shot of the window interior, one close of the bead line on the sill, one of the AC exterior sleeve if you can see it from the ground.

  Why this matters: a leak above an intact window with a dry wall below, during wind-driven rain, is almost always exterior — head-jamb flashing, AC sleeve seal, or siding/trim above. The fact that the AC was recently installed is worth telling maintenance even if the install checks passed; flashing can be subtly displaced and sealant takes weeks to fully cure.

Emergency threshold — call building maintenance emergency line (or 911 if no building line) NOW if any of these:

  - Water reaches, drips onto, or is visibly creeping toward the nearest outlet, switch, lamp, or the AC's own power cord or plug.
  - Sparks, buzzing, flickering lights, a tripped breaker, or any burning / hot-plastic smell.
  - Water is pooling on the floor and spreading beyond the immediate sill area.
  - Ceiling or wall above or beside the window begins to sag, bulge, soften, or drip from a new location.
  - Leak intensifies sharply instead of tapering as the storm passes (could indicate larger envelope failure).
  - Anyone — you or Kibo — gets a tingle or shock from anything metal in the room. Get Kibo out first.

  If none of those are happening, the towel-and-pan approach gets you through the storm. Document, do the exterior ground-level check once rain stops, then contact maintenance non-emergency with the photos and timeline — they will want them.

One more: while lightning is frequent and close, stay back from the window glass and the AC unit. Occupying the room at normal distance from the window is fine; just don't lean on the sill or work over the AC.

Here's a rewrite that aligns with the established facts on the North Pier token workflow:

    The canonical token package is the single source of truth. Figma edits and edits to generated files are not, on their own, authoritative: a token change enters the system when Design opens a pull request against the canonical package, and the paired Figma change goes in at the same version. Renames use the rename template (old and proposed names, affected surfaces, rationale, pure rename vs. semantic change); pure renames get a fast paired review, semantic changes need a short ADR entry in the design-system decision log before review. Once the canonical package version is published, the rename propagates as platform-binding pull requests; the previous name is retained as an explicit alias that emits deprecation warnings in every generated format, passes the same case-fold uniqueness check as primary names, and is removed after the deprecation window so old-name references fail validation.

    Every publish reruns the pinned generator and the drift check; nothing publishes on schema-validation or drift failure. Drift failures are routed, not bypassed: hash-only mismatches are packaging nondeterminism owned by the build lane; semantic mismatches are real drift owned by the canonical-token lane; if both occur, both fixes are required. That is the opposite of the established rule — canonical names must be case-fold unique across all formats, and the Surface.Muted / surface.muted collision was resolved by renaming in the canonical source, not by appending an Android suffix. REVIEW: deployment.environment label contract (revised, 2024-06-26)

Strong improvements over the prior proposal:
  - Explicit allowlist (3 values); cardinality budget = allowlist size, no slack
  - Lowercase-before-validation closes the casing bypass
  - Omit-on-missing removes one default-to-unknown path
  - Reject-before-publish is the right control point
  - Explicit "no unknown fallback" intent

Is it enforceable as written?
Not fully. The contract declares behavior but does not pin behavior to specific enforcement points. Three pieces are under-specified:
  (a) what "reject" does to the metric
  (b) where the per-tenant budget is counted and what happens on exceed
  (c) what metrics-router and rollup-service do when the label is absent

Gaps that still allow a fourth value on the wire:

1. Rejection semantics undefined.
   "Reject before metrics publication" has three plausible readings: drop
   the metric, publish with the label omitted, or publish with a sentinel.
   Only the second is safe. The first loses legitimate telemetry; the third
   reintroduces "unknown" (or a raw value) as a fourth series on the wire.
   REQUIRED: on rejection, publish the metric with deployment.environment
   omitted entirely. Pin this; do not leave it implicit.

2. SDK-side default not addressed.
   The OTel SDK in the producing service may carry its own default for
   deployment.environment (commonly "unknown", "default", or the env var
   name). If the SDK populates the attribute before the collector sees it,
   "unknown" can reach the wire even with the collector's allowlist, because
   the collector forwards attributes rather than second-guessing SDK choices.
   Past precedent here: SDK defaults have been a recurring source of ingest
   errors — treat as a known failure mode, not a theoretical one.
   REQUIRED: SDK MUST NOT emit a default; OR the collector MUST overwrite
   any SDK-supplied value with the allowlisted-or-omitted outcome.

3. Producer set not enumerated.
   "Required executable path: OTel collector -> metrics-router -> rollup-
   service" is correct for the path but does not say it is the ONLY path.
   Any service publishing deployment.environment via direct SDK push, a
   sidecar, or a different collector is outside the contract.
   REQUIRED: enumerate all current producers of this label and bind each
   to the same normalize/validate/reject path.

4. Metrics-router default on missing label unspecified.
   If metrics-router synthesizes a default when the upstream label is
   absent, "unknown" reappears at the next hop even though the collector
   omitted it.
   REQUIRED: metrics-router MUST NOT synthesize a default.

5. Rollup-service consumer behavior unspecified.
   Rollup aggregates on labels. If rollup assumes the label is always
   present and inserts a default on read, "unknown" appears in rollup
   output. A missing label is a distinct series key, not a synonym for any
   of the three allowlisted values.
   REQUIRED: rollup MUST treat a missing label as a fourth series key.

6. Cardinality budget enforcement point and exceed action missing.
   "Per-tenant distinct-value budget: 3" needs an enforcement location
   and an exceed action. Recommend reject-further-writes for that tenant
   on this label with an alert. Clamping to first-3-seen is harder to
   reason about and harder to alert on; avoid it.

7. Lowercase is the only normalization stated.
   "Prod " (trailing space), "Prod\t", full-width "prod" (U+FF50), and
   NFC/NFD variants all lowercase to strings that fail the allowlist and
   will be rejected — correct outcome. BUT if any producer trims or
   unicode-normalizes before reaching the collector, the same input can
   land as "prod" on one path and "Prod " on another, breaking parity.
   REQUIRED: normalization happens in exactly one place (the collector),
   and downstream hops MUST NOT re-normalize.

8. Empty string, null, and whitespace-only inputs not classified.
   Are these "missing" (omit) or "malformed" (reject)? Specify. Recommend
   reject as malformed — closer to the safe side.

9. Pre-validation logging.
   If the raw value is logged at DEBUG or in error messages before
   validation, it appears in logs and any log-derived metrics. Not on the
   wire, but it re-enters cardinality if log fields are ever treated as
   labels. Log only the allowlisted/normalized outcome, or hash-only.

10. Historical data from the prior contract.
    Storage may already contain deployment.environment = "unknown" or
    other non-allowlisted values from the rejected proposal. The new
    contract needs a migration: either a re-emit window with a deprecation
    alias, or a hard cutover with pre-cutover series quarantined and
    excluded from cardinality accounting.

Direct answer to the silent-fourth-value question:

  "unknown" — not silently, IF rejection = omit, AND the SDK carries no
  default, AND router and rollup do not synthesize one on missing. As
  written, two of those three are unspecified.

  Raw user input — not silently, IF rejection = omit (not drop, not
  sentinel), AND there is no parallel producer path that bypasses the
  collector. As written, the producer set is not enumerated and rejection
  semantics are undefined.

Minimum additions for enforceability:
  - Pin rejection to "publish with deployment.environment omitted".
  - Forbid any default at SDK, collector, router, or rollup.
  - Enumerate producers; bind each to the path.
  - Pin cardinality enforcement point and exceed action.
  - Classify empty/null/whitespace as malformed.
  - Add a migration plan for historical series.

Bottom line: the proposal's intent is sound and closes most of the prior
risk, but it is not enforceable until items 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 are
written into the contract with named enforcement points. Items 7-10 are
secondary but should not ship without an answer.

# Review of the proposed incident-load response shape

## 1. Blockers in the proposed schema

The proposed response has three independent blockers, plus one derived smell:

**a. `debug_incident_refs` does not belong in an external payload.** It is described as containing internal incident identifiers. That is exactly the kind of internal-ID leakage the external contract was written to exclude — the same class of failure that sank the internal read-model export reuse on May 15. Internal incident IDs are not a "debug" affordance that gets a free pass on the wire; they're an attribution handle and a correlation key into internal systems. They must not be serialized to an external response, returned in headers, logged in caller-visible error bodies, or rendered in UI cards. If internal refs are needed for diagnostics, they live in server-side logs scoped to the request, with the same allowlist discipline as the rest of the contract.

**b. The proposed missing-source behavior — `incident_count=0`, `active_minutes=0`, `source_updated_at` omitted — is exactly the bug the contract already rejected.** This is the canonical fail-open pattern: a broken or absent source collapses to "nothing happened." Zero is semantically "we observed zero permitted incidents." `unknown` is "we cannot tell." The two are operationally different — zero is a positive signal about activity; `unknown` is a signal about the observation pipeline. Merging them means a silent ingest regression will look like a quiet service.

The May 9 decision locked the behavior: counts ≥5 → numeric; 1–4 → literal `"suppressed"` token; 0 → numeric zero; absent permitted source → explicit `unknown` with no value timestamp. The May 17 contract examples and the June 4 focused test both reinforced this. The proposed shape reverts to the May 8 sketch that was superseded.

**c. The field name `source_updated_at` is wrong, and `active_minutes` is out of scope.**
- The contract field is `source_observed_at` — the upstream source observation time, present only when a permitted source event exists. `source_updated_at` invites a freshness read of the *response*, not the *source*, which is the exact confusion the June 4 test was added to prevent.
- `active_minutes` is not in the established contract. It is a derived metric that invites interpretation ("how much of the window was the service in incident state?") and is precisely the kind of synthesis that has historically been pushed back when added without provenance backing. If Product Engineering has a use case, it needs its own contract decision — not a field-name slot in this response.

**d. The window is undefined in the schema.** The contract uses a fixed 30-day window. The proposed fields `window_start` / `window_end` imply the window is caller-controlled or arbitrarily scoped. A caller-controlled window on a permission-safe summary is a re-introduction of the query-volume-delta class of signal that was excluded from v0. If the window is fixed, it should be stated as such and the fields should either be omitted or be echo-only of the contract constant.

## 2. Corrected fail-closed external behavior

For a permitted source event existing:
```
service_id, window_days=30,
incident_count: <integer ≥5 | literal "suppressed" for 1–4 | 0>,
source_observed_at: <timestamp from the source observation>,
provenance: { source_ref: <permissioned link> }
```

For an authorized request with no permitted source event in the window:
```
kind: "unknown",
source_observed_at: omitted,
observation_attempted_at: <separately labeled>,
no incident_count, no source_ref, no debug fields
```

For denied access:
```
HTTP 403,
code: "permission_denied",
state: "denied",
no value timestamp, no observation_attempted_at, no source_ref,
no incident_count
```

Notes on what this preserves:
- Zero is zero; `"suppressed"` is `"suppressed"`; absent source is `unknown`. Three distinct states, three distinct operational meanings.
- `source_observed_at` is the upstream observation time and only appears when there is a permitted source event. It is never used to imply freshness of an `unknown`.
- `observation_attempted_at` is a separate, explicitly labeled field so a caller can tell *when we tried to look* versus *when the source observed something*.
- Authorization happens before lookup. A denied request reveals neither timestamp field, the source_ref, nor any aggregate. That is what stops ERR-4-class ambiguity.
- `debug_incident_refs` is server-side only. If a caller needs to correlate to internal artifacts, they have access to the source system; otherwise they don't, and the contract stays permission-bounded.

  Rice (cook now, cool, fridge):
    1 cup long-grain white rice, rinsed
    1¾ cups water or low-sodium broth, pinch of salt
    Bring to boil, cover, low 15 min, off heat 5 min, fluff, cool uncovered 10 min, then cover and refrigerate. It reheats better than freshly-cooked rice for this dish.

  Chicken marinade (one bowl, big enough for 4 thighs):
    Juice of 1 lime + zest of that lime
    3 tbsp olive oil
    1 tsp kosher salt, several grinds of black pepper
    Half the chopped cilantro (stems are fine)

    1 pint cherry tomatoes, halved (quarter if large)
    1 small handful cilantro, chopped
    1 garlic clove, minced (optional, nice)
    1 lime, cut into wedges for serving
    Reserve the second lime for finishing

  Peaches (small bowl, covered, in the fridge):
    2 peaches, sliced into wedges
    Toss with a small squeeze of the reserved lime and a pinch of sugar
    Cover and refrigerate

Pull the chicken out of the fridge 20 minutes before you start so it loses the chill.

 0:00   Preheat oven to 425°F. Pat the chicken thighs very dry with paper towels. This is what makes the skin crisp.

 0:05   Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a 12-inch cast-iron or oven-safe skillet over medium-high until shimmering. Lay thighs SKIN DOWN and leave them alone.

 0:12   Skin should be deep gold and release cleanly. Flip. Scatter corn, tomatoes, and garlic around the chicken. Drizzle a little olive oil over the veg, salt lightly.

Short answer: the sequence is broadly adequate for a small, source-confirmed leak — but only if "after the wall dries" is verified with a moisture meter, and only if the trigger conditions below are met before Friday's masonry and the first post-work check. Otherwise the timeline is too slow.

What's working in the plan:
  - Source identified and reachable. An open head joint above a window is a classic leak path, and a temporary seal plus scheduled permanent masonry work addresses the root cause.
  - Damage is localized. Only an 8-inch patch above the window is damp; the wall beside the outlet is dry and there is no ceiling bulge — water has not tracked laterally into the ceiling or far down the wall.
  - The AC is exonerated. No glass break and no AC-attributable pattern, so the diagnosis does not depend on disturbing the AC install.

Where the plan needs sharpening:

1. The location of the damp patch is suspicious. Water entered at the head (top), and water in a wall cavity tracks downward via the paper facing of drywall. A damp patch on the interior face above the window usually means the cavity behind it is wet, even if the surface a few inches away looks dry. Plan accordingly: surface dryness of a small patch does not mean the cavity is dry.

2. "Wait until dry, then repaint" only works if you measure dry. A pin or pinless moisture meter on the patch and surrounding area should be back to baseline (typically <15–16% on a pin meter, or matching an unaffected reference spot on a pinless meter) before any primer or paint goes on. Painting over a still-damp wall traps moisture and feeds the exact mold problem you are trying to avoid — and paint will blister later even if no mold forms.

3. "Recheck after masonry work" is the right cadence for a contained, source-confirmed leak. Anything in the lists below is a reason not to wait for that recheck.

Faster interior opening — open the wall sooner (within 48–72 hours of the source being sealed, not after the full masonry/repaint cycle) if any of the following:

  - The damp patch grows in area, darkens, or develops a defined "wet line" moving down the wall.
  - Moisture meter readings on the patch are not measurably trending down within 48 hours of the temporary seal. Water in a closed cavity does not evaporate fast; a flat or rising reading means the cavity is holding more water than the surface shows.
  - The drywall feels soft, crinkles when pressed, or the paper facing bubbles.
  - Paint or texture in the area blisters, swells, or pulls away from the wall.
  - You see or smell anything musty. A musty odor already means active microbial activity — that is an opening trigger, not something to monitor.
  - The wall above or beside the patch was previously patched or painted over, or you have any reason to think this has been wet before — prior moisture plus new moisture is a high mold-risk scenario.
  - The same window has leaked before, or the head joint was open long enough that multiple rain events got in.

Mold assessment — call an independent mold inspector (not the painting contractor) before any cosmetic work if any of the following:

  - Musty smell anywhere in the bedroom, especially near the window or in the closet on that wall.
  - Visible discoloration beyond the current damp patch — black, dark green, or orange spotting, not just water staining.
  - Anyone in the household is immunocompromised, has asthma, severe allergies, or a mold sensitivity. Kibo counts here too — pets track spores out of the room, and small-breed respiratory systems are sensitive.
  - Moisture readings stay >16% after 72 hours of drying, or climb between checks.
  - You open the wall and find wet insulation, wet wood framing, or visible growth on the back of the drywall. At that point the remediation scope is bigger than paint.

One practical note specific to this window: because the AC is in it, do not run the AC through the first few days after the masonry work. The cold surface at the AC sleeve will condense moisture out of the still-wet wall and onto the AC, which slows drying and dumps condensation where you do not want it. If the bedroom is uncomfortable without the AC, a closed-window dehumidifier in the room for 3–5 days after masonry will do more than the AC would.

Net: the sequence is reasonable for a small, source-confirmed leak — fix the source, let it dry, verify with a meter, then repaint. The decision point that matters is the 48–72 hour moisture check. If the patch is shrinking and readings are dropping, stay the course. If readings are flat, the patch grows, or any odor appears, open the wall before painting and do not let the painting schedule drive the timeline.

Bottom line: as written, three independent ways to corrupt readiness on retry or restart — watermark assigned before the write, no idempotency key, and a cache that can't survive crash. Needs a transactional outbox (or equivalent durable marker) and a monotonic CAS-style watermark advance.

HAZARDS

1. Watermark ordering
- cache[tenant].watermark = maxTimestamp(rows) runs BEFORE store.write. On write failure the cache claims "ready at T" when nothing is durable; on crash that entry is gone anyway (in-memory only). It's dead state that evaporates on restart and misleads in-thread consumers between assignment and write.
- No monotonicity. A later batch with an older maxTimestamp overwrites a higher in-memory value, and on retry/emit can publish a regressed watermark downstream.
- Backfill-specific: maxTimestamp(rows) is almost certainly behind the current live watermark. The code emits whatever the batch contains instead of max(currentDurable, candidate). On a backfill of older data this actively regresses downstream readiness.

2. Retry / idempotence
- store.write(rows) has no idempotency key. Retries re-write. Safe iff the store dedups on (tenant, event_id); unsafe if it upserts on (tenant, ts) — a retry of a backfill row could clobber newer state.
- emitReady runs once per successful write. If emit fails after write succeeds, retry both writes again AND emits again. Downstream sees two publishes for the same watermark — fine if it dedups on (tenant, watermark), poison if not.
- The whole batch is the unit of retry. No partial-progress marker. If batch=1000 and write fails at row 700, retry duplicates 1..699 plus writes 700..1000.

3. Crash recovery
- Cache is lost on restart. After a crash post-write/pre-emit, the next call restarts from scratch. If write isn't idempotent you duplicate; if it is you merely re-emit (recoverable).
- After a crash mid-batch with no idempotency keys, you can't tell which rows landed. Retry either duplicates or skips, both silently.
- The in-memory watermark gives zero protection across restarts. It isn't the system watermark — it's bookkeeping that disappears.

SAFER SEQUENCE (transactional outbox per (tenant, batch))

    applyBatch(tenant, batch_id, rows):
        candidate_wm = maxTimestamp(rows)
        current_wm   = store.readWatermark(tenant)        # durable, monotonic

        if candidate_wm <= current_wm:
            # backfill rows already covered; record audit, do not emit
            store.markBackfillSeen(tenant, batch_id)
            return nil

        idempotency_key = (tenant, batch_id, row_seq)     # stable across retries

        txn begin:
            store.writeRows(rows, key=idempotency_key)    # dedup at store layer
            store.advanceWatermark(tenant, candidate_wm)  # CAS: only if candidate > current
            store.outboxEnqueue(tenant, candidate_wm, batch_id)  # durable readiness marker
        txn commit

    publisherLoop:
        for each marker in outbox:
            emitReady(tenant, marker.watermark, marker.batch_id)  # downstream dedups on (tenant, wm)
            outbox.delete(marker)                                  # only after successful emit

Properties:
- Crash anywhere -> outbox is the source of truth for "must publish." Nothing emitted is unbacked.
- Retry -> store dedups by idempotency_key; outbox dedups by (tenant, watermark); downstream dedups by (tenant, watermark). Three independent safety nets.
- Monotonic -> watermark advance is CAS; stale batches short-circuit without emitting.
- Backfill-safe -> candidate_wm <= current_wm skips emission cleanly; you still get an audit marker.

ASKS FOR CYRUS BEFORE THE PATCH LANDS

1. What's the store's natural dedup key? (tenant, event_id) or (tenant, ts) upsert? The answer decides whether idempotency keys are needed on writeRows or only on the outbox.
2. Does downstream emitReady dedup on (tenant, watermark), or is each emit treated as a fresh signal? If not, the outbox gives at-least-once and the receiver becomes the duplication point.
3. Is the live rollup pipeline running concurrently with the backfill? If yes, watermark advance MUST be CAS against a durable current, not max-of-this-batch — otherwise backfill races ingest and pins the watermark at an old value.
4. Is there a per-tenant mutex or partition key in the cache today? If multiple workers call applyBatch for the same tenant concurrently, the in-memory watermark races; the durable CAS fixes that, but the current cache[tenant].watermark line actively makes it worse.

If 1–4 come back clean, the outbox version is a small patch and a much safer backfill.

Ankle sounds like a low-grade lateral sprain. By the standard screening rules (Ottawa), you screen negative: you can bear weight (four steps without giving way) and you have no focal bony tenderness on the lateral malleolus. That combination makes a clinically significant fracture unlikely enough that plain films are not required up front. The inversion mechanism plus swelling below the outside ankle bone fits a typical Grade I to II anterior talofibular ligament stretch.

Immediate care, next 48 to 72 hours

  Protect. A lace-up ankle brace or a semi-rigid stirrup limits inversion and lets you walk without re-rolling. If you do not have one, a figure-8 elastic wrap from the base of the toes to mid-calf is a fair stand-in; snug, not tight.
  Elevate. Above heart level when you are sitting.
  Compression. Same idea as the wrap, or a compression sleeve.
  Ice. 15 to 20 minutes at a time, every 2 to 3 hours while awake, with a cloth barrier. Helpful for pain even though the evidence for speeding healing is thin.
  Avoid HARM for the first 72 hours: Heat, Alcohol, Running or massage of the area. Aggressive lateral-ligament stretching also tends to backfire early.
  Pain control. Acetaminophen around the clock is fine. If you want an NSAID, defer it to day 2 or 3 so the early inflammatory phase is not blunted, then ibuprofen 400 to 600 mg with food up to TID.
  Gentle motion. As soon as tolerated, draw the alphabet with the big toe or do pain-free dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. Early controlled motion generally does better than strict immobilization.

Walking for the apartment viewing

  Yes, ordinary walking is reasonable. With a brace, supportive closed shoes (running shoes, not flats or sandals), and acetaminophen on board, you should manage a 30 to 60 minute showing. Take the elevator over stairs. If a unit is on a second or third floor walk-up, ask to defer or reschedule that one. Skip the moving of any heavy boxes or furniture.

Signs that should prompt urgent evaluation (same day, ED or ortho urgent care)

  Inability to bear any weight at all, even a single step.
  Visible deformity or a bone that looks out of place.
  Numbness, tingling, coolness, or color change in the foot (neurovascular concern).
  Open skin over the injury.
  Pain sharply localized to the medial malleolus, the navicular, or the base of the fifth metatarsal. These are separate Ottawa sites and each warrants films.
  Pain and swelling that sit above the joint line between the tibia and fibula, or pain that worsens when you squeeze the calf and try to dorsiflex. That points toward a syndesmotic (high ankle) injury, which is a different animal and should be seen promptly.
  Severe pain that does not respond to a reasonable dose of OTC medication.

Signs that should prompt a non-urgent appointment within about a week (PCP, sports med, or ortho)

  Pain that has not meaningfully improved after 5 to 7 days of the above.
  Swelling unchanged or worse after 3 to 5 days.
  A sense of the ankle giving way when you walk, or persistent instability.
  No return to running or soccer within 2 to 3 weeks.

A typical Grade I to II lateral sprain in a healthy adult resolves in 2 to 6 weeks. If you want to be thorough, balance and proprioception work (single-leg stand, then eyes-closed progression) starting in week 1 or 2 is the single best predictor of not re-rolling it next time you play.

==============================================================================
PART 1 — PER-ATTEMPT OBSERVATIONS
==============================================================================

The metrics list in the proposal is a run-level summary, not a per-attempt record. To preserve attribution, every push attempt must carry:

  For every push (1..600):
    - push_seq
    - push_outcome: accepted | rejected_at_accept | blocked_during_apply | timeout | error
    - gen_before_push, gen_after_push
    - cleanup_triggered (bool), cleanup_duration_ms
    - retained_readers_held (count, age_ms)

  For stress attempts only (seq % 50 == 0), additionally:
    - setup_duration_ms (time spent arranging retained readers)
    - pre_arrangement retired_gen_count (expected: 4)
    - blocked_at: accept | apply | post_apply
    - fifth_gen_observed (bool — did the 5th retired gen actually materialize?)
    - in_flight_retire_ops at moment of block

"Largest cleanup pause" collapses attribution — record every cleanup duration, derive max as a summary field. Without per-attempt cleanup_duration_ms, a single slow cleanup looks identical to a sequence of normal cleanups plus one outlier.

==============================================================================
PART 2 — BLOCKED-PUSH INVARIANT (must be explicit)
==============================================================================

The proposal does not state what "blocked" means. State it:

  INVARIANT: A stress attempt at seq % 50 == 0 must NOT leave a 5th retired
  generation persisting past the cleanup window for that attempt.

    - pre_arrangement retired_gen_count == 4 (baseline)
    - stress push attempted with retained readers in place
    - if accepted: retired_gen_count may transiently reach 5, MUST return to <=4
      within the staging cleanup-pause budget
    - if rejected at accept: retired_gen_count stays at 4, no cleanup triggered
    - cleanup is complete when retired_gen_count <=4 AND in_flight_retire_ops == 0

The invariant under test: the cleanup correction drains retired generations within budget. The test FAILS if:
  - 5th gen persists past cleanup window on a stress attempt
  - cleanup_duration_ms exceeds the existing staging cleanup-pause limit
  - any non-stress push (seq % 50 != 0) observes retired_gen_count >= 5

==============================================================================
PART 3 — STOP CONDITIONS (proposal lists symptoms, not thresholds)
==============================================================================

The current list ("active-generation inconsistency, route-parity failure, dropped series, reload failure, restart, cleanup pause above the existing staging limit") is unfalsifiable as written. Replace with quantified gates, each attributed to a specific push_seq:

  STOP-A: retired_gen_count >= 5 on any NON-stress push.
           Attribution: cleanup did not complete between stress attempts.

  STOP-B: cleanup_duration_ms > existing_staging_cleanup_pause_limit.
           The plan MUST cite this number explicitly. Do not leave as
           "above the existing staging limit" — that is not a threshold.

  STOP-C: active_gen_id changes between consecutive non-stress pushes
           WITHOUT a corresponding reload event. (route-parity failure
           with attribution to the exact transition.)

  STOP-D: dropped_series_count delta > 0 across any 50-push window.

  STOP-E: reload_failures > 0 across any 50-push window.

  STOP-F: restarts > 0 across any 50-push window.

  STOP-G: p99 drift > 20% from run baseline.
           (Reuse the 2024-06-05 canary threshold. Do not invent a new
           staging number without sign-off.)

  STOP-H: heap delta from run start > +10%.
           (Reuse the 2024-06-05 canary threshold.)

  STOP-I: route_set_hash regression — hash of next 50 pushes != hash of
           prior 50 with same input, with no corresponding config change.

On any STOP-X: halt, record push_seq, the triggering observation, and the gen/route/heap snapshot at that moment. Do not auto-resume.

==============================================================================
PART 4 — RECOVERY (this is the proposal's weakest part)
==============================================================================

"After a blocked push, allow the harness to continue once cleanup completes" is exactly the auto-retry pattern that blurs attribution. Replace with:

  RECOVERY-1: On a blocked stress attempt, the harness RECORDS the block
              and PAUSES. No automatic continuation.

  RECOVERY-2: A human operator (Wes, primary deploy-pipeline owner) inspects
              the per-attempt ledger and confirms whether the invariant held
              (5th gen drained within window) or failed.

  RECOVERY-3: If invariant held, operator resumes at the NEXT push_seq with
              an explicit "resume_after_block" annotation. The next push is
              observed with heightened scrutiny (full per-attempt record,
              not run-level summary).

  RECOVERY-4: If invariant failed, sequence is HALTED. No retry of the
              failed stress attempt — the failure is the data point.
              Re-plan required.

  RECOVERY-5: Backoff between stress attempts must be explicit and human-paced,
              not derived from cleanup duration. Auto-resume on cleanup
              completion obscures whether the next push succeeded due to
              genuine cleanup or due to timing skew.

No automatic retries. Every push after a block is a new, attributed decision. Backup scope (per Wes daylight: backup != primary) does not extend to resume authorization — that stays with primary.

==============================================================================
PART 5 — ISOLATION GAPS
==============================================================================

The proposal does not specify:

  ISO-1: Staging traffic profile. Single-tenant dedicated, or shared with
         other staging workloads? If shared, quiesce other workloads for
         the duration of the 600-push sequence; otherwise attribution
         between this exercise and concurrent staging traffic is impossible.

  ISO-2: Reader-retention mechanism. Real slow-consumer path, or mock/test-only
         hold? Mock holds isolate from production code paths but do not
         exercise the real retention trigger. State explicitly which is used —
         the choice changes what is being tested.

  ISO-3: Canary vs 100% in staging. The proposal implies 100% of the staging
         metrics-router fleet. Confirm or correct.

  ISO-4: Build/branch isolation. Pin to a specific commit SHA of
         metrics-router. PR #423 may have follow-up commits; without a pin,
         a rerun tests different code.

  ISO-5: Reader retention duration. If variable, the 5th-gen attempt is
         non-deterministic. Fix at a specific duration (e.g., 2x the normal
         export interval) and document.

==============================================================================
PART 6 — MISSING OBSERVATIONS
==============================================================================

  OBS-1: gen_before_push / gen_after_push per attempt (not just active_gen_id
         snapshots).

  OBS-2: Time from "retained readers arranged" to "push attempted" — separates
         setup cost from router behavior.

  OBS-3: Whether the 5th-gen attempt was blocked at accept vs after-accept —
         different code paths, different failure modes.

  OBS-4: Cleanup duration per retired generation, not just the largest.
         The largest is a summary; the distribution is the signal.

  OBS-5: Memory recovered (heap delta post-cleanup vs pre-stress), not just
         heap snapshot.

  OBS-6: Sequence integrity on route_set_hash — monotonic check across all
         600 pushes, not just within 50-push windows.

  OBS-7: in_flight_retire_ops at the moment of each block. Was the router
         mid-cleanup when the stress push arrived?

==============================================================================
BOTTOM LINE FOR WES
==============================================================================

The proposal's structure (600 pushes, every 50th as a stress attempt) is sound. The execution details are not:

  1. Auto-resume after a blocked push must be removed; replace with human-
     attributed pause/resume (RECOVERY-1..5).
  2. Stop conditions must be quantified (STOP-A..I). "Above the existing
     staging limit" is not a threshold.
  3. Per-attempt observations must replace run-level summaries (Part 1).
  4. Isolation (traffic, reader mechanism, build pin, retention duration)
     must be specified before run (ISO-1..5).
  5. The existing staging cleanup-pause limit must be cited as a number in
     the plan, not referenced as "the existing limit."
  6. The blocked-push invariant (Part 2) must be in the run plan verbatim
     so the failure criterion is unambiguous.

Until those are addressed, the exercise will produce data that cannot be attributed to specific causes, and a failure cannot be distinguished from a slow cleanup. This review authorizes nothing beyond staging preparation. No production rollout is implied or approved.

I have enough context from prior reviews. Here is the precise review.

────────────────────────────────────────
REVIEW OF REVISED ROLLUP-SERVICE BACKFILL PSEUDOCODE (post-July 5)
────────────────────────────────────────

Residual defects in the revised pseudocode

1. Watermark advance and batch result are not atomically committed.
   The function performs `writeWatermark(tenant, batch.end)` and then `writeBatchResult(tenant, batch.id, result)` as two independent store operations. A crash between them leaves the durable watermark at `batch.end` with no result written for that batch. Because `current = readWatermark(tenant)` returns the advanced value, the next invocation takes the `batch.end <= current` early-return path and returns `already_done` without ever writing the batch result. The aggregate is permanently lost.

2. Readiness is published from the attempted value, not from a durable readback.
   `readiness.publish(tenant, batch.end)` is invoked immediately after the second store write using the in-process argument, without reading either the persisted watermark or the batch result back from storage. There is no way to distinguish a successful commit from a half-applied one. Downstream consumers therefore see readiness for state that may not exist on disk.

3. The idempotency key is only batch-scoped and is not recorded with the write.
   The store has no record of `(tenant, batch.id)` ever having been processed. The watermark is the only durable artifact, and `readiness.publish` carries no deduplication key. A redelivered retry that arrives after a previous successful commit, or that races with a concurrent worker, will see `current >= batch.end`, take the early-return, and publish readiness a second time. Concurrent invocations can also both pass the watermark read and both write the result.

4. Retry behavior does not recover from the partial-progress window.
   "Caller invokes `process` again with the same batch after any error" only works if every observable failure mode either committed everything or committed nothing. The current pseudocode admits a third state — watermark advanced, result missing, readiness not yet published — and the retry path will not recover from it; it will mask it as `already_done`.

5. The watermark write is an unconditional overwrite.
   The conditional in the previous draft (advance only when candidate > current, with monotonic guard) is gone. Two workers retrying the same tenant can race on `writeWatermark`: the slower one's stale `batch.end` can clobber the faster one's higher value. This regresses watermark monotonicity, which the May 28, 2024 invariant requires.

6. No per-tenant serialization point.
   Nothing in the function prevents two `process(tenant, …)` invocations for the same tenant from interleaving. The earlier draft at least implied a single in-memory watermark per tenant; this draft relies entirely on the store, with no CAS or transaction and no lease. The worker-reassignment race that the March 8 fix closed for the live path is reintroduced here for the backfill path.

7. Recovery semantics on restart are undefined.
   After process restart, the in-memory `current` is lost and there is no `attempt_id` recorded anywhere. The function cannot tell whether a given `(tenant, batch.id)` was committed, partially committed, or never started. The only signal is the watermark, which is now the wrong signal because it is advanced independently of the result.

────────────────────────────────────────
REQUIRED CORRECTIONS
────────────────────────────────────────

A. Single atomic commit of watermark + batch result + idempotency record.
   The watermark advance and the batch result write must be one transaction in the backing store. If the store cannot do cross-row transactions, the batch result must be the durable source of truth and the watermark must be derived from it (max `end` over committed results) on read. A separate `committed_batches` row keyed on `(tenant_id, batch_id)` must be written in the same transaction.

B. CAS or monotonic guard on the watermark.
   The watermark write must reject any candidate ≤ current persisted value, even on the backfill path. The May 28 invariant applies regardless of whether the work originated from live completion or a maintenance backfill.

C. Idempotency key is `(tenant_id, batch_id, attempt_id)`.
   `attempt_id` is assigned at lease issuance, incremented only after lease expiry without ack or explicit abort, and never reused. The committed row stores `attempt_id` so a redelivered retry that observes a committed `(tenant_id, batch_id)` returns `already_done` without re-running `recompute` and without re-publishing readiness.

D. Outbox or equivalent for readiness publication.
   The readiness event for `(tenant, batch.end, batch.id)` is written to a durable outbox row in the same transaction as the batch result. A separate publisher reads the outbox, sends to readiness, and deletes the outbox row only after a confirmed send. Retry of `process` after a crash must observe the outbox row and resume from "publish pending," not re-run the whole batch.

E. Per-tenant serialization.
   Backfill work for a given tenant must execute under a per-tenant lease or partition key. Without it, two workers retrying the same `(tenant, batch.id)` race the watermark, the result write, and the outbox. This is the same hazard that the worker reassignment test on March 8, 2024 closed; the backfill path needs the same protection.

F. Retry contract restricted to true transient failures.
   "Retry after any error" must be narrowed to transient store or publisher errors that left no observable side effect. After a partial-progress crash, the retry must perform recovery (read committed-batch row, finish outbox publish if pending) rather than re-enter at the top of `process`. A poison batch (repeated failure with no progress) must be marked and surfaced, not retried indefinitely.

G. Recovery path explicitly restated in code or comments.
   On restart, before evaluating any new batch, the worker must scan the outbox for unsent readiness rows for that tenant and publish them, then resume normal processing. Uncommitted draft state from a previous process lifetime must not carry over.

────────────────────────────────────────
SEQUENCE REQUIRED FOR THE PR
────────────────────────────────────────

The corrected `process(tenant, batch)` must run, in this order and only this order:

  1. Acquire per-tenant lease; assign `attempt_id` if none exists for `(tenant, batch.id)`.
  2. In one store transaction, on the unique key `(tenant_id, batch_id)`:
     a. if a committed row exists with `attempt_id` ≤ current attempt → return `already_done`;
     b. else write the batch result, advance the watermark via CAS (reject if candidate ≤ current), and insert an outbox row `(tenant, batch.id, batch.end, attempt_id)`.
  3. After commit, attempt to publish from the outbox; mark the outbox row sent only after confirmed publish.
  4. Release the lease only after step 3 succeeds or the outbox row is durable for a later publisher.
  5. On any error before the transaction commits: abort, release lease, allow caller retry under the same `attempt_id`.
  6. On any error after commit but before publish: caller retry must observe the committed row and the outbox row and resume at step 3 without re-running `recompute`.

Pre-PR questions Cyrus still owes an answer on
  - The exact idempotency key on the store side (the smallest safe one, per the May 28 invariant).
  - Whether the store supports cross-row transactions; if not, the fallback derivation of the watermark from max committed batch.
  - Whether the readiness target is idempotent on `(tenant, batch.id)`; if not, the outbox must dedupe there too.
  - The per-tenant serialization mechanism (lease, partition key, or single-worker-per-tenant).
  - The poison-batch signal and alerting path, so a stuck batch does not silently block the tenant's watermark.

────────────────────────────────────────
REVIEW VERDICT
────────────────────────────────────────

Request changes. The watermark is now in the right place, but the commit, idempotency, and readiness paths still violate the cross-service invariants: atomic write is missing, the idempotency key is not recorded, readiness is published from an attempted value rather than a durable readback, and per-tenant serialization is absent. The pseudocode must be revised per A–G above before Cyrus's team turns it into a PR. Implementation, deployment, and operational ownership remain with Cyrus's team; my scope here is the design-review invariants only.

Suggested next step: ask Cyrus for a revised draft that shows the transaction boundary explicitly, names the per-tenant serialization mechanism, and restates the recovery path on restart. Once those three are visible in the pseudocode, the remaining questions reduce to the pre-PR list above and the validation evidence list from the May 29 regression requirements (89.9s included / 90.1s excluded, lagging watermark blocks, rebalance reload, pre-commit crash publishes nothing, post-commit crash recovers without double count, repeated compactions identical).

The contract is clear on all three disputed points. Let me write the review.

**Review: Implementation sketch vs. proposed fail-closed contract**

The sketch encodes the right *intent* in two of three places but fails it on three concrete points. Each maps directly to a clause in the proposed contract.

**1. "unknown" → OMIT is wrong; it must be REJECTED.**

The proposed contract says there is no `unknown` fallback on this label — omission is reserved for *missing* input, and an explicit `unknown` value is treated the same as any other non-allowlisted input. The sketch collapses these two states: `if raw is missing` and `if value == "unknown"` both return `OMIT`. After normalization that means `"unknown"` and `"UNKNOWN"` and `" unknown "` and `" unknown"` all silently disappear into the same omitted-series bucket, indistinguishable from a tenant that never set the attribute.

Required correction:

  - Missing input → `OMIT` (label absent on the wire; this is a first-class state).
  - Non-empty input that does not normalize to an allowlisted value, **including the literal string `"unknown"`** → `ERROR`. Drop the series or omit the label per the rejection policy, increment `exporter_labels_dropped_total{reason="unsupported_deployment_environment"}`, and rate-limited debug-log a hash of the raw value. Never emit `"unknown"` on the wire. The metrics-router must not synthesize a default, and the rollup-service must treat a missing label as a distinct fourth series key rather than mapping it to `unknown`.

**2. The validate-then-trim order is wrong.**

The sketch calls `lowercase(trim(raw))` and *then* checks the allowlist. Two consequences:

  - A bare-whitespace input like `"   "` becomes `""` after trim and would match `if value == "unknown": return OMIT` only if the author also tested `""` there — they did not. In the current sketch, `"   "` reaches the allowlist check and returns `ERROR`, which is fine, but `"   "` and `""` and the truly-missing case all collapse into the same wire behavior for the wrong reasons.
  - Trimming is a presentation concern that should happen only on values that survive validation, so log/drop accounting reflects the raw producer shape rather than a normalized one.

Required correction: validate the **trimmed, lowered** value against `{"prod", "staging", "dev"}`, but do the missing-vs-empty-vs-present branching on the raw input first:

  normalize(raw):
    if raw is missing OR raw is null: return OMIT
    trimmed = trim_ascii(raw)
    if trimmed == "": return ERROR          # whitespace-only is malformed, not missing
    value = lowercase_ascii(trimmed)
    if value == "unknown": return ERROR      # explicit unknown is not a missing-input signal
    if value in {"prod", "staging", "dev"}: return value
    return ERROR

The decision on whether to drop the series or emit the metric without the label should be made in the publication path, not here — but that decision must be the same one the contract makes for every malformed input, including `unknown`.

**3. The per-tenant budget check is in the wrong place and does the wrong thing on exceed.**

The sketch publishes the metric first and then "alerts if tracker exceeds 3". That admits a fourth distinct value onto the wire — the budget becomes a *post-hoc* observation rather than an enforcement point. The contract is explicit: the budget is enforced before publication, exceedance rejects further writes for that tenant on this label, and clamping is forbidden. Alerting alone is insufficient.

Required correction:

  - Maintain the per-tenant distinct-value set at the edge (collector or router, before the metric is emitted).
  - On the publication path, after a value has been validated:
    - If the tenant's set already contains this value, allow publication.
    - If the tenant's set does not contain this value and `size(set) >= 3`, reject publication of this label for this tenant. Increment `exporter_labels_dropped_total{reason="deployment_environment_budget_exceeded"}` and emit a per-tenant alert to the runbook owner. Do **not** clamp to the first three, do **not** silently emit as `unknown`, and do **not** synthesize a default.
    - Otherwise, add the value to the set and publish.
  - The global distinct-value budget of 3 also has to be enforced the same way at the global scope (or the per-tenant check is meaningless).
  - The alert is a *signal*, not the enforcement point. Move the `if tracker exceeds 3` line out of the publication path and into the runbook/alert path that triggers after rejection has already happened.

**Other items the sketch is missing and the patch should add before it advances**

  - The pre-trim, pre-lowercase raw value must not be logged. Logs may contain only the normalized allowlisted outcome or a hash, so a rejected value cannot re-enter cardinality through log-derived metrics.
  - The producer set has to be enumerated (SDK, collector, router, rollup, sidecar), with each routed through the same normalize/validate/reject path; direct SDK pushes and sidecars are out of contract unless explicitly covered.
  - The historical-series migration plan is not in scope of this sketch but blocks merge: storage may already contain `unknown` and other out-of-allowlist values, and the contract requires either a re-emit window with deprecation alias or a hard cutover that quarantines pre-cutover series and excludes them from cardinality accounting.
  - Cross-service parity fixture (24h post-export series, existing label identity preserved, OTLP receiver rewrite verified) is required before the patch advances; silent allowlist expansion, default/missing-value labels, and unnamed cardinality-budget ownership are all prohibited by sign-off.

Send these corrections back to Product Engineering and ask them to resubmit with: (a) `unknown` reclassified as `ERROR`, (b) the missing/empty/whitespace branching moved ahead of normalization and allowlisted on raw input shape, and (c) the per-tenant (and global) 3-value budget enforced as a *pre-publish* rejection gate with a drop counter and runbook alert, not a post-publish alert.

The entry carries two overlapping cleanup-pause sections. Both state the same stop thresholds, but one is older (rationale) and the other is the accepted boundary (current). Rollback conditions differ in count between the two.

Stop thresholds (cleanup-pause wording)

The 2024-05-30 "Generation / cleanup guidance" section says:
  - "Retired objects accumulate above 4 on any canary pod"
  - "Cleanup pauses exceed 100 ms on any canary pod"
  - Either holds → pause additional configuration pushes.

The 2024-06-18 "Accepted push-resume boundary" section says:
  - "Retired generation count crosses more than four (i.e. > 4 retired generations on a single pod)"
  - "Stop-the-world cleanup pause exceeds 100 milliseconds on a canary pod"
  - "Either condition by itself is sufficient to stop further pushes."

Both sections agree on the numbers: retired > 4 and pause > 100 ms. They are equivalent — the second is the explicit accepted boundary and the first remains as underlying guidance.

Resume conditions (2024-06-18, single bounded push)

All four must hold at the same time:
  - Retired generation count ≤ 1 on every canary pod
  - p99 returned to baseline for the canary slice
  - Heap returned to baseline for the canary pod(s)
  - The five verification checks clean: active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series = 0, reload failures = 0, restarts = 0

Immediate re-pause: any stop threshold recrossed → pause immediately, no waiting for a second crossing.

Rollback conditions — here is the discrepancy that matters

2024-05-30 "Generation / cleanup guidance" lists THREE hard rollback triggers:
  1. Active-generation inconsistency across canary pods
  2. Non-zero route-delivery divergence
  3. Any non-zero dropped-series count

2024-06-18 "Accepted push-resume boundary" lists FIVE rollback conditions:
  1. Active-generation inconsistency across canary pods
  2. Non-zero route-delivery divergence
  3. Any non-zero dropped-series count
  4. Any reload failure in the canary window
  5. Any restart in the canary window

HARNESS STRUCTURE RECOMMENDATION

Three named phases, all first-class in the record.

The fix is to stop treating "blocked attempt -> cleanup -> retry" as one push. It is three phases with their own identities. Add a fourth (decision gate) that gates the retry.

PHASE A — BLOCKED-ATTEMPT PHASE
  request_id      = push_n:attempt_k   (k=1 for the first attempt)
  recorded fields: request_id, config_hash, sent_at, response_status,
                   response_body, decision=blocked, block_reason
  invariant check: snapshot active routes BEFORE send;
                   snapshot again AFTER response received;
                   assert equality; FAIL the harness (not warn) on mismatch

PHASE B — CLEANUP-INTERVAL PHASE
  interval_id     = cleanup_n:m        (between attempt k and k+1)
  recorded fields: interval_id, started_at, ended_at, cleanup_events,
                   routes-stable-across-interval=true/false
  This phase is its own observable. It cannot be elided from the final
  record even if attempt k+1 is never attempted.

PHASE C — DECISION-GATE PHASE
  gate_id         = gate_n:m           (one per possible retry)
  recorded fields: gate_id, requested_at, decision_token (signed:
                   operator name + timestamp + reason),
                   decision=proceed|abort
  Default: abort. The harness cannot transition Phase B -> Phase D
  without an explicit decision_token recorded here. Auto-proceed is
  not a behavior.

PHASE D (CONDITIONAL) — RETRY PHASE
  request_id      = push_n:attempt_k+1, distinct from attempt k
  Reachable only via a Phase C with decision_token=proceed.
  Carries forward config_hash from the blocked attempt so the
  relationship is explicit (push_n groups the attempts; attempt_k
  distinguishes them).


WHAT THIS GUARANTEES

1. Distinct request identities preserved.
   request_id distinguishes attempt k from attempt k+1 even when the
   harness "replays" the same configuration. The push_n grouping makes
   the relationship queryable without collapsing identities.

2. Blocked push cannot change active routes.
   The before/after routes snapshot in Phase A is a hard assertion,
   not a warning. On mismatch the harness aborts BEFORE cleanup,
   BEFORE the decision gate, BEFORE any retry.

3. Separate decision required before retry.
   Phase C is mandatory. The harness halts after Phase B until a
   decision_token is recorded. No automatic transition.

4. Blocked attempt, cleanup interval, and any retry remain separately
   identified phases.
   Each phase has its own ID space and its own start/end. Even if
   Phase D never executes, Phases A and B remain first-class.


RECORDING SHAPE

  push_n=<n>
    attempt_1
      request_id          = push_n:attempt_1
      sent_at, response, decision=blocked, block_reason=...
      routes_before, routes_after, routes_equal=true|false
      cleanup_observed=true|false
    cleanup_1
      interval_id         = cleanup_1
      started_at, ended_at, events=...
      routes_stable=true|false
    gate_1
      gate_id             = gate_1
      requested_at, decision_token=..., decision=proceed|abort
      (default: abort — no transition without token)
    attempt_2
      request_id          = push_n:attempt_2
      parent_attempt      = attempt_1        (forward-reference, not collapse)
      sent_at, response, decision=...
      ...


OPERATIONAL NOTES (runbook-aligned)

  - Owner path: the operator who records the decision_token is the
    owner of record for Phase C. Primary/backup stays in metadata,
    not in identity.
  - The before/after routes snapshot reads from the same source the
    production router would consult (runbook's operator path), so
    "no change" is the same observation production would make.
  - A Phase-A invariant failure is a HARD FAIL distinct from
    decision=blocked. Two findings:
      "blocked as expected"   (no harm, harness continues to B)
      "blocked but routes changed"  (block did something it shouldn't;
                                     harness aborts the whole run)


MINIMAL HARNESS LOOP

  emit attempt_1   (record request_id, sent_at)
  assert routes_after == routes_before
    if not equal: HARD FAIL, abort run
  record decision=blocked, block_reason
  emit cleanup_1   (record interval_id, started_at)
  HALT — wait for decision_token
  on decision=proceed:
    emit attempt_2 (request_id distinct from attempt_1)
  on decision=abort:
    close push_n with status=aborted, no retry


One thing worth flagging: this treats the attribution flaw as a structural problem (phases collapsed), not a logging problem (more verbose logs). Adding fields to a single combined record would not fix it — the retry would still inherit the blocked attempt's identity downstream. The split into phases with their own IDs is what keeps the blocked attempt visible after the retry succeeds.

Why this is a hard fail (not a "response looked fine" pass)
  - The run produced a clean response envelope (no protected value reached the wire) AND violated call order (adapter invoked before the 403 was returned).
  - These are independent assertions. A clean envelope does not satisfy the authorization-order contract, and authorization order was the only thing the negative case actually tested.
  - Treating envelope cleanliness as sufficient is exactly how this slipped through. The gate must reject any run where the two assertions are not both evidenced.

Shared authorization wrapper — required shape
  - Single chokepoint mediating every path to a source adapter: lookup, importer page-fetches, retry, and publication (per Iris's existing fail-closed safeguards).
  - Authorization evaluates to allow/deny BEFORE any adapter invocation. "Decide then fetch" is the only legal sequence; "fetch then decide" is a contract violation regardless of the resulting envelope.
  - Tenant_id is part of the cache key (AUTH-2 invariant, retained).
  - Deny path returns HTTP 403 with permission_denied (ERR-4 invariant, retained) and never reaches an adapter.
  - Allow path proceeds to the adapter with a fresh authorization context; retries do not reuse a prior snapshot.
  - The wrapper is the only legal entry to adapters. Any code path that touches an adapter without going through the wrapper is itself a gate failure, independent of any test result.
  - Cache behavior: a cached allow returns 200 with kind="absent"/unknown-state semantics if the permitted source is missing — denial is not re-derived from source absence (existing invariant, retained).

Negative call-order acceptance criteria (the test bar)
  - Each negative fixture must produce TWO independent assertions, both required, neither sufficient alone:
    - Assertion A — Response correctness: HTTP 403 not_authorized (or permission_denied), no protected field, no source timestamp, no inferred unknown payload. This is what the July 12 run already passed.
    - Assertion B — Call-order correctness: zero source-adapter invocations for the denied request. Evidence is the adapter-call trace (span/telemetry), not the response.
  - A fixture passes only when both A and B pass. A pass on A with a fail on B is a gate failure (this is the July 12 case).
  - Call-order evidence must be captured at the wrapper boundary, not at the adapter boundary — adapters can be invoked by tests, fixtures, or background jobs, and only the wrapper trace distinguishes "the wrapper decided deny" from "the wrapper was bypassed."
  - Negative fixtures must cover, at minimum:
    - explicit-unknown unauthorized (the July 12 case)
    - absent permitted source for an unauthorized caller
    - stale permitted source for an unauthorized caller
    - malformed permitted source for an unauthorized caller
    - cross-tenant unauthorized (tenant_id mismatch)
  - Each fixture must record: decision_source (cache_hit / cache_miss / live), policy_generation, wrapper invocation timestamp, adapter-call count (must be 0), and response envelope.
  - The fixtures must be runnable as a contract test, not just a manual probe — otherwise the call-order assertion is not actually exercised.

Separation rule going forward (the thing to keep distinct)
  - "No leakage in the response" is a content assertion.
  - "Authorization preceded source access" is an order assertion.
  - Readiness evidence must present them as separate rows per fixture; merging them into a single pass/fail hides the exact failure mode that occurred on July 12.
  - Reviewer checklist reads: A ✓ / B ✗ / decision: fail — not "response was clean, gate passed."

Short controlled return is reasonable today; another full week off isn't warranted given your current function. The mild tightness on harder lateral cut is the one residual sign worth respecting, and the protocol below is built around it.

ASSESSMENT

    Lateral ankle sprain (most likely grade I, possibly early grade II
    based on your description), roughly 5+ days out.

    Pain-free on walking, straight-line jog, single-leg calf raises,
    and forward hops. No instability, no swelling. These cover most
    standard return-to-sport gates.

    The only positive finding is tightness (no sharp pain) on higher-
    load lateral cut. That's the provocative direction for a lateral
    ligament injury, so it's the right thing to respect -- but tight-
    ness without pain during the provocative test at 5+ days is
    acceptable for a graded return with guardrails.

    Deferring another full week when functional tests are passed is
    over-conservative and just costs you deconditioning.

WARM-UP (non-negotiable, ~20 min before any ball touches)

    1. Self-mobilization (2-3 min): ankle circles both directions;
       knee-to-wall dorsiflexion drill (slow, into end-range); peroneal
       and calf foam roll or massage ball.

    2. Cardio ramp (5 min): easy jog -> moderate jog. No sprinting yet.

    3. Activation (3-5 min):
       - Single-leg balance, eyes open, 30s x 3 each side
       - Single-leg calf raises 15 x 2 each side
       - Banded lateral walks 10 each direction x 2 (band at forefoot
         for peroneal activation)

    4. Progressive loading (5 min), in this exact order. STOP the
       warm-up and do not play if any step produces sharp pain, a
       "catch," or instability:
       small forward hops -> small lateral hops -> medium lateral hops
       -> low lateral shuffle -> 50% lateral cut -> 75% lateral cut
       -> full lateral cut. ~3-4 reps per step.

    5. First touches at walking-to-jogging pace before joining play.

PARTICIPATION LIMITS (first session only)

    - Cap actual play at ~30-45 minutes. Do not run a full 60-90 min
      pickup on day one.
    - First 15 min: stay at ~70% intensity. Avoid being last defender
      back (high-stakes cuts). No contested headers or 50/50 balls --
      those produce unexpected lateral loads.
    - Build to full intensity across the session only if tightness
      stays mild and unchanged from baseline.
    - Stop the session at the cap above regardless of how it feels.
      This is a graded return, not a test of how far you can push.

STOP CRITERIA -- stop immediately and do not return that day if:

    - Sharp pain or a "catch"/"tweak" in the ankle. Anything more than
      your current baseline mild tightness.
    - Any feeling of giving way or instability.
    - New or returning swelling.
    - Pain that increases during play rather than staying at baseline.
    - Noticeable loss of push-off strength on the affected side.

AFTER THE SESSION

    - Re-test: 10 single-leg calf raises and a medium-effort lateral
      hop should remain pain-free and stable.
    - If baseline tightness is unchanged or better the next morning:
      continue graded return next session, push to ~60 min.
    - If tightness persists >24h, worsens, or any stop criterion
      triggered: take 3-5 more days of rest plus rehab, then re-test.
      Do not push through to the next session.
    - Daily rehab regardless: banded eversion (peroneals) 3x15; single-
      leg balance progressing to eyes-closed or foam; hop progression
      forward -> lateral.

This is general guidance applied to a self-assessment, not a substitute for an in-person exam. If tightness does not improve over the next 2-3 sessions, or if you ever feel a true give-way episode, see your clinician -- that's worth a formal eval rather than more self-management.
