Diagnosis check first: a split at the valve-stem/rubber junction is a tube-side failure (bond line / age), not a tire failure. Your no-glass-no-wire-no-sharp-rim findings confirm the casing and rim tape are not the cause. A correctly sized replacement tube is the right fix; do NOT install the new tube without re-inspecting one more time, because the most common reason a "new tube fails immediately" is that the cause was actually in the rim/tire and got missed.

PRE-INSTALL (with tube still out)

1. Tire still on the rim, one or both beads seated. Leave it there.
2. Rim tape: run your fingertip around every spoke hole under the tape. You should feel no raised nipple edges and no tape gap. If the tape has shifted or you can feel a nipple poking through, replace the tape now, not after the new tube goes in.
3. Rim well: drag a cotton ball or your fingertip (slowly, with light pressure) around the inside channel of the rim. Any snag means a sharp edge - file or sand it smooth before proceeding.
4. Tire casing: with the tube out, flex the tire and look from the inside for embedded glass/thorn/wire that the outside view missed. Run your finger (with a glove) around the inside of the casing. If you find anything, pull it. The stem-bond failure means the casing is probably innocent, but verify.
5. New tube: inflate it just to round shape (a few PSI, then deflate) before installing. This confirms it's not defective and makes it easier to seat without pinching. Inspect for any mold flash or visible defect at the stem bond.

INSTALL SEQUENCE

6. Insert the valve through the rim valve hole first. The valve stem must go in straight - if it angles, the hole is wrong (Schrader vs Presta, or wrong-size rim hole) and forcing it will split this tube too.
7. Tuck the tube into the tire all the way around the circumference. Push it into the rim's well (the drop channel in the middle of the rim cross-section), not up against the bead. A tube sitting in the well cannot get pinched.
8. With both hands, work the second bead of the tire onto the rim. Use plastic tire levers only - never a screwdriver. The last 6-8 inches usually needs a lever; lever only the bead, never the tube.
9. Before using any lever on the last section, look at the tube through the gap and confirm it is fully tucked under the bead, not caught between bead and rim.

PRESEATING AIR (the answer to "how much air before seating")

10. With the tire fully mounted but not yet inflated to spec, add air in stages:
    - Pump to ~5 PSI (road) or ~10 PSI (mountain). The tube should be visibly rounded under the tire but the tire should still be soft enough that you can press the sidewall in with your thumb.
    - At this low pressure, walk around the wheel and look at the tire's bead line on both sides. The bead should sit evenly below the rim edge all the way around. A section that bulges out or sits high means the tube is pinched under the bead at that spot.
    - Run your hand around the outside of the tire feeling for any "bubble" or soft spot - that is a pinch.
    - If you find a pinch: deflate fully, push the bead off the rim at that spot with your thumbs (no lever), reseat the tube into the well, remount the bead, re-add air, and recheck. Do NOT inflate past preseat pressure with a pinch present - it will cut the tube.

PINCH AVOIDANCE - rules that prevent the failure mode that killed the last tube

- Tube fully tucked into the rim well before any lever work near the last 6-8 inches.
- Valves straight through the rim hole. A crooked valve = the tube is twisted under the bead = pinch waiting to happen.
- Never inflate before confirming the bead is evenly seated all the way around on both sides.
- Never use a sharp tool anywhere near the tube.
- If you have to stop and start the lever work, every time you stop, look through the gap and verify the tube is below the bead.

INFLATION TO SPEC

11. Inflate to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall. Stay under the max. For a rear tube failure of this type, I'd err toward the middle-to-upper end of the recommended range rather than the bottom, since the stem bond was the weak point and you want the tube well-supported by the casing.
12. Cap the valve (if Presta, close the locknut). Finger-tight only on Presta cores.

HOLD AND PRE-RIDE CHECKS - do these in order, do not skip

13. Static hold (immediate): squeeze the tire firmly with both hands at 8 points around the circumference. You should feel firm, even resistance. Any soft spot = pinch, deflate and reseat.
14. Valve check: the valve stem should be perfectly perpendicular to the rim and should not move when wiggled. If it wiggles or leans, the tube is twisted or the valve hole is wrong - deflate and fix.
15. Bead-line visual: both sides, all the way around, bead sits evenly below the rim edge. Any high spot = tube under the bead.
16. Spin check: lift the bike, spin the rear wheel, watch the tire pass the brake pads (if rim brakes) or the frame. The tire should not wobble side-to-side or up-and-down. A tire that "hops" as it spins means the tube is unevenly seated.
17. Pressure hold (5-minute test): wait 5 minutes, re-check pressure. A small drop (1-2 PSI) is normal as the tube stretches and the tire seats. A drop of more than 5 PSI means the tube is not sealed against the rim or there is still a slow leak - find it (soapy water around valve, bead, and tire) before riding.
18. Load check: with the wheel back in the frame (if you removed it), sit on the bike with your full weight on the saddle and push down hard on the bars. The tire should not visibly deform asymmetrically and the valve should stay straight. Re-check pressure after this load.
19. 24-hour pressure check (ideal): leave the bike overnight and check pressure in the morning. If it held overnight, the install is good. If it dropped, you have a slow leak somewhere - usually valve core, bead/rim interface, or a casing pinhole, in that order.
20. First ride: in a low-traffic area, ride 50-100 meters and re-check pressure and feel. Then a short neighborhood loop. Then a normal ride. Do not go straight from install to a long or remote ride.

ORDER-OF-OPERATIONS SUMMARY

Inspect rim tape, rim well, tire casing -> preshape new tube -> valve through rim hole -> tube into rim well all the way around -> mount second bead with plastic levers only -> inflate to preseat pressure (5 PSI road / 10 PSI MTB) -> check bead line and feel for pinches around full circumference -> inflate to sidewall spec -> squeeze test at 8 points -> valve alignment check -> spin check -> 5-min pressure hold -> reinstall in frame -> loaded sit-check -> overnight hold -> short test ride.

If preseat inflation shows any pinch, deflate and reseat before going further - that one step is what separates a tube that lasts years from a tube that splits on the first curb.

Pre-flight assumption I'm making from your language ("rim drags against one brake pad once per revolution"): this is a RIM-brake rear. The whole sequence below assumes that. If it's actually a disc-brake rear, the "pad" you're seeing is at the rotor near the hub, not the rim, and the procedure is different — tell me and I'll re-issue for disc.

================================================================
DIAGNOSTIC SEQUENCE — do these in order, stop and fix at the first failure
================================================================

1. TIRE vs. PAD — rule out the tire as the contact first
   - Spin the wheel slowly by hand. Watch whether the TIRE (rubber) is what's passing the pad, or the rim's brake track is. A bead that didn't fully seat symmetrically can make the tire stand proud of the rim on one side.
   - Pass: tire clears pad all the way around with visible daylight.
   - If the tire is the contact, deflate, reseat the bead (check the bead line is even all the way around against the rim), reinflate. Don't continue.

2. WHEEL SEATED IN DROPOUTS — symmetric and bottomed
   - Loosen the QR / thru-axle. With the wheel loose, push the bike forward so the axle drops fully into the dropouts. The non-drive-side axle end should sit flush with (or just inside) the outside face of the dropout.
   - Look down the seatstays from behind: the tire should be equidistant from each seatstay.
   - Look down the chainstays from the right side: same check.
   - Pass: axle flush both sides; tire equidistant from both stays; no twist in the wheel.
   - If asymmetric, the wheel is tracking sideways. The brake centering step later will be masking this, not fixing it — reseat first.

3. QR / THRU-AXLE TENSION — the one that bites rear wheels under pedaling
   - QR (skewer): close the lever. It should require firm palm pressure to fully close. You should feel an imprint on your palm. If your fingers can close it, the cam is under-tensioned and the wheel can pivot in the dropouts under hard pedaling — that's a real-world hazard on a rear wheel. Open, tighten the adjusting nut 1/4–1/2 turn, close, retest.
   - Thru-axle: torque to the frame manufacturer's spec. Don't guess on carbon — over-torque cracks the frame, under-torque lets the axle walk. Typical ranges are 5–8 Nm road / 12–15 Nm MTB, but the frame spec wins.
   - Pass: lever closes with firm palm pressure (QR); axle does not move when you try to twist the wheel laterally with the bike held.

4. WHERE IS THE RUB HAPPENING — this is the masking check
   - Lift the bike, spin the wheel slowly.
   - Question A — the rub is at the same ROTATIONAL position of the wheel each turn (a specific spot on the rim passes the pad): lateral trueness issue on the rim. Do NOT fix this by centering the brake. You are about to mask a warp.
   - Question B — the rub is constant in angular position around the pad (the pad is just too close to the rim regardless of which part of the rim is passing): brake centering or wheel-tracking-in-frame issue. Safe to adjust.
   - If A: stop. The wheel needs truing on a stand before you ride. If you're going to true it yourself, a 0.5 mm lateral runout at the brake track is roughly the threshold for noticeable rub; beyond that, the brake will pull toward the high side under hard braking (rear-wheel brake torque is smaller than front, but it's not zero, and a loaded rear under pedaling plus braking is the failure mode). For anything more than a trivial wobble, shop it.
   - If B: continue to step 5.

5. BRAKE CENTERING — only do this after 1–4 pass
   - Side-pull rim brake: centering screw on the brake arm or at the cable yoke. Quarter-turn at a time, spin the wheel to check, repeat.
   - V-brake / linear-pull: centering screw at the arm pivot, plus a spring-tension balance done via the pad-side spring nuts (loosen one, tighten the other a quarter-turn to shift the caliper).
   - Pass: rim clears both pads with daylight on at least 5 full revolutions, no audible or tactile rub.

6. RIM TRUENESS SANITY CHECK — even after step 5 passes
   - With the wheel spinning, watch the rim's lateral runout relative to the pads. The rim should not visibly approach either pad by more than ~1 mm at the brake track.
   - If you "fixed" the rub by centering the brake but the rim still has a high spot, you will feel it again the first time you brake firmly on a bumpy surface. That is the masking failure mode the user named. Don't ship it.
   - Pass: rim tracks in the middle of the pad gap, lateral deviation not perceptible to the eye at the brake track.

7. FUNCTIONAL BRAKE CHECK
   - Squeeze the lever fully. Pads contact the rim evenly (both sides touch at the same lever travel), the lever does not bottom out against the bar, and on release both pads retract the same distance.
   - Pass: firm, even contact; lever has reserve travel; pads retract symmetrically.

================================================================
PRE-RIDE GATES — every one must be true
================================================================
  [ ] Wheel spins freely with no pad contact for ≥5 revolutions
  [ ] Tire clears pad all the way around (no tire/pad contact)
  [ ] QR lever requires firm palm pressure to close, OR thru-axle torqued to frame spec
  [ ] Axle ends flush in dropouts both sides
  [ ] Tire equidistant from both seatstays and both chainstays
  [ ] Rim tracks centered between pads, no >1 mm lateral wobble at brake track
  [ ] Brake applies and releases evenly, lever does not bottom out
  [ ] Wheel does not shift when you stand beside the bike, grab the saddle, and push the bike forward hard

================================================================
ROUTING ON FAILURE
================================================================
- Trueness gate fails: do not ride. Truing on a stand is the correct fix; do not chase it by re-centering the brake or by "just loosening the QR a bit so it sits where it wants." Both are band-aids on a rear wheel.
- Seating / tension gate fails: redo that step and re-test from step 4.
- Functional brake gate fails: usually pad retraction (sticky pivot), cable tension, or a pad that's worn unevenly — all of those have nothing to do with the wheel and need their own fix.

If you tell me the brake type (and if disc, rotor size and whether mechanical or hydraulic), I can tighten this up where the centering step is. The wheel-side checks above don't change.

Short answer: yes, the window stops; no rollback is required (and there is no rollback to perform), because the five hard rollback triggers never fired.

Why the window stops

The 2024-07-25 owner-led rule treats every gate breach as an immediate stop. The label-name parity check is one of those gates — it is a hard pre-publication gate, not an advisory preflight. Nadia's open `metrics-router#414` encodes exactly that: a push whose manifest label name does not match the production contract and the rollup-service consumer must be rejected before activation. Cross-service label-name parity has been a hard gate since the 2024-10-24 Cardinality Guardrails first cut, and the runbook treats stale-label pushes as preflight concerns rather than runtime signals.

What you described fits the gate exactly:

    Manifest label        : deployment_env
    Production contract   : deployment.environment
    Rollup-service consumer: deployment.environment
    Gate result           : rejected before publication
    Active routes         : unchanged
    Retired generations   : unchanged (no new retired gen created)
    Full health set       : at baseline

None of the operating thresholds (retired gens <=4, pause <=100 ms, full health baseline) actually fired — the row never made it that far. The gate itself fired. Either way the rule is the same: a gate breach stops the window immediately. Wes stopping without trying rows 2 and 3 is correct.

Why there is no rollback

The five hard rollback triggers are:

  1. Active-generation inconsistency
  2. Route-delivery divergence
  3. Dropped series (non-zero)
  4. Reload failure
  5. Restart during the canary window

None of them fired, and a pre-publication rejection cannot fire any of them by construction:

    Trigger                          | State here
    ---------------------------------+----------------------------
    Active-generation inconsistency  | N/A — no generation became active
    Route-delivery divergence        | N/A — active route set unchanged
    Dropped series                   | N/A — no reload occurred
    Reload failure                   | N/A — reload was not attempted
    Restart                          | N/A — no reload occurred

The 2024-06-18 boundary is explicit on this: rollback requires one of those five; with all five absent and baseline clean, the correct response is hold-and-investigate, not roll back. The May 13, 2024 evidence (73 accepted, 2 rejected before activation, no rejected generation active) was treated as proof the gate was doing its job, not as a rollback event. This case is the same shape.

Rollback description for the change record

Use a non-rollback entry. The text should read something like:

    Rollback: not required.
    Reason  : Row 1 was rejected by the label-name parity preflight before
              publication. Manifest emitted `deployment_env`; production
              contract and rollup-service consumer expect
              `deployment.environment`. No generation was activated, no
              retired generation was created, no reload was attempted, and
              no route change occurred. The five hard rollback triggers
              (active-generation inconsistency, route-delivery divergence,
              dropped series, reload failure, restart) did not fire. The
              prior active generation continues to serve. Full health set
              remained at baseline for the duration of the window.
    Action  : Window stopped per 2024-07-25 rule. Manifest must be
              corrected (`deployment_env` -> `deployment.environment`) and
              re-submitted under a fresh Alex decision. No push is
              pre-authorized by the rejection.

Do not write a rollback command, a deploy_id to roll back to, or a "rollback performed at HH:MM:SS" line — there is no rollback action to record. Writing one would falsely imply a published state existed that needed to be undone, which is exactly what the pre-publication gate prevented.

What Alex decides next

Three things, in order:

  1. Confirm the stop. (Stop is automatic under the rule; Alex's confirmation is just acknowledgment, not a fresh push authorization.)
  2. Decide whether the manifest fix is a one-row correction inside the same window or a new window. Under the 2024-07-25 rule a new window requires a separate Alex decision after a fresh full health baseline. A corrected row inside the same window is also a separate decision — the original opening decision did not pre-approve any row result.
  3. Either way: nothing runs until Alex says so. The recovery-push carve-out (one push after full health baseline under Alex decision) is technically available because baseline never moved, but it still requires the fresh Alex decision and is not implied by the rejection.

Also worth flagging for the change record: this is the second confirmation that the parity preflight is blocking correctly (cf. May 13, 2024 evidence). It is gate-behavior evidence, not rollback evidence. Keep the two categories separate in the postmortem so it does not get misread as a canary regression later.

Classification (two separate axes, by design)

Serving-safety evidence — CLEAN / PASS
  - Final old-holder routing response at 4 ms: old holder answered only inside its authorized window.
  - Old-holder serving gate closed at 12 ms: a clean cutover boundary, with no late responses after that point.
  - No later old-holder response: zero stale-serving from the old holder.
  - Exactly one serving holder throughout: no overlap, no two-holders window, no gap with two.
  Net: the cluster never answered with a non-owner, and never answered with two owners. The serving-safety contract held end to end.

Availability evidence — DEGRADED (gap + tail), separate axis
  - Replacement serving began at 1.26 s: a ~1.26 s window where no holder was serving. That is an availability gap measured against user latency, not a serving-safety failure.
  - p99 1.8 s for ~70 s: elevated tail while the replacement acquired leases and any backlog drained.
  - No errors, no restarts: the degradation is acquisition/ramp latency, not a fault state.
  Net: users waited longer than the steady-state SLO; the system was not unsafe.

Why the availability delay is NOT stale-serving
  Stale-serving is "an old/revoked holder kept answering past its lease." Here the old holder stopped at 12 ms — correct serving-safety behavior. The 1.26 s is the time between "old holder correctly stopped" and "new holder correctly started," i.e. lease-transfer / replacement-acquisition latency. It is an availability number (how long did nobody serve?) and not a serving-safety number (did anyone serve when they should not have?). Collapsing them would mis-diagnose the drill and push the wrong control.

Per the shard-keeper runbook (rb_1789241064338, lease-convergence exit checks), the existing post-failover gates are already satisfied by what you reported (one holder at all times, no stale-owner traffic past the gate). What is missing is the latency-side picture, which is what a threshold change actually depends on.

Measurements Alex should collect before touching a lease-transfer latency threshold

1. Per-stage decomposition of the 1.26 s. Where did the time go? At minimum:
   - t_failover_trigger → t_candidate_elected
   - t_candidate_elected → t_candidate_ready
   - t_candidate_ready → t_lease_acquired_on_replacement
   - t_lease_acquired → t_first_successful_response_served
   Without this split, "1.26 s" is a black box and any threshold change is uninformed — tightening it may move the bottleneck, loosening it may hide a real regression in one stage.

2. Replacement-candidate readiness timing in this drill. The March 18 staging drill showed a ~5x gap between `ready` and lease convergence (18 s vs 96 s). Mirror that comparison here: when did the chosen replica report `ready` relative to 1.26 s? If `ready` happened at, say, 200 ms and lease acquisition ate the rest, the threshold belongs on the lease path, not the readiness path.

3. Lease-renewal interval for this shard. The runbook requires "two full lease-renewal intervals" of stale-owner watch; the threshold change needs the same number to size the watch window and to know whether 1.26 s is inside one interval, exactly one interval, or several.

4. Lease-epoch timestamps on both sides. When did the new holder's epoch first appear, and when did the old holder's epoch last appear? Monotonic advance across the cluster is a precondition (per the runbook entry); without the timestamps you cannot tell whether 1.26 s includes an epoch-revocation round-trip.

5. Cause of the old holder's 12 ms gate closure. Voluntary step-down, lease-revoked, or fenced. Each implies a different latency budget: a voluntary step-down usually removes a revocation round-trip from the 1.26 s; a fenced closure usually adds one.

6. Baseline distribution of lease-transfer latency across prior drills and prod failovers. Percentile-by-percentile (p50 / p95 / p99 / max), not a single observation. A threshold should sit at a chosen percentile of the empirical distribution; one drill at 1.26 s is not a distribution.

7. Shape of the 70 s p99 tail. Flat elevation, falling tail, or bimodal? If it tracks a backlog drain, the relevant number is queue depth at t=0 and drain rate, not raw p99. If it is bimodal (early ramp vs late stragglers), the threshold needs sub-buckets.

8. Request volume during the drill. Latency under load is not latency at idle. Was the 70 s tail load-correlated, and how does the load compare to the production traffic profile the threshold is meant to protect?

9. Scope of "no errors." Confirm explicitly: zero 5xx to clients, zero timed-out client connections, zero internally-logged errors during the 1.26 s window. "No errors" in this report is clean, but a threshold change should be defended on the strictest of those three readings.

10. Whether "replacement serving began at 1.26 s" means first-byte-of-first-request, first-successful-request-bucket, or first-quantile-stabilized. The choice changes the number by tens to hundreds of milliseconds and changes where the threshold lands.

Rule of thumb before any change: do not edit the threshold until items 1, 2, 3, 6, and 8 are on paper for at least this drill plus the prior N drills. The other items harden the picture but those five are what make the threshold defensible.

STOP CONDITIONS (any one trips; first three are rollback, server-health is stop-and-assess)

1. Deadline
- Any single request at or above 3.0s e2e.
- OR ingest-client p99 e2e ≥ 2.5s sustained over a 5-minute window during the canary (vs the synthetic observed max 2.24s — gives ~10% buffer above what we've actually seen, not above the deadline).

If observability can't tell us which attempt the server processed, that's the stop — it doesn't matter whether the actual count was 1 or 2.

- Post-transmission retry observed even once. The synthetic reported retries only after explicit connection-acquisition failure before transmission; a retry after the request was transmitted is a behavior regression, hard stop.

Given the freezer ambient reached 24°F (well below the 40°F danger threshold) and nothing leaked, this is mostly a salvageable incident. One item goes, two stay. The critical reading is the freezer's peak ambient temperature — because it never crossed 40°F, the standard 2-hour danger-zone discard rule doesn't apply to the meat or fruit.

Below is the breakdown using current USDA guidance. The three buckets you asked for: REFREEZE, COOK PROMPTLY, DISCARD.

ICE CREAM (soft)
Category: DISCARD
The 24°F freezer reading alone doesn't tell you the ice cream's actual temperature. Ice cream softens and loses structure well below its own melting point — typically soft/scoopable around 20-25°F and fully liquid around 10-15°F depending on fat and sugar content. At 24°F ambient after 3 hours, the carton has likely gone through significant structural breakdown.
  - Per USDA, ice cream that has melted should be discarded, not refrozen. The reasoning is structural: refrozen melted ice cream develops large ice crystals, emulsion breakdown, and a grainy/icy texture that is unpleasant to eat even when safe.
  - Dairy also warrants more caution than other foods because of Listeria and other pathogen history.
  - If you want to be technical: ice cream that is still semi-firm (soft-serve consistency, holds a peaked shape) could be refrozen, but expect noticeable quality loss. Liquid = discard, no question.
  - Throw it out. The replacement cost is low relative to the risk and quality tradeoff.

CHICKEN BREASTS (sealed, firm ice crystals, ~30°F surface)
Category: REFREEZE or COOK PROMPTLY — both are safe
This is the easiest call. All your indicators are favorable:
  - Sealed package = no contamination during the thaw
  - Firm ice crystals present = still mostly frozen through, not deeply thawed
  - 30°F surface reading is well below the 40°F danger threshold
  - During the open period, the chicken's core likely tracked 5-10°F above ambient — putting it in the high 20s to low 30s at peak, still well below 40°F
  - 3 hours is below the 2-hour-at-above-40°F discard rule
Two good options, pick based on when you'll use them:
  - Refreeze now if you won't cook within 3-4 days. Safe; texture/moisture may suffer slightly on thawing.
  - Cook promptly (within 1-2 days) and refreeze the cooked dish. Better end quality — cooked chicken holds texture better than twice-frozen raw chicken, and you get a ready meal.
Discard only if: any off odor, slimy texture, or discoloration when you open the package. Smell is your best safety test here.

FROZEN BERRIES (partly thawed, 34°F)
Category: REFREEZE
  - 34°F is below the 40°F danger threshold
  - Remaining ice means no significant bacterial growth window opened
  - Fruit is generally more forgiving than animal products
  - USDA: berries with ice crystals that stayed below 40°F can be refrozen; safety is not in question
Quality note: refrozen-thawed berries will be noticeably softer/mushier than original. Best uses after refreezing are smoothies, baking, cooked sauces, or jam — not as a standalone fruit where texture matters.
Discard only if: visible mold, off odor, or a fermented/alcohol smell when you open the bag.

GENERAL CLEANUP NOTES
  - Wipe down the freezer interior and the drawer with a mild bleach solution (1 tbsp bleach per gallon of water) or hot soapy water before restocking. Condensation from the thaw is a breeding surface for bacteria and mold, especially in the drawer gasket and any drip areas.
  - Check your freezer thermometer accuracy. Hanging air thermometers can read several degrees off from the actual food temperature. A small thermometer sealed inside a cup of water (or in a bag of crushed ice water) gives a more reliable reading.
  - If the freezer rises above 40°F for more than 2 hours in any future incident, the discard rule applies to all perishable frozen food regardless of how it looks or smells.

Bottom line: toss the ice cream, keep and refreeze the chicken and berries, sanitize the freezer, and you're back to normal.

This is similar to the 7/30 interdigital abrasion — superficial flap on a pad edge, no FB or infection signs — so the same general approach applies, with a few pad-specific notes.

Immediate cleaning (do once now)
- Rinse the paw under lukewarm water or a dilute chlorhexidine solution (the blue chlorhexidine, diluted to a pale tea color; or just plain water if that's what you have). Gentle stream, ~30–60 seconds.
- Pat dry with a clean cloth or paper towel. Do not rub the flap.
- Do NOT use hydrogen peroxide (cytotoxic to healing tissue), rubbing alcohol, or undiluted chlorhexidine on the wound itself.
- Do NOT apply Neosporin/antibiotic ointment right now — pads contact ground and he'll lick it off; ingestion of the petrolatum base can cause GI upset, and ointments on pads just pick up dirt. If a vet subsequently decides it's needed, they'll prescribe a pad-safe option.

Should you trim anything yourself?
- Do NOT trim the flap. Even a loose-looking pad flap is usually still partially vascularized and acts as a natural biologic dressing. Cutting it can re-open a wound, cause bleeding, and remove tissue that would otherwise re-adhere or slough cleanly on its own.
- Trimming hair around the paw is fine if needed to keep the area clean and to see the wound clearly — use blunt-tip scissors and cut parallel to the skin, not pointing into it. Keep hair out of the wound bed.
- If over the next 24–48 hours the flap turns dark/black, leathery, and clearly non-viable, a vet can trim it under sedation; that's a clinic job, not a home job.

Protection
- Keep him from licking. Licking macerates the wound and slows healing more than almost anything else. If he's licking repeatedly, use an e-collar (the rigid plastic cone or a soft inflatable/comfy collar) — measured to extend just past the nose when he lowers his head.
- A bitter-tasting deterrent spray (e.g. bitter apple) on the fur just above the pad can help, but it must not get into the wound.
- Booties: brief use only — put one on just before the walk for pavement/grit protection, and remove it immediately after coming inside. Leaving a bootie on indoors traps moisture and macerates the pad, which makes things worse. If he won't tolerate a bootie, skip it; cleanliness and dryness indoors matter more than outdoor coverage.
- Between walks: paw dry, no licking, no soaking. Skip baths/swimming until healed.

Walk limits for the next 48–72 hours
- Short elimination walks only — out and back, paved or familiar clean surface. No long walks, no hikes, no rough terrain, no hot pavement (back-of-hand test: if you can't hold it on the asphalt for 5 seconds, it's too hot for him).
- Avoid tall grass, weeds, and seed-head areas (foxtails/awns migrate into wounds — relevant risk in many areas).
- No running, jumping, or rough play until the flap is stable.
- Wipe and dry the paw after every outing, even if he didn't obviously dirty it.
- Recheck the flap at 24 hours and again at 48 hours. Most superficial pad flaps like this re-adhere or form a firm scab within 2–3 days if kept clean, dry, and lick-free.

Signs that mean URGENT (ER or same-day vet, not a wait-and-see call)
- Active bleeding that doesn't stop with gentle, steady pressure applied for 10 minutes.
- A visible foreign body still embedded (thorn, glass shard, grass awn) — pulling it yourself can drive it deeper.
- Paw held completely off the ground, or sudden severe lameness.
- Rapidly spreading swelling, especially tracking up the leg; heat that's obvious to the touch.
- Purulent (yellow/green/grey) discharge, foul odor, or any discharge that looks like pus rather than clear fluid.
- Cold, pale, blue, or dark-purple toe pad — vascular compromise.
- Flap torn further or pad torn deeper, exposing the fatty digital cushion underneath (yellow, lobulated tissue).
- Aggressive, non-stop licking/chewing that you can't interrupt — risk of self-trauma escalating.
- Systemic signs: lethargy, refusing food, fever, vomiting.

Signs that mean REGULAR vet care (call the office, appointment within 24–48 hours)
- Redness that's the same or worse at the 48-hour mark instead of settling.
- Mild clear or pink-tinged oozing that persists beyond the first day.
- A loose flap that hasn't re-adhered by day 3 and is clearly dangling, or that flips up with each step.
- A mild limp that doesn't resolve by 48 hours.
- Any crack, fissure, or second wound developing nearby.
- You can see the flap starting to lift and a raw wound bed underneath.

If none of those develop and the flap looks calmer/drier at 24–48 hours, you're on the right track and he likely won't need a visit at all — same disposition as the 7/30 event. If you do end up calling, mention the prior 7/30 abrasion so they can compare healing trajectory.

Kibo's soft-but-formed stool with no blood, vomiting, lethargy, or appetite change is in the mild/recovering range after a 7-day antibiotic — antibiotics commonly disrupt gut flora, and what's happening now is consistent with that rather than a red flag.

HOME PLAN (next 24-48h)
- Small, frequent bland meals: boiled skinless chicken + plain white rice, no seasoning/oil/bones (roughly 1/3 chicken to 2/3 rice). 3-4 small meals instead of normal portions.
- 1-2 tbsp plain canned pumpkin (NOT pie filling — no sugar/spices) stirred into a meal can help firm stool.
- Fresh water always available. If he's not drinking normally, low-sodium chicken broth (no onion/garlic — check the label) to encourage intake.
- Resume his normal diet gradually over 2-3 days once stool firms.
- Optional, vet-approved: a canine probiotic (FortiFlora, Proviable) is reasonable post-antibiotic; just mention it to his vet at next contact so they know.

DO NOT GIVE WITHOUT VET ADVICE
- Human anti-diarrheals — Imodium/loperamide dosing is dog-specific and can be unsafe; Pepto-Bismol contains salicylates. Both can also mask a worsening picture.
- Dairy (yogurt, milk, cheese) — many dogs are lactose intolerant; it usually makes loose stool worse.
- Table scraps, fatty/rich/fried food, bones, new treats/chews during this window.
- Anything with onion, garlic, chives, grapes, or xylitol.
- Human probiotics not labeled for dogs (some contain xylitol or strains not suited to dogs).
- Stopping, restarting, or extending any medication on your own.
- Fiber supplements (psyllium, etc.) without guidance — dose matters.

CALL HIS REGULAR VET (non-urgent)
- Soft stool persists past 48h, or trends worse (looser, more frequent, larger volume).
- Any new mucus, blood, or black/tarry stool.
- Appetite drops meaningfully, or vomiting starts (even once), or water intake drops.
- New lethargy, abdominal discomfort, hunching, or repeated unproductive posturing to poop.
- Separately: Kibo's pad from 9/2 still has its own recheck triggers (redness spreading, discharge, worse weight-bearing, no clear improvement at 48h). Those apply to the paw independently of the GI picture — if anything on the pad changes, that's also a regular-vet call.

SEEK URGENT/ER CARE
- Repeated vomiting, especially retching without producing anything, or can't keep water down.
- Large-volume bloody or profuse watery diarrhea.
- Collapse, severe weakness, pale or tacky gums.
- Distended/bloated abdomen with restlessness or unproductive retching (bloat — higher concern for deep-chested breeds; I don't have his breed noted).
- Suspected toxin ingestion.
- Extreme lethargy or unresponsiveness.

When in doubt, his regular vet can triage by phone and direct you to urgent care if needed.

The bounded observation is sufficient evidence to convene a release review. The release decision itself — removing the time bound — is a separate act and still requires explicit decisions.

Sufficiency of the bounded observation

The 100% rollout produced clean data against every relevant gate:

  - Numerical stop did not fire. 70 deadline hits over 81,760 requests (~0.086%); peak rolling 10-minute rate 0.098%. Volume is large enough that the rate is signal, not noise, and stayed below whatever threshold the numerical stop encodes.

  - The consistency invariant held. Every deadline case retained observable `accepted` state and none was retried; there were zero duplicate request identifiers. Read together: the client treated deadline-reached requests as committed on the server side and did not retry, and the server side never observed (or never acted on) duplicates. End-to-end consistency preserved.

  - Connection-acquisition failures were correctly bounded. 82 pre-transmission failures were retried once and only once — the safe boundary, since no data has left the client yet. They did not surface in error rate or p99.

  - Downstream health baseline held. ingest-edge error rate and p99 stayed within 6% of pre-push baseline for the full hour. No reload/restart, no dropped series, no parity regression — none of the rollback-class triggers fired.

  - Window discipline held. Single bounded 100% push under an owner-led window; baseline restored afterward. Not a recovery push.

That is a clean window. It belongs on the table for a release decision.

What is still required before removing the time bound

A clean bounded observation is necessary; it is not the release decision. Removing the bound is a separate act that requires three explicit decisions, none of which the observation itself provides:

  1. Cross-service determination. Per the Feb 27 framework, Alex is the final approver on cross-service releases, scope limited to cross-service invariants, failure modes, ownership seams, and escalation boundaries. The question for `ingest-client#87` is whether removing the bound changes an invariant, failure mode, or ownership seam visible to another service — e.g., ingest-edge SLO behavior under sustained 100%, retry/duplicate semantics visible to downstream consumers, error-rate attribution. The owner must state the determination explicitly. If cross-service, a fresh Alex decision is required to remove the bound. If contained to ingest-client/ingest-edge with no seam change, the owner can proceed under owner-led window authority.

  2. Monitoring ownership for the unbounded state. While bounded, deadline-hit rate, p99, and error rate were watched as part of window discipline. Once the bound is off, three things need a named owner: who watches the deadline-hit rate long-term and at what threshold it pages; who owns the ingest-edge error budget that the observation kept within 6% of baseline; and where the rollback trigger lives — client config, ingest-edge rate-limit, or deploy pipeline. This must be declared before the bound comes off, not after; otherwise the safety net the bounded observation provided disappears without a replacement.

  3. Explicit rollback criteria for the post-bound state. The bounded window's rollback criteria were implicit in the gates. The unbounded steady state needs named triggers — deadline-hit rate threshold over a defined window, p99 rise over baseline, duplicate-ID detection, etc. — and a named owner for the rollback call. This is the runbook entry for the steady state, and it should exist before the bound is removed.

Distinguishing the two

  Bounded observation answered: "Does 100% rollout behave correctly under observation?" — yes.

  Release decision answers: "Do we keep it at 100% without the time bound, and who watches it?" — not yet decided, and not automatic from a clean window. A clean bounded observation removes the need for further bounded pushes; it does not by itself authorize the unbounded steady state.

Practical next step: owner states the cross-service determination, declares the post-bound monitoring owner and thresholds (and rollback triggers), and — if cross-service — requests the fresh Alex decision. Once those three are recorded, the bound can come off.

REPACKING SEQUENCE (8 book boxes → under 35 lb, apt + 1 shelf row still usable)

Goal: shed ~7-13 lb per box. Books are the only thing in them, so we redistribute books, not add filler. Towels/linens get used to stabilize the small boxes in the truck, not to hide weight.

Phase 1 — Stage (10 min)
  - Put the 6 small boxes, a bathroom scale, a roll of packing tape, and a sharpie in one spot.
  - Pull 4-6 bath towels and a fitted sheet within reach.
  - Clear ~3 ft of floor next to the heaviest box pile.

Phase 2 — Weigh and rank (15 min)
  - Weigh each book box (stand on scale holding it, subtract your weight; record on the box flap).
  - Sort boxes into: heaviest (46-48), middle (43-45), light (42-43). The "light" ones may not need touching.
  - Weigh or eyeball the 6 small boxes empty so you know the tare (~1 lb each).

Phase 3 — Redistribute by weight, not by topic (45-60 min)
  - Open one heavy box at a time. Pull the densest items first (textbooks, hardcovers, coffee-table books, board games).
  - Sort pulled items into three buckets:
      A. "Small box" — paperbacks and small hardcovers only. Cap each small box at ~30 lb hard (paperbacks pack tight fast). That gives you ~180 lb of redistribution capacity across 6 small boxes, more than the ~80 lb you need to shed.
      B. "Usable shelf row" — the row you designated. Leave it accessible: do not pack anything from it. It stays as your working library through the move-out window.
      C. "Towel bundle" — anything awkward (odd-shaped hardcover, single art book). Wrap 2-4 books in a bath towel burrito-style; these go on top of linens in a suitcase or duffel for transport.
  - Re-weigh each original box. Target 32-33 lb, not 35 — that gives margin for the mover to grab without re-gripping.
  - Re-tape and re-label.

Phase 4 — Close out (10 min)
  - Each small box gets a soft item (towel, t-shirt, pillowcase) as 2 inches of top padding before sealing, so paperbacks don't shift.
  - The one usable shelf row: face the spines out, leave a clear path to it, and put a piece of painter's tape across it that says "DO NOT PACK" so anyone helping you later sees it.
  - Stack the now-compliant book boxes last on the truck (top of load, against a wall) so nothing crushes them.

Net: 8 boxes now under 35 lb, 6 small boxes in service, towels used as padding, one shelf still browsable.

DRYWALL ANCHOR PATCH (two ordinary anchors, no paint today, paint-ready later)

Assumes the common plastic conical anchors (the kind that came with a shelf or mirror). If either anchor is a molly or toggle, see the note at the bottom.

1. Remove the screw first. Phillips or drill on reverse-out.
2. Back out the anchor. Grip the flange with needle-nose pliers and rock it side-to-side while pulling straight out. It will come. If it spins freely without backing out, tap it slightly INTO the wall cavity with a hammer until the flange sits just below the paper face — do not crush the paper around it. This is the standard "punch and patch" move; the hole is now internal and you only have a small dimple to fill.
3. Trim. Run a fresh utility knife blade around the hole to cut any raised or fuzzy paper. Wipe with a dry cloth.
4. First coat. Lightweight spackle (DAP DryDex goes on pink, dries white — useful for spotting missed spots). Press it into the hole with a 1-inch putty knife, slightly overfilling. Let dry per label.
5. Sand. 150-grit sanding sponge, light pressure, just flush with the wall. Knock the dust off with a dry cloth, then a barely-damp cloth.
6. Second coat if needed. Any visible depression or anchor outline gets one more thin pass, dry, sand.
7. Stop here. The patch will be visibly matte-white against paint but structurally and visually acceptable for the handoff walkthrough. Paint (or just a dab of primer on the spot) can happen any time before handoff.
8. Mark it. Put a small arrow of painter's tape next to each patch with "SPACKLE — TOUCH UP" so neither you nor anyone helping forgets.

Optional upgrade (still not "painting today"): one light pass of a quick-dry primer (Zinsser Bulls Eye 1-2-3, or any latex primer) over the patch takes 5 minutes and makes the spot disappear under any paint later. Strictly optional.

If one of the anchors is actually a molly bolt or toggle:
  - Molly: unscrew the bolt, then grip the metal sleeve and rock it out the same way. If it won't budge without tearing the paper, cut the head off with a hacksaw blade or snips, push the rest into the cavity, and patch as above.
  - Toggle: tighten the bolt until the toggle drops into the cavity, then patch the resulting ~1/2-inch hole the same way (you may want a self-adhesive aluminum patch screen behind the spackle for that size — any hardware store, $3).

Order of operations for the day: do the anchor patch FIRST while the boxes are still stacked against the wall and you have clear access. Then repack. Anchors take 20 minutes for both; you won't want to do them after the shelves come down.

WHAT'S WORKING

The fact that he settles the moment his bed is back in its usual corner tells you the anchor is intact. The plan below is built around not breaking that anchor.

SAFE AREA SETUP

Pick one room or one corner that packing does NOT enter. That space stays as static as possible for the rest of the packing phase. In it:

    His bed stays in the usual corner. Don't rotate, don't wash the cover, don't replace it.
    Water and food bowls stay put, on the usual schedule.
    A worn t-shirt or blanket of yours draped on or near the bed. Your scent is doing more work than any product.
    A long-lasting food toy (stuffed Kong, Toppl, lick mat with wet food) given only when a packing block starts, so it becomes the "good thing that happens when boxes move" association.
    A baby gate, closed door, or exercise pen to physically keep him out of the active packing zone. He's following you between rooms because the rooms keep shifting; the gate removes the choice and lowers his vigilance.
    Optional low-cost additions: an Adaptil diffuser in that room's outlet, and a calm-music or white-noise playlist to mask tape and stretch-wrap sounds.

If he already likes a crate, that can be his den instead of the bed-corner. Same principle: familiar, covered, undisturbed.

ACTIVITY TIMING AROUND PACKING BLOCKS

    1. 30 to 45 minutes before a block, take him on a sniff walk or do a 10-minute scatter feed in the yard. The goal is to lower arousal, not tire him physically.
    2. Block starts. Settle him in the safe area with the stuffed toy, close the gate, and pack outside that room.
    3. Keep blocks to 60 to 90 minutes max, then a real break: tools down, sit on the floor near him for 10 minutes, let him re-check on you.
    4. Hold meal times and walk times to his normal clock. Predictable routines matter more right now than the volume of exercise.
    5. For the loudest stretches (tape guns, stretch wrap, furniture shifting) either schedule them during his walk or have someone keep him company. Save the noisiest work for one block and recruit a friend, dog-walker drop-in, or sitter for that window if you can.
    6. Avoid packing right before you leave the house. He should not associate your departure with the sound of boxes.

BEHAVIORAL AND PHYSICAL SIGNS THAT WARRANT VETERINARY ADVICE

Call your vet sooner rather than later if any of these show up. They cross from manageable stress into a welfare or medical concern.

Behavioral:

    Pacing or following that does NOT stop when his bed is back in the corner and the room is quiet. His current pattern is "settles when bed returns." If that breaks, it is escalating.
    Sudden destructiveness aimed at doors, crates, walls, or windows.
    New guarding, snapping, or growling at people he has known.
    Hiding combined with refusal to come out for meals or treats for more than a few hours.
    Restlessness at night, inability to settle for sleep across two nights.
    House-soiling when previously reliable.

Physical:

    Panting at rest that does not resolve within 10 minutes of packing stopping.
    Trembling or shaking when the environment is calm.
    Repeated vomiting, or any diarrhea, especially with blood or mucus.
    Refusing food or water for 24 hours, or refusing treats outright. He currently takes treats, so treat refusal in a food-motivated dog is a meaningful signal.
    Excessive licking of a paw or flank to the point of raw skin.
    New limping or stiffness.

If you see one physical sign plus a behavioral one, that is a same-day vet call, not a wait-and-see.

ONE OPTIONAL PREP FOR THE MOVE ITSELF

If the move is soon, start a parallel plan for the new place: bring his unwashed bed cover and a worn item of yours into the new space first, set up the corner before he arrives. Same anchor, new walls.

PLAN: One-pan chickpea-spinach rice with hard-boiled eggs and lemon-yogurt sauce.

Why this solves the holding problem:
  - Hard-boiled eggs sit safely in cold water in the fridge for 2+ hours. You cook both portions of egg NOW; yours goes on the plate warm, hers waits in the fridge in cold water and is at safe, just-cooled texture by 9:30.
  - Spinach gets wilted INTO the rice (steamed under the lid), not left as loose leaves. Braised in starch it does not oxidize or go brown/soggy over the next hour.
  - Rice pilaf holds covered off-heat for an hour and reheats in 4-5 min with a splash of water. Yogurt sauce holds cold with no last-minute work.
  - Active time: ~25 min. Cleanup: 1 pot, 1 pan, 2 small bowls, 1 cutting board.

TIMELINE (assuming 7:15 PM start):

7:15  Eggs into a small pot, cover with cold water, high heat. While it heats:
      drain chickpeas, rough-chop spinach, pull yogurt + lemon + spices.

7:25  Water boils. Timer 9 min. Meanwhile, wide lidded skillet over medium:
      oil, then 1 tsp cumin, 1/2 tsp coriander, pinch chili, 30 sec.
      Add chickpeas, toss 1 min. Add 1 cup rice, stir 30 sec.
      Add 1.5 cups water + big pinch salt. Simmer.
      Scatter spinach on top (do NOT stir — lid-steams it clean). Cover, lowest heat, 18 min. Do not peek.

7:34  Eggs into ice bath (or cold running water in a bowl). Peel under running water.

7:40  Rice done. Kill heat, keep lid on. Halve eggs. Plate YOUR portion now:
      scoop of rice, one warm egg half, dollop of lemon-yogurt sauce, cracked pepper.
      Eat. You have 5 min before the walk starts.

7:45  Walk Kibo. Before you leave:
      - Devika's egg halves into a small bowl of cold water, into the fridge.
      - Rice stays covered on the counter (or lowest heat if your kitchen runs cold).
      - Yogurt sauce stays cold.

8:15  Back. Loosely cover the rice pan or move to fridge — either works.
      Yogurt sauce is fine on the counter.

9:25  Reheat her rice: low heat, splash of water, lid on, 4-5 min. Plate rice,
      her egg (drained from cold water), yogurt sauce, pepper.

9:30  Devika walks in to a hot plate.

NOTES:
  - If you only have 2 eggs (one each), this still works — just one half per plate.
  - If you want her egg warmer than just-cooled: in the last 2 min of rice reheating,
    nestle her halves into the pan with the splash of water, lid on. Comes out warm.
  - The spinach stays bright because it was never submerged and never sat alone.
    That is the whole trick.

Session plan — mild lumbar stiffness, no red flags, sub-max volume.

Goal: keep Tuesday session light enough that Saturday's packing block starts with the same back you have now, not a worse one.

1. Warm-up (~15 min, non-negotiable)

Cardio ramp (5 min): easy bike or row, just enough to warm tissue, not enough to fatigue the back.

Ground mobility (~5 min):
  Cat-cow x 10, slow, full breath each rep
  World's greatest stretch, 5 each side
  90/90 hip switches x 8/side
  Glute bridge x 10 with 2-sec pause at top
  Dead bug x 8/side — strict, back pressed flat. If you cannot keep neutral, drop dead bugs and just do more bridges.

Wall ramp (~5 min): easy traversing at waist height, no dynamic moves, gradually increase angle. End with two problems well below your max grade (V0–V2 range, whatever that is for you). Stop here if stiffness hasn't loosened. If still tight after 10 min on the ground, consider it a sign and reschedule to Thu.

2. Movement limits for the session

  No compression problems (squat starts, roof jams, anything that loads the lumbar vertically).
  No drop knees, no cross-body reaches, no big rotational moves.
  No dynos, no deadpoints, no campus moves, no max-effort lock-offs.
  No high feet that pull the lumbar into deep flexion.
  Keep arms bent. Straight-arm hangs load the back more than bent-arm climbing at the same grade.
  Climb with legs. If a move wants you to pull with the back, downclimb or step off.
  Submaximal effort only — RPE ≤ 7. Treat this session as movement quality, not grade.
  1–2 attempts per problem. If it's not clicking quickly, move on. No projecting today.
  Plan the descent — drop from low holds, land with bent knees, don't compress on landing.

3. Volume cap

  Aim for 6–8 problems total, spaced out. Sit and rest 3–5 min between problems, walk around between sets. If you hit 5 problems in 40 min and feel fine, stop there. More is not better today.

4. Stop criteria — leave the wall immediately if any of these hit

  Any sharp pain, anywhere in the back.
  Any referral down the leg or into the glute.
  Numbness, tingling, or sudden weakness in either leg.
  Pain at rest that wasn't there before (you said none now — protect that).
  Pain during a rep that is worse than the warm-up baseline.
  Lumbar fatigue that makes neutral-spine climbing hard to hold — sloppy form is the precursor to a tweak.
  Any "catch" feeling, even a brief one. Walk away.
  Hard cap: ~50 min wall time. Harder cap: 6 problems. Whichever comes first.

5. After the session

  Walk out, hydrate. If anything feels tight in the next hour, gentle heat (warm shower / heating pad 15 min), not ice — stiffness responds to warmth. No stretching the back into flexion today; gentle extension (cobra press-ups x 10) only if it feels relieving, never forcing range.

6. Saturday decision rule

Your instinct to give yourself an out is the right one. Here is the order I'd attempt, with a hard stop after attempt 2.

ATTEMPT ORDER (lowest cosmetic risk first)

1. Rubber band in the socket.
   Lay a flat strip of rubber band across the stripped hex socket, then press the original-size hex bit firmly into it. The rubber fills the rounded-out corners and gives the bit fresh bite. Use steady, even downward pressure. No hammer, no ratchet. Try once. If it does not break free, stop and reassess.

2. Next-size-up hex bit.
   The larger bit should drop into the existing socket profile and contact the high points the smaller bit skipped. Apply firm hand pressure and slow, even torque. Stop the instant you feel the bit cam out or the socket start to mushroom. If it spins without biting, the socket is done. Go to the brace plan below.

3. Painter's tape plus manual screwdriver (only if 1 and 2 both failed and you accept cosmetic risk).
   Fold painter's tape into the socket to pack it denser, then use a flat-head that matches the socket width. Expect possible marring of the wood around the opening. This is the last step before giving up.

WHAT TO SKIP
Locking pliers on this screw. The socket is recessed in the wood, so the pliers cannot grip the screw head without slipping onto the surrounding wood and crushing the finish. Higher cosmetic damage than the screwdriver method, with no better odds of removal.

WHEN TO STOP AND BRACE
Stop and brace the bookcase the moment any of these is true:
  - The rubber band attempt did not release the screw on the first real try.
  - The next-size-up bit cammed out even once.
  - You see any mushrooming of the socket walls or any scuff or crush on the wood around the screw.
  - You have spent more than about five minutes of total effort.

You have already met every condition that matters for the move: the structure is rigid, there is no wobble, no cracked wood, and the assembled remainder fits through the doors. A stripped socket does not change that. The remaining risk of pushing further is purely cosmetic damage to a joint you do not need to free today.

BRACING THE JOINT FOR THE MOVER
Goal: keep the one connected side panel from swinging open or shifting during the move.

Using what you have on hand:
  1. Cut a piece of cardboard to span the corner. It should be wide enough to wrap onto both faces of the joint (side panel plus adjoining rail) and long enough to cover roughly six inches along each face.
  2. Bend the cardboard into an L that hugs the inside corner of the joint.
  3. Wrap painter's tape tightly around the joint and cardboard, four to six passes, pulling the tape taut as you go. Each pass should overlap the previous by half its width.
  4. The cardboard spreads the pressure so the tape does not print through to the finish.

Then:
  - Put a piece of painter's tape on a visible face of the bookcase and write on it: "Loose side panel, handle as one piece, do not tilt."
  - Tell the mover verbally when they arrive. The brace is invisible from outside, so the verbal handoff is the actual safety step.

That gives you a fully rigid, move-ready piece without risking the wood finish on a screw that is not actually blocking the move.

Recommendation: certified check.

Reasoning:

The $55.80 is the only argument for the card, and it buys you nothing. The receipt, the settlement timing, and the mover's relationship are identical either way — the 3% is just the mover passing through their processor fee. You aren't trading speed for cost, because you have the check in hand by Thursday; you're just paying $55.80 for the privilege of adding a third-party dependency (terminal, network, processor, issuer auth) at the worst possible moment.

The risk asymmetry is the deciding factor. With a check you've already obtained, the only failure modes are "lost it" or "forgot it" — both entirely under your control. With a card, the failure modes are external: terminal down, signal gone, processor hiccup, fraud hold on a large charge, declined for an unexpected reason. Any of those at 3:55 PM with a 4:00 PM building cutoff is a problem you can't fix in the room. With the check, your worst case is a trip back to the car.

Operational:
- Get the check Thursday and put it directly in the folder/envelope with the moving documents. Don't remove it until you're handing it over.
- At unload end: check → signed receipt → building management before 4 PM.
- The receipt is your protection against any "we never got paid" claim, same as a card charge record would be — so you're not giving up anything on that axis.

Net: $55.80 saved, and you remove a meaningful failure mode from the critical path. Easy call.

COLD-CHAIN DECISION

Items and what they need:
- Yogurt, milk, cooked lentils, raw spinach, raw eggs: keep below 40F. All go in the cooler.
- Frozen berries: keep frozen if possible, but partial thaw is recoverable if you use them the same day.
- Condiments: most opened jars (mustard, ketchup, hot sauce, soy, vinegar) tolerate a few hours at room temp. Skip the cooler for these — they ride on the truck and you free up cold space for what actually needs it.

Why this works: the truck carries non-perishables and condiments; you carry perishables in the car on the late-morning South Slope trip. Realistic cold-chain window is roughly 7:30-8:00 AM (when food leaves the Park Slope fridge) until you can put it back in a South Slope fridge — probably 2-4 hours total. With four packs and a medium cooler, you have more cold capacity than you need for that window, which is exactly the margin you want.

COOLER PACKING (cold-sink method)

Pre-chill: if the cooler has been sitting warm, drop one frozen pack in, close the lid, and let it pull the interior down for 15-20 minutes before loading food. Skip if the cooler has been stored somewhere cool.

Load order, bottom to top:
1. Two frozen packs flat on the bottom — the cold base.
2. Densest, highest-water items in the middle: the milk carton and the two lentil containers. Thermal mass benefits most from being surrounded by cold.
3. Eggs still in their carton (the carton cushions and protects — don't break eggs out into a bag).
4. Yogurt, then spinach in its bag with the air squeezed out.
5. Two remaining frozen packs against the sides and on top — surround the food with cold.
6. Frozen berries last, at the very top so you can pull them straight into the freezer on arrival.

Stuff a folded towel or paper into any air gaps. Tight packing holds cold; air pockets let it escape.

CAR PLACEMENT

Passenger compartment or footwell, never the trunk. A closed trunk in sun runs 10-20F hotter than the cabin. Keep the cooler shaded — a reflective sunshade draped over it adds a real margin. Avoid opening it repeatedly; each opening is a cold leak.

TEMPERATURE CHECK ON ARRIVAL

Probe the center of one of the lentil containers — it's the densest item and tells you the worst case.

- Under 40F: everything is fine, put it all straight into the fridge.
- 40-50F: still safe — you've been under 2 hours above 40F, well inside the limit. Refrigerate and plan to use milk and yogurt first over the next day or two.
- Over 50F: the chain broke. Yogurt and milk are the canaries — discard if they smell or taste off. Cooked lentils, eggs, and spinach tolerate this range better; still use them that day, cooked through. When in doubt, throw it out.

Wipe the probe between items.

FIRST-NIGHT MEAL: LENTIL AND SPINACH FRITTATA

Uses almost everything in one pan, ~25 minutes, minimal cleanup — right call for a moving day.

Ingredients: 4-6 eggs, both portions of cooked lentils, roughly half the spinach (save the rest for breakfast), a small splash of milk, salt and pepper, a tablespoon of oil or butter.

Method:
1. Heat the oven to 375F if using it. In an oven-safe skillet, warm the oil. Add the chopped spinach with a pinch of salt and cook just until wilted, 1-2 minutes.
2. Whisk the eggs with the milk and a pinch of salt. Pour over the spinach. Scatter the lentils across the top, pressing them in slightly so they don't all sink.
3. Stovetop-only path: cover and cook on the lowest flame 10-12 minutes until the center is just set. Oven path: cook on the stovetop 3-4 minutes until the edges set, then transfer to the oven for 10-12 minutes.
4. Cut into wedges. Good warm or at room temperature.

Side: yogurt with the frozen berries. Thaw the berries on the counter for 10 minutes, or eat them half-frozen like a granita. Finishes off the last perishables.

Leftover frittata keeps 3-4 days in the fridge, so this also covers lunch the next day.

All five cold-sensitive items fit in one medium cooler with four packs. No waste expected if the probe reads under 50F on arrival. Condiments ride the truck. First-night meal consumes nearly everything except half the spinach — minimal leftovers to think about.

The glare is a reflection problem: sun comes through the window, hits the right monitor's screen, and bounces into your eyes. With the window unobstructed as a hard constraint, the cleanest fix is to redirect the reflection rather than block the sun.

Recommended, in order of effectiveness and disruption:

1. Right monitor (do this first - 30 seconds, zero layout change):
   Pivot the right monitor on its swivel base so its face is parallel to the window wall rather than angled inward toward you. In a typical dual-monitor setup each screen angles toward the user - that inward angle is exactly what catches the side-window reflection and bounces it straight at your face. Rotating the right monitor so its face points more toward the window (or directly away from it) sends the reflected sun back toward the window instead of into your eyes. If the monitor stand only allows tilt and not swivel, tilt the top edge 5-10 degrees back toward the window instead - that redirects the bounce toward the ceiling.

2. Shade during 2:30-4 PM only:
   Drop the upper third of the shade and leave the lower two-thirds open. Afternoon sun enters through the top of the window at that hour, so shading the top portion cuts most of the direct glare while the window stays clearly visible from below - it is not "blocked," just filtered at the angle that matters. If the existing light-filtering material is too sheer to fully solve it, clip a temporary panel over that upper strip for those 90 minutes.

3. Skip desk rotation:
   The Ethernet run along the baseboard and the chair's door clearance both work as-is. Rotating the desk to chase 90 minutes of daily glare would disturb the layout you just verified works - not worth it when #1 alone should solve the reflection.

4. Skip the lamp:
   Repositioning a lamp adds fill light, which can reduce perceived contrast in dim rooms, but it does not stop a direct sun reflection bouncing off glass. Do not bother unless #1 and #2 still leave the right monitor washing out on Monday.

Net plan: adjust the right monitor's angle now, test it at the window during a glare window this afternoon if possible, and stage the partial shade close as the 2:30-4 PM backup for Monday. Total time on the layout itself is under five minutes.

Quick clinical read first so you know where I'm coming from: the picture — bilateral, symmetric, worse with eccentric load (stairs), relieved by warmth, no focal sharp pain, no neuro/vascular/systemic findings — fits exertional myalgia / DOMS from two move days, not a structural injury. Devika's call (no more lifting tonight) is the right one. Plan below.

TONIGHT (conservative)
  - Stop lifting. Anything left in boxes that needs moving waits for tomorrow or for help. This is the single highest-yield thing.
  - Hydration: aim for clear-pale urine by morning. Moving + stair-climbing + (probably) sweating depletes volume, and under-hydration is what makes DOMS feel worse and what tips mild muscle injury toward rhabdo.
  - Protein + carbs at dinner and a snack before bed (e.g. dinner protein source + a small bowl of cereal, milk, or a banana with yogurt). Muscle repair needs substrate, not just time.
  - Analgesia: acetaminophen 500-1000 mg PO, up to 3 g/24h, OR ibuprofen 400-600 mg PO with food, up to 1200 mg/24h OTC. If you have any renal, GI, or liver history pick one rather than both; either is fine for an isolated night.
  - Heat vs ice: since warmth already helped and there's no acute swelling, stick with warmth — 15-20 min warm shower, hot pack, or heating pad on the sorest spots before bed. Skip ice unless a specific spot becomes acutely tender or swollen.
  - Gentle movement: short walk around the block or up/down one flight, slow, just to keep things from stiffening overnight. No stretching to "work it out" — that mostly just adds eccentric load on already damaged fibers.
  - Sleep position: if shoulders are worst, avoid sleeping directly on them; a pillow under the arm or a slight side-lying rotation off the shoulder helps. For thighs, a pillow under the knees if on your back.

SUNDAY PICKUP SOCCER
  - Default: skip it, or play only if morning self-check passes. DOMS from a move weekend typically peaks 24-72 h after the trigger, so Sunday morning is exactly when you'll be at your worst. Sprinting, cutting, and kicking on freshly damaged thigh and shoulder girdle muscles is a real strain/tear risk and meaningfully worsens next-week soreness.
  - If you really want to play, gate it on all of these being true at wake-up:
      1. Pain is symmetric, diffuse, and ≤ 4/10 at rest.
      2. No focal tenderness — pushing on any one spot is not dramatically worse than the surrounding muscle.
      3. Stair descent is nearly normal (the stairs test is the most sensitive of yours).
      4. No swelling, no bruising, urine is normal color.
      5. You can jog in place pain-free for 2-3 minutes.
  - Even if all pass: warm up 10-15 min before touching a ball, avoid max-effort sprints and high kicks for the first 15 min, and stop the moment anything focal or sharp shows up. Substituting as goalie or half-field walking is a reasonable middle path.
  - Tell the group you're coming off a move weekend and may sub yourself out early; that's a normal sentence.

WARNING SIGNS — seek same-day medical evaluation (urgent care / ED) if any of these appear, now or overnight:
  - Urine turns dark brown, tea-, or cola-colored, especially with decreased output. This is the rhabdomyolysis signal and is time-sensitive (hydration within hours matters).
  - Severe pain out of proportion to what you'd expect from soreness, especially in one calf or thigh, or pain that worsens rather than improves over the next 24-48 h.
  - Focal swelling, a palpable lump, or new bruising in one limb that wasn't there tonight.
  - Calf or thigh becomes hot, swollen, tender along one side, especially with no trauma that explains it — DVT window after prolonged exertion plus dehydration is real, even if the absolute risk is low.
  - Numbness, tingling, or weakness in a limb, or pain that radiates — none of which you have tonight.
  - Inability to bear weight, a joint that locks or gives way, or a pop you can localize.
  - Chest pain, pressure, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, or cough — none of which you have tonight, but exertion plus dehydration plus age plus any cardiac history changes the threshold.
  - Fever > 38 C / 100.4 F, or chills — argues for something other than pure DOMS.
  - Soreness that is still clearly worsening past 72 h rather than plateauing or improving.

If none of those appear and Sunday morning feels like the typical DOMS curve, you can resume light activity and treat it as a normal week. If it lingers past Tuesday with no improvement, that's worth a non-urgent primary care visit — not an emergency, just a check-in.

None of this is a substitute for being seen, and I'm an AI not a clinician, but the pattern you described is reassuring and the plan above matches what you'd get from a sports-med or primary care colleague tonight.

IMMEDIATE SAFE RESPONSE

  What you described is the textbook low-battery chirp: one beep ~every 60 sec, LOW BATTERY on the display, no symptoms in either adult, and your independent plug-in CO monitor is clear. That's reassuring, but treat the next few minutes as confirmatory, not as dismissal.

  1. Confirm the pattern. Press and hold the TEST button on the unit for ~5 seconds. You should hear its full alarm pattern (a loud repeating 3-beep for smoke, or 4-beep for CO) regardless of battery state. That proves the unit still functions and isn't currently detecting an event.

  2. Silence the chirp for tonight if you can't get a replacement battery right away. On most combination units, holding the silence/test button for about 10–15 seconds quiets the low-battery chirp for roughly 8 hours. Check your model's manual for the exact hold time, since it varies by manufacturer.

  3. Replace the backup battery. Even on hardwired units, the chirp means the 9V (or AA / lithium) backup cell is dead. Twist the unit off its mounting bracket, swap the battery, remount it, and press TEST again.

  4. Check the manufacture date stamped on the back of the unit. If it's more than 10 years old, that's an end-of-life chirp and a fresh battery will not fix it — replace the whole alarm.

  5. If the chirp returns after a known-good battery, replace the whole unit. Don't keep silencing a chirping alarm indefinitely — it costs you the protection the device exists to provide.

HOW TO TELL A LOW-BATTERY CHIRP FROM AN ACTIVE ALARM

  Low-battery chirp:
    one short beep every 30–60 seconds, constant cadence, no acceleration, often paired with LOW BATTERY (or BAT) on the display, no voice announcement.

  Smoke alarm (fire event):
    three loud beeps, pause, three loud beeps, repeating — the "T-3" pattern. Display or voice typically says FIRE.

  Carbon-monoxide alarm (CO event):
    four loud beeps, pause, four loud beeps, repeating — the "T-4" pattern, deliberately distinct from smoke. Display or voice says WARNING: CARBON MONOXIDE or shows a ppm reading.

  End-of-life:
    chirp every ~30 seconds with END or REPLACE on the display. A fresh battery will not silence it; the entire unit must be replaced.

WHEN TO LEAVE OR CALL 911 INSTEAD OF TROUBLESHOOTING

  Leave the apartment immediately and call 911 from outside (or a neighbor's) if any of the following is true:

    The unit is sounding a repeating 3-beep or 4-beep pattern, not a single chirp.
    The display reads a CO ppm value or shows CARBON MONOXIDE / GAS.
    Anyone in the home has headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, blurred vision, or flu-like symptoms without fever — including Kibo, since pets typically show CO signs (restlessness, lethargy, vomiting) before people do.
    More than one person or pet feels unwell at the same time, even mildly.
    You smell something unusual — sharp chemical odor, gas, or burning with no visible source.
    You can't confirm what the unit is doing (no display, no second CO monitor, no way to test it).

  Do not open windows first if you suspect CO — just get out. Fire department will measure the atmosphere with a calibrated meter before you re-enter. Do not go back in until they've cleared both the unit and the air.

  If none of those triggers apply and the pattern stays a single chirp with LOW BATTERY on the display, you're safe to troubleshoot as above.
