Pressure verdict (bottom line)

Both readings sit inside the 50-75 psi sidewall spec, with the rear ~3 psi higher than the front — that's the correct direction for weight distribution (rear carries ~60% of rider+gear load on most frames). At 33°F ambient, your gauge is reading true cold pressure; no warm-to-cold correction is needed (a tire filled at room temp would lose ~6-7% pressure cooling to 33°F, but you measured outdoors). The values are slightly below the geometric middle of the range, which is conservative and actually beneficial in cold/winter conditions because the larger contact patch improves grip on slick surfaces.

There is no tire-pressure-based reason not to ride. The bigger exposure here is surface ice in shaded patches, which the checklist below treats as a separate domain.

Pre-ride checklist

Tire-pressure concerns
  1. Confirm the readings haven't drifted since you measured (cold tires, valve straight, gauge seated). If anything feels soft on a thumb-press test, re-measure before mounting up — but no re-pressurization is needed otherwise.
  2. Visually re-scan sidewalls and tread for the same defects you already cleared (bulge, exposed casing, new cuts). Cold rubber hides casing damage less than warm rubber, so a second look at the contact patch and sidewalls is cheap insurance.
  3. Check that the valve stems are seated straight and caps are finger-tight; a slow leak that you can't hear indoors becomes obvious in cold air.
  4. Note: don't top off just to hit mid-range. Mid-to-lower in the spec is the conservative cold choice.

Surface-ice risk
  1. Feel the air on exposed skin — if 33°F is also windy, frost will have formed on shaded asphalt even where the road looks dry.
  2. Look at your planned route from memory: where are the north-facing slopes, tree-canopy streets, bridge decks, overpasses, underpasses, metal drainage grates, painted crosswalks, and curb edges? These freeze first and dry last.
  3. Brake test at walking speed in the driveway or at the start of the ride — confirm both brakes still bite cleanly in the cold; cable-actuated brakes lose a few percent of power when wet or icy.
  4. Lights on, even daytime — shaded patches in winter are dim and ice is hardest to read in low contrast.
  5. Visibility layers: clear or photochromic lenses if you wear glasses, since cold + wind fogs them.

Route plan

  - Prefer sun-exposed streets, south-facing slopes, and well-trafficked arterials (other cars do your road-clearing).
  - Avoid or descend cautiously: bridges and overpasses (cold air underneath freezes them even when ambient is above 32), shaded north-facing grades, alleys with poor drainage, leaf piles (wet leaves are nearly as slick as ice), metal grates and painted surfaces.
  - Keep the loop short and out-and-back if possible so you retreat along a known-warm path rather than committing to a long cold return.
  - Tell someone your route and expected return time — cold-weather mechanicals or falls warrant a quicker check-in than summer ones.

Stop conditions (any one of these ends the ride)

  - You see a visible glaze, rime, or reflective sheen on the road surface ahead.
  - You feel a skid, wash, or any single wheel losing traction — even a small one. It means the next patch will be worse.
  - A tire pressure change: audible hiss, sudden handling change, or visible bulge/cut that wasn't there at the start.
  - Brake performance degrades noticeably, or a brake starts rubbing/squealing in a new way.
  - Numbness in fingers or toes that affects braking, shifting, or balance — cold injuries compound fast on a bike.
  - Planned time limit reached; in near-freezing temps, planned duration should be ~70% of what you'd ride at 50°F because cooling and metabolic cost both rise.

Separation, in one line: tire pressure is a non-issue here — 55/58 in a 50-75 spec at 33°F is conservative and correct. The ride's risk lives entirely in the surface-ice domain, and the checklist treats that as a visibility, routing, and early-stop discipline problem rather than a tire-pressure one.

ASSESSMENT: ORDINARY CHARGER WARMTH

Normalizing to 70°F room temp:
  Brick:        104°F  (ambient +34°F)
  Plug body:     76°F  (ambient + 6°F)
  Outlet face:   77°F  (ambient + 7°F)

Why this reads as normal:
  - Most quality 65-100W USB-C bricks (Apple, Anker, GaN third-party) measure
    100-120°F at the hottest spot under sustained 60W+ draw. The plastic case
    IS the heatsink; surface temp is expected to rise.
  - The outlet face is only ~6-7°F above ambient. A failing outlet (loose
    backstab, worn contact, undersized for load) typically runs 15°F+ above
    ambient at the face, because resistance at the contact interface is where
    the heat lives.
  - The brick-to-outlet delta is ~28°F, with heat flowing OUT of the brick
    (designed) rather than BACK from the outlet. That's the healthy direction.

Likely cause: near-full 65W draw (CPU/GPU work + depleted battery). As the
battery tops off, the brick should cool.

SAVE THESE NUMBERS AS BASELINE. Re-measure in the same three spots after
30 min and 2 hr. Trend should be flat or falling as charge completes —
NOT a monotonic climb.

SAFE MONITORING (during normal use)

  - Re-measure brick / plug / outlet at 30 min and 2 hr from cold start.
  - Hand test: distinctly warm, never painful to hold 5+ seconds.
    Comfort cutoff is roughly 115°F; ~120°F is the "too hot to hold" line.
  - Listen for new or rising coil whine / buzz. Some whine at light load
    is normal; loud or growing = degradation.
  - Confirm laptop still reports expected charge rate (Battery / power stats).
  - Place brick on a hard, non-flammable, non-insulating surface. Don't
    bury it under paper, fabric, or in a drawer — the case + convection
    is its only cooling.

UNPLUG NOW IF ANY OF THE FOLLOWING

  - Brick too hot to hold comfortably (>120°F / 49°C at the surface).
  - Any smell: sweet, ozone, burnt plastic, or fishy (electrolytic cap venting).
  - Any discoloration on brick, cable strain-relief, plug pins, or outlet.
  - Buzzing that's new, louder, or coming from the outlet rather than the brick.
  - Laptop charging drops in/out, or brick status LED changes behavior.
  - Plug feels looser than before, OR outlet face starts approaching brick
    temperature (heat conducting back through the plug = failing contact).
  - Any sparking, scorch marks, or melting on brick / cable / plug / outlet.

ELECTRICIAN ESCALATION CRITERIA

Call an electrician for any of:
  - Outlet face >100°F under load (anything >25°F above ambient is suspicious;
    >30°F means real resistance at the contact).
  - Buzzing from the outlet itself, not the brick.
  - Outlet feels loose when inserting/removing the plug.
  - Discoloration, scorching, melting, or cracking on the outlet or plug pins.
  - Breaker tripping under normal charger load (a 65W brick on a 15A circuit
    pulls ~0.55A — a trip means a different load shorted or the breaker is bad).
  - Warmth reproduced on other outlets in the same room (panel/wiring issue,
    not the charger).
  - Outlet is backstab-wired (push-in termination) on a high-load circuit —
    these fail more often than side-screw terminations; recommend converting
    to side-screw.

BUILDING / MANAGEMENT ESCALATION

Relevant if this is in a leased office, coworking, or shared space where the
wiring belongs to the building:
  - Multiple outlets or neighboring units showing similar symptoms — points
    to a common cause or panel issue rather than a single device.
  - Building-side damage (scorched panel, tripped building breaker).
  - Per lease, infrastructure electrical is landlord's responsibility —
    forward any of the above electrician findings to building management.

OWNER-SIDE NOTE

If Devika's laptop and brick are hospital-issued (likely, given charting on a
shared work-room setup), the brick is organizational property. Replacement
lifecycle belongs to the hospital, not personal. If any of the unplug-now
criteria ever trigger, request a replacement through IT/MDU rather than
buying personal.

BOTTOM LINE

This looks like ordinary duty-cycle warmth, not a failure precursor. The most
reassuring signal in your numbers is the outlet face being only 6-7°F above
ambient — that's a healthy, low-resistance contact. The single most useful
ongoing habit is to feel the outlet face once when she first plugs in
(record it) and recheck monthly; it should stay near ambient.

Backup-first sequence for Anya — 512 GB drive, 9 GB free, Nov 5 backup stale
===============================================================================

WORKING SPACE TARGET (direct answer)
- A major macOS update typically needs 25–35 GB of free space; a minor/security update needs ~15–20 GB.
- On her 512 GB drive, target at least 35–40 GB free before clicking "Update Now" — that means reclaiming at least 26–31 GB from the current 9 GB.
- Leave headroom: the updater builds its own working set, and a post-update cache rebuild can take another few GB transiently.
- If macOS itself asks for more space mid-install, let it purge local snapshots and iCloud-evictable files automatically rather than retrying with less free.

STOP CONDITIONS — do not proceed past these if any are true
- External drive is encrypted and the password isn't known / drive hasn't been unlocked since Nov 5.
- macOS doesn't see the drive, or shows the wrong volume (e.g. a partition that's been reformatted).
- Time Machine shows a backup chain error, "Backup disk image could not be created," or any red banner.
- She has not verified that today's backup completed and contains her recent files.

PART 1 — VERIFY A FRESH BACKUP (do this before touching storage)

1. Plug the external drive directly into the laptop. Avoid hubs/docks if possible; if unavoidable, confirm the dock has its own power.
2. macOS will likely prompt "Do you want to use this drive to back up with Time Machine?" → click Use Backup Disk.
3. If no prompt: Apple menu → System Settings → General → Time Machine. Confirm the disk is selected. Toggle it off and back on if needed to force re-detection.
4. If the drive is encrypted and macOS asks for a password: enter it and choose Remember This Password in My Keychain.
5. Open Time Machine in System Settings and click "Back Up Now" (or right-click the Time Machine menu-bar icon → Back Up Now).
6. Watch the menu-bar icon. When it returns to its idle (non-spinning) state, the backup is done. First backup after a 5.5-week gap can take several hours depending on what changed.
7. VERIFY: enter the Time Machine timeline. The most recent entry must be dated today (Dec 14, 2024). Step back through time on 2–3 different files (a recent document, a recent photo) and confirm older versions exist. If the latest backup is still Nov 5, stop and investigate.

PART 2 — LET LOCAL SNAPSHOTS RELEASE (this is the biggest single win)

Time Machine keeps local snapshots on the boot drive as a buffer when the external isn't connected. Connecting the external and completing a fresh backup causes macOS to thin these snapshots automatically.

- After the backup completes, wait ~10–15 minutes without rebooting. macOS will reclaim the now-redundant local snapshots.
- This alone often reclaims 10–40 GB on a drive that's been off-backup for weeks. From 9 GB free, this step frequently takes her to 30+ GB before any manual cleanup.

PART 3 — CHECK STORAGE BREAKDOWN

Apple menu → About This Mac → More Info → Storage tab → wait ~30 seconds.

Note two things:
- Available vs Purgeable: macOS distinguishes truly free space from space it will reclaim on demand (local snapshots, iCloud eviction, caches). Purgeable is fine — it counts toward what the updater will use.
- The category breakdown (Apps, Documents, Mail, Photos, System, Other). It tells her where the bulk is.

PART 4 — SAFE MANUAL CLEANUP (in this order)

4a. Empty Trash. Often 1–10 GB sitting unnoticed.

4b. ~/Downloads. Delete .dmg/.pkg installers after install, duplicate PDFs, mail attachments that are also in Mail, old zip files. Do not delete anything she can't redownload or doesn't have elsewhere (receipts, tax docs, etc.).

4c. Old iOS device backups — usually the single biggest hidden category:
    ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/
    Each device backup can be 10–50+ GB. Sort by size in Finder. Delete backups for devices she no longer owns or has already replaced with a different backup. This does NOT delete data on the iPhone/iPad itself — it only removes the on-laptop copy.

4d. Mail housekeeping: Mail → Mailbox → Erase Junk Mail, then Erase Trash. In Mail → Settings → Accounts → Advanced, reset the attachment cache. Mail's main database in ~/Library/Mail should NOT be touched manually (see "DO NOT DELETE" below).

4e. Browser caches: small (0.5–3 GB) and self-rebuild. Optional.

4f. Developer caches if any are present (safe to delete; regenerate on demand):
    ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData
    ~/.cache/Homebrew
    ~/Library/Caches/com.docker.docker
    ~/.npm, ~/.next, .yarn build caches
    Old .ipsw files if she's an iOS developer

4g. Large files by size: Finder → Recents → sort by size, OR System Settings → General → Storage → Manage → Review Files → Large Files. Move or delete.

PART 5 — CONFIRM SPACE BEFORE UPDATING

- About This Mac → Storage must show ≥ 35 GB free (purgeable + available combined).
- If still short, revisit 4b (Downloads) and 4g (Large Files). If Photos is large (>100 GB), consider Settings → Photos → Optimize Mac Storage to keep thumbnails local and originals in iCloud. This is reversible but worth deciding deliberately.

PART 6 — RUN THE UPDATE

- System Settings → General → Software Update → Update Now.
- Plug into power. Stable network. Do not close the lid. Do not interrupt.
- If the updater asks for more space mid-install, let it auto-purge — do not cancel and retry.

PART 7 — POST-UPDATE VERIFICATION

- After reboot: log in, open Mail/Messages/Photos, confirm apps launch.
- Confirm the external drive still appears as a Time Machine destination and that an hourly backup has resumed.
- Do not delete or reformat the external drive until at least one verified post-update backup has completed.

DO NOT DELETE MANUALLY
======================

In ~/Library (anything outside the paths listed in Part 4):
- ~/Library/Mail — Mail's message database. Even "cache" folders here can force Mail to rebuild or lose state.
- ~/Library/Messages — Messages history and attachments.
- ~/Library/Containers — sandboxed app data for many modern apps.
- ~/Library/Keychains (login.keychain-db) — saved passwords, certificates, Wi-Fi credentials.
- ~/Library/Application Support in general — only delete the specific MobileSync/Backup/* entries in Part 4c.
- ~/Library/Caches in general — only the specific dev/cache entries in 4f. Random cache folders look deletable but some are app boot-critical.
- Anything owned by "root" or "system" — that's macOS itself.

In user folders:
- Pictures/Photos Library.photoslibrary — the canonical master. Deleting it deletes the originals.
- Documents, Desktop, Downloads subfolders with current work — review first.
- Anything from iCloud Drive folders without confirming it's elsewhere or backed up.

On the backup drive:
- Any Backups.backupdb folder, the sparsebundle, or .MobileBackup folders. Touching the Time Machine volume can invalidate the entire backup chain.

General:
- Files she's not 100% sure about.
- Files found by a third-party "cleaner" app (MacKeeper, CleanMyMac, etc.). The built-in Storage tab is the only authoritative view; commercial cleaners routinely flag system files and silently purge user data.

EDGE CASES WORTH FLAGGING

- If the external is encrypted and the password was forgotten: stop. A factory reset of the drive means losing the Nov 5 backup. Recover the password first.
- If she has multiple iOS devices tethered regularly, MobileSync/Backup is almost certainly the largest reclaimable category and is worth checking before anything else.
- If the backup disk has been used for anything else since Nov 5 (different Mac, file storage, formatting): the chain may be broken. Time Machine will tell her at first connection — if it offers to "start a new backup," decline and investigate rather than accept.
- If the update itself fails partway through with a "not enough space" error despite ≥ 35 GB free: boot into Safe Mode (hold Shift at startup) and re-run the updater from there — Safe Mode clears some caches the regular boot cannot.

The execute-style tool isn't available in this environment, so I'll work the arithmetic by hand (the numbers are small and exact).

**Headline numbers**

- Per-day use, prior: 252 / 30 = 8.400 kWh/day
- Per-day use, new: 286 / 31 = 9.226 kWh/day
- Δ per-day use: +0.826 kWh/day, about +9.8% on a per-day basis

That +0.83 kWh/day is the real-use delta once you strip out the extra day in the billing period. It's the single most important number, because the bill total ($90.52 vs whatever prior) mixes three things you have to separate: more days billed, more kWh used per day, and estimate reconciliation.

**Why the "estimated" flag on the prior reading matters**

An estimated read isn't wrong, but it is a guess. Two ways the new bill can look higher even if your actual usage didn't change:

1. The Nov 11 estimate was too low → the utility "under-billed" the prior period → the catch-up kWh get pushed into the next bill, making Dec's usage appear inflated even though your real consumption was steady.
2. The estimate was too high → the prior bill was over-stated → Dec's bill looks like a drop, not a rise. (Not your case here, since Dec is the higher one.)

You can't tell which way the estimate went without the raw readings, which is exactly why the meter readings matter more than the kWh totals on the face of the bills.

**The comparisons you need before calling or disputing**

Pull these four items first; they answer every other question:

1. Prior bill: the START meter reading and END meter reading for the 30-day period (the one ending Nov 11). The bill shows only the END reading and that it was estimated. The START reading is the one you need to confirm.
2. New bill: the START meter reading and END meter reading for the 31-day period ending Dec 12 (actual). New bill gives you the actual END reading — you need the START reading too.
3. Actual cumulative kWh across the combined 61-day span: (new END reading) − (prior START reading). That is the ground-truth consumption for the whole window, independent of any estimate.
4. The prior bill's supply charge, delivery charge, and total new charges (the dollar split, not just kWh), so you can compare per-kWh rates apples-to-apples.

Once you have those, run three checks in this order:

Check A — Estimate reconciliation. Subtract the prior period's billed kWh (252) from the actual kWh used in that same window (new START reading − prior END reading). If actual was, say, 270 kWh, then ~18 kWh of "Dec usage" was really Nov catch-up, and ~34 kWh is true December use. If actual was 250, then Dec is genuinely ~36 kWh above Nov's real pace. This single check tells you whether to dispute or accept the kWh number.

Check B — Per-day normalization. Compare 8.40 vs 9.23 kWh/day (computed above). Anything within ~10–15% is plausibly weather/behavior driven for a winter billing period in NYC (heating load, shorter daylight, more indoor time). Anything beyond that is worth a question, not necessarily a dispute.

Check C — Rate check. Compute implied $/kWh on the new bill: 90.52 / 286 ≈ $0.3165/kWh. Split it: supply 34.32 / 286 ≈ $0.1200/kWh, delivery 56.20 / 286 ≈ $0.1965/kWh. Compare both halves to Con Ed's published tariff for your service class (the bill header lists the rate class — usually a "SC" or residential rate code). If the supply or delivery $/kWh has crept up versus the prior bill, part of the $90.52 is rate, not usage. That's not disputable, but it's worth knowing before you call so you don't argue about the wrong line item.

**Which readings actually matter, ranked**

1. New bill START reading (the number you don't have yet — call or check the online account).
2. Prior period START reading (same).
3. New bill END reading (actual, 12/12 — on the bill).
4. Prior period END reading (estimated, 11/11 — on the prior bill).

Readings 1 and 2 are what unlock Check A. Without them you can do Check B and Check C but not the estimate reconciliation, and the estimate flag is the part most likely to make the bill look "wrong" when it's actually correct.

**What to do with the result**

- If Check A shows the estimate was off by a lot (say >20 kWh) and Check B per-day use is close to the prior, the bill is mostly estimate catch-up, not real increased use. Pay it but ask the utility to correct the estimated read going forward, or request a real meter read.
- If Check A shows the estimate was close and Check B shows a real per-day jump, the usage increase is genuine — look at weather (HDD for the period), any new appliance, occupancy changes, and a heat-pump/space-heater draw before disputing.
- If Check C shows a rate change larger than Con Ed's filed tariff allows, that's a bill error worth disputing in writing.

# Assessment: Layered SDK Validation + Server 413 Backstop (Option D / Hybrid)

The owners' layered candidate is structurally different from the three options previously framed: it combines client-side pre-transmission rejection (in the SDK) with a server-side deterministic 413 (the December 5 replay contract) as a backstop for nonconforming clients. That's not Option A (per-client 2,000-point cap), not Option B/C (server soft rejection with partial-resend semantics), and not "documentation only." It's worth taking seriously on its own terms, then comparing honestly.

## What this candidate actually proposes

- SDKs reject batches >8,000 points *before transmission*, return an error to the caller, and instruct the caller to split.
- Ingest-edge retains the validated December 5 contract: 413, zero accepted points, rejected_points = submitted, reason `oversized_batch`.
- Two current clients adopt SDK validation immediately; one older client relies on the server backstop initially.
- The 8,000-point threshold and the 413 envelope are not changed.

## Strengths relative to the other options

1. **The server contract is already replay-verified.** The December 5 replay (25,000/25,000 with deterministic 413, zero accepted, exact accounting, compliant requests unchanged) is the strongest evidence in this whole workstream. The candidate does not re-litigate that.
2. **It moves the failure from "accepted at server, then partially or atomically rejected" to "client never sends an oversized batch."** For adopting clients, the 413 path is exercised only by older/nonconforming clients and during SDK upgrade windows — the bulk of traffic shifts to a cheaper, pre-transmission rejection. This compresses the surface area of the contract without weakening it.
3. **It is owner-aligned.** Client-side validation is in the SDK owners' lane; server backstop stays with ingest-edge. No cross-service invariant gets crossed (413 is still 413; 429 admission refused; 503 internal failure).
4. **It does not require partial-resend semantics, idempotency-key subsetting, or per-point identification on retry.** The known gap (OTLP receiver's rejected-points count may not give clients enough information to subset retries) becomes moot for the two adopting SDKs because they reject before sending.
5. **It does not collapse the threshold to 2,000.** The fleet-wide 99.6% / 0.4% tail distribution stays handled; only the 0.4% tail gets rejected, and only the older client population initially drives that through the 413 path.
6. **Tail risk reduces over time as SDK adoption increases.** The 413 backstop's load is expected to decay; the contract is needed but rarely exercised.

## Failure modes specific to this layered candidate

These are the honest questions, not advocacy against it.

**A. Two-layer correctness drift.** The SDK validates "above 8,000 points"; ingest-edge also validates "above 8,000 points." If the two definitions ever diverge (counting scope: pre- or post-attribute validation? raw vs. decoded? after retry coalescing? including rejected points from a prior attempt in the same request?), the layered design produces the worst kind of bug: clients that pass SDK validation and still hit 413, or clients that fail SDK validation when the server would have accepted. The December 3 staging wrapper fix (duplicate `Content-Encoding: gzip`) is a reminder that two-layer encoding contracts drift in practice. **Evidence needed: a single canonical counting spec, used by both SDKs and ingest-edge, with test fixtures that exercise boundary cases (8,000 vs 8,001, post-attribute-filter count, count after dedup within request).**

**B. The older client's experience.** For the one client that does not adopt SDK validation, the candidate is functionally identical to the standalone 413 option — it will hit the server backstop. That means whatever evidence you would require for a standalone 413 (production measurement at the 8,000-point threshold, retry/correctness/support-load behavior) is still required for *that subset of traffic*. You don't get to skip that evidence just because the candidate is "layered." The replay validated the wire behavior; it did not validate what the older client does on receiving 413 (does it retry, split, page someone, drop?). **Evidence needed: production canary or shadow for the older client class specifically — observed behavior on first 413, split latency, support tickets during the observation window.**

**C. SDK error surface becomes user-facing.** A pre-transmission SDK rejection is a new client-visible failure mode. Callers have to be told to split. If the SDK error message, error code, or documentation is ambiguous, callers will mis-handle it (retry unchanged → continue to be rejected locally forever; silently drop → data loss; retry forever after random backoff → local amplification). The November 21, 2024 proposal that asked clients to "retry using ordinary exponential backoff" was already blocked on this exact failure mode — plain exponential backoff on an oversized batch is unacceptable. The candidate dodges that for the server side but inherits it on the client side unless the SDK explicitly does not retry its own pre-transmission rejection. **Evidence needed: SDK rejection error contract documented; verified behavior of each adopting SDK on receiving the SDK-side error (no silent retry, no silent drop, clear split instruction); a fixture proving the SDK does not loop locally.**

**D. Caller code paths and observability.** When ingest-edge rejects, you have server-side counters (accepted, rejected, reason) and can dashboard the 413 rate. When the SDK rejects pre-transmission, those points never reach the server, so dashboards and quota/billing under-count submissions unless the SDK also reports the rejected count to telemetry. The unresolved "permanent batch disposition and persistence, audit, telemetry, retry-counter, quota, and billing treatment" list is *more* exposed under this candidate, not less, because a non-trivial fraction of "oversized" events now never reach ingest-edge at all. **Evidence needed: how attempted/accepted/rejected accounting reconciles when the SDK rejects pre-transmission; telemetry schema for SDK-side rejections; quota and billing treatment of locally-rejected points (do they count against the tenant's submitted-points quota?).**

**E. The 8,000-point threshold is the same across both layers.** That's good for consistency, but it ties the threshold decision to this candidate. If the right threshold turns out to be different from 8,000 (higher to reduce reject rate, lower to bound queue behavior), changing it is a coordinated SDK + server change across multiple client populations. The earlier distribution analysis suggested choosing 8,000 over 2,000 reduces the reject rate but does not reduce contract complexity — that observation applies here too. **Evidence needed: validated production distribution at 8,000 (replay was 25,000 requests; we don't know the steady-state population above 8,000 across all tenants, only that the bounded tail exists); confirmation that 8,000 is the right shared threshold rather than the SDK adopting a tighter bound and the server keeping a looser one.**

**F. Migration window and rollback.** The candidate assumes SDK validation is adopted per-client over time. During the migration, three behaviors coexist: SDK-rejecting clients (new path), the older nonconforming client (server 413), and any not-yet-upgraded SDK on the same version that previously emitted oversized batches. The two adopting clients are a sample, not the population — behavior of the rest of the SDK matrix during upgrade windows is unmeasured. **Evidence needed: upgrade-window telemetry for at least one full SDK-major-version rollout; rollback plan if SDK validation misfires (e.g., the SDK incorrectly rejects batches the server would have accepted).**

**G. The 88% utilization question does not disappear.** The Option A 2,000-point cap analysis modeled ~88% peak local client queue utilization. The layered candidate doesn't impose that cap — it uses 8,000. So local queue absorption under a 9,600-point burst (or higher, if nonconforming clients send larger batches) is a different curve. The 82% previously observed on a different client without the cap-shaped burst pattern suggests the upper bound is somewhere below saturation, but the candidate's specific burst shape (whole batch rejected client-side vs. 1.2× the cap split into compliant sub-batches) hasn't been replayed. **Evidence needed: replay or measured burst of the older client class at sizes above 8,000 to confirm local queue absorption and server backstop arrival rate stay within the existing envelopes (decode-wait p99 ≤131 ms baseline, request p99 ≤20 ms trigger threshold, retired gen <2).**

## Comparison to the other options, briefly

- **vs. Option A (hard 2,000-point client cap):** Layered candidate rejects ~0.4% of batches instead of altering API surface for the other 99.6%. Lower blast radius. But it requires SDK + server coordination and the older-client evidence Option A doesn't need.
- **vs. Option B/C (soft server rejection above 8,000 with Retry-After and partial-resend):** Layered candidate avoids the partial-resend problem entirely for adopting clients. Lower contract complexity. But it pushes the same correctness burden onto the SDK and onto callers, and leaves the older client on a server path that still needs the same evidence Option C lacks.
- **vs. documentation only:** Layered candidate is strictly more defensive — it actively prevents oversized traffic and bounds the older client to a deterministic server response. Documentation only leaves the reproduced latency path (the Oct 4 2.69 s p99 at 10k×10s) possible.

The layered candidate is the strongest *structural* option on the table, but the open evidence list is not shorter than Option C's — it shifts, with new items added (two-layer counting, SDK error surface, telemetry reconciliation, migration window) and old items preserved for the nonconforming client subset.

## Minimum evidence before permanent disposition

If you want a decision-ready package, the owners need to provide:

1. **A canonical counting spec** for "points per request" — same definition in SDK and server, with fixtures covering 8,000, 8,001, post-validation count, post-coalescing count, and behavior on the boundary.
2. **SDK error contract** for pre-transmission rejection: error code, message, retry/non-retry guidance, observable telemetry — confirmed by each adopting SDK owner in writing, with a fixture proving the SDK does not loop locally on its own rejection.
3. **Production-or-shadow evidence for the older client class** receiving 413: arrival rate, retry/split behavior, support tickets, quota/billing reconciliation, across at least one seven-day window with the canaried SDK changes live.
4. **Migration-window plan**: SDK matrix inventory, rollout order, rollback procedure if SDK validation misfires (rejects a batch the server would accept), and a stop condition consistent with the July 25 framework (retired ≤4, pauses ≤100 ms, full health baseline).
5. **Telemetry reconciliation**: attempted = accepted + rejected holds across both layers; SDK-side rejected points are observable to the platform with a bounded-cardinality reason field; quota and billing treatment of locally-rejected points is decided.
6. **Validated steady-state distribution above 8,000 points** across the full tenant population, not just the bounded tail replay sample — needed to size the backstop's load and confirm 8,000 is the right shared threshold.
7. **Canary plan with explicit abort criteria**, consistent with prior ingest-edge canaries (retired gen <2, p99 drift <20%, heap <10%, no dirty signals; soak past the failure point before promotion). Note the "no Friday/holiday/eve-of-long-weekend" rule for the watch window.
8. **Owner-map confirmation** that this remains SDK-team-led for client-side validation, ingest-edge-team-led for the server backstop, with the cross-service invariant (413 = oversized, 429 = admission refused, 503 = internal failure) explicitly preserved and re-stated in the runbook.

Assessment of the 2024-12-20 OTel collector staging load test
================================================================

Note up front: 2024-12-20 is a Friday, so even setting the framework aside, this is not a day a production push would land per the standing no-Friday/no-holiday convention.

1. Objectives vs. result
------------------------

Accounting (did all forwarded traffic reach the collector?):
  Met, within the bounded envelope. Edge-gateway forward counts match
  collector receipt counts across all three channels (gzip OTLP/HTTP,
  uncompressed OTLP/HTTP, gRPC) with no unexplained gap. The split
  across the three channels is accounted for rather than collapsed into
  a single aggregate, which is the right shape for this kind of test.

Valid-traffic preservation (does the collector preserve the quality
of the traffic it is asked to forward?):
  Met, narrowly. Error rate at 0.08% is at baseline (no regression),
  and p99 +4 ms is small enough to call negligible for a single
  bounded run. Nothing in the report indicates dropped series, parity
  loss, reload/restart events, or other 7/25-framework rollback
  triggers. The framework's retired<=4 / pause<=100ms gates are not
  explicitly reported in what you've given me, so I can only say the
  result is consistent with staying inside them, not that they were
  measured.

Stability under malformed input (does a hostile input class poison
valid traffic?):
  Met for the test as designed. All 200 deliberately malformed gzip
  requests were rejected; valid traffic was unaffected; no collector
  crash; no forwarding loop. That confirms the basic isolation
  property the test was designed to probe.

2. What this result does NOT authorize
--------------------------------------

It does not authorize any of the following, and treating it as
anything more than a staging result is the specific failure mode to
avoid:

  - A production push of any kind. Per the 7/25 framework, any prod
    push requires a fresh Alex decision after an owner proposal, with
    a full health baseline taken at push time and the
    retired/pause/health gates re-evaluated against that baseline.
    This test provides none of those.
  - A longer shadow. A 900K-request bounded run is not the same shape
    as the multi-day shadow the framework contemplates before a prod
    authorization; extending it is a separate owner proposal and a
    separate decision.
  - Load beyond the tested envelope. The test is bounded in request
    count, payload mix, duration, and concurrent-fault surface. It
    does not cover sustained peak, burst above the tested rate,
    realistic payload-size distribution, backpressure, disk/queue
    saturation, multi-tenant contention, network failure modes,
    mixed valid+malformed interleave at scale, adversarial payloads
    (gzip bombs, truncation, header smuggling), or collector
    restart/recovery under fault.
  - Skipping the owner-proposal step. The collector workstream owner
    still owns the implementation, telemetry, and release; the test
    result does not move that.
  - Treating the 0.08% / +4 ms numbers as a baseline. They are
    equal-to-baseline / negligible-on-this-run, not a baseline
    themselves. A new baseline must be captured at prod-push time
    under the framework.
  - Treating it as a precedent for adjacent changes. Wrapper,
    collector config, edge-gateway config, and pipeline provenance
    are distinct change surfaces; a clean result on one does not
    transfer to another.

3. Bottom line
--------------

The test met its accounting, valid-traffic, and stability objectives
as scoped. It does not authorize a production push, a longer shadow,
an extension of the envelope, or a bypass of the 7/25 framework. The
next step, if anyone wants to move toward prod, is an owner proposal
with a fresh Alex decision, not a re-read of this result.

Compatibility evidence reads as sound across the four dimensions that actually matter for the design choice:

1. Local pre-flight (both newer SDK languages): 50k attempts each, 100% rejected locally, zero network transmission. The local check fires and stops the oversized payload before it leaves the process, and both languages behave the same way.

2. Local semantic correctness: splitting the same data produced complete accepted-point accounting. The local rejection is not a lossy heuristic — it's semantically equivalent to "batch exceeds cap, split it, all points still land." No silent data loss.

3. Server-side validation (older client / ingest-edge path): 10k oversized attempts, each got a validated HTTP 413. The edge returns the right code — not silent accept, not 500, not a hang.

4. Older-client recovery: no unchanged retry on 413, succeeded after splitting. This is the dimension I'd most worry about (retry storms, edge amplification, backpressure), and it's not present.

The one item that didn't pass cleanly is the SDK error text on one language. The programmatic error code is correct, so any automation branching on the code works. The text just says "batch too large" without surfacing the 8,000-point cap — operators reading the message won't learn the actual number from it.

Position on whether to correct the text before the permanent design choice:

The text correction should not gate the design selection.

- Behavioral correctness is intact. All four compatibility dimensions above hold regardless of what the SDK string says.
- The framework gates I care about for this kind of change (consistency, parity, dropped series, reload, restart, retry behavior, edge validation) are all satisfied. The SDK string doesn't touch any of them.
- The text gap is independent of the design disposition. Whether the permanent design is "layered with 8k cap," a different cap, edge-only, or whatever, the SDK still ought to tell the operator the actual limit. Decoupling keeps each scope clean.
- It's a well-scoped, low-risk owner-led fix. It can land in the same window as the design rollout or as a small follow-up push; it doesn't need to be bundled into the design decision.

Worth raising as a follow-up but not a gate:

- If 8,000 becomes the permanent cap, the SDK error string becomes part of the long-term public contract. A "batch too large" message that doesn't name the number pushes every operator into docs or support to find it. Cheap to fix, real friction avoided.
- The 10k-attempt evidence is for one older client. The compatibility claim generalizes to "older clients that behave like this one" — no unchanged retry on 413, recovery via split. If there's a known variant that loops on 413 or doesn't split, that's an owner-side migration/rollout concern, not a design gate.

Within my scope (cross-service guardrails / escalation boundaries), the evidence supports proceeding to the owners' permanent disposition choice. The SDK text fix is a recommendation to the owner, not a condition on the design.

WHAT YOU'RE DEALING WITH
- A stalled burr grinder with a stone jammed in the burrs and a brief hot-electrical smell from locked-rotor current. The smell is the insulation off-gassing, not necessarily failing yet — but it tells you something got hotter than designed.
- Until the stone is out and the inspection below passes, treat the unit as "do not energize."

UNPLUGGED JAM-REMOVAL SEQUENCE
1. Confirm the plug is physically out of the outlet (not just switched off). Don't put fingers near the burrs until step 5.
2. Wait 5 minutes unplugged. If your grinder has any electronics (display, timer, dose counter, soft-start), the board's capacitors can hold charge for several minutes even with the plug pulled. The wait bleeds that off.
3. Remove the hopper. Tip beans back into their bag — check the beans for more stones.
4. Remove the upper burr / burr carrier per your grinder's normal disassembly. Use the release the manufacturer designed (latch, twist, or screw). Don't pry with metal — you'll chip the burr edges or bend the carrier.
5. With the upper burr out, the stone should be loose or easily accessible. Pick it out with a non-conductive tool: wooden chopstick, wooden skewer, plastic tweezers, or the grinder's own cleaning brush. Don't use a metal screwdriver inside the burr chamber.
6. Brush out ground coffee and chaff from both burrs and the grind path with a dry brush.
7. Don't reassemble yet — go to Inspection first.

INSPECTION (still unplugged, hopper and upper burr off)

A. Foreign-object check
   - Stone fully removed, no fragments under the carrier, in the chute, or between teeth
   - No packed chaff/grounds that would still stall the motor

B. Burr condition
   - No chipped, bent, or broken teeth on either burr
   - No browning, blackening, or scorch marks on the burr faces
   - Carrier sits flat — no warping

C. Burr rotation by hand
   - Place a wooden or plastic tool against the lower burr teeth and try to rotate. It should turn smoothly with light, even friction. Any scraping, catching, gritty feel, or wobble = stop here.
   - If you can reseat the upper burr by hand (still no power), rotate again — should still feel smooth and concentric.

D. Motor housing — exterior only, do not open
   - Sniff around the ventilation slots. Any lingering hot-electrical or burnt smell?
   - Look at the housing near the motor and around the switch: any discoloration, brown halos by the vents, melted sheen on the plastic?
   - Run your fingers along the entire cord, especially the plug and the strain relief where the cord enters the housing. Any stiffness, bulging, exposed copper, or discoloration?
   - Look at the plug blades: any darkening or pitting.

E. Switch feel
   - Press the on/off or pulse button with the unit unplugged. Mechanically normal — no looseness, sticking, or crunch.

F. Outlet (the one it was in)
   - Visual check of the face: any darkening or melt marks? You already said no heat — visual is still worth doing.

DECISION: TEST ONCE OR LEAVE OUT OF SERVICE

May test once — ALL of these must hold:
   - Stone fully removed, chamber clean
   - No chips, scorching, or discoloration on burrs or housing
   - No burnt smell from the vents after the chamber is clean
   - Burrs rotate smoothly by hand (with and without upper burr seated)
   - Cord and plug look and feel normal
   - Outlet face looks normal
   - Switch feels normal

Leave out of service (or replace) — ANY ONE of these:
   - Any scorch, brown halo, melted sheen, or discoloration on the housing, vents, burrs, or cord
   - Lingering electrical smell from the motor area once the burr chamber is clean
   - Cord stiff, discolored, or damaged at either end
   - Plug blades darkened or pitted
   - Burrs chipped or visibly damaged
   - Burr rotation rough, gritty, scraping, or wobbly
   - Outlet face shows any darkening
   - The grinder tripped an internal thermal fuse and won't reset via normal means

Why the conservative bar: a brief hot-electrical smell means insulation got hot enough to off-gas. Once windings or switch contacts have been thermally stressed, the next failure often happens later, under normal load, with no warning. The cost of a replacement grinder is low; the cost of a smoking outlet or a fire isn't.

If you do test once: plug directly into a wall outlet (no power strip, no extension cord, no surge protector — those can mask a fault), run it empty for 10–15 seconds with the hopper off, then stop it. Listen for new electrical noise (buzzing, crackling) and watch/smell for any new odor from the vents. If anything is off, unplug and retire the unit. If it's clean, you can run a small dose through and call it good.

ON THE MOTOR HOUSING — DON'T OPEN IT
- Some grinders (anything with electronics, larger induction-style motors, or a soft-start board) have capacitors that can hold a painful or dangerous charge even unplugged.
- Without a discharge resistor, a schematic, and the service manual, opening the case is the part most likely to hurt you or ruin the unit. The exterior checks above are the deepest safe inspection.

PREVENTING THE NEXT STONE
- Small pale stones in beans are almost always field stones that survived harvest and weren't removed at the roaster. Rare but real.
- A quick visual scan of beans before pouring into the hopper catches most of them. Sifting beans against a lamp makes pale stones easier to spot than under overhead kitchen light.
- Some people use a coarse mesh sieve to sift beans before grinding — adds a minute, catches most small stones.

The thin section is already safe — keep it off the heat. The thick section needs to reach 145°F in its geometric center; resting it off-heat won't get 126°F there, so you have to put heat back into it. The trick is finishing only the thick part.

SALMON

1. Slice or separate the thin tail end off. Put it on a warm plate, tent with foil, set aside. It will hold for 10–15 min without drying out.
2. Put the thick portion back over direct heat just long enough to drive off surface chill — hot skillet, 60–90 sec per side — then move it to a rack (not a sheet pan) in a 275°F oven. Air needs to circulate around it.
3. Probe the thickest part. Pull at 145°F. Expect 5–10 min depending on how thick.
4. Tent loosely, rest 1–2 min. Carryover will even out the gradient between the 126/133°F pockets.

Skip the "low-temp hold for X minutes" trick — it's equivalent to 145°F but requires you to babysit a probe, and you're serving a baby. Just go to 145°F.

Why: Anya is in the higher-risk group, so 145°F throughout (not the 130–140°F time-temp alternatives) is the right target. Thick fillets always carry a temperature gradient — only the center reading matters.

VEGETABLES

- Off the burner, lid on (or foil tent), in the same pan. 10–15 min is fine; they won't overcook.
- If the salmon delay stretches past ~15 min, drop the burner to its lowest setting with the lid on, or slide the covered pan into a 170°F oven. Stir once before serving.
- Don't leave them uncovered at room temp.

Serve the thin portion to whoever's eating first if someone's hungry; Anya's portion comes off once the thick section clears 145°F.

Devika's badge is a physical-access token only here (no keys, meds, or PHI on it, and her separate auth app on her phone is the 2FA for logins). That shapes the right order of operations: deactivate the physical token tonight, check that nothing logged into her accounts, then do the Monday walk-in. Below is the sequence you can run together tonight, plus Monday.

TONIGHT — containment + reporting (do this now, in order)

1. Call hospital security, don't wait. Use the after-hours / on-call line (badge loss is usually a 24/7 line; the main switchboard can route you). If she doesn't have it, the hospital operator number on the staff intranet page works. Call, don't email — email isn't monitored overnight.

   Have ready when she calls:
     - Full name, employee ID (if she knows it), department / unit
     - Last confirmed use: scan-out Friday 7:05 AM
     - Where she's already searched (coat, work bag, apartment entry area) and that she hasn't found it
     - Confirmation: no keys, no meds, no patient info attached

   Ask security to do these four things on the call and read back the answers:
     a. Deactivate the badge in the access-control system right now and log it (get a ticket / incident reference number).
     b. Pull the audit trail for that badge since Friday 7:05 AM and tell her whether it's been used again. If yes, get the door, time, and any associated camera review — that's the only way to know whether someone walked into a restricted area.
     c. Tell her whether the badge alone opens doors, or requires PIN / second factor at the door. If PIN-required, risk drops meaningfully; tell her anyway.
     d. Tell her the Monday replacement procedure: where to go, hours, what ID to bring, whether there is a temporary badge or only a permanent one, and who (charge nurse / manager) needs to be notified.

2. Write down immediately after the call: officer name, ticket/incident number, time of call, the answers to a–d. Screenshot or photograph the notes. This is what you'll reference Monday.

3. Do not: keep searching the apartment (she's already covered her usual spots — turning the place upside down won't recover it tonight and may distract from the call), post about it anywhere, or share the badge number with anyone outside security.

TONIGHT — account / remote-access checks she should ask for or do herself

The badge is almost certainly not her remote or workstation credential. Hospital remote access (VPN, EMR off-site, email) is username + password + the auth app on her phone — and the phone is still in her possession. Still worth verifying, because some hospitals do pair badge + PIN for workstation login on-site:

  - Hospital SSO / EMR portal (web): sign in, look for "active sessions" or "sign out everywhere" and use it. This kills any browser session someone else might be in if she ever left herself logged in on a shared or lost device.
  - Work email (web): same — check "recent activity" and sign out other sessions.
  - Auth app on her phone: confirm the token still generates codes (it does, because she has the phone). If the hospital uses Okta/Duo/Microsoft/Google authenticator, that's the credential that matters; the badge is not a backup.
  - Password change: only if she sees a login she doesn't recognize, or if she reuses the hospital password anywhere else. Don't preemptively rotate everything — the bigger signal is anomalous logins.
  - Ask security or the IT helpdesk (often a separate number from security — get it from the staff directory): "Was the badge used to log in to any workstation, and is workstation login badge+PIN or badge-only?" That tells you whether the badge compromise extends to on-site systems.
  - If she uses the badge to unlock a phone-pairing or proximity auto-unlock feature on her hospital-issued device or laptop, ask security how to revoke that pairing.

Net: she controls the critical credential (auth app + phone). The badge is a physical key; deactivation neutralizes it.

MONDAY MORNING — replacement sequence

  1. Arrive 20–30 minutes before shift to the security office (most open by 6 AM; confirm hours from the Saturday call).
  2. Bring: government photo ID, employee ID if she has the card, the ticket/incident number from Saturday's call, and her phone (auth app).
  3. Get either a permanent replacement or a temp/loaner badge; if temp, ask when the permanent one is ready and whether she needs to come back.
  4. Test the new badge before leaving security: at least her unit's main door, a medication/supply room if she uses one, and the staff entrance she'll come in through Monday and onward. Confirm it logs a swipe.
  5. Notify her charge nurse / unit manager per hospital policy — most require the employee to report a lost badge to their supervisor even after security has it. Do this before shift start so it doesn't come up mid-shift.
  6. Complete any written incident report HR or security requires (some hospitals require a signed form even after the verbal report).
  7. If for any reason the replacement isn't ready Monday AM, ask security on Saturday's call about escorted access or a manager-approved interim — don't assume she'll be locked out; most hospitals have a documented fallback.

One thing to keep in mind: this is a physical-token incident, not a credential compromise. The reporting path is hospital security, not (usually) a HIPAA breach notification — there's no PHI on the badge and no indication anyone's used it. If Monday's audit review comes back showing post-7:05-AM swipes, that's a different conversation (security + her manager + possibly employee health), but it's a follow-up, not the first move.

CHRISTMAS EVE — 6:30 PM SERVICE TIMELINE
(4 lb unstuffed whole chicken + roasted potatoes + sautéed green beans)

4:30 PM — PREP BOTH
  - Pull chicken from fridge; let it lose the chill 15-30 min for more even cooking
  - Pat the bird very dry (this is what crisps the skin), season inside and out with salt/pepper, optional herbs or butter under the skin
  - Cut potatoes into 1.5" pieces, toss with oil and salt

4:45 PM — CHICKEN INTO A 400°F OVEN
  - Breast-up on a rack in a roasting pan
  - 4 lb unstuffed at 400°F: target ~1 hr 15 min, but cook to TEMP not to time
  - Don't open the oven for the first 50 min

5:00 PM — POTATOES INTO A 425°F OVEN
  - Sheet pan or roasting pan, single layer
  - Higher temp than the chicken because potato pieces are denser than breast meat
  - 1.5" cubes at 425°F: ~50-60 min total

5:55 PM — FIRST TEMP CHECK (the leg/thigh is the slow part)
  - Instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of the inner thigh, parallel to the body, NOT touching bone
  - You're looking for 155-160°F in the thigh — that's your cue to pull
  - Why pull at 160°F: the thigh coasts up 5-10°F during rest, and the breast runs 5-10°F cooler than the thigh in the oven, so when the thigh hits 165°F post-rest, the breast is safe too
  - If still under 150°F: 10 more min, recheck
  - Don't probe the breast yet — it always finishes first and tells you nothing useful this early

6:00 PM (or whenever thigh reads 160°F) — PULL EVERYTHING
  - Chicken to a cutting board, tent LOOSELY with foil (tight foil steams the skin and ruins the crisp)
  - Potatoes out — either tent on the stovetop or slide them back into the turned-off oven with the door cracked (or a 170°F "warm" drawer if you have one)
  - Skim drippings now if you want a quick pan sauce

6:00-6:20 PM — REST (this 20-min window is what makes the whole plan work)
  - Chicken climbs from ~160°F to 165°F+ without drying out the breast
  - Potatoes hold heat
  - Use this window to trim the green beans and set out your sauté pan

6:20 PM — GREEN BEANS ON
  - Hot pan, oil, optional garlic, then beans
  - 4-5 min sauté until bright green and crisp-tender (olive-drab and soft = overdone)
  - Salt, finish with butter or lemon off heat
  - Done at 6:25 — same minute you carve

6:25 PM — CARVE & VERIFY (second and definitive temp check)
  - Remove legs/thighs, slice breast meat off the carcass
  - Re-probe the cooked meat at the thickest point:
      Breast: must read ≥165°F
      Thigh:  must read ≥165°F
  - If anything reads 160-164°F (rare if you pulled at 160°F): put that piece on a sheet pan at 400°F for 5 min, recheck
  - If anything reads under 160°F (very rare): back to the oven in 5-min increments until 165°F

6:30 PM — PLATE & SERVE

FOOD-SAFETY NOTES
  - The thermometer is the only reliable indicator. Clear juices and a wiggly leg are NOT safe tests for poultry.
  - Probe locations: breast = thickest side section; thigh = inner thigh, parallel to the body, off the bone.
  - The 160°F-pull + 20-min-rest is the trick that lets you serve a juicy breast and a safe thigh at the same meal — if you wait for the breast to hit 165°F in the oven, the thigh is past 180°F and dry.
  - If you're behind and the thigh hasn't hit 160°F by 6:05 PM, just leave the bird in 5 more minutes — don't crank the heat.

WHY THE VEGETABLES STAY HOT
  - Potatoes ride the oven for an hour, then hold in residual oven heat for the rest window — they're still steaming at 6:25.
  - Green beans are started at 6:20 and finish at 6:25 — five minutes on the heat, straight to the plate. Nothing is held, nothing gets cold.

Hand computation:

  Kettle:      1,500 W
  Toaster:     1,450 W
  Combined:    2,950 W
  Current (I = P/V) at 120 V:
    Kettle:    1,500 / 120 = 12.50 A

    Combined:  2,950 / 120 = 24.58 A

A 15 A breaker is sized to hold ~80% continuously (NEC continuous-load rule), so the practical continuous ceiling is ~12 A, and even a momentary trip typically occurs well before 24 A. 24.6 A into a 15 A circuit is a clear, expected trip — not a wiring fault signature.

Yes — the combined load explains the trip. Here's the full picture:

1. Does the load explain the trip?
  Yes. At 120 V, the two together draw ~24.6 A (kettle ~12.5 A + toaster ~12.1 A). That's roughly 164% of the breaker's 15 A rating — the breaker did exactly what it's designed to do. The fact that the breaker reset normally, holds set with everything unplugged, and the receptacle shows no heat/odor/discoloration/buzzing/spark/play is consistent with an overload trip, not a wiring fault. A fault (short, arc, ground, or loose connection) would typically re-trip with no load, trip again immediately, or show one of those physical signs.

2. Why this circuit is so easy to overload
  15 A × 120 V = 1,800 W is the *nameplate* limit. Code derates continuous loads to 80%, so the practical limit is ~1,440 W sustained. Either appliance alone is right at the edge. The kettle especially can spike a bit above its nameplate during the heating cycle. Kettles and toasters are both resistive, high-surge loads that should never share a small-appliance branch circuit.

3. How to reuse the two appliances safely
  Rule: never run them at the same time on the same 15 A circuit. Either of these is fine solo:
    - Kettle alone on the kitchen circuit — fine, near the limit but acceptable.
    - Toaster alone on the kitchen circuit — same.
  Together — pick one of these instead:
    a. Stagger: boil the kettle first, pour/move it off, then start the toaster. Don't restart the kettle until the toaster has ejected and cooled a cycle.
    b. Move one off the circuit: use the toaster in another room on a different 15/20 A circuit (living room, bedroom, office) if you have one you can confirm is on a separate branch. Don't assume — kitchen counter circuits in most homes are dedicated small-appliance circuits and *must not* be shared with other rooms per NEC 210.52(B), so an adjacent room receptacle is usually a different circuit, but verify by tripping the kitchen breaker and seeing what else goes off.
    c. If you toast a lot and boil a lot at the same time, a long-term fix is an electrician adding a second small-appliance circuit to the kitchen (NEC actually requires *two* 20 A small-appliance branch circuits for the kitchen counters — so a kitchen with only one 15 A circuit is itself a code concern worth flagging).

4. How to manage them so you don't paper over a real wiring problem
  What you want to distinguish: "expected overload trip from two heavy loads" vs. "breaker tripping because the circuit is failing." A few guardrails:
    - Trip pattern check: if a trip occurs with only *one* appliance running — especially a low-draw one — that's not load, that's the circuit. Stop using it and get it looked at.
    - Reset behavior: a healthy overload trip will let you reset cleanly after the load is removed and the breaker cools a minute. If the breaker won't reset, resets but trips again with nothing plugged in, or feels hot to the touch, treat it as a fault, not an overload — don't keep cycling it.
    - Receptacle inspection (you already did this and it's clean — good baseline): feel the plug and the faceplate after a normal run with one appliance. Warm is plausible on a heavy 12 A load; hot is not.
    - Don't daisy-chain power strips or use extension cords for either appliance — resistive loads at this wattage on a 14-gauge cord is a real fire risk.
    - Don't replace the 15 A breaker with a 20 A to "fix" it. That's the most dangerous response and is a code violation if the wire is 14 AWG (which a 15 A circuit almost certainly is). 20 A breakers require 12 AWG wire.

5. When to involve management / an electrician
  Involve management / landlord now (informational, non-urgent) if any of these:
    - You want to confirm the circuit rating and what's on it — the breaker label and the actual wire/breaker sizing aren't always the same, and a 15 A label on a 14 AWG circuit with frequent trips is worth documenting.
    - The kitchen has only one small-appliance circuit (which is itself a code issue per NEC for current kitchens — older kitchens grandfathered, but worth flagging for a remodel).
    - You want a second 20 A small-appliance circuit added.
  Call an electrician (non-emergency) if you observe at any point going forward:
    - Trip with a single appliance running.
    - Breaker won't reset, or trips again with nothing plugged in.
    - Receptacle, plug, or breaker feels hot; any discoloration; any buzzing; any smell; any sparking on insertion.
    - Lights on the same circuit dimming or flickering when an appliance kicks on (beyond the normal brief blink from a refrigerator compressor).
  Call an electrician / utility emergently (or 911 if you see active sparking or smoke) for:
    - Smoke, scorch marks, persistent burning smell, visible arcing, or a breaker that keeps tripping immediately after reset with nothing connected.

Net: the trip is explained by load, not by a hidden wiring problem. Run them one at a time on that circuit (or move one to a different verified circuit), don't swap the breaker, and use the single-trip / single-load / receptacle-temperature signals above as your tripwire for escalating.

Read on the threshold crossing

A 7/420 = 1.67% error rate crossed the 1% line on a canary panel whose bracketing intervals are clean and whose volume is one to two orders of magnitude below normal. The deciding evidence is the shared internal synthetic request identifier across all seven failures: that is not seven independent user requests failing — it is one synthetic probe repeatedly landing on a 5xx path inside the same 5-minute window, or several probe invocations from one probe source firing in the same bucket. The numerator is dominated by one probe identity, not by distributed user traffic.

Concretely:
- The canary panel as a whole did not regress. Latency, egress reconciliation, and the zero-error windows on either side argue the route-decision plane is healthy.
- The crossing is a small-N artifact. At N=420, a single failing probe identity is enough to push the ratio above 1%; a genuine regression would move both the ratio and the absolute count.
- This is the classic denominator-collapse false positive. Holiday-evening traffic on a canary subset gives exactly the conditions where one probe-only failure looks like a panel regression.

Treat it as a probe anomaly that tripped the wrong alert, not as an incident on the canary.

Immediate evidence to pull, in order

1. The seven 500 records: confirm the shared identifier is a synthetic probe ID (probe name / probe group / probe-region), not a tenant or end-user ID. The description implies it; verify it explicitly.
2. The 5xx cause on those records: exception class, upstream call, target endpoint/version/region. Look for whether the probe exercises a code path real traffic does not (specific header set, edge input, single-region call), or whether it is hitting a known-flaky dependency.
3. The probe's history against this canary: is this a one-off, or does the same probe ID fail intermittently at this rate? A long-run failure rate on that probe ID contextualizes whether the alert threshold is even the right instrument.
4. Blast-radius check on the canary cohort: even though egress and latency look fine, confirm no general-prod traffic shares the failing code path, and that the canary's error path is isolated.
5. Whether the alert fires only on the canary panel or also on a rollup that includes the same probe traffic. If the rollup is also tripping because the probe is mirrored there, the same fix applies one level up.

No code rollback, no canary abort, no page. Evidence points to a probe-driven false positive.

A safer alert formulation

The underlying defect is that error-rate percentage is being evaluated against a window where the sample is too small to mean anything. Three complementary fixes; pick the cheapest, or stack them:

A. Volume floor. Gate the percentage on a minimum request count in the window:
    error_rate_5m > 1% AND request_count_5m >= V
   with V set near the panel's "normal" lower bound. For a panel that usually sees tens of thousands per 5m, a floor around a few thousand is enough to silence near-idle alerts without losing sensitivity to real regressions. Highest leverage, easiest to reason about, no math change.

B. Confidence-aware threshold (Wilson lower bound on the error proportion). Alert when the lower end of the confidence interval on the observed error rate exceeds the SLO:
    wilson_lower(error_count, request_count, z) > 0.01
   Concretely on this observation: at z=1.645 the Wilson lower bound on 7/420 is about 0.91%, comfortably under 1%; the alert correctly stays quiet. At higher N the rule converges on the 1% line. More principled than (A); requires either a metrics backend that supports it or a small pre-aggregator.

C. Probe-aware exclusion. Identify synthetic probe traffic by a label or request ID and exclude it from both numerator and denominator. The label effectively already exists, since all seven failures share an identifier. Cleanest fix for exactly the pattern you saw; requires that probe labels be reliably attached, which is its own small failure mode to monitor.

Practical stack for this panel: (C) if probe labels are trustworthy, plus (A) as a backstop for any other low-volume regime. (B) is the right single rule if you want one formulation that works across panels with very different traffic shapes without per-panel tuning.

One thing worth not doing: lowering the threshold to chase a phantom page. The 1% rule is fine; the problem is applying it without a volume guard or a probe guard. Keep the threshold, tighten the precondition.

WORKING READING

What you describe — full rest clears ADL pain, gentle resisted wrist flexion is mildly provocative, and the undercling pattern has now reproduced twice — is most consistent with a low-grade medial-epicondyle / common-flexor-tendon irritation (a flexor / pronator tendinopathy picture, not a tear, not a bony injury, no neurovascular signs). That's a load-capacity problem, not an inflammation problem, so the fix is graded reloading, not more rest. More rest past symptom resolution will just lower your capacity and make the first undercling session re-flare it.

This is a plan, not a diagnosis. If anything below doesn't fit, or if any red flag appears, formal sports-medicine or PT eval is the right move.


ASSUMPTIONS I'M USING
- Timeline: you restart graded loading today (you've had ~7 days of relative rest and symptoms are at this baseline).
- "Bouldering partner, standing Tue/Thu gym sessions" — I'll anchor the plan around those days, with Wed/Fri/Sat/Sun off.
- "Full motion, normal grip, no swelling, no bony tenderness" — taken at face value. If any of those is actually worse than reported, jump to RED FLAGS below.


STAGE 0 — PAIN MODULATION + BASELINE (Days 1–7)

Goal: confirm the tendon tolerates static load, calm down symptom reproduction, and establish a baseline you can compare later weeks against.

What to do (3 of your 7 days this week — Tue / Thu / one weekend day):
- Wrist-flexion isometric: forearm supported on a table, palm up. Press your palm into your other hand (or a table leg / immovable object) at ~30–40% of max, hold 30–45 seconds, 4 reps. Pain during the hold should stay ≤3/10.
- Wrist-extension isometric: same setup, palm down, ~30% effort, 30–45 s × 4. Often tolerated and worth doing for balance.
- Pronation / supination isometric: light hammer in hand, resist twist against the table or your other hand at low effort, 4 reps each direction.

Dose: 1 session/day on training days, 1 set OK on off-days if you want.

Advance to Stage 1 when ALL of these are true for at least 2 consecutive sessions:
- Isometric pain ≤2/10
- No after-pain >1/10 lasting >1 hour
- No new symptoms (numbness, tingling, aching at rest)
- Sleep and morning are unaffected


STAGE 1 — TENDON CAPACITY (HEAVY-SLOW) (Weeks 2–3)

Goal: build actual load tolerance in the flexor / pronator group so climbing-specific demands stop being a surprise.

What to add (Tue / Thu / Sat or Sun, ~3 days/week):
- Eccentric-emphasis wrist curls: light dumbbell (start 1–2 kg; a full soup can is fine), forearm supported, palm up. Lower for 3 seconds, lift in 2 seconds. 3 sets × 10–12 reps.
- Reverse wrist curls (palm down): same scheme, lighter if needed.
- Pronation / supination with hammer or light dumbbell: 3 × 10 each direction.
- Continue Stage 0 isometrics on the days in between, but only if Stage 1 sessions are clean.

Loading rule: when 3 × 12 at a given weight feels easy AND post-session pain ≤1/10, add 0.5–1 kg next session. Don't add weight faster than once a week.

Hold / regress Stage 1 if:
- Pain during a set climbs above 3/10
- Post-session pain >2/10 lasting >24 hours
- Morning stiffness in the elbow / forearm >15 minutes after a session
- The undercling simulation pattern starts to show up during wrist curls → drop weight by ~30% for a week, don't push through

Advance to Stage 2 when ALL true for ≥2 sessions:
- 3 × 12 wrist curls at ≥3 kg (or equivalent) with no during-or-after pain >1/10
- Grip feels symmetric opening a jar / carrying groceries
- No symptom reproduction from a brief sub-maximal undercling hold (≤5 seconds, large hold)


STAGE 2 — CLIMBING PREP / GENERAL CAPACITY (Weeks 3–5)

Goal: bridge from wrist-curl capacity to finger / forearm capacity under body-weight demands.

Add, on top of Stage 1:
- Dead hangs: both arms, large jugs, 3 × 20–30 s. Progress to single-arm hangs with feet on a chair or foot-loop (assisted), 3 × 10–15 s.
- Therapy putty: sub-maximal squeezing (don't crush it), 2–3 min, 2×/day on off-days.
- Light farmer's carry: 2 × 30–40 m with moderate weight.
- Keep Stage 1 wrist work twice/week; drop isometrics.

Advance to Stage 3 (climbing reintroduction) when ALL true for ≥1 week:
- Single-arm hangs (right arm) for 10–15 s without pain, ≥3 reps
- Grip strength feels ≥90% of left (rough self-test: hang a loaded pack from each hand — should feel even)
- No reproduction of the undercling-type ache from any of the above
- Stage 1 loading continues to be clean


STAGE 3 — RETURN TO CLIMBING, AVOIDING UNDERCLING (Weeks 5–8)

Goal: prove the tendon tolerates real climbing load while deliberately NOT loading the undercling pattern.

Rules for this stage:
- 2 sessions/week max, 30–45 min each. Quality over volume.
- Hold selection priority: jugs > pinches > slopers > open-hand crimp with thumb-off > half-crimp > full crimp.
- Avoid: undercling, side-pulls that load the wrist in deep flexion, dynamic moves, max-effort problems.
- Top-rope or easy boulder; sub-maximal effort (RPE ≤7/10).
- Stop the session if you feel the familiar undercling-type ache anywhere in the forearm — not just at the elbow.

Stop / regress if:
- Ache during the session OR aching the next morning → next session drop volume by ~30% and downgrade hold size
- Morning stiffness >15 min or any pain at rest → take a full week off climbing, stay on Stage 2, then retry
- Any grip feels sharp, pinching, or reproduces 2/10+ → that grip is banned for this cycle

Advance to Stage 4 when ALL true for ≥2 sessions:
- Two clean climbing sessions with no during-or-after pain
- No morning stiffness
- Wrist curls from Stage 1 still progressing without flare


STAGE 4 — UNDERCLING REINTRODUCTION (Weeks 8+, often later)

Goal: bring back the specific pattern that reproduced symptoms, very gradually.

Sequence:
- First undercling contacts: large holds, low-angle wall, 3–5 moves, full rest between. One session/week only.
- If clean (no during-session pain, no 24h flare): keep volume low for 2 sessions.
- Then: smaller holds, more moves, up to 2 sessions/week with undercling.
- Then: steeper walls and longer problems.
- Last: dynamic undercling moves and max-effort undercling problems.

Rules for the whole Stage 4:
- 24h rule: any after-pain >1/10 → next session drop one step back in the sequence
- Never introduce a harder undercling within 48h of a harder Stage 1 lift
- If the undercling pattern reproduces twice in this stage (same way it did twice during your rest period), stop the undercling progression entirely and go to PT/sports-medicine — two reproductions is your early warning that capacity isn't there yet


GLOBAL YELLOW FLAGS (HOLD / REGRESS)
- Pain during loading >3/10
- Post-session pain >2/10 lasting >24 hours
- Morning stiffness >15 minutes
- Symptom pattern broadening (now hurts on multiple grips that were clean before)
- Grip asymmetry you can actually feel in daily life
- Two consecutive sessions showing any of the above

If you hit any of these: drop one stage for ~1 week, don't load through them.


RED FLAGS — STOP GRADED LOADING, ARRANGE EVAL

Any of the following should trigger a sports-medicine or PT evaluation, sooner rather than later:
- Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the fingers or hand (especially ulnar-side — ring & pinky)
- Visible swelling, bruising, or a lump at the elbow
- Bony tenderness when you press on the medial epicondyle (sharp, localized)
- Loss of motion (can't fully flex or extend the elbow or wrist compared to the other side)
- Locking, catching, or a sense that something is "giving way"
- Pain at rest or pain that wakes you from sleep
- No improvement at all after 4 weeks of consistent Stage 0–2 work, OR symptoms worsen despite reducing load
- Any acute "pop" or sudden sharp pain during loading

PT/sports-med is also the right call, even without a red flag, if:
- You're not confident self-prescribing load progression
- You want a real grip-strength measurement and a tailored program
- You climb at a level where small deficits matter


ADJUNCT NOTES (OPTIONAL)

- Ice / NSAIDs: short-term use for pain relief is fine, but don't lean on either during the loading stages — they can blunt the tendon-adaptation response if used around every session.
- Bracing / counterforce strap: an off-the-shelf elbow strap worn just below the medial epicondyle can take the edge off Stage 0–1 symptoms. Don't use it as a substitute for loading.
- Wrist position warm-up before Stage 1 work: 2–3 min of gentle wrist circles + light putty, then start.
- Sleep / grip position: avoid sleeping with the wrist fully flexed under a pillow or body — a simple neutral-wrist wrist brace at night for the first 2–3 weeks can reduce morning symptoms.


SUMMARY OF YOUR NEXT 2 WEEKS

Today (Sat): Stage 0 isometrics, one short session.
Tue / Thu / Sun: Stage 0 isometrics. Re-assess after Thu.
End of week 2: if Stage 0 clean, move to Stage 1 (wrist curls, 3×/week).
End of week 3: if Stage 1 clean, add dead hangs (Stage 2).
Weeks 4–5: if Stage 2 clean, plan a low-key Stage 3 return (no undercling).

No climbing before Stage 3. No undercling before Stage 4. Each stage has explicit advance / hold / regress gates — don't time-box past them.


ONE LAST THING

I built this from the self-check data you gave me and from your climbing context. If your grip strength isn't actually symmetric, if the elbow has any point-tenderness on the bone, or if there's any nerve symptom you didn't mention, skip the plan and book the evaluation — those are the cases where self-loading is the wrong tool.
