PRE-UPDATE CHECKLIST

Do all of this before clicking "Update Now."

A. ANCHOR THE RECOVERY PATH

  1. Backup verified - confirmed. Note the date/time of the most recent successful backup and that it includes the post-cleanup state.

  2. Make a second backup if the external is your only one. A bootable clone (Carbon Copy Cloner / SuperDuper) is the strongest safety net - if the internal drive becomes unbootable, you can boot FROM the clone. Time Machine alone is a data backup, not a bootable one.

  3. Locate the FileVault recovery key. If FileVault is on and the password is forgotten post-update, the recovery key (or iCloud recovery) is the only way back in. Confirm you can read it.

  4. (Optional but recommended) Make a bootable macOS installer USB for the CURRENT macOS version (not the target one). If the internal drive fails to boot, internet Recovery works but is slow; a local USB boots in seconds.

B. CONFIRM HEADROOM

  5. 28 GB is the install footprint. macOS stages files on a separate APFS volume during install; on Apple Silicon this is automatic, on Intel it can be tighter. Watch for any preflight warning at install start. If it complains about space, stop and free more - do not override.

  6. 41 GB free minus 28 GB needed = 13 GB after install. Workable but not lavish. If the workshop recording is multi-GB, temporarily moving it to the external during install gives breathing room and keeps it off the disk during the update.

C. INVENTORY THINGS THAT OFTEN BREAK ACROSS UPDATES

  7. List login items (System Settings -> General -> Login Items). Some get disabled and need re-enabling.

  8. List apps that install kernel/system extensions: security tools, VPN clients, virtualization (Parallels/UTM), NTFS or non-Apple file-system drivers, audio interfaces. These are the most likely to need updates after a major OS bump.

  9. Note Apple ID password and 2FA device. App Store / iCloud may re-prompt.

  10. Note any custom trackpad / keyboard / dictation shortcuts - some reset.

D. ENVIRONMENT

  11. Quit every app. Finish or pause any browser uploads/downloads.

  12. Pause Time Machine (menu bar -> Stop, or disable in Settings) until the update is fully done and verified.

  13. Disable sleep schedule and "Wake for network access" in Energy settings - the Mac should not sleep during install.

  14. Confirm Bluetooth peripherals are charged; better, use a wired keyboard/mouse if the installer might need input.

  15. Timing note: it's holiday week. Apple Store / phone support has limited hours if something goes sideways. The recovery path below should not need them, but worth knowing.

INSTALLATION SEQUENCE

  1. System Settings -> Software Update -> confirm target version and read release notes. Note any known issues.

  2. Click "Update Now" (or "Restart to install" if the download is staged).

  3. Mac reboots into the macOS Installer. Black screen with Apple logo and progress bar - normal. Do NOT power off, close the lid, or press the power button.

  4. Installer runs (15-45 minutes typical). One or two automatic reboots are normal.

  5. Mac boots to login screen (or directly to desktop if FileVault is off and auto-login is on).

  6. Log in. Answer first-run prompts (Apple ID, terms, Siri, analytics). Skip iCloud sign-in if anything looks off - come back to it.

  7. Let "Setting up your Mac" finish indexing before judging performance.

FIRST-RESTART VERIFICATION

  1. macOS version: Apple menu -> About This Mac -> confirm version matches target.

  2. Disk health: Disk Utility -> select internal drive -> First Aid -> Run. Validates the APFS container post-install.

  3. Storage sanity: About This Mac -> More Info -> Storage. Purgeable should have content; System data shouldn't balloon.

  4. Re-anchor the backup: resume Time Machine or re-mount the external. Run one successful backup on the new OS. This is the first confirmation the new OS can read/write the external drive cleanly.

  5. Core app smoke test: Safari, Mail, Calendar, Notes, Messages, Terminal, Finder, System Settings. Each opens and responds.

  6. Workshop materials smoke test: open the recording, slides, source files; verify sizes/dates and that they open. Open one app whose data lives in Application Support and confirm it loads its library.

  7. Network: Wi-Fi associates, captive portal accepts (if any), cloud sync works.

  8. Audio + mic + camera permissions: quick test in FaceTime or Photo Booth. Permission resets after major updates are common.

  9. Login items / agents: Activity Monitor -> Energy tab - confirm expected background helpers are present.

  10. Sleep/wake test: close lid, open, confirm clean wake.

RECOVERY PATH IF INSTALL FAILS

Three failure shapes; each has a recovery.

A. Installer hangs or fails midway, then reboots

  1. Force shutdown (hold power 10s). Boot normally.

  2. Open Software Update - retry. If it fails again, boot into Recovery: power on holding Cmd+R (Intel), or hold power until "Loading startup options" then click Options -> Continue (Apple Silicon).

  3. From Recovery: Reinstall macOS -> select the internal drive -> install. This reinstalls the OS over existing data; it does NOT wipe the disk. Safe first attempt at recovery.

B. Mac boots into Recovery by itself, or shows a folder-with-question-mark

  1. Try internet Recovery: Cmd+Opt+R (Intel) or Options -> globe icon (Apple Silicon).

  2. From internet Recovery: Disk Utility -> First Aid on the internal drive -> Run. Then Reinstall macOS.

  3. If the boot volume is missing or damaged beyond Repair, escalate to backup restore (see Total failure below).

C. macOS reinstalled but user data or apps look corrupt

  1. Boot normally. Use Migration Assistant (in /System/Applications/Utilities) to selectively restore from the Time Machine backup.

  2. If FileVault password is forgotten, use the recovery key on the FileVault lock screen - "Reset it using the recovery key." Without it, data is unrecoverable.

RECOVERY FROM TOTAL FAILURE

If the disk is unrecoverable or install will not complete:

  1. Boot from the bootable macOS installer USB: hold Option on Intel; on Apple Silicon, hold power -> Options -> select the USB.

  2. Disk Utility -> erase the internal APFS container. This IS destructive - only do this if you've decided to restore from backup.

  3. Reinstall macOS from the USB onto the erased drive.

  4. Migration Assistant -> import from Time Machine or external backup.

  5. Re-authorize apps, re-sign into iCloud, redo custom settings.

The OS can be reinstalled in 30-40 minutes; the user data cannot. The backup is what matters most.

Good that you haven't pressed it closed or plugged it in. A ~2 mm seam on a case that wasn't designed to open means internal pressure is already pushing on the seam. The cell is mechanically compromised; treat it as damaged lithium-ion from here on out.

CURRENT STATE READ
Your signs (cool, no smoke/odor/hiss, no discoloration, no puncture, unpowered) mean the cell is currently stable. A swollen Li-ion cell is not "fixable" by squeezing it back — it is at elevated risk of thermal runaway, and the risk rises the longer it sits, gets warm, or is mechanically stressed. So the goal is: stop disturbing it, isolate it where a failure would do the least damage, and get it out of the apartment to a proper disposal channel on your own schedule rather than after it vents.

ISOLATE IT IN THE APARTMENT (RIGHT NOW)
- Move it to a hard, non-flammable, room-temperature surface (concrete floor, ceramic tile, stone countertop). Avoid wood, carpet, upholstery, paper, bedding.
- Pick a spot away from people, pets, and exit paths, but where you can see it from across the room.
- Place it on/in something that contains a vent or fire: a metal pot, metal bucket, or a glass/ceramic bowl with a layer of dry sand, dry cat litter, or vermiculite. The pack sits ON the inert material; the material absorbs heat and any electrolyte that might weep.
- Do NOT seal it in an airtight container or plastic bag — if it vents, pressure needs to release somewhere other than into your face. A loose lid or open top is correct; a ziplock is wrong.
- Do NOT put it in a refrigerator/freezer "to slow the reaction." Cold-then-warm cycling + condensation on the cell is worse, and a frozen swollen cell can crack on thaw.
- Keep it away from direct sun, radiators, the oven/stove area, and any heat source.
- Leave it alone. No pressing, no flexing, no charging, no discharging, no "test" with a cable.
- If you have a cheap LiPo safety bag (the thick fire-resistant pouches sold for RC/drone batteries), put the pack in that, then in the pot. It is not a guarantee, just an extra layer.

CONTAINER FOR TRANSPORT
- Use a rigid, non-conductive, lidded or partially-covered container: a plastic tote, a 5-gallon bucket, a metal paint can with a loose-fitting (not airtight) lid, or a sturdy cardboard box lined with a bag of sand/cat litter.
- Cushion so it cannot slide, rattle, or have the terminals touch anything metallic. Tape over the USB ports with electrical tape so nothing conductive bridges them. Avoid packing peanuts (static) and anything flammable as the primary cushioning.
- Surround (not bury against) the pack with sand, dry cat litter, or vermiculite so a vent is partly smothered and any liquid is absorbed.
- Keep the container cool in transit: car trunk in mild weather is fine; do NOT leave it in a closed, sun-heated car. Bring it straight to the drop-off; don't leave it in the car overnight.
- Transport on the ground, not on a soft seat where it can flex.
- Treat it as you would any hazardous package: stable, upright, labeled enough that anyone handling it (a rideshare driver, a friend) understands it is a damaged battery.
- Do NOT carry it on public transit in a backpack pressed against your body. If you must use transit, use a rigid bucket with a lid you can set on the floor away from you, and keep stops short. The question said "not loosely" — a rigid, cushioned, vent-tolerant container meets that bar.
- Do NOT fly with it. Airlines and the FAA prohibit damaged or swollen lithium batteries in carry-on AND checked baggage. There is no exception for "small" or "carefully packed." Ground transport only.

DISPOSAL (NOT HOUSEHOLD TRASH, NOT CURBSIDE RECYCLING)
Lithium-ion packs — especially visibly damaged ones — are household hazardous waste / universal waste, not municipal solid waste. Putting one in a trash bag or recycling bin risks a garbage-truck fire and is illegal in many jurisdictions.
Channels that typically accept damaged/swollen Li-ion packs:
- Municipal Household Hazardous Waste (HHW) facility or drop-off day. This is the most reliable channel for a swollen cell. Many cities accept by appointment; some have walk-in days.
- Call2Recycle (call2recycle.org) drop-off locator — Home Depot, Lowe's, Best Buy, Staples, and many auto/electronics retailers participate. Policies on damaged cells vary by site; call ahead and say "swollen / damaged lithium-ion power bank" so they don't turn you away at the counter.
- The manufacturer or retailer if they have a take-back program (Apple, Anker, Goal Zero, etc.).
- Some fire stations will accept damaged cells, but this is jurisdiction-dependent — call first.

When you hand it off:
- Tell the staffer it is swollen/damaged and not to charge, drop, or compress it.
- Keep it in your transport container until they take it from you; don't pre-deposit it in an unsupervised bin.

EMERGENCY SIGNS — RESPONSE CHANGES IMMEDIATELY
Any of these means the cell is going into or through thermal runaway. Stop what you're doing, evacuate people and pets from the room (and close the door to slow fire spread), and call 911 / your local emergency number. Then re-evaluate only with professional guidance.
- Hissing, popping, crackling, whistling — the cell is venting gas and likely electrolyte vapor.
- Smoke of any color, even a thin wisp.
- Sweet, sharp, or solvent-like chemical smell (often described as sweet/ether-like). You may smell it before you see anything.
- Heat: the case becomes warm or hot to the touch. A stable damaged cell is at room temperature; warming means exothermic reaction has started.
- Sudden increase in the seam gap, or any new bulge, blistering, or discoloration of the wrapper.
- Fire or visible flame. Lithium-ion flames can jet, reignite, and burn extremely hot. Do not try to smother with a small cloth; if you have a Class D extinguisher or a large amount of water and a clear exit path, you can attempt it, but your default should be evacuate and call 911. Do not pick up a flaming or smoking power bank.

WHAT NOT TO DO (QUICK REFERENCE)
- Do not charge it, even briefly, to "see if it still works."
- Do not press the case back together.
- Do not puncture, bend, or drop it.
- Do not put it in water, salt water, or a freezer.
- Do not put it in household trash, mixed recycling, or e-recycling drop boxes that don't explicitly take damaged cells.
- Do not transport it in a checked bag, carry-on, or anywhere it can be flexed or shorted.
- Do not leave it where a pet, child, or cleaning robot can knock it off a surface.

REASONABLE TIMELINE
You don't need to evacuate your apartment or rush tonight, but you also shouldn't let it sit for weeks. Once it's isolated in the pot/inert material on a non-flammable surface, the next reasonable step is to identify your nearest HHW facility or Call2Recycle site (call ahead about damaged cells), package it as above, and move it out of the home within a day or two.

- Percent increase: 36 / 168 = 0.2142857... = 21.43% (rounded to 21.4%)

A 21% jump on a renter's policy, in a market where the typical driver is "building-area rate revision," is meaningfully above general premium trend (~6-8% YoY). Worth confirming the stated reason and shopping at least one comparator before accepting; the renewal premium itself is small enough that the real risk is in the coverage terms, not the $36.

Questions to verify before renewing or comparing alternatives
Organize as a single request to the current carrier and as the comparison list when pulling a quote elsewhere.

Like-for-like coverage (confirm the renewal matches the current declarations exactly)
1. Personal property limit: $40,000 stated. Is that the current limit or a quoted limit the carrier may have auto-indexed? If indexed, what was it last year?
2. Loss of use: $12,000. Is this "actual loss sustained" (preferred) or a fixed cap tied to a % of the property limit (common in cheap policies)?
3. Personal liability: $300,000. Is this per-occurrence with a separate aggregate, or per-occurrence only? Is there a medical-payments-to-others sublimit (often $1,000-$5,000)?
4. Does the renewal change any of these limits, sublimits, or named-insured/address information versus the current declarations page? Even if the dollar amounts shown are the same, the structure can shift.

Deductible structure
1. The $500: is it a single all-perils deductible, or are there separate deductibles for wind/hail, hurricane, or named-storm?
2. Is a higher deductible (e.g., $1,000 or $2,500) available with a premium credit? On a sub-$250 policy the dollar savings are modest but worth knowing.
3. Are any special-category losses (water backup, jewelry, electronics) subject to their own deductible?

Exclusions and sublimits that erode coverage silently
1. Water damage / sewer / sump backup: included, sublimited, or excluded? In NYC older buildings this is the most common denial pathway.
2. Mold: sublimit or excluded; what is the cap?
3. Hurricane/wind: separate deductible? (NY carriers sometimes apply one even for inland boroughs.)
4. Theft from a vehicle or away from premises: covered under personal property, or sublimited?
5. High-value categories — jewelry, watches, furs, silverware, art, collectibles, bikes, musical instruments, cameras: each typically has a per-category sublimit (often $1,000-$2,500) that is far below replacement cost. Anything above those caps needs to be scheduled on an inland-marine / personal-articles rider.
6. Dog-breed exclusions if relevant to the household (varies by carrier and breed; pit-mix, rottweiler, etc. are commonly excluded or surcharged; some carriers have no breed list).
7. Liability exclusions: business use of the unit (home office / 1099 work), short-term-rental hosting, and incidental room-rental all commonly excluded or only covered via endorsement.
8. Roommates / non-listed occupants: any non-listed person residing at the address is typically not covered for liability or property. Confirm everyone in the household is a named insured or listed resident.

Replacement-cost questions (the single largest coverage gap on most renter policies)
1. Is the personal property written on replacement-cost basis or actual cash value (ACV)? This is the headline question. ACV can pay 30-60% of replacement cost on older electronics, furniture, and appliances.
2. Is replacement cost applied uniformly across all perils, or only to certain causes of loss?
3. Is there an extended-replacement-cost or "guaranteed replacement" option, and at what premium?
4. Ordinance-or-law coverage: does the policy pay to bring damaged items up to current code/standard, or only to the original standard?
5. Pair-vs-set clause: if one item in a set is damaged, is the whole set payable, or only the single item?
6. Inflation guard: is the property limit automatically indexed each year, and by what index? If yes, the $40,000 figure on the renewal may not be the actual current limit.

Commercial / discount questions before accepting
1. Multi-policy discount if auto is with the same carrier.
2. Claims-free / loyalty discount.
3. Autopay, paperless, and paid-in-full discounts.
4. Whether "building-area rate revision" is being applied uniformly across their book or only on this policy — if only yours, ask for the specific rate filing or territory code being used.

Practical sequencing
- Pull the current declarations page (PDF) and compare line by line to the renewal declarations; do not rely on the renewal summary alone.
- Get one competing quote (Lemonade, AssurantConnect via GEICO, or a NY-domestic carrier like NYCM if eligible) with the same limits, replacement-cost basis, and deductible so the comparison is apples-to-apples.
- If the current carrier's renewal matches the existing coverage on a replacement-cost basis with no new exclusions and the same deductible structure, the $36 may be reasonable to accept given the cost of switching (new deductible reset, new inspection/cancellation timing). If any of the above has shifted, the renewal notice is the trigger to shop.

Does the $18 savings compensate? — No, almost certainly not on its own.

1. Deductible shift ($500 → $1,000)
   - You are self-insuring an extra $500 per claim.
   - Breakeven: $18 / $500 ≈ 3.6% probability of any single claim landing in the $500–$1,000 band over the policy year.
   - A renter with normal exposure (kitchen fires, theft, water damage from upstairs neighbors — common in NYC multi-unit buildings) crosses that 3.6% threshold easily. One such event and the $18 is gone, with another $482 out of pocket on top.

2. Loss-of-use cut ($12,000 → $8,000)
   - This is not annual cash flow; it's tail coverage. It pays additional living expenses if the unit becomes uninhabitable (fire, major water, etc.).
   - $4,000 of headroom ≈ roughly 2–6 weeks of temp housing in NYC at modest rates; less if you need a pet-friendly short-term rental (you have Kibo).

3. Net read
   - You are paying $18 to accept +$500 of self-insured deductible risk and -$4,000 of loss-of-use headroom. That is a poor trade on financial grounds alone. Here's the plan, ordered by what to do in the next few minutes and what to watch for through midnight.

RETREAT SETUP (do these in the next 15-20 minutes)

The bedroom closet is the right call - he's chosen it, and that's a denning instinct. Don't move him to a "better" spot; honor it.

- Bed, water, treats are already in place. Add a worn t-shirt or blanket of yours if one is handy - your scent calms more than another dog's.
- White noise machine: position it as close to the closet as the cord allows. Set it loud enough to mask voices and conversation, not so loud it drowns out his cries. Run a fan on low in the room for a second steady-noise layer.
- Close curtains/blinds fully - even with windows shut, the flashes can trigger him.
- Close the bedroom door so hallway noise is dampened.
- Skip the crate unless he goes in voluntarily and is crate-trained. Forcing a crate on a panicked dog can cause injury.
- Lick-distraction: if you have xylitol-free peanut butter, plain yogurt, wet dog food, or a Kong, smear it on a plate or stuff it and leave it in the retreat. Licking is a self-soothing behavior; this can settle him faster than anything else you can offer tonight.

YOUR EVENING RHYTHM

You:
- Eat in or near the retreat so he's not alone. Keep your own reactions calm - don't startle at bangs, don't coddle him when he's pacing. Sit nearby, hand him a treat when he settles for a few seconds, let him come to you.
- Background TV or low music is fine.

Food and water:
- No big meal for him in the next hour - stress vomiting is common. Small treats as "settle" rewards are fine.
- Water stays available. Some stressed dogs drink more; that's normal.

Bathroom trips:
- Leash on, even in a building hallway. Use a harness if he pulls or could bolt. Short leash, stay with him the entire time.
- Time it to a lull between bangs if you can. Earlier evening is usually quieter than the 11:30-12:15 window.
- Carry a flashlight and a cleanup bag.
- If he freezes at the door or refuses to walk, don't force it. A pee pad indoors, if you have one, is fine - holding it for a few hours won't hurt him.

NORMAL ANXIETY (monitor at home, no vet call)

Pacing, panting, hiding, trembling, lip-licking, whale eye, whimpering, clinginess, occasional treat refusal, dilated pupils. This can run for hours through the worst of it. He's already showing some of these - none of this on its own is an emergency.

URGENT - CALL THE EMERGENCY VET NOW

- Repeated vomiting, or any vomit with blood
- Diarrhea with blood, or black/tarry stool
- Collapse, fainting, loss of consciousness
- Seizure (paddling, loss of body control, loss of bladder/bowel)
- Gums that are pale, white, blue, or brick-red instead of healthy pink
  -> Quick check: lift his lip now while he's calm, learn his normal pink. Recheck during a peak - if it's off, that's the single fastest vital sign you can read.
- Belly feels tight, swollen, or drum-like, especially with retching or trying-to-vomit-with-nothing-coming-up. This can be bloat/GDV - minutes matter, go immediately.
- Open-mouth breathing at rest with heaving ribs when he isn't hot - that's respiratory distress, not stress-panting.
- Self-injury: breaking through a door, window, or crate; any bleeding.
- Sustained non-response: won't take a favorite treat, won't look at you, doesn't react to his name for more than a couple of minutes. Sustained shut-down is worse than trembling-and-pacing.

DISTRESS YOU CANNOT IGNORE BECAUSE YOU'RE ALONE

Between bangs, watch for two things:

1. Gum color. Pink = ok. Anything else = emergency.
2. Breathing. Should settle toward a normal resting rate within 30-60 seconds of a bang. Still panting hard between bangs, plus off-color gums, plus restlessness = not just stress.

EMERGENCY CONTACTS - HAVE READY BEFORE YOU NEED THEM

- Nearest 24-hour emergency veterinary hospital: have the address in your phone, not just the name. NYE Uber/Lyft availability drops; if you have a car, know the route now.
- ASPCA Animal Poison Control: 888-426-4435
- Pet Poison Helpline: 855-764-7661
- If you can't transport him alone because of his size or his panic, call the ER first - some give stabilization advice by phone and a few dispatch.

ONE-LINE VERSION
Closet retreat + steady noise + your calm presence + lick-distraction. Short leash, harness, flashlight for bathroom. Pink gums and breathing-that-settles-between-bangs = wait it out. Off-color gums, hard belly, seizing, collapse, sustained non-response = go now.

FOLLOW-UP (not tonight, but worth doing)
If fireworks reliably set him off, schedule a vet consult in early January to talk through next year's plan - prescription anti-anxiety meds for the event, desensitization training, and whether a ThunderShirt-style wrap helps him. That's a January conversation, not a NYE one, and it's the right way to handle the recurring side of this.

Smallest sequence that distinguishes the three, in order. Each step is observation by the generator itself (introspection flags, dry-run, hash compare); none of them is a hand edit to the generated iOS file. Stop at the first step that points at a cause.

1. Cache-busted regenerate the iOS target and hash-compare.
   - Delete the existing iOS artifact and re-run the iOS generator with the clean / no-cache flag the build supports (or blow the generator's content-addressed cache for that target).
   - Diff the new iOS output's spacing token against the canonical package's spacing value.
   - If they match now: stale generated output. Root cause is a skipped regen or a stale cache; nothing in the canonical or the generator is wrong. Stop.
   - If they still mismatch: the iOS generator actually executed against the current canonical and still emitted the old value. Continue.

2. Print the canonical artifact each generator consumed.
   - Run the iOS generator and the web generator both with their manifest / input-hash / print-source mode enabled in the same session.
   - Compare the two records: canonical version, hash, path, or ID.
   - If they differ: canonical-package problem in the narrow sense -- the canonical's value is right, but the iOS generator is pointed at a different snapshot than the web generator. The fix is re-pointing the iOS generator's canonical reference, not editing the iOS output. Stop.
   - If they match: both generators consumed the identical canonical. Continue.

3. Compare generator versions and observe parse-side behavior.
   - Record the iOS generator's version and the web generator's version.
   - Run the iOS generator in a verify-input / dry-run / dump-parsed mode so it prints the spacing value it parsed from canonical before any emit step.
   - Three branches:
     - Parsed value already wrong (mismatches canonical): generator bug at the parse or schema layer, independent of version. Escalate with the parsed-vs-canonical diff.
     - Parsed value correct and iOS generator version differs from web's: generator-version drift. Pin the iOS generator to web's version, re-run. If iOS now matches, root cause confirmed.
     - Parsed value correct and versions already match: an emit-layer bug specific to the iOS format. Escalate with the parsed-vs-emitted diff and both generator versions.

Why this order is the minimum.
- Step 1 isolates the cheapest, most likely cause (regen-skipped or stale cache) with one rebuild and one compare. If it fires, the rest is unnecessary.
- Step 2 is needed only if Step 1 fails, and it is the only step that distinguishes "the canonical exists correctly but iOS is not looking at it" from "the canonical is genuinely the problem." It runs in seconds via existing manifest flags.
- Step 3 is needed only if both above pass, and it splits the remaining generator-side failures into parse / version / emit, which have different fixes.

Throughout, every signal comes from the generator's own introspection. Anya's lane and workflow are untouched; the question collapses to which knob to turn, not which line in the iOS file to patch.

Bottom line: the $18 annual savings does not reasonably compensate. The doubled deductible alone wipes out the savings on the first claim, and the competitor narrows coverage in the categories most likely to be claimed in a NYC apartment.

Cost math
  Annual savings: $18 (~$1.50/month)
  Extra deductible on any one claim: +$500
  Net if you file one claim: −$482
  Breakeven: ~0.036 claims/year, i.e., one covered event every ~28 years.

Coverage gaps, item by item

Deductible: $500 to $1,000
  Doubles out-of-pocket on every claim. Two minor claims in a year = −$982 net. A higher deductible also tends to suppress small claims, which is fine until a bigger loss lands.

Water backup: included to excluded
  NYC apartments are heavily exposed (older stacks, ground-floor units, storm surcharge on combined sewers). The current endorsement typically covers damage and tear-out in the $2K–$10K+ range. On the competitor this is a full gap, not a sublimit. Buying it back as a rider typically costs $30–$75/year, which alone exceeds the $18 savings.

Off-premises bicycle theft: $40K blanket to $1,500 sublimit
  The largest practical exposure. NYC bike theft is high and most incidents are off-premises (street racks, transit, workplaces). A reasonable road, gravel, or e-bike runs $1,500–$4,000+; anything above $1,500 is uninsured, and you still pay the higher deductible on top.

Electronics: $40K blanket to $2,500 sublimit
  Laptop + camera + audio + tablet + bike computer easily clears $5K–$10K in a typical household. The $2,500 cap leaves a $2,500–$7,500+ gap on a single electronics loss.

Loss-of-use: $12,000 to $8,000
  NYC displacement costs add up fast (hotel + food + transit). $4,000 less ALE can be burned through in 2–4 weeks for two adults.

Risk scenarios against the $18 saved
  - one minor claim (any cause): lose money
  - off-premises bike theft: likely lose money
  - water backup event: likely lose money, possibly uncovered entirely
  - electronics loss above $2,500: lose money
  - displacement beyond ~2 months: lose money

The competitor is doing the classic sublimit-and-deductible play: cheaper on premium, more risk transferred to you in the categories most likely to be claimed.

Recommendation
  Keep the current carrier at $204. Before renewing, ask the current carrier three things:
    1. confirm the $40K replacement-cost property limit still has no bike or electronics sublimits
    2. what the water-backup endorsement limit actually is (some carriers cap at $5K–$10K)
    3. whether claims-free, autopay, or bundle discounts apply

If you and Devika still want to switch for reasons beyond price (claims experience, app, service), ask the competitor to quote with water-backup added back and the bike/electronics sublimits raised, then compare apples-to-apples. The headline $186 is not a meaningful number as quoted.

I will use a few facts I know about bicycle drivetrain diagnosis directly. Nothing in memory or session history is bike-specific, so this is a fresh, self-contained answer.

Your symptom pattern (skip only under hard load, only in the smallest cog, otherwise indexed, no visible damage) is a classic stress-test signature: it tends to point at one of four things, in roughly this order of likelihood — bent derailleur hanger, worn chain on a worn cassette, a chipped small-cog tooth, or loose cassette/freehub. A stiff link and indexing error usually present differently (across cogs, or with visible shift quality issues) but they are still worth ruling out. Below is a phased sequence so you can stop as soon as the cause is clear.

SAFE STATE BEFORE YOU START

Workstand is best. If none, flip the bike so it rests on handlebar and saddle, drivetrain up. Do not grip the brake levers while the bike is inverted (some hydraulic systems can trap air if the lever is held down). With the bike on the ground, hold the rear brake on and lift the rear of the bike so the rear wheel spins freely for the moving checks. Do all pedaling checks with hands well clear of the chain; do not wear loose clothing or gloves near the cogs.

PHASE 1 — STATIC VISUAL AND TACTILE (no tools)

1. Sight the rear derailleur hanger. Crouch behind the saddle and look down the right chainstay toward the rear axle. The two derailleur cage plates should look parallel to the cassette face. Any twist, kink, or visible offset, even 1–2 mm, is meaningful. The hanger can be bent from an impact you did not feel at the time (bike leaning against a post, a curb hop, transport clamp). Subtle hanger bend is the single most common cause of "only skips in the smallest cog, only under load, otherwise everything is fine."

2. With the wheel off the ground, pedal backward slowly and watch the chain pass over the upper jockey pulley and across the cassette. Listen for a regular tick. A tick at one consistent position (one link) is a stiff link. A tick that drifts or only happens in certain cogs is often a stiff link too. Skip or jump while you are pedaling by hand usually means a stiff link or a damaged tooth.

3. Grab the chain at the smallest cog with your thumb and push forward as if simulating a hard pedal stroke. Watch the tooth of the smallest cog as the chain tries to climb over it. If the chain lifts visibly onto the tooth face, that cog's teeth are hooked/worn. On a healthy cog, the chain stays seated at the base of the tooth.

4. Shift through every gear, including the smallest, and watch from directly above and directly behind. The chain should sit centered on each cog's width. Any cog where it visibly sits closer to the next larger cog, or hangs off the edge of the smallest cog toward the spokes, is misindexed (or hanger-bent, which mimics indexing).

PHASE 2 — WHEEL AND CASSETTE SECURITY

5. With the bike on the ground, grab the front of the rear tire and try to rock the wheel laterally in the dropouts. Any clunk or play = wheel not properly seated or axle not properly clamped (QR lever tension, thru-axle torque). Fix before anything else: a loose rear wheel under hard pedaling can skip the chain off entirely and is a ride-ending hazard on its own.

6. Remove the rear wheel. With the cassette up, try to rotate the cassette by hand against the freehub. It should be locked — no independent rotation. If it spins on the freehub, the splines are worn or the cassette is not torqued. If it shifts axially (push-pull) at all, the cassette is not properly clamped. This is a "do not ride" finding.

7. With the wheel off, spin the freehub rapidly by hand. It should spin freely for many seconds and click loudly going forward. A rough, crunchy, or short-spinning freehub points at bearing failure inside, which can also manifest as skipping under load.

8. If you have a cassette lockring tool and torque wrench, the cassette lockring spec is typically 40 Nm. Do not ride with a loose lockring — it can shift under power and either skip or lock the wheel.

PHASE 3 — CHAIN WEAR (the most common underlying cause)

9. Use a chain wear indicator (go/no-go gauge) on a taut section of chain. The two thresholds to know:
   - 0.5% elongation: chain should be replaced soon; cassette likely still serviceable.
   - 0.75% elongation: chain and cassette should both be replaced; riding on a new chain against a worn cassette typically produces exactly your symptom — skipping only under hard load, often worst in the smallest cog because the chain wraps less of it.

10. Without a gauge: measure 12 full links (pin to the same pin 24 half-links away). New chain = 304.8 mm (12.000 in). Replace chain if ≥ 305.6 mm (12 1/16 in). Definitely replace chain and inspect cassette if ≥ 307.6 mm (12 1/8 in). For 11- and 12-speed chains the replacement threshold is tighter; treat any measurement over 305.6 mm as urgent.

If the chain is at or past 0.75% and you find any hooked/shark-fin shaped teeth on the small cog (Phase 4 below), the diagnosis is "worn chain wore the cassette," and the right repair is both parts. Installing only a new chain on a worn cassette typically re-creates the skip within a few rides.

PHASE 4 — COG-TOOTH INSPECTION

11. Remove the rear wheel and hold the cassette up to a strong, raking light. Rotate each cog slowly. Teeth should be asymmetric — a smooth ramp on the leading edge, a hooked trailing edge. Worn teeth look symmetrical (the ramp is gone), pointed like a shark fin, or curled into a hook. Inspect the smallest cog first and most carefully. Any single tooth that is chipped, bent, missing, or visibly different from its neighbors is enough to cause the skip — that single bad tooth is what the chain hits on every hard stroke.

12. Run a rag across the cassette face. Built-up grime can pack between teeth and cause the chain to lift; clean and re-check. This is a long shot but cheap to rule out.

PHASE 5 — INDEXING

13. With the bike in a stand (or flipped), shift into the smallest cog and look from behind the saddle straight down the cassette. The chain should sit centered on the cog. Quarter-turn the barrel adjuster at the rear derailleur or shifter: clockwise (typically) moves the derailleur outboard (toward the spokes — chainline lengthens), counter-clockwise moves it inboard. Watch the chain respond. Stop the moment it is centered on each cog.

14. While pedaling lightly, shift up and down through the full range. Every upshift should land cleanly with a small audible click. Every downshift should move crisply. If the small cog specifically is sluggish going on or off, the high (H) limit screw may be wrong, or the cable has stretched just enough to lose the top gear.

Indexing-only problems can be ridden to a shop, but the skipping symptom you described is unlikely to be pure indexing given that you say shifting is otherwise indexed.

PHASE 6 — STIFF LINK

15. If Phase 1.2 pointed at one specific link: with the chain on the bike, find that link and gently flex it side-to-side about 10 degrees in each direction, repeatedly, while lubricating it. Most stiff links free in under a minute this way. If a link will not free, the chain is unsafe and needs replacement — a link that refuses to flex under hand force will fail under body weight on the pedals.

WHAT TO DO AT EACH FINDING

- Hanger visibly bent: stop, take to a shop for hanger alignment or replacement. You can ride there only if the bend is truly minor and your route is flat, direct, and you avoid standing on the pedals. A bent hanger is one skip away from the chain jamming between cassette and spokes, which can lock the rear wheel.
- Hanger alignment gauge confirms a misalignment you cannot see by eye: same as above.
- Chain at or past 0.75% wear: replace chain, inspect cassette; if cassette shows hooked teeth, replace both. Do not commute on the current setup under load.
- Small cog has any single damaged tooth: replace cassette (or single-cog if you have a matched donor and the right tools). Do not ride under load until repaired.
- Cassette rocks on freehub, or lockring is loose: shop. Do not ride.
- Wheel rocks in dropouts: secure the axle first (proper QR closure or correct thru-axle torque). Re-check skip. If wheel still skips after wheel is secure, deeper issue — shop.
- Stiff link freed and chain wear is fine: ride cautiously, re-check skip under load in a low-risk place (flat road, no traffic) before resuming normal use.
- Indexing off only on the small cog and fixed by barrel adjustment: ride cautiously and re-check under load.

CRITERIA FOR LEAVING THE BIKE UNRIDDEN UNTIL A SHOP LOOK

Any one of these is a "do not ride, even to the shop" finding:

- Chain elongation ≥ 0.75% AND any hooked/shark-fin teeth visible on any cog.
- Cassette not positively locked to the freehub (visible/audible movement, lockring loose).
- Rear wheel has any lateral play in the dropouts.
- Derailleur hanger is visibly bent or twisted.
- Small cog has a chipped, bent, missing, or visibly asymmetrical tooth.
- Freehub bearings feel rough, crunchy, or short-spinning.
- A stiff link that will not free after flexing and lubrication.

You can ride cautiously to a shop (flat route, no standing on pedals, no traffic load) only if every one of the above has been ruled out, the cause is something you cannot fix in your space (e.g., hanger alignment tool, cassette replacement), and the wheel is firmly seated in the dropouts.

RENEGOTIATION FROM 1 Gbps TO 100 Mbps — WHAT IT MEANS

1000BASE-T needs all four twisted pairs. 100BASE-TX falls back to two. A drop to 100 Mbps is the classic fingerprint of one pair (or one contact on one pair) failing — not a config or ISP-line issue. The fact that a single reseat restored 1 Gbps and held for an hour points to a marginal contact, not a hard break. Expect recurrence until the marginal element is replaced.

LEAST-DISRUPTIVE SEQUENCE (ordered, each step before scope grows)

  1. Capture baseline state now (link is currently up)
     - Router admin: WAN page — link rate, duplex, uptime, TX/RX error counters
     - Modem admin: LAN/ethernet port status page (most modems show port link-rate and counters)
     - Router log: export or screenshot. Flag every prior WAN renegotiation, CRC/FCS error, dropped frame. Note timestamps.
     - Cost: zero. This is the evidence file everything else is compared against.

  2. Inspect the short patch cable end-to-end
     - Both RJ45 plugs: bent pins, green oxidation, jacket pulled back from the strain-relief boot (the ~3 cm behind the plug is the highest-stress zone)
     - Bend radius: tight staples, door pinches, coils smaller than ~4× cable diameter
     - Run a finger along the jacket — soft spot, flat spot, stretch mark from furniture
     - Any of the above → mark cable suspect, but keep it for step 4 evidence

  3. Reseat both ends deliberately
     - Unplug, wait 5 s, plug back in until the click
     - Confirm 1000/Full within ~30 s
     - Outage cost: ~5–10 s

  4. Substitute the cable — the single move that resolves most of these
     - Swap in a known-good Cat5e or Cat6 patch, ≤2 m if you have one
     - Park the original cable; do not discard yet — it may become evidence
     - Hold 1 Gbps for 10+ minutes of normal traffic before declaring the substitute good
     - Sustained-load check: run an extended speedtest or a wired iperf3 between two clients while watching the WAN rate. If it drops mid-load on the new cable, the cable is not the sole culprit.
     - Outage cost: ~30–60 s

  5. Port swap
     - Routers rarely have a second WAN port — check before assuming
     - More useful: try a different LAN port on the modem. If the substitute cable still negotiates to 100 Mbps on a different modem port, the modem's Ethernet handoff is suspect → ISP territory.
     - Outage cost: ~30–60 s

  6. Watch the error counters over ~1 hour of organic traffic
     - Devika's charting + your browsing is fine load — no need to synth traffic
     - Stable 1 Gbps, zero CRC/FCS increment → cable was the issue, stop here
     - Stable 1 Gbps but counters increment → port or EMI; move the cable away from any power brick, USB hub, or fluorescent ballast
     - Drops back to 100 Mbps under load → thermal, marginal port, or upstream — escalate

  7. Power-cycle only if the link degrades during the sequence
     - Modem first; wait for full sync (all status lights steady, optical light stays normal), then router
     - Outage cost: ~2–5 min for modem resync
     - Repeat power-cycles more than twice in a week = ISP evidence on its own

EVIDENCE THAT JUSTIFIES CONTACTING THE ISP

You are ready to call when you have, on paper or screenshots:

  - Sustained failure to hold 1 Gbps with a known-good cable on a known-good port
  - Modem-side log entries naming T3/T4 timeouts, OFA alarms, loss-of-ranging, or LAN/Ethernet port errors (not cosmetic link-rate fields)
  - Recurrence after power-cycle
  - The failure tracking only the modem's Ethernet handoff — nothing on your router's LAN side
  - Timestamp correlation: modem uptime/link-rate reset at the same moment your router logged the WAN renegotiation

Do not call with: "I reseated once and it came back" (single observation), or "the router says 100 Mbps" (your equipment talking). Do call with: "with my own cable on your modem, the modem's own diagnostic page shows port errors, the link still negotiates to 100, and the modem event log shows X at these times."

TWO NOTES SPECIFIC TO THIS SETUP

  Optical light held steady during the stall, so the failure is downstream of the ONT. The ISP conversation, when it comes, is about the modem's Ethernet handoff or its config — not the fiber drop. That framing keeps the call short and on-target.

  Timing for Devika: 100 Mbps is generally fine for EHR traffic, but the simultaneous stall on wired and 5 GHz means the router reset during renegotiation — a real 30–90 s outage for her. The cable swap in step 4 is worth landing before her next chart-heavy shift, not after.

Short answer: yes. Any incomplete automatic closure of a spring-gate clasp — before or after cleaning — is a retirement criterion for use with Kibo. The clasp is a single point of failure holding a 25–35 lb dog that can lunge; a gate that doesn't fully seat on its own cannot be trusted to seat under load. Below is the cleaning and unloaded test sequence to confirm the diagnosis, plus the reasoning.

Why this matters specifically with a front-clip harness

  A spring-gate clasp fails by "rollout": the harness D-ring slides across the partially open gate under load and pops out. Front-clip harnesses amplify this because the attachment point sits at the chest, so any sideways pull converts into a twisting/lateral force on the gate rather than a straight pull. Kibo never got loose this time because the leash happened to hang in a low-load orientation. That is luck, not safety.

Safe cleaning sequence (do this before testing)

  1. Remove the clasp from the leash if it's a swiveling/bolt-snap style that unscrews, or leave attached if it's a fixed eye. Work over a towel so you don't lose the small spring if it disassembles.
  2. Lukewarm rinse (not hot) to dissolve road salt and slush residue. Salt is the most likely culprit — it packs into the spring pocket, corrodes the pivot pin, and adds drag.
  3. Soft brush (an old toothbrush is ideal) with a drop of mild dish soap. Work around the gate pivot, the inside of the nose where the gate seats, and along the spring pocket. Do not pry the gate past its normal travel.
  4. Rinse thoroughly with clean lukewarm water. Any soap residue will attract grit and worsen the problem.
  5. Dry completely. Compressed air or a hair dryer on low is fastest; otherwise air-dry 24 hours. Moisture trapped in the spring pocket is what makes salt-jammed clasps fail again within a few walks.
  6. Optional, only after fully dry: one tiny drop of dry silicone or PTFE lubricant on the pivot. Avoid WD-40 as a long-term lube (it strips factory lube and attracts dirt); a one-time WD-40 flush followed by drying and re-lubing is fine if salt is packed in.
  7. Do not disassemble the spring itself unless the clasp is designed for it (most are not). If a spring comes out, the clasp is not user-serviceable to a reliable standard — retire it.

Unloaded test sequence (no dog, no harness, no force that mimics the dog)

  1. Hold the clasp body in one hand, gate facing you, in good light.
  2. Press the thumb lever slowly. The gate should open smoothly with light pressure and you should feel a clean detent.
  3. Release the lever. The gate must snap fully closed under spring power alone. No halfway, no sticking, no hesitation.
  4. Look at the gate-to-nose junction against a bright background. Any visible light gap means the gate is not seating.
  5. Repeat open/close 20 times. Consistency matters — a clasp that closes 18 of 20 is not acceptable.
  6. Press the gate tip inward with a fingertip as if trying to open it without the lever. Only the lever should be able to open it. If you can push the gate open with finger pressure alone, the spring is shot.
  7. Static load test. Hang a 10–15 kg bag from the closed clasp on a fixed eyebolt. Watch the gate for 60 seconds. Any creep open = fail.
  8. Dynamic load test. Same weight, give it a sharp tug and a bounce. Gate must stay fully seated.
  9. Side-load test (this is the front-clip harness scenario). Hook the closed clasp onto a fixed D-ring and pull sideways. Gate must not roll open or even partially unseat.
  10. Listen. Many bolt snaps give a small audible click when fully closed. Silence or a mushy close often correlates with partial seating.

Decision

  - If the gate returns only partway at step 3, or shows any gap at step 4, or fails any of steps 6–9: retire. Do not return to service with Kibo.
  - If it passes every step after cleaning: technically functional, but the fact that it exhibited partial closure during normal use means the spring or pivot was already compromised. The honest call is still to retire it from primary Kibo use. It can be kept for non-safety tasks (securing a crate, hanging something at home) if you want, but not for a walk.
  - Use your intact backup leash. When you replace this one, consider a stainless or marine-grade bolt snap if slush exposure is going to be recurring — January in NYC will eventually get any plated steel clasp.

One housekeeping note: I'd retire the leash, not store it for later re-evaluation. The temptation to "try it again on a short walk" after a successful cleaning is the failure mode that gets dogs loose.

Pre-flight
- Navigate to the retailer via your own bookmark or a typed URL — not the alert link.
- Use a clean browser profile or a private/incognito window; have the password manager ready to autofill the new credential.
- Note the alert timestamp and the breach corpus name for your records.

1. Independent sign-in
- Confirm you can sign in with the current (now-known-exposed) credential from your trusted device.
- If sign-in fails, shows an unexpected MFA challenge, or lands on a "verify your recovery info" page you did not initiate, stop — that is a separate incident (possible active takeover) and changes the sequence.

2. Password replacement
- Generate a new high-entropy password in the manager; let the manager save it before you submit.
- Change the password; do not approve any "link this account to another login" or "keep me signed in everywhere" prompts during the flow.
- Confirm the manager now holds exactly one entry for this account and the old credential is overwritten.

3. Session revocation
- Open the security/sessions area and "Sign out all sessions" / "Sign out everywhere." Most retailers expose an "Active sessions" or "Devices" list — review it for anything unfamiliar before revoking.
- Re-authenticate on the device you control. Disable "trust this device" if it was on for devices you no longer use.

4. MFA audit
- Confirm every registered factor is one you set up. Remove anything you do not recognize.
- Prefer an authenticator app (TOTP) or hardware key over SMS or voice; if SMS/voice is the only factor, migrate it to an app while you still have access.
- Regenerate backup/recovery codes; store the new set in the manager and delete the old ones.

5. Recovery options audit (especially important on a dormant account)
- Recovery email: confirm it is the address you expect. Replace if it has been changed or if the mailbox provider is no longer yours.
- Recovery phone: confirm it still routes to a SIM you control. A recycled number here is the most common dormant-account takeover vector — if the number is no longer yours, change it to one you control before anything else can be changed against it.
- Security questions, if used: treat their answers as compromised and replace with random stored values, or disable the questions if the platform allows.

6. Saved-payment review
- Enumerate stored cards and wallet methods: cardholder name, last four, brand, billing address.
- Remove anything you do not recognize. For cards you keep, note the issuer and the last four so you have a baseline.
- Confirm no shipping address has been added or changed.

7. Activity and notifications
- If the retailer exposes login history or account activity, scan for IPs, cities, and device classes you do not recognize.
- Enable sign-in alerts and new-device alerts if available.
- Confirm the notification destination is your current address.

Broader-action triggers — escalate if any of the following appear after the password change:
- An order, refund, store-credit load, gift-card issuance, or address change you did not make.
- A payment method, recovery email, recovery phone, or MFA factor change you did not make.
- An active session you cannot terminate, or repeated successful sign-ins from unrecognized locations.
- A password-change confirmation email you did not initiate (suggests the actor is already inside).
- The retailer confirms that the breach also exposed stored payment-card data, full SSN/DOB, or other PII sufficient for account takeover or identity fraud.
- Any unauthorized merchant authorization on a card that was stored on the account, or any other unexpected activity on the underlying card issuer account.

If any of those fire:
- Replace the stored card(s) by requesting new numbers from the issuer, not just by removing them from the retailer — a stored PAN may already be exfiltrated.
- Place a fraud alert with one bureau (which propagates) or a credit freeze if PII beyond the credential was exposed.
- Rotate any other accounts that share the recovery email or recovery phone if those were modified during the incident.
- File a report with the retailer and the card issuer; preserve timestamped screenshots of the unauthorized activity.

Because the credential is unique and MFA was in place, the disclosed password alone is unlikely to enable takeover — the sequence above invalidates the leaked credential, locks out any prior silent access, and verifies that the recovery surface is still yours. If steps 1–7 complete cleanly with no unfamiliar activity, no broader credential or card action is justified.

Bottom line: based on what you described, replacing saved cards and rotating unrelated credentials are not warranted by the evidence. What does matter is preserving a specific set of records so the incident remains reconstructable.

Why no card replacement
  - No orders were placed, no saved-payment methods were changed, no checkout path was engaged. The cards on file are still your own enrollment, untouched by the attacker.
  - The retailer-side risk is zero in the evidence; the issuer-side risk is unchanged from before the breach.
  - Defense-in-depth reissuance with the card issuer is a reasonable personal choice but is not evidence-driven here. If you do it, treat it as a one-time issuer reissue rather than a churn of the retailer record.
  - The cheaper, equally informative action is to watch your card statements for 60-90 days at a low threshold.

Why no rotation of unrelated credentials
  - The password was unique and not reused, so the compromise has no propagation surface to other accounts.
  - You already rechecked recovery address and MFA enrollment, both intact. There is no signal that other accounts are exposed.
  - Rotating credentials without a reuse or compromise signal is churn that creates its own risk (lost access, broken stored logins, no signal-driven prioritization) and dilutes future alerts.

What this evidence does and does not establish
  - Establishes: one read-only session on 2024-12-29 from an unfamiliar Windows device, profile-page view only, no persistence indicators, contained by your own actions.
  - Does not establish: how the unique, non-reused password was obtained. The security history you have is an in-account record; the vector sits outside it. That is the only meaningful open question and matters more than anything in-account.

Records to retain
  1. The security history export itself. It is the primary evidence: sign-in timestamps, device identifiers, IP addresses if surfaced, user-agent. Store it with a clear filename containing the export date.
  2. The unfamiliar device's identifying fields from the export — device fingerprint or device ID, OS string, IP, and the exact UTC timestamp of the session. These are the lead for any future pattern match.
  3. Timestamps and counts for your containment actions: password change, session revocations (number of sessions killed), and the export. These anchor the post-incident baseline.
  4. A snapshot of the current recovery address, captured after your recheck, showing it is unchanged. Same for MFA enrollment: factor types, enrollment dates, no new factors.
  5. The retailer's case or ticket number if you opened one, plus the date/time and the response received. Establishes the vendor-side record.
  6. A short incident summary you write yourself — timeline, scope (single session, read-only, profile page), impact (none observable), containment taken, records preserved. This is what makes the rest of the records actually usable later.
  7. Any communication with the retailer, preserved in full. Email headers and the original retailer reply, not just a summary.

Storage posture
  Keep the export and summary in a location you control that is independent of the retailer account. An encrypted folder on a device not used to sign in to that account, a read-only archive, or a printed copy all satisfy the goal: the records survive independently and are not co-located with anything else that might be compromised. The retailer can lose or purge its logs; yours cannot.

What to watch for going forward
  - Any post-containment sign-in reusing the same device ID or IP family.
  - Password-reset emails you did not initiate.
  - New MFA factors you did not enroll.
  - Card or bank statement anomalies at a low threshold.
  - Recurrence of unfamiliar-device sign-ins on other accounts, which would change the vector question.

One follow-up worth doing when you have time
  The export tells you what happened inside the account. The interesting question is upstream: how did the attacker obtain a unique password? Realistic candidates are a phishing path specific to this account, malware on a device you used to sign in, or a retailer-side breach. If any of those surface later, that becomes the actual fix; everything in-account is downstream of it.

The preservation contract: nothing on the cloud side is touched (no deleting, no scope changes, no disabling iCloud Backup) until the encrypted local backup exists on disk AND you have proven it can be read with your password.

Phase 0 — Inventory and screenshot (5 minutes)
  Goal: know exactly what is at risk before you touch anything.
  1. On the iPhone: Settings → [your name] → iCloud → Backups. Screenshot the entry for "This iPhone." Record: date of last successful backup (should be Dec 26) and size. This is your baseline.
  2. In the same screen, open Manage Storage and screenshot the breakdown. Identify the top 3–5 items so you know what to free later (Phase 4).
  3. On the phone: Settings → [your name] → iCloud → note the toggle for "Messages in iCloud." If it is OFF, messages live only in device backups (cloud and local) — that is what you are racing to capture locally.
  4. Confirm at least 30 GB free on the computer. A full backup is roughly the size of used storage on the phone.
  5. Memory test: think about anything deleted from the phone since Dec 26 — messages, photos, notes, app data. Those exist ONLY in the stale cloud backup. If anything matters there, that is the single copy you are racing to preserve. Make a list.

Phase 1 — Choose and record the encryption password
  Do this BEFORE plugging in. If you lose this password, the backup is unrecoverable — even Apple cannot help.
  - Use a unique strong password (12+ chars, ideally a passphrase of 4–5 random words).
  - Record it in your password manager AND on paper stored somewhere safe.
  - Do NOT reuse your Apple ID password.
  - You will re-enter this password every time you back up OR restore from this backup.

Phase 2 — Create the encrypted local backup
  Mac (Ventura and later):
    1. Connect via USB cable. Avoid Wi-Fi for this one — slower and more failure modes.
    2. Open Finder. The iPhone appears in the sidebar under Locations.
    3. Select the iPhone. Trust the computer; enter the iPhone passcode when prompted.
    4. Under Backups, choose "Back up all of the data on your iPhone to this Mac."
    5. Check "Encrypt local backup."
    6. Set and confirm the encryption password (the one from Phase 1).
    7. Click "Back Up Now." Do not disconnect.
    8. The status bar shows progress. Encryption adds overhead — a 15 GB backup typically takes 30–60 minutes over USB.
    9. Backup is done when Finder shows "Last backup to this Mac: [today]" with today's date.
  Windows (iTunes):
    1. Install/update iTunes from apple.com (desktop version has clearer paths than the Microsoft Store version, but either works).
    2. Same cable → trust → passcode flow.
    3. Phone icon → "This Computer" → check "Encrypt iPhone Backup" → set password → "Back Up Now."
  Note the backup location:
    - Mac: ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/<device-hash-or-uuid>/
    - Windows (desktop iTunes): %APPDATA%\Apple Computer\MobileSync\Backup\<hash>\

Phase 3 — Verify (the step most people skip; do not skip)
  Pass all three checks below before touching the cloud.
  Check A — Size and timestamp sanity:
    - Open the backup folder (location from Phase 2).
    - Confirm most recent file modifications are within the last few hours.
    - Confirm total folder size is in the right ballpark — typically 5–30 GB on a phone with real data. Under 1 GB on a phone that has data means the backup is incomplete; stop and re-run.
    - Confirm Manifest.plist exists and opens (XML). Its presence is a strong signal of a well-formed backup.
  Check B — Open with password (proves encryption is correct AND the backup is not corrupted):
    - Use a tool that reads encrypted iPhone backups. Two good options:
      - iMazing (free trial): iMazing → Browse Backups → select the backup → enter password. If it loads, you can browse Messages, Contacts, Call History, Notes.
      - iBackup Extractor (free tier): File → Open Backup → choose the folder → enter password.
    - If the tool rejects the password, the password is wrong — do NOT delete the backup, just re-enter.
    - If it loads but reports corruption, the backup is bad — re-run Phase 2 before proceeding.
  Check C — Visual confirmation:
    - In the same tool, scroll through Messages and confirm recent threads are present.
    - Export one thread as PDF or CSV to a separate folder as an extra "I have proof" copy.

Phase 4 — Only after Phase 3 passes, touch the cloud
    1. Free iCloud space: delete large items identified in Phase 0, offload iCloud Drive files, manage photo storage. Do NOT delete the existing iCloud device backup yet.
    2. Verify Settings → iCloud → Backups still shows the Dec 26 (stale) backup. Freeing space does not auto-delete existing backups.
    3. Plug the phone in, lock it, connect to Wi-Fi. iCloud Backup re-runs automatically once there is room (usually within hours, often that night).
    4. Confirm Settings → iCloud → Backups now shows a backup dated today. The Dec 26 one has been replaced.
    5. Belt-and-suspenders: keep the encrypted local backup for at least a few weeks. After that, archive it to an external drive if you want to free computer space. Do not rely on a single local copy of irreplaceable data long-term.

What NOT to do until Phase 3 passes
  - Do not Manage Storage → delete the iCloud backup for this iPhone. Even though stale, it is the only copy of anything deleted from the phone since Dec 26.
  - Do not toggle "iCloud Backup" off and back on. That triggers a fresh backup once re-enabled and may consume the freed space before the local one is verified.
  - Do not change backup scope (toggle off any app category) until the new backup completes successfully.
  - Do not erase or reset the phone.
  - Do not store the encryption password only in your head.

Failure modes during Phase 2
  - "Backup failed" or stops mid-way: usually cable, USB port, or trust prompt. Try a different cable/port, re-trust, retry.
  - Encryption prompt never appears: another backup tool (iMazing, iBackup Extractor, etc.) may be holding the connection. Quit those, retry.
  - Backup completes but Manifest.plist is missing or folder size is tiny: do not trust it. Delete that folder and re-run Phase 2.

What the local backup actually preserves vs. the cloud one
  Both an iCloud backup and an encrypted local backup of the same phone contain the same logical data: messages, app data, device settings, keychain (with encryption), Health, call history. Photos in iCloud are NOT in either backup — they live in iCloud Photos independently and are unaffected by this. The local backup you are about to make is strictly newer than the Dec 26 cloud one, which is a feature — provided nothing irreplaceable was deleted from the phone between Dec 26 and now (your Phase 0 list).

BLUF: Lock the card now; do not replace yet. A single small pending authorization with the card still in your hand is the textbook "card-testing" pattern — fraudster validates the number, then attempts a larger charge within hours-to-days. Locking blocks the follow-on without disrupting your pending $1.00, your auto-pays, or your saved payment methods.

1. Immediate containment (next 2 minutes)
  - Open your issuer's app directly (or type the issuer URL yourself — do not use a link from any text/email about this charge). Lock or freeze the card.
  - Reversible in seconds. Blocks new authorizations at the merchant network level. Does not cancel the pending $1.00.
  - Leave the pending transaction alone. If fraud, it will drop in 1–7 business days when no matching capture posts.
  - Do not call any number sent to you in a text/email about the charge — only the number on the back of the card or your most recent statement.

2. Independent verification (next 30 minutes, before you forget the details)
  - In the issuer app, capture the full transaction detail screen: exact descriptor string, MCC (merchant category code), terminal ID, city, timestamp. A common trick is a descriptor close to a real merchant — verify character-by-character.
  - Sign in from a fresh session (force-close and reopen the app, or use a desktop browser). If MFA behaves normally and you see no unfamiliar sessions/locations, your account login is likely not compromised — good signal, but doesn't rule out the card number being harvested elsewhere (breach reuse, skimmer, phishing purchase).
  - Independently look up "NORTHSTAR DIGITAL" yourself — descriptor alone is ambiguous. Many small real SaaS, ad-network, domain, or subscription merchants show up unfamiliar. Search the name plus "scam" / "fraud" / "legit"; check whether it has a real web presence with a verifiable address. Note what you find and when.
  - I cannot verify the merchant for you from here — treat your own search result as the basis, not the absence of one.

3. Evidence to preserve (screenshot before you do anything else)
  - The pending transaction screen (merchant, $1.00, 8:41 PM, "pending" status).
  - The expanded detail screen if the app has one.
  - Your card-on-file screen showing the last four and that the physical card is with you.
  - The account activity / login history page if shown — clean history is evidence that the issuer account itself wasn't taken over.
  - Keep (don't delete) any automated email/SMS the issuer sends you about this charge.
  - Note the time you discovered it. Date/time-stamped screenshots are fine; an export or PDF is better if the app offers it.

4. Replacement criteria — replace the card only if any one of these triggers:
  - A second unfamiliar authorization appears on this card, even another small one. That confirms card-testing; replace.
  - The $1.00 actually posts (instead of dropping off) and you did not authorize it. File dispute + replace.
  - The issuer, when you call, recommends replacement.
  - You simply want closure now. Replacements are typically free, 3–7 business days; this is reasonable but more disruptive than the situation strictly requires.
  - If none of these happen and the $1.00 drops in a few days with no further activity, you do not need to replace.

5. Lock vs. replace right now
  - Lock now. Replacement is more disruptive than a single pending $1.00 warrants:
    - Any auto-pay or subscription on this card will need the new PAN/CVV; gym, streaming, utilities, etc. — easy to miss one.
    - Mobile wallet (Apple/Google Pay) token needs re-provisioning.
    - Saved cards in browser autofill break.
  - Lock lets you watch safely for 24–72 hours. If clean, release and move on. If anything else shows up, replace from inside the locked-card flow (most issuers route replacement without you having to unlock first).

6. When you contact the issuer (use the back-of-card number)
  - Tell them: unfamiliar pending $1.00 from "NORTHSTAR DIGITAL" at 8:41 PM, no purchase made, physical card in possession, login/MFA normal.
  - Ask them to: (a) confirm whether they've already flagged or blocked the descriptor, (b) put a note on the account to watch for follow-on attempts, (c) tell you their hold window before any matching capture is auto-released, (d) whether they want you to dispute now or wait until it posts.
  - Do not read the full card number aloud unless you dialed the official number yourself.

What would change this recommendation upward (i.e., replace immediately):
  - The card was ever out of your sight today — even briefly at a restaurant, hotel front desk, or repair shop.
  - A second pending auth of any amount from any merchant.
  - Any sign the $1.00 has actually posted rather than being a true pending hold.
  - Login or MFA behavior was even slightly off (unexpected prompt, push you didn't request, device you don't recognize).

What would change it downward (relax — keep using the card, no lock needed):
  - The independent lookup shows "NORTHSTAR DIGITAL" is a real, verifiable company you have a plausible reason to have transacted with (subscription you forgot, free-trial conversion, ad-network charge tied to a service you use).
  - The issuer confirms it's a known recurring small charge on your account and you recognize it after the detail check.

The most likely outcome is the $1.00 drops in a few days with nothing else appearing, in which case you release the lock and do nothing further. The whole point of the lock is to make that outcome free.

## Generation / cleanup guidance (added 2024-05-30)
==============================================================

The checks above cover CPU, memory, queue depth, route-delivery
divergence, dropped series, and restarts. This section adds the
checks that are otherwise invisible during a canary: active vs
retired generation counts, epoch drain, matcher cleanup, and
stop-the-world cleanup pauses.

### What to compare
- Compare p99 by pod against active generation count and retired
  generation count for that pod. A pod can look quiet on aggregate
  p99 while a retired generation is leaking hot objects into the
  cleanup queue.
- Track stop-the-world cleanup pauses (the long-tail GC /
  matcher-table compaction pauses) alongside p99. A clean p99 with
  rising cleanup pauses means the next config push will stall.

### Pause additional configuration pushes when either holds
- Retired objects accumulate above 4 on any canary pod — old
  generation objects are not being drained; another config push on
  top will worsen the leak.
- Cleanup pauses exceed 100 ms on any canary pod — matcher-table
  compaction is already in stop-the-world territory; more config
  will lengthen the pauses, not shorten them.

In either case, hold the next push, drain, and re-check before
resuming.

### Required verifications before resuming
After the pause condition clears, verify all of the following
before allowing the next configuration push:
1. Active-generation consistency — every canary pod reports the
   same active generation ID.
2. Route parity — route-delivery divergence (already in the
   baseline checks above) holds at zero.
3. Dropped series — held at zero.
4. Reload failures — zero in the canary window.
5. Restarts — zero in the canary window.

All five must hold. A clean p99 alone is not enough.

### Evidence to capture
For the canary record, capture:
- Generation evidence: per-pod active generation ID, per-pod
  retired generation count (peak and at-resolution), and the
  epoch-drain timestamp.
- Heap evidence: per-pod heap high-water mark during the canary
  window, and any stop-the-world cleanup pause duration over 100 ms
  (timestamp, pod, duration).
- Attach both to the canary record alongside the existing p99 /
  error-rate / dropped-write / rollup-lag captures.

### Rollback rules (do not weaken the existing criteria)
- Do not roll back solely because a transient p99 spike recovered.
  The bar above already requires the five verifications to hold; a
  p99 spike that self-recovers while generations stay consistent,
  route parity holds, dropped series stay at zero, reload failures
  stay at zero, and restarts stay at zero is consistent with canary
  warmup, not a regression.
- Do roll back for any of:
  - Active-generation inconsistency across canary pods (mismatched
    generation IDs after the push).
  - Route divergence — non-zero route-delivery divergence between

## approval wording)  ← what Wes specifically needs
==============================================================

The owner-led config window rule below replaces the prior per-push
approval framing. It extends — and does not replace — the Generation
/ cleanup guidance above and the baseline checks at the top of this
entry.

### Window opening
Each owner-led config window requires a fresh opening decision from
Alex. Without an opening decision, no pushes proceed under this rule.

### What operators may do inside the window
Mapped operators may make single-file pushes while all of the
following hold:
- Retired generations remain at four or fewer on every canary pod.
- Cleanup pauses remain at 100 ms or below on every canary pod.
- The full health set returns to baseline after every push.

A push that leaves the full health set at baseline is in-window. A
push that does not is out-of-window — see stop rules below.

### Stop rules — the window stops immediately
The window stops immediately when either of the following holds:
- Retired generations exceed four on any canary pod.
- Cleanup pauses exceed 100 ms on any canary pod.

Either condition by itself is sufficient. The window stops the
moment a threshold is crossed; no second crossing is required.

### Recovery and the next push
After the window stops and the thresholds clear:
- A fresh decision from Alex permits exactly one fully observed
  push.
- That single push is bounded — it is not a return to the prior
  window's cadence.
- Capture the same generation + heap evidence listed in the
  "Evidence to capture" section above for that push.
- If the full health set does not return to baseline after that
  push, the single-push permission does not extend further.

### Opening a new window
Another window requires a separate fresh decision from Alex, made
only after the single bounded push above has returned the full
health set to baseline. The previous window's opening decision does
not carry forward.

### Rollback conditions (unchanged)
The following remain rollback conditions, in addition to the rules
in the Generation / cleanup section above. Roll back on any of:
- Consistency — active-generation inconsistency across canary pods.
- Parity — non-zero route-delivery divergence.
- Dropped series — any non-zero dropped-series count in the canary
  window.
- Reload — any reload failure in the canary window.
- Restart — any restart in the canary window.

These five remain rollback conditions even if p99 has returned to
baseline, even if the heap has returned to baseline, even if cleanup
pauses have come back under 100 ms, and even if retired generations
have drained back to four or fewer. A clean threshold picture does
not talk anyone out of the rollback.

- Alex remains the primary owner.
- Wes remains the practical backup.
- Wes is not becoming the primary owner. The owner map is
  unchanged.

**Why silent mapping is prohibited:**

- The bounded contract admits only `prod`, `staging`, `dev` on the wire; missing input is omitted. Everything else — `unknown`, `qa`, malformed values, arbitrary raw strings — is rejected before publication.
- Silent `qa` → `staging` rewriting fabricates a deployment classification. That breaks provenance: the metric would claim a workload shipped from staging when the producer actually labeled it QA. Downstream parity (rollup-service consumer reading the same labels) would then report a producer-consumer mismatch against an invented value, not a real one.
- The three-value tenant distinct-value budget (`{prod, staging, dev}`) exists precisely to prevent a fourth value from being smuggled in via coercion. Silent mapping is the cheapest way to erode that ceiling without anyone noticing.
- The producer side is the place to fix this. The staging release owner needs to either (a) send `staging` when the workload is genuinely a staging workload, or (b) omit the label when the producer cannot truthfully assert an environment.

A staging producer that emits `qa` because QA is its internal vocabulary still emitted `qa`; that is a producer contract drift, not a normalization question.
