Here is a minimal setup. I am assuming a typical South Slope layout (entry → living room → hall → kitchen / bedroom / work-room / bathroom); swap room names to match yours.

PRINCIPLE (applies to every room)
- Find the ceiling head (small brass/chrome disc). Picture a 3-foot circle on the floor directly under it.
- Inside that circle: move anything freestanding — floor items (rugs, baskets, shoes, mats, scales, laundry hampers) AND anything tall enough to block a pole sweep (floor lamps, tall plants, coat racks, floor mirrors, chairs). Push them to a wall edge or stack them just outside the circle.
- Leave wall-mounted items, built-ins, and anything already against a wall outside the radius alone.
- The 6-foot pole is vertical, so the constraint that matters is "nothing in the circle tall enough to obstruct the pole going up to the head."

PER-ROOM CHECKLIST (do a 30-second pass per room tonight)
- Living room (likely first stop): rug corner, floor lamp, side table, plant, shoes, toy bin.
- Hallway: floor baskets, shoe pile, bags.
- Kitchen: trash can, kick stool, pet bowls, floor mat in front of sink if it falls under the head.
- Bedroom: laundry basket, floor mirror, chair with clothes, under-bed bins that protrude.
- Work-room: see below.
- Bathroom: bath mat, scale, hamper, basket. Toilet and vanity stay.
- Kibo's holding room (see below): clear the 3-ft radius tonight while you are already on the move.

WORK-ROOM (the only room with extra path rules)
- 3-ft radius under the head: clear as above.
- Door path: clear the door's swing arc — nothing on the floor within ~3 ft of the hinge side, and nothing hanging on the back of the door.
- Window path: clear ~3 ft of floor in front of the window and make sure the window can be opened and reached. If a chair or part of the desk blocks sill access, scoot it aside. Tie back curtains if they hang into the floor radius or block the operator.

KIBO — PICKING THE HOLDING ROOM
Pick the room that is all three of these:
  1. OFF the inspectors' walking path from your front door (they do not pass through it to reach other rooms).
  2. Last in the sequence they will hit (farthest from entry, or the smallest side room).
  3. Equipped with litter box, water, and a familiar blanket or bed.

Best fits in a typical apartment: a bathroom off the hall (small, head usually near the door, Kibo can hide in the tub or a carrier during the brief check) or a back bedroom that inspectors reach last.
Bad fits: a bedroom the hallway funnels inspectors through, or the living room.

Set up tonight: litter box, water bowl, blanket, one toy. Close the door from tonight so Kibo acclimates.

KIBO MOVING SEQUENCE
- Tonight, before bed: holding room set up, door closed.
- Tomorrow 8:40–8:50 AM: move Kibo into the holding room with a treat; latch the door. Confirm water and litter are reachable.
- 8:55 AM: one quick apartment pass to confirm nothing migrated back into any 3-ft circle overnight. Crack the work-room window if the inspection calls for it.
- 9:00–11:00 AM: stay home. When inspectors reach Kibo's room, briefly contain Kibo (carrier, or close him in the tub / behind the litter box) while they check the head. Door closed again before they move on.
- ~11:00 AM, after they leave: open Kibo's door.

ENTRY PATH = the route inspectors walk from your front door through the apartment. If your hallway forces them past Kibo's door to reach anything else, pick a different holding room — that is the one constraint that, if violated, defeats the "away from the entry path" rule.

That is the whole plan: ~15–20 minutes of floor-item shifts tonight, one door routine tomorrow morning, no disassembly.

Outline below — minimum questions the one-page feasibility proposal must answer. Each section names what the proposal needs to resolve, not what I'd commit to. Customer interpretation stays with Iris; nothing here authorizes the feature or changes the active preview.

  Row-level authorization
    - Does the on-screen read-only authorization grant suffice, or is an
      explicit "export" scope required per requester?
    - Authorization check: per-row at generation, or dataset-level gate
      upstream of generation? What is the fallback when a row's
      authorization cannot be resolved mid-job?
    - Does the dataset contain rows the requester is authorized to view on
      screen but not to receive in a durable artifact? How is that filtered?

  Tenant binding
    - Single-tenant export only, or multi-tenant bulk? If multi-tenant,
      what identifier is emitted on every row to confirm binding on receipt?
    - Where is cross-tenant leakage prevented — query layer, export pipeline,
      or both? Defense-in-depth or single chokepoint?
    - How is the tenant scope communicated to the requester before generation
      and verified in the delivered file?

  Provenance and source timestamps (per 2025-04-03 completeness rule)
    - How does the export pipeline populate tenant_id, published_service_id,
      published_owner, source_record_id, and source_timestamp on every row?
    - Behavior when source_record_id or source_timestamp is null: hard reject
      the affected rows, reject the whole export, or generate with a visible
      gap marker? (Null in either field currently = scan fail.)
    - Are these fields emitted as CSV columns, or held in a sidecar manifest?
      What is the contract for downstream consumers?

  Stale-to-unknown behavior
    - Does the export mirror the on-screen stale-to-unknown policy exactly,
      or does export have stricter freshness requirements?
    - For rows that have aged past the staleness threshold: drop, mark
      "unknown," or carry the stale timestamp with an explicit caveat?
    - Is there a defined staleness horizon beyond which export is refused
      outright, regardless of authorization?

  Export retention and delivery
    - Where is the generated file stored, for how long, and who can
      re-download it?
    - Delivery channel: signed URL, email attachment, secure transfer, or
      other? Expiry on the delivery token?
    - Retention window aligned with Harbor Health's data-handling
      obligations (HIPAA / BAA / contract terms)? Who owns the decision on
      the retention number?
    - On deletion, is the file purged, or only access revoked? Audit trail
      of either.

  Excluded fields
    - Explicit allowlist vs explicit denylist — which is the contract for v1?
    - Which fields visible in the preview are excluded from export (internal
      IDs, free-text clinical notes, derived values, unpublished metadata),
      and on what basis each is excluded?
    - Are excluded-field decisions documented in the runbook so they survive
      staff and contract changes?

  Auditability
    - Per export: requester, timestamp, authorization scope checked, row
      count, output hash, delivery channel, retention expiry, recipient
      identity.
    - Audit log retention, location, and who can read it.
    - Can the export be replayed or reconstructed from the audit trail, or
      is the audit only a record of occurrence?

  Failure modes
    - Partial delivery vs all-or-nothing on job failure.
    - Authorization change mid-job — abort, complete with current snapshot,
      or surface a per-row delta?
    - Provenance failure mid-job (row discovered to have null source_record_id
      or source_timestamp after generation starts) — retry, skip, fail the
      whole export?
    - Retry semantics and idempotency: can a failed export be safely
      re-requested without duplicating downstream artifacts?

  Is read-only on-screen authorization sufficient for a generated file?
    - The proposal must answer this directly, not by inheritance. Generated
      files persist, are transferable, and outlive the authorizing session —
      that is a different threat model than on-screen read-only.
    - If yes, the proposal must state the conditions under which it is
      sufficient and any compensating controls.
    - If no, the proposal must specify the additional authorization scope
      (purpose-binding, recipient-binding, time-bound consent, or other) and
      who grants it.

Review of Product Engineering's one-page Lantern CSV feasibility proposal against the established framework

Scope of review. Product Engineering's proposal (as relayed by Iris) generates CSVs from the currently visible deploy-movement and published-ownership cards, reuses the on-screen authorization decision, and retains generated files for seven days in a shared object-store prefix. The active preview remains unchanged; no implementation or customer authorization exists. The review below uses the seven categories named in the ask, with the two structural categories Iris separately flagged (tenant binding; stale-to-unknown) folded into authorization and provenance so no requirement is dropped.

A. Authorization — blocking
  The proposal "reuses the on-screen authorization decision" for a generated file that is persistent, transferable, and re-downloadable. That is a different authorization object from an in-room read: on-screen authorization is per-request and ephemeral; a retained file is a new artifact with its own distribution surface, recipient set, and replay window. Persistent and transferable artifacts require explicit, separate authorization, not inherited scope. As written, the proposal offers no grantor, no scope expansion, no compensating control, and no decision on whether the existing read-only pilot authorization covers a downloadable artifact. This is the same failure-mode class as Lantern's importer-retry-after-revocation pattern: relying on a snapshot of an authorization that no longer matches the artifact's lifetime. Unresolved.

B. Provenance (incl. source timestamps and stale-to-unknown) — blocking
  1. No row-level provenance contract is defined for the file. The April 3, 2025 completeness rule requires every approved export row to carry tenant_id, published_service_id, published_owner, source_record_id, and source_timestamp, with null source_record_id or source_timestamp treated as a scan failure. The proposal does not state which fields land in the CSV, whether each row carries its source_record_id and source_timestamp, or what happens when a permitted source is absent at generation time.
  2. No generation-time freshness or explicit-unknown behavior is specified. A CSV generated from a snapshot of cards must define whether each row reflects the card state at the moment of generation, whether stale permitted sources are written as the row or replaced with `unknown`, and what the per-row `unknown` sentinel looks like in CSV form (the on-screen rule uses a typed unknown, not a blank). Without this, the file is structurally a partial provenance leak — bounded on-screen, unbounded in the file.
  3. Generation-time is not defined as a derivation boundary. The on-screen freshness marker uses max(observed_at) from the served event set; a CSV must fix the generation instant and either carry it on every row or in a header, and it must be re-evaluated against each source's freshness at generation, not at last render.

C. Retention — blocking
  1. "Seven days in a shared object-store prefix" is unauthorized for the current read-only pilot. The pilot's wrapper scope is provenance-backed deploy events, published ownership, timestamped incident-load summaries, and explicit unknown states — i.e., read-only in-room signals. A seven-day retained file is a new artifact class with its own retention policy and is not covered by the existing authorization.
  2. Retention ownership is unassigned. The proposal does not name a retention owner, a deletion procedure, or a verification path that deletion actually occurred. Past object-store experience (the repeated five-minute prefix-listing job) shows that retention hygiene needs explicit scheduling and verification, not a passive prefix.
  3. Re-download access during the retention window is unstated. If a recipient can re-fetch the file via the object-store URL during the seven days, that is effectively a longer-lived authorization surface than the pilot permits; if they cannot, the delivery mechanism and one-time token need to be specified.

D. Delivery — blocking
  1. No delivery channel is defined. On-screen → file → recipient has at least three viable shapes (signed URL, attached file, in-product download), each with different authorization, audit, and re-download properties. The proposal names none.
  2. No delivery-token expiry, recipient identity binding, or re-download policy is defined. Without these, the seven-day retention window is functionally open access to anyone with the URL.
  3. HIPAA/BAA/contractual alignment is not addressed. Harbor Health's request originates from an internal release-review workbook, but the file would carry customer-scoped deploy-movement and ownership data. Storage location, access permissions, re-download access, delivery-token expiry, and deletion behavior must align with Harbor Health's data-handling obligations before any artifact exists.

E. Exclusion (excluded fields and inference) — blocking
  1. No exclusion-list enforcement is specified for the CSV. The May 15, 2024 contract explicitly excluded internal room names, employee IDs, permission IDs, owner-map IDs, raw incident text, and ownership inferred from room context. The proposal does not enumerate which fields are forbidden, where the exclusion is enforced (generation-time allowlist vs. card-level filter), or what happens if a forbidden field would have been in the on-screen card. The on-screen exclusion contract is enforced read-side; a generated file needs its own enforcement layer.
  2. Inferred ownership and raw incident text must remain excluded by construction. The proposal generates from cards, which already excludes those, but the proposal does not state that the generator inherits the same allowlist or prove it under test.
  3. Cross-signal contamination risk is not addressed. A file that lets a recipient join deploy-movement and ownership rows offline recreates the query-delta and management-chain rollup patterns that v0 explicitly excludes. The proposal does not limit row cardinality, row ordering, or per-recipient file shape in a way that prevents offline re-joining.

F. Auditability — blocking
  The established audit requirement for any export is: requester, timestamp, authorization scope, row count, output hash, delivery channel, retention expiry, and recipient identity, plus retention, storage location, access permissions, and replay/reconstruction policy. The proposal names none of these. Without an output hash, a tampered or substituted file is undetectable. Without recipient identity, distribution is untracked. Without replay/reconstruction policy, a second request for the same window is undefined (does it generate a new file with a new hash? is the old file invalidated? does the second request require a fresh authorization?). Authorization-before-lookup at file-generation time must be specified, including the wrapper entry point — the resolver-local workaround pattern was already rejected for preview lookups and would be rejected here.

G. Failure modes — blocking
  1. Partial delivery and authorization changes during generation are not specified. What happens if authorization changes mid-generation? What happens if the source adapter fails after some rows are written? Past importer failure modes required reauthorization before each source-page fetch and immediately before publication, with invalidation of partial imported material on denial; a CSV generator needs analogous fail-closed semantics.
  2. Idempotent re-request is undefined. The wrapper contract requires that retries use a fresh authorization context rather than a cached allow; the CSV analog must say whether a re-request within the retention window generates a new file, invalidates the prior file, or is denied.
  3. Provenance failures during generation (null source_record_id or null source_timestamp) are not addressed. The April 3, 2025 rule treats these as scan failures; the generator must say whether a single failing row fails the whole file, fails only that row (with explicit unknown), or is treated differently at generation time vs. scan time.
  4. Stale-during-generation is not distinguished from stale-at-render. A card that was fresh when viewed but stale at the moment the file is written must be either re-evaluated or written as `unknown`; neither is specified.

H. Cross-cutting gaps
  1. The proposal is feasibility-stage and has not been implemented or authorized by customers. The active preview remains unchanged; that boundary is preserved.
  2. Customer interpretation remains Iris's responsibility. The technical gaps above are not a request for Iris to redefine scope; they are a request that any future proposal address each category concretely before review resumes.
  3. The seven-day shared-prefix retention is, on its own, sufficient to keep this at feasibility: it is a new artifact class that the existing read-only pilot authorization does not cover.

PRE-RIDE FRONT-WHEEL / BRAKE INSPECTION (no tools needed)
Goal: tell harmless pad rub from anything that needs a shop.

1. FREE-SPIN ISOLATION
   Lift the front end, brake off, spin and let it coast. Crouch and listen at three spots:
     - Above the tire / fender
     - Beside the brake caliper (or rotor, if disc)
     - Beside the hub
   Sound loudest at the brake = pad / rotor / rim contact.
   Sound loudest at tire / fender = tire contact or debris.
   Sound loudest at hub, or pitch follows wheel speed rather than position = bearing.

2. PAD CONTACT CHECK
   With the wheel still, sight down the caliper from above and from behind the fork.
     - Rim brake: each pad should clear the rim by ~1-2 mm and land on the braking track, not the tire or below the rim.
     - Disc brake: rotor should sit centered in the caliper slot, no visible warp when spun slowly.
   Squeeze the lever lightly while watching the contact. If the rub appears or worsens, the pads / caliper are the source. If the rub is identical lever-released vs lever-applied, the pads aren't the cause.

3. TIRE / DEBRY PASS
   - Check clearance between the tire and: fork crown, fender, brake arms, frame. Look for shiny rub marks on the tire sidewall or paint.
   - Run a finger or cloth lightly around the tread and sidewalls; pull any clearly external shard (glass, wire, thorn) you can see. Don't dig into the casing.
   - Spin slowly and watch the contact patch for any bulge, hop, or visible debris rotating with the wheel.

4. SPOKE + RIM TENSION
   - Squeeze adjacent spoke pairs at the flange. Tension should feel uniform. A noticeably softer spoke is loose.
   - Pluck a few spokes like a guitar string. Healthy spokes ring; a thud or much lower pitch = loose or broken.
   - Sight the rim edge against a fixed reference (fork blade, pad edge) while spinning slowly. Any new side-to-side or up-and-down hop? Any visible bend?

5. HUB / BEARING
   - Wheel off ground, hands on each axle end (or the dropout flanges for QR). Rock fore-aft and side-to-side. Click / clunk / play = bearings.
   - Free-spin for about 10 seconds, then immediately touch the hub. Warm is fine; hot is a bearing problem — stop.

6. QUICK-RELEASE / AXLE CLOSURE (you already cycled it — verify)
   - Closed lever should leave a clear imprint in your palm.
   - With brakes applied, try to rock the wheel fore-aft in the dropouts. Any movement = QR isn't clamping; STOP.
   - Skewer should sit perpendicular to the dropout face when closed.

INTERPRETATION
   - Pad rub that disappears when you re-center the caliper or loosen and re-seat the wheel = rideable after a quick re-adjust.
   - Rub that persists with the caliper centered, or that changes when you squeeze the lever = misaligned caliper, sticky piston, or pad contamination. Ride cautiously to a shop; not a workout.
   - Sound independent of the lever, located at the tire = debris or tire bulge. Clear debris and recheck; bulge = stop.
   - Sound at the hub with roughness, play, or heat = stop.

STOP — DO NOT RIDE UNTIL A SHOP CHECKS IF YOU FIND:
   - Visible rim crack, dent, or any new runout (side-to-side wobble), even small.
   - Any loose spoke, or more than one thud on the pluck test.
   - Free-spin grinds and stops within 1-2 seconds, or the hub gets warm / hot.
   - Bearing play on the rock test, or a rough gritty feel.
   - Brake lever pulls to the bar, feels spongy, or braking power drops during the inspection.
   - QR / axle not clamping (wheel moves in dropouts under load) — catastrophic if it fails at speed.
   - Bent rotor (disc) or visibly warped rim edge.
   - Rub that worsens when you apply the brake before the lever is anywhere near its limit.
   - Any heat at the hub or rim after a short free-spin.

If none of those are present and the scrape is light, intermittent, and unchanged by the lever, it's almost certainly pad rub or a small debris shard. Clear any visible debris, re-center the wheel, and ride the first minute cautiously to confirm the sound doesn't worsen before committing to a longer route.

Steady rain with no thunder is a "shorten, don't skip" situation — the bathroom need is real and a known-loop walk with belly coverage beats a wet marathon. Given Kibo's prior pad laceration (9/2/24) and that a wet paw is easier to nick or irritate, lean conservative on exposure but not on the trip itself.

1) Walk length and route
- Target 15–20 minutes — enough for potty + a real sniff, short enough that the undercoat doesn't soak through.
- Pick your shortest known "bathroom loop" rather than exploring. Familiarity = faster business, less hesitation in rain.
- Sidewalk-first, grass-second. Avoid tall wet grass and leaf piles (burrs, hidden debris, irritated paw pads given his history).
- Avoid standing water and storm drains. Step around curb puddles.
- Stay within ~1–2 blocks of home so you can cut the walk short cleanly if anything shifts.

2) Gear and towel setup
- Harness and leash: confirm clip still dry/functional before clipping on. Quick-dry lead is nicer; standard is fine.
- Raincoat with belly panel and a high collar — the chest/belly soak is what chills them afterward; a back-only slicker doesn't do much.
- Skip booties unless Kibo already wears them without a fight — forcing them adds stress and lengthens the outing. A paw-wax barrier (e.g. Musher's Secret) is a reasonable substitute if you have it.
- You: hooded rain shell, waterproof shoes, one free hand (umbrella + leash + poop-bag is too many variables).
- Towel station before you leave: one towel flat by the inside door as a landing mat, a second dry towel ready inside on a towel rack or chair back. Keeps wet dog from running through the apartment before you can grab him.

3) Paw and coat cleanup on return
- Paws first: wipe each pad and between the toes with a damp cloth or unscented paw wipe to get mud and grit off before he lies down. Given the 2024 pad infection, this is the step not to skip.
- Towel the belly, chest, armpits, and inside of the thighs — those areas trap water and stay damp longest.
- Quick once-over on legs and tail; full rub-down only if he's noticeably soaked.
- If he's truly drenched, a low/cool blow-dry on the undercoat helps; otherwise air-dry with the towel station blocking access to couch/bed until he's dry to the touch.
- Quick harness check: dry the harness webbing before re-clipping next time so it doesn't mildew.

4) Conditions that justify shortening or bailing
- Thunder, lightning, or sudden wind gusts — even distant thunder is a reason to head home.
- Rain escalating from steady to heavy/downpour, or hail.
- Kibo shaking, tail tuck, whale-eye, repeated paw-lifting, or actively refusing to move forward.
- A limp or favoring a paw (any pad sensitivity given prior injury → call it and recheck at home).
- You losing visibility or footing on slick pavement.
- A stray dog or any street incident you don't want to manage one-handed in the rain.

If none of those trigger and he potties within the first 5 minutes, the 15–20 minute loop is the right shape.

Reading Iris's sample against the Apr-4 readout contract, here's how it lands:

The issue is clean and the contract is already on her side.

Canonical unit is `explanation_request_id`, not HTTP response row.
The Apr-4 readout fields are defined per request: total explanation requests, eligible combined, completed combined renders, valid over-24h, stale-or-missing as explicit unknown, eligible renderer failures. A retry is one logical request hitting the evidence base twice; it should count once in every field. Bucket classification (eligible combined, separate, unknown, renderer failure) is a property of the request's underlying data, which doesn't change between retry attempts on the same ID. The 6 IDs × 2 attempts = 56 rows is overcounting by 12% in the sample, and that bias propagates into every rate.

What the fix looks like
- Dedup by `explanation_request_id` before any field count.

THE DEFECT (logical-request vs. attempt-counting)

A "logical request" is the unit of authorized intent — one thing the caller asked the system to do. An "attempt" is one execution against that intent. The defect collapses the two: the counter that should report "how many logical requests were processed" instead sums attempts, so a single retrying request registers as N requests.

Symptoms this produces:

  - Inflated throughput / load counts; rate limits and SLOs computed on the wrong base.
  - Broken idempotency: dedupe keyed on (caller, target) instead of a stable authorized request id means retries can be treated as new work and double-apply side effects.
  - Lost retry telemetry: success-after-retry becomes indistinguishable from first-try success; mean-attempts-to-success vanishes.
  - Skewed release scoring. Under the rule that live=rollback and replay/mirror=mismatch investigation and the two are never combined, a comparison surface that mixes live attempts with replay attempts will report divergence that is actually retry noise, and vice versa — false rollbacks and false clean signals are equally possible.
  - Broken audit: the audit log is asked "did this logical request complete?" and answers "attempts 3 of 5."

Root cause is a missing primary key. Logical requests have no stable identifier at the boundary; whatever id exists is per-attempt, so dedupe has nothing stable to dedupe on.

THE CORRECTION (concise)

Define two distinct entities with a 1:N relationship, each with its own counter and its own audit trail.

Logical request
  - Identity: a stable "authorized request id" issued by the caller at the boundary. Authorization is bound to the id at issuance (signed envelope, or id derived from an authorized session/credential), so possession of the id alone is insufficient to spoof retry of someone else's request.
  - Counted exactly once per id for every system-wide metric that asks "how many requests": volume, latency p50/p99, error rate, billing, SLO attainment, release-scoring inputs.
  - Side-effect set is idempotent on id; replays of the same id do not create new logical state.

Attempt
  - Identity: a per-execution attempt id, parented to the logical request id.
  - Counted independently: attempt_count, retry_count, terminal_attempt_index, time-to-terminal-attempt — these are attempt-shaped metrics and stay on the attempt axis.
  - Audit: each attempt appends one record keyed (request_id, attempt_id) with auth context, payload hash, outcome, and timestamp. The logical-request audit row is the parent; attempt rows are children.

The two axes never substitute for each other. A retry storm shows up as high attempt_count on a small set of logical requests, not as inflated logical volume; replay divergence shows up as attempt_count differing from live on the same id while the logical outcome is held constant.

REGRESSION-TEST REQUIREMENT

For each canonical retry fixture (transient failure then success; partial failure then success; permanent failure; retry storm; unauthorized retry of an existing id; concurrent attempts under one id) the test must assert all of the following:

  1. Logical-request count equals the number of distinct authorized request ids in the fixture, never the number of attempts. A fixture that issues one logical request and retries it 5 times must report logical_count == 1 and attempt_count == 5. The inverse fixture (5 distinct ids, 1 attempt each) reports logical_count == 5 and attempt_count == 5.
  2. Side-effect dedupe: re-running the same request id end-to-end produces exactly one logical outcome row; no duplicate mutations, no duplicate downstream events keyed on the request.
  3. Attempt auditability: every attempt is retrievable individually by (request_id, attempt_id) with auth context, payload hash, outcome, and timestamp. Attempt rows are append-only; a later attempt never rewrites an earlier attempt's outcome.
  4. Live-vs-replay logical parity: replay/mirror of the same request id set produces identical logical_count and identical logical outcomes to the live run, regardless of differing attempt_count between the two runs. Divergence in attempt_count alone is not a release-scoring failure; divergence in logical_count or logical outcome triggers the live=rollback / mirror=mismatch-investigation rule.
  5. Authorization binding: an attempt presented with a valid request id but no/expired/wrong-scope auth envelope is rejected or recorded as an unauthorized-attempt event without creating or advancing a logical request. Logical_count is unchanged.
  6. Concurrent-attempt collapse: N concurrent attempts issued under one authorized request id resolve to one logical request with terminal outcome determined by exactly one attempt; the others terminate as no-ops on the logical state and remain visible in the attempt audit.

Acceptance: all six assertions pass for the full fixture set on every release. A regression that re-introduces attempt-as-logical counting fails assertions 1 and 4 first; a regression that loses auth binding fails 5; a regression that loses append-only attempt audit fails 3.

Notes for the test harness
  - Fixtures must be replayable: the test takes a recorded (request_id, payload, auth) set and runs it against live and against replay/mirror; the comparison is on logical-request outcomes, not on attempt sequences.
  - Attempt_count is reported but not asserted equal between live and replay — only counted, and only checked for non-negativity and for matching the fixture's intended retry shape.
  - Unauthorized-attempt coverage needs at least one fixture per rejection mode (missing envelope, expired envelope, wrong scope, id from a different tenant).

The pattern you describe — one repeatable contact point per revolution, laterally true wheel, firm braking, no heat, no visible pad damage, and a centering QR change that did nothing — is a misaligned left brake pad, not a wheel-true issue. The pad has shifted laterally (or its toe-in is wrong) so that only one edge of the pad crosses the brake track once per rotation. Centering the QR wouldn't affect it because the rim isn't moving laterally relative to the pad; the pad is in the wrong place.

On the ride question:

  - A short low-speed verification is compatible with the symptoms as reported — a parking-lot roll forward, brake to a stop, feel the rim temperature, listen for any change. This is a diagnostic, not a ride.
  - A ride of any real distance is not. Sustained pad rub on the brake track will, over time, cut a groove into the rim's braking surface. A grooved rim brake track is a wear-out part: once it's worn or gouged, the rim is unsafe regardless of how the pads look afterward.
  - You don't need a shop for this specific issue. Pad re-alignment on a side-pull caliper (5 mm Allen on the pad-retaining bolt, re-center over the brake track, re-set toe-in) is owner-level maintenance. If you'd rather not do it yourself, walk or transport the bike — don't ride it to the shop.

Findings that make the bike unsafe to ride — check these before and during any test:

  - Pad contacts the tire side of the rim rather than the brake track (shreds the tire; this is not your symptom, but worth confirming visually)
  - Pad hangs off the brake track onto the rim sidewall
  - Visible groove, gouge, or shiny wear line on the rim at the contact point
  - Dark streak on the rim at the contact that doesn't wipe off (pad material embedding)
  - Heat in the rim after a minute of spin — smell, or hot to touch
  - Wheel no longer spins freely, or develops lateral wobble during spin (means the rim wasn't truly true, or something shifted)
  - Braking becomes soft, spongy, or pulls to one side
  - The rhythmic scrape changes into continuous drag (pad fully displaced, or contamination)
  - Loose or "pinging" spoke under load, or any visible spoke movement at the nipple
  - Quick release not fully seated — cam closed under handle force, not just resting against the closed position

If any of those appear, the bike is not rideable until corrected.

What the runbook and prior record require

Generation state is three independent fields: active_generation (what's serving), last_validated_generation (latest that passed validation), and last_attempted_generation (latest reload candidate regardless of outcome). The advancement rule is hard: advancing active_generation is gated behind successful validation and an atomic config-pointer swap; reload_start updates only last_attempted_generation, validation failure records a rejected last_reload without changing active or last_validated generations, and the atomic commit updates active_generation and last_validated_generation under the same lock. The generation invariant is attempted >= validated >= active, and endpoint reporting must expose violations rather than conceal them. active_generation is the only field that indicates what is serving traffic. This was the lesson from the 442 case: the /healthz endpoint returned 200 with config_generation=442 even though generation 442 failed validation and was never activated, and Support was misled into believing the rejected configuration was healthy and active.

Verdict

Request changes.

The change, as described, exposes active_generation directly on the status endpoint before validation passes and before the atomic config-pointer swap commits. That is the exact failure shape that the existing rules are written to prevent. Eleven seconds of an endpoint reporting generation 619 as active while serving still on generation 618 is not "no production effect" — it is the same class of bug as the 442 case, with the only mitigation being the brevity of the window. A dashboard sample landed in that window, which is the whole point of the field: downstream consumers will sample it, alerts will key off it, and any postmortem will read the wrong answer.

Specific issues to address in the PR before merge

1. active_generation is not the field to surface for "what we are trying to become active." Surface last_attempted_generation and last_validated_generation instead, and keep active_generation strictly read from the post-swap snapshot under the same lock that guards the atomic config-pointer swap. The status endpoint must observe only complete old or complete new generation states.

2. The eleven-second window is the bug, not a property of the change. If the code path that assigns the candidate to the field executes before validation, the field is exposed before it is valid. The fix is the order: assign to last_attempted_generation on reload_start, leave active_generation untouched on validation failure, advance active_generation only inside the atomic commit under the swap lock. active_generation must not be mutated outside that lock.

3. Separate liveness from configuration readiness. The status endpoint should expose a readiness object with active, last_validated, last_attempted, reload outcome, timestamps, and a last_reload object that carries the validation error and rejected candidate's sub-cache state when applicable. A failed validation should be observable as a failed reload — not as an advance and a quiet revert.

4. The dashboard sample that captured generation 619 needs to be reconciled. The sample is real evidence of a consumer believing the wrong generation; treat it as the bug, not as an isolated sample that happens to be wrong. Whatever scrape, panel, or alert recorded it must be inspected and the panel label provenance (live vs. validation-only) verified against the Cardinality Guardrails and runbook expectations.

5. Add a fixture that asserts the regression directly: candidate generation N with a validation failure leaves active_generation at N-1 for the entire window, the status endpoint reports active=N-1 throughout, last_attempted_generation=N, last_validated_generation=N-1, and last_reload carries a rejected status with the validation error. The fixture should also assert no status sample in the window reports active=N. The May 6, 2025 revised PR pattern (parse and compile candidates before acquiring the publication lock, readers observe only complete old or new generations) is the right shape to mirror here.

6. Cross-service boundary: the status endpoint is read by rollup-service and by support tooling. Confirm the label set and panel provenance (live vs. replay vs. mirror) match Cardinality Guardrails preflight and the Sept 12, 2026 review rule that live-path panels must be distinguishable from validation-only panels.

What the change is not

This is not a canary response case and does not engage the metrics-router canary runbook. No routes changed, no production state changed, no canary was running. The rollback conditions in the runbook (consistency, parity, dropped series, reload, restart) are not triggered here. The relevance of the runbook is only the rules it documents about how generation state must be reported and how atomic publication must be done — those are baseline rules, not canary-specific ones.

- The status payload schema exposing active, last_validated, last_attempted, and last_reload with the validation error and rejected candidate state when applicable.

- Confirmation that the dashboard sample that recorded 619 has been traced to a consumer and that the consumer's panel provenance has been verified (live vs. validation-only).
- A note in the PR description that this is a status-endpoint correctness change to the generation-reporting path, not a metrics or routing change — so reviewers and the on-call know where to look if a future regression reports through the same surface.

This is a blocking defect, not a corner case. A preflight cache key that does not encode the fixture version cannot produce valid Cardinality Guardrails production-review evidence as proposed.

Why it fails the gate:

  - The shared parity fixture is the authoritative cross-service parity check for covered label-name changes. A "pass" returned from a stale fixture version is not a pass — it is evidence that the gate was bypassed.
  - The new bounded `storage_region` case in v18 is exactly the contract boundary that has caused real past incidents: the Feb 13, 2024 `shard_region` → `storage_region` rename with the rollup-service reader still on the old key, and the Jan 16, 2025 `storage_zone` vs `storage_region` drift producing zero matched consumer reads. Skipping the v18 case on a cache hit means the defect class the fixture exists to catch can reach review.
  - Cardinality Guardrails preflight is one of three required checks (preflight + alert-source classification + owner sign-off + the executable fixture running the current version). A preflight that silently omits a required case fails preflight regardless of what v17 said about the same commit.
  - Treating a prior-version verdict as authoritative is structurally similar to the "sampled / non_authoritative" rule — incomplete or stale evidence cannot serve as a production pass.

What the cache must do before this proposal is approvable:

  1. Cache key includes the fixture version (or a fixture content hash), not only the commit SHA. A fixture version bump must invalidate prior entries.
  2. A cache hit on commit `a81c4e2` against v17 must not satisfy a v18 preflight request — equivalent to "the fixture version is part of the verdict inputs, full stop."
  3. A regression test demonstrating the corrected behavior: bump fixture to v18, re-run preflight on `a81c4e2`, observe a cache miss, observe v18's `storage_region` case actually executing, and observe the candidate's verdict being produced from v18 (not carried over from v17).
  4. Documented invalidation trigger for fixture version bumps. It cannot be "happens to differ because of an unrelated field" — the version must be a first-class key component.
  5. Re-run the candidate against the corrected cache with fixture v18 and either record a clean v18 pass or keep the candidate blocked. The current "pass via stale cache hit" is not retroactively acceptable evidence.

Scope: this stays inside the first-cut Cardinality Guardrails scope (label-change preflight). Not asking for telemetry rewrite, legacy-aggregator retirement, replay expansion, router enforcement, or any of the deliberate non-goals.

One thing to confirm before approval: who owns the cache layer? If it sits inside Cardinality Guardrails' own preflight path, the fix is local (key = commit + fixture version, with version-bump invalidation). If it is a shared infra cache owned elsewhere, this needs to be raised to that owner, because the cache has to honor the gate's verdict inputs — and a cache that can override a required preflight case is the wrong abstraction regardless of who owns it.

Recommendation: block the proposal as written. No production review or release has occurred, which means this is the right time to catch it — before any green evidence is on record from the stale cache.

Residual bug is exactly what you described. The cache key (commit_sha, fixture_version) is content-keyed on the input fixture, but the verdict depends on the rule set in force at evaluation time. Those two are independent: rule edits that don't touch fixture data leave the key unchanged, so a cached verdict computed under the looser rules gets served as authoritative against the stricter rules. False positive.

Three ways to close it, in order of blast radius:

  1. Add a rule_set_version (or policy_version) to the cache key. Key becomes (commit_sha, fixture_version, rule_set_version). Bump rule_set_version on any rule edit. One-line cache change, one extra dimension, no retrofit of existing fixtures. Lowest risk for a no-review, no-release posture.

  2. Fold the rule set into the fixture_version itself — content-address fixture_version over (fixture data + rules). Any rule change naturally bumps the version. Structurally nicer because it kills the "did we remember to bump rule_set_version?" failure mode for the next rule edit too, but it redefines what "fixture version 18" means and breaks any in-flight references.

An idempotency key has one job: uniquely identify the *request as the sender defined it*, so that a genuine retry returns the original outcome and a *different* request is never mistaken for a retry. Truncating the request_id to its first 32 characters discards exactly the information a caller relies on for uniqueness. - 1,200 distinct points submitted under a second request_id.
- Caller receives the *first* request's success response.
- Caller's local log shows "accepted."
- Platform actually accepted 0 of the 1,200 points.

That is silent data loss on a path with no client-visible error. The caller cannot detect it from their side, cannot retry to recover (the response says success), and has no signal that anything is wrong until they notice a missing series downstream. The duplicate-response path is the worst possible failure shape for an idempotency layer — it hides loss behind a success.

**Why this will fire in production**

Collision probability on a 32-character prefix is not negligible at real request volumes. Any caller that generates request_ids with a fixed scheme (timestamp + counter, UUIDv4 with a shared namespace header, request ID + sequence number, etc.) will produce prefixes that repeat. **Assessment of the revised design**

The revised design materially closes most prior gaps (file-wrapper retrieval-time authorization, policy_generation + file-grant cache invalidation, row-level tenant binding, excluded-field enforcement with offline re-join protection, retrieval-time freshness with explicit-unknown). Two cross-service failure-shape gaps remain:

1. **Support-admin attribution.** The proposal lets support administrators mint replacement downloads, but it doesn't preserve the original customer requester identity in the audit trail or in the new file grant. That breaks recipient-binding on replay/re-download and creates a provenance hole — the audit log will attribute the file to the admin rather than to the customer who originally requested it.

2. **In-progress revocation.** The design doesn't specify behavior for an already-open download stream when authorization is revoked mid-stream. The contract requires revocation to convert a cached allow to 403 not_authorized even without a policy_generation bump (bounded to ~5s), but for in-flight bytes there's no defined terminal state. Need: drain-and-terminate vs revoke-on-next-byte, bounded TTL on in-flight streams, behavior under concurrent membership-revocation races (fully pre- or fully post-revocation, no partial bodies), and the audit record for the truncated stream.

Both are reviewable on design + test evidence; neither authorizes implementation or customer access.

Approach: cook the chicken low-effort in the oven, use the cook time to assemble everything cold, boil water for couscous in the last 10 minutes. Walk Kibo first so he's settled before Anya walks in. Plate at 5:50, hot food on the table at six.

TIMELINE

  4:00–4:30 PM   Walk Kibo (normal late-afternoon loop)
  4:30           Wash hands. Pat chicken thighs dry, season (salt, pepper,
                 olive oil, lemon zest). Set on a parchment-lined sheet pan
                 skin-up. Leave on counter.
  4:35           Oven on at 400°F.
  4:40           Wash hands AGAIN before touching anything else. Now work
                 only with the salad stuff:
                   - Yogurt sauce: yogurt + squeeze of lemon + salt
                     (grated cucumber or garlic optional). Bowl, fridge.
                   - Slice cucumbers and tomatoes. Container, fridge.
                   - Cut lemon wedges. Plate, counter.
                   - Wash fruit, set on a platter, counter.
                 Wipe the counter where the raw chicken was. From here on,
                 raw chicken does not touch the counter again.
  5:10           Chicken into the oven. Set a timer for 33 minutes.
                 (35–38 min total cook time for bone-in thighs at 400°F;
                 pull a couple minutes early because they keep cooking
                 while resting.)
  5:35           Kettle on (or pot of water to boil).
  5:40           Boil water. Pour over couscous in a bowl, cover with a
                 plate, set aside. Pull salad veg and yogurt sauce from the
                 fridge so they aren't ice-cold.
  5:43           Pull chicken onto a CLEAN plate (not the raw-chicken pan
                 or sheet). Tent with foil. Internal temp should read
                 175°F+ — thighs are best at 175–185, juices clear, no
                 pink at the bone. If you don't have a thermometer, cut
                 into the thickest one and check.
  5:48           Fluff couscous with a fork, transfer to a serving bowl.
                 Dress the salad lightly (olive oil, lemon, salt) OR put
                 dressing on the side so it doesn't wilt.
  5:50           Arrange on the table: couscous, salad, chicken (skin up,
                 lemon wedges alongside), yogurt sauce in a small bowl,
                 fruit platter. Light a candle if you want.
  5:55           Wash hands, wipe counters, run the cutting board and knife
                 through hot soapy water. Done.
  6:00           Open the door. Anya walks into a hot meal on the table.

FOOD SAFETY (the only rules that actually matter)

  - Wash hands before AND after raw chicken. Don't skip the second wash.
  - Raw chicken stays on one cutting board / pan. Cooked chicken lands on
    a clean plate, not the pan it went in on.
  - If anything (counter, board, towel) touched raw chicken, hot soapy
    water before it touches salad stuff. Or: do all salad prep first,
    refrigerate, then handle chicken. Either order works as long as raw
    and cooked don't share a surface.
  - Thighs to 175°F internal, not 165°F like a breast. The 175 number is
    what makes them tender, not just safe.
  - Yogurt sauce and dressed salad: under 2 hours at room temp is fine,
    so a 30-min dinner window is no problem. Don't dress the salad until
    5:48.
  - In June heat, don't let the raw seasoned chicken sit on the counter
    past 5:00. If you fall behind, put it in the fridge and pull it when
    the oven's ready.

LOW-EFFORT SERVING AND CLEANUP

  - Everything serves out of the dish it was made in. No plating
    individual portions.
  - Parchment on the sheet pan means the chicken pan goes straight to
    soak. No scrubbing.
  - Use the couscous mixing bowl as the serving bowl. Use the salad bowl
    as the serving bowl. Same for the sauce.
  - One round of cleanup after Anya leaves: stack bowls, run dishwasher,
    wipe counters, sweep. 10 minutes.
  - Coffee/tea and the fruit platter on the counter from arrival — gives

KEEPING IT RELAXED (since you flagged this)

Recommended policy: treat the quarter-end snapshot as an immutable observation record, and treat post-close source corrections as timestamped amendments that mutate fields of existing observations but never generate new adoption or failure counts.

Components:

1. Frozen snapshot at quarter close
   - Once quarter close fires (1st business wk after quarter close, per the standing agreement), the snapshot becomes append-only.
   - Each deduplicated observation (dedup key: team + release_candidate + canonical-package version) gets a stable observation_id.
   - The full snapshot is checksummed and timestamped at close. No in-place edits, no row deletions, no count recomputation after the fact.

2. Amendment ledger, not observation log
   - Corrections arriving after quarter close are written as amendments, not as new observations.
   - Each amendment carries: amendment_id, observation_id (FK to the original), received_at, corrected_field, old_value, new_value, source_correction_ref (ticket, vendor notice, etc.), submitted_by, verified_by, applies_to_future_quarters (boolean), invalidates_observation (boolean).

3. Identity preservation — the no-double-count guarantee
   - Amendments change fields of an existing observation; they do not change its observation_id or dedup key. The same release remains one observation, possibly with corrected attributes. It cannot be counted twice.
   - Adoption and failure counts for the frozen quarter are derived only from the snapshot's deduplicated observations at close time. Amendments never add, remove, or rebucket rows in the count.

4. What amendments explicitly are not
   - Not new adoption events.
   - Not new failure events.
   - Not recomputed period totals.
   - Not a replacement of the snapshot.

5. Two views, never silently merged
   - Default published quarterly view = frozen snapshot only. Headline numbers come from this.
   - Companion "as-corrected" view = snapshot joined to its amendments, labeled as post-close corrections and dated. This is a footnote artifact, never the headline.
   - Either view is independently auditable; the join is auditable separately. No silent blending.

6. Auditability primitives
   - Snapshot integrity check on access: rehash and compare; mismatch = investigate, do not auto-fix.
   - Amendment ledger is append-only and ordered by received_at.
   - Every amendment has a chain-of-custody trail (submitter, verifier, source ref).
   - The original quarter is readable without amendments; the amendments are readable without recomputing the quarter.

How this maps to the constraints:
  Frozen quarter stays frozen  ->  snapshot is immutable + checksummed.
  Don't lose the correction     ->  amendment ledger is required, append-only.
  Don't count the same release twice  ->  amendments mutate fields, not identity; no new count rows.
  Timestamp + link to original  ->  amendment_id -> observation_id FK + received_at.
  Not new adoption or failure   ->  counting rule scopes to snapshot; amendments carry applies_to_future_quarters and invalidates_observation flags but never enter the period count.

Boundary call-outs worth flagging to Anya before she writes it up:
  - If a correction invalidates the observation entirely (release rolled back before adoption could be measured), the amendment sets invalidates_observation = true, but the snapshot count is unchanged. The observation is excluded from future quarters, not retroactively removed from the frozen quarter.
  - If a correction changes team attribution, the frozen quarter's per-team counts use the original attribution; the corrected attribution takes effect from the next quarter onward.
  - If Anya wants the as-corrected view cited alongside headline numbers, it goes in the same artifact but in a labeled separate section, never blended into the headline.

One forward-looking note: if Anya adopts this shape, the operational procedure (snapshot freeze command, amendment intake form, integrity-check cadence, the two-view rendering rule) belongs in a runbook entry under her measurement lane, not in conversational memory. That way the policy travels with the review and doesn't depend on this thread being reread.

PRACTICAL HEAT PLAN — JUNE 19-23, 2025
Alex + Kibo, South Slope apartment, bedroom AC off through Monday

WHAT TO DO THIS EVENING (THURSDAY 6/19) BEFORE THE ADVISORY HITS
- Open windows on the shaded/north side of the apartment after outside drops below indoor temp (usually after 8-9 PM) to flush residual heat. Run fans blowing IN.
- Stage a "cool kit" in the living room and one by the bed: ice packs in pillowcases, a damp cotton sheet, electrolyte packets, dog water bottles.
- Freeze water bottles, a damp towel or two, and a couple of low ice trays for Kibo's water bowls.
- Confirm you have a working indoor thermometer (or use a weather app indoor reading) so you can actually track indoor temp over the next four days.

FRIDAY-SUNDAY SHADE AND FAN STRATEGY
- Keep blinds/curtains CLOSED on south and west windows all day. Open them only after the sun is off them.
- East windows: close by 10 AM.
- Cross-flow setup: one fan blowing out a cracked window on one side, one fan blowing in on the other, ideally through the living room. Ceiling fans set counterclockwise (forward spin = summer).
- Do NOT aim a fan directly at Kibo. Dogs cool by panting and foot pads; direct airflow masks the cues (panting, drool, posture) that tell you they are overheating.
- Overnight lows around 76°F mean outside air won't cool the apartment much. Expect indoor temps to settle in the high 70s to low 80s; if it climbs above 85°F sustained, see "leave the apartment" below.

WHERE TO SLEEP THROUGH SUNDAY
- Sleep in the LIVING ROOM, not the bedroom. Living room typically has better cross-ventilation and isn't on the broken unit's wall.
- Damp top-sheet trick: lightly mist a cotton sheet, sleep under it. Evaporation drops skin temp without making you shiver.
- Ice pack in a pillowcase under the sheet at the hip or shoulder works better than a frozen pillow, which just numbs one spot.
- If indoor stays above 82°F overnight, consider relocating for Fri-Sun nights: a friend with AC, a pet-friendly hotel, or an NYC cooling center (call 311 for current sites — most accept dogs).

KIBO WALKS — TIMING AND ROUTE
- Pavement rule: 7-second back-of-hand test. If you can't hold the back of your hand to the sidewalk for 7 seconds, Kibo's paws can't take it.
- At 90°F ambient, sun-baked asphalt reaches roughly 135-150°F — a paw burn in seconds.
- Walk windows: early morning 5:30-7:30 AM, and evening after 8:30 PM. Skip midday Fri-Sun.
- Routes: shaded side streets, grass strips, dirt paths. Avoid asphalt intersections and the sunny side of the block.
- Bring a collapsible bowl and water for Kibo. A 15-minute walk in 85°F+ heat can push a dog into heat stress.
- Wipe paws with a cool damp cloth after each walk — pads absorb and radiate heat.

HYDRATION — BOTH OF YOU
- Alex: roughly 8-12 oz water per hour while awake during the advisory. Add electrolytes (Nuun, Liquid IV, or 1/4 tsp salt + splash of juice in 16 oz water). Cortado in the morning is fine; switch to cold water or electrolyte drinks for the rest of the day.
- Kibo: two water stations in different rooms (kitchen + wherever you are). Add ice cubes to one. Frozen low-sodium bone broth or plain wet-food "pupsicles" work as enrichment + hydration. Refill at least twice daily. If Kibo isn't drinking, mist food with water or stir in a spoon of wet food.
- Watch urine output: dark or decreased = dehydration in either of you.

CLEAR THRESHOLDS — WHEN TO LEAVE OR SEEK HELP

Leave the apartment (go somewhere air-conditioned):
- Indoor sustained temp above 85°F AND you can't pull it below 82°F within an hour of effort.
- Either of you showing early heat-stress signs (below).
- Options: NYC cooling center (311), library branch, mall, any cafe/bar with AC, friend or family. Kibo is welcome at most cooling centers and at indoor public spaces that allow dogs.

Alex — heat exhaustion (call primary care if not improving in 30 min):

Wes's draft rule is wrong on three independent counts. Here's the breakdown, grounded in the June 11 facts and the existing runbook language:

**1. Wrong cause attribution.**
A negative `route_snapshot_age_seconds` on June 11 was a *symptom* of host-time skew (the instance's wall clock jumped forward ~7 minutes, so the snapshot's recorded timestamp read as "in the future" relative to the new wall clock). It was not evidence of a route-generation mismatch. The runbook's April 15 debrief section "Host-maintenance rejoin gate" and the related April 12 / June 11 incident memories make the same point: an instance reporting a generation that doesn't match the fleet is a generation mismatch (April 12 reported 611 vs. fleet 612); a current-generation instance with a clock-derived negative snapshot age is a host anomaly, not a mismatch.

**2. The instance was on the current generation.**
June 11 had no generation divergence. Per the incident record: "the current generation on the isolated instance, no route or configuration change." A "route-generation mismatch" rule presupposes that the instance is reporting a stale or wrong generation. That condition did not exist here.

**3. Recovery was instance replacement, not config rollback.**
The recovery action was deploy-pipeline instance replacement after canary isolation. The active configuration was correct, unchanged, and stayed in place. Rolling it back would have replaced a correct config with a prior correct config and left the host-clock defect on the still-running peer fleet unaddressed. This is also why the event was not classified as an owner-led window — it was an instance-level host anomaly, not a config-push regression.

**What the rule should actually say (proposed wording):**

> If `route_snapshot_age_seconds` is negative on an instance, treat it as evidence of host-time skew on that instance, not a route-generation mismatch. Confirm the instance is on the fleet's current active generation; if so, the canary should isolate it and the instance should be replaced through the deploy pipeline. Do not roll back the active configuration. Capture the host-clock evidence (NTP offset, magnitude and direction of the jump, clock source) and apply the host-maintenance rejoin gate before releasing isolation.

**A few process notes before you reply to Wes:**
- The canary runbook already has the right vocabulary: "active-generation consistency," "current active generation reported," and the host-maintenance rejoin gate (six conditions, isolation until all six hold). Wes's draft conflicts with all of it.
- Per your standing rule, "live = rollback, replay/mirror = mismatch investigation. Never combined." A negative snapshot age on a single instance, with the fleet otherwise on the current generation and clean health, is not a live regression signal.
- I'd push back on Wes rather than silently rewriting the rule. He's listed as a reviewer on `ingest-edge#221` (merged), so this is plausibly a metrics-router runbook edit he wants landed before something else. Worth asking whether he's seen the host-maintenance rejoin gate section — if not, that's the gap to close first.

Stinger removal with a straight scrape (not pinch/tweezers — squeezing injects more venom) was the right move, and the cool rinse helps. Kibo's clean April baseline plus his September '24 pad laceration infection history makes this local site worth extra watch. Structured plan below.

IMMEDIATE CARE (next 1-2 hours)

Cold compress on the pad:
- Wrap a few ice cubes or a bag of frozen peas in a thin dish towel — never bare ice on skin.
- 10 minutes on, 10 minutes off. Repeat 2-3 cycles over the next few hours.
- Goal: slow venom spread, numb pain, reduce swelling.
- Stop if Kibo shows discomfort or the pad looks blanched.
- After 24h, switch to warm compresses if residual swelling persists — warm encourages resolution.

Pad hygiene:
- Gentle chlorhexidine or dilute povidone-iodine rinse once today, pat dry. (You already have chlorhex from last year's protocol.)
- Inspect between toes and pads for any other stingers, thorns, or clover debris — clover patches can hide multiple insects.
- Put an e-collar on now if he'll lick. Licking + a puncture + outdoor flora = the exact pathway that turned into last year's pad infection.

DO NOT GIVE (without vet direction)

- Ibuprofen / naproxen / Aleve — toxic to dogs (GI ulcer, kidney injury).
- Acetaminophen / Tylenol — toxic; liver damage and red-cell injury in dogs.
- Aspirin — only if your vet explicitly doses it; not standard for stings.
- Topical benzocaine, lidocaine, hydrocortisone, calamine, or "drawing salves" — risky if licked; not formulated for dogs.
- Essential oils (tea tree, lavender, etc.) — toxic even topically.
- Benadryl (diphenhydramine) — often recommended online, but: only after calling your vet or an ER line for a weight-based dose, only if Kibo has no other conditions/meds, and only if any mild swelling is spreading. It is NOT a substitute for the emergency signs below.

ACTIVITY LIMITS (next 24-48h)

- Leash walks outside for bathroom breaks only — short, slow, on clean surfaces (avoid grass/clover/heated pavement).
- No running, jumping, off-leash play, fetch, or stairs.
- Mild intermittent lameness for 12-24h is expected.
- Skip Ren's Tuesday/Thursday bouldering gym session and Sunday pickup soccer for at least 48-72h, until Kibo is fully sound.

MONITORING — EVERY 2-3 HOURS FOR 24H

Systemic / allergic reaction signs → URGENT VETERINARY CARE (ER, not wait-until-Monday):
- Facial, muzzle, lip, or eyelid swelling
- Hives or raised welts anywhere (ears, belly, groin common)
- Vomiting or diarrhea
- Excessive drooling, sudden panting, or labored breathing
- Restlessness, agitation, or sudden weakness/lethargy
- Pale gums (should stay bubblegum pink)
- Collapse, stumbling, inability to stand
- Repeated pawing at face/mouth
These signs typically appear within 15-30 minutes but can be delayed several hours. Anaphylaxis in dogs progresses fast — go now.

Local site worsening → CALL YOUR VET SAME DAY, ER IF RAPID:
- Swelling spreading up the leg or visibly larger after 4-6 hours
- Increasing pain — won't bear weight at all, or growls when paw is touched
- Redness spreading, hot to the touch, streaking up the leg
- Discharge, pus, foul odor, or a dark scab that grows
- Limping worse instead of better after 48h
- Fever signs: warm dry nose, lethargy, inappetence >24h
- New lameness on a different leg (suggests systemic spread or a missed second sting)

Given Kibo's prior pad infection, treat any of the above as a same-day vet call rather than wait-and-see.

24-HOUR FOLLOW-UP

- Pad should be less pink, less swollen, and Kibo closer to normal weight-bearing.
- Resume routine short walks only after fully weight-bearing without a head-bob.
- Note the clover loop location — early-summer clover blooms track bee/wasp activity. Worth flagging for future walks.

ONE LAST THING

Confirm your ER vet number and primary vet number on speed-dial now while things are calm — South Slope to BluePearl/VERG/etc. — so you're not searching contacts if a reaction starts.

PREVENTIVE PLAN — KIBO, July 4 (intermittent neighborhood fireworks, late afternoon into evening)

Baseline check confirms he's fine to manage this at home with environment + behavior; nothing here requires meds or a vet visit preemptively.

1) EARLIER LONG WALK — front-clip harness + leash

  - Aim for two outings: a brisk sniff-walk mid-morning (~10:00–11:00) and a longer one early-to-mid afternoon (~14:00–15:00), so you're back inside well before dusk.
  - Front-clip harness is the right tool here: it steers without throat pressure, gives you clean control if he tries to bolt at a bang, and reduces tracheal strain if he lunges. Two-finger check at every strap before leaving; make sure clips are fully seated and leash is sound.
  - Route: familiar, low-traffic, away from parks, fields, and water where neighbors tend to set things off. Stay within easy retreat distance of the apartment.
  - Length: 45–60 min of sniff-rich walking. Mental fatigue (nosework) tires a dog faster and more calmly than physical pace alone.
  - ID: tags secure; microchip registration already current (South Slope, 3/5/25).
  - If a bang fires while you're out: don't fuss, don't coddle, don't drag. Pause, cue an easy known behavior (sit, hand target, eye contact), reward, then choose a quieter direction. The front clip gives you clean steering.
  - Heat: July 4 in NYC is usually hot. Bring water for him, walk in shade, palm-test the pavement (back of hand to asphalt 5 sec — too hot for you = too hot for him), and pivot to grass if needed.
  - Do NOT leave him unattended in a yard, on a balcony, or in a car, even briefly. Startle plus open space equals an escape.

2) WINDOWS AND CURTAINS

  - Close and lock every window. Even a one-inch crack lets in flashes and amplifies sound.
  - Draw curtains/blinds fully. Light flashes travel far and are often as alarming as the bangs themselves.
  - Mask sound with steady, low-frequency background: a fan, AC, white-noise machine, or a calm playlist (classical, "Through a Dog's Ear"). Keep volume moderate — enough to flatten peaks, not so loud it startles on its own.
  - Avoid any window fan pointed at his bed; aim airflow away from him so he can self-regulate temperature.

3) QUIET INTERIOR RESTING AREA

  - Pick one room away from the street side — bedroom, bathroom, walk-in closet, or interior den. Smaller and more enclosed reads as a den.
  - Set up before the first expected bang:
      - His bed with a blanket that smells like you or Devika.
      - A covered crate if he's crate-comfortable (drape a towel over the top and sides, leave the door open).
      - A long-lasting chew held in reserve for after the first bangs: frozen stuffed Kong, lick mat with plain peanut butter or plain yogurt, bully stick under supervision. Licking/chewing releases calming endorphins.
      - Water available, not in a huge bowl (anxious dogs gulp and may vomit).
      - Optional: Adaptil (dog-appeasing pheromone) diffuser if you have one — plug in now, effect builds over hours. Without it, a worn cotton t-shirt of yours draped over his bed works similarly.
  - Stay in the room with him. Be matter-of-fact and calm. Quiet presence, slow breathing, occasional gentle stroke. Avoid over-comforting — that can reinforce fear — and avoid frustrated/annoyed tone if he paces or whines.
  - Keep lights dim; minimize sudden movements in and out of the room.

4) FOOD AND BATHROOM TIMING

  - Breakfast: normal, on schedule (already done).
  - Don't feed a large meal within 2–3 hours of expected firework onset — stress on a full stomach can trigger vomiting/regurgitation.
  - Last outdoor potty break: ~16:00–17:00, before the evening peak. He may refuse to go out later even if he needs to; have pee pads by the door as a fallback.
  - Hold the frozen Kong/lick mat for after the first bangs start — gives him a task at the moment he needs one.
  - If he has any stress-sensitive GI history: skip dinner or offer a small, bland meal (plain boiled chicken + white rice) earlier in the day. Otherwise his normal dinner is fine if it's well before evening.

5) DO NOT IMPROVISE WITH HUMAN MEDICATION

  No OTC human drug for people without explicit vet direction and a weight-based dose. Specifically:

  - Acetaminophen (Tylenol): toxic — liver failure, facial swelling, can be fatal.
  - Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin): toxic — kidney failure, GI ulcers.
  - Naproxen (Aleve): toxic, narrower margin.
  - Aspirin: sometimes prescribed by vets at specific doses, but never self-dosed — GI bleeding, drug interaction risks.
  - Diphenhydramine (Benadryl): sometimes used under vet direction, BUT never substitute "PM," "D," "Allergy & Sinus," or "Cold & Flu" products — pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine are toxic to dogs, and dose is weight-specific.
  - Melatonin: sometimes used; avoid any product sweetened with xylitol (toxic).
  - CBD, THC, edibles, gummies: unregulated; THC is toxic to dogs.
  - Alcohol, tea tree oil, concentrated peppermint/citrus essential oils: toxic.

  For future fireworks events (NYE is often worse than July 4), call the vet in advance. Options a vet may prescribe or recommend:

  - Trazodone — situational, given 1–2 hours before the trigger.
  - Gabapentin — sometimes combined with trazodone.
  - Sileo (dexmedetomidine oromucosal gel) — FDA-approved for noise aversion in dogs.
  - Clomipramine or fluoxetine — for chronic/severe cases; takes weeks to work, so it requires planning.

  Historical note worth flagging: acepromazine used to be prescribed for noise phobia but is now generally NOT recommended — it sedates without addressing fear and can make some dogs more reactive to noise.

  For today, with no current distress: behavioral + environmental plan only. Do not improvise.

6) SIGNS THAT REQUIRE URGENT VETERINARY HELP

  Call your regular vet's after-hours line or the nearest 24-hour ER (have both numbers saved in your phone and on the fridge before evening) for any of these:

  - Breathing: rapid/shallow panting that doesn't slow in a quiet room, labored inhale, blue/pale or purple gums, persistent gagging/choking sounds, profuse drooling.
  - Collapse: can't stand, wobbly gait, fainting.
  - Persistent vomiting or diarrhea, especially with blood.
  - Seizure activity: paddling, loss of consciousness, post-event disorientation that doesn't resolve in 10–15 minutes.
  - Bloated/distended abdomen with non-productive retching — bloat is an emergency regardless of cause.
  - Escape-injury signs: torn toenail with active bleeding, lacerations, bleeding from mouth, sudden lameness or favoring a limb.
  - Heat-stress overlap: bright red gums, panting that won't slow in a cool room, vomiting in heat (also a July risk).
  - Allergic-type: sudden facial swelling, hives.
  - Pain cues: vocalizing, trembling, hunched back, snapping when touched, refusing to move.
  - Straining to urinate with no output (especially in males — urinary blockage is an emergency).
  - Prolonged unresponsiveness or disorientation after the noise stops.

  Note: mild lip-licking, ears back, low tail, and pacing in response to a bang are normal noise sensitivity, not emergencies — handle those with the behavioral plan in section 3 (calm presence, redirect to a chew, no fuss).

Quick pre-evening checklist (run through ~16:00):

  - All windows closed and curtains drawn.
  - Resting room set up with bed, worn-shirt blanket, water, Adaptil on.
  - Background sound (fan/playlist) running at low steady volume.
  - Frozen Kong / lick mat ready in freezer.
  - Pee pads by the door.
  - Vet ER number visible (phone + fridge).
  - Kibo's collar/harness ID visible if you take him out for one last quick break.

If the bangs turn out to be milder than expected, you can stand down the strict version of the plan; the core is windows closed + a den + a chew + calm presence. Have a good quiet day.

Here is the analysis and the blocking review comment.

ANALYSIS (missed-reload defect)

Root cause shape. The metrics-router config watcher is subscribed to fsnotify.Write on routes.yaml. Deployments stage a candidate file and atomically rename it over the watched path. That rename is a Create on the directory plus an inode replacement on the file. A Write-only subscription on the original inode fires zero events for the new inode, so generation 619 reached disk while the process kept serving 618. The defect is "silently stale": no event, no failed-reload signal, no observable divergence.

Why content-based detection matters. Even with rename/create handled, a touch(1), a permission flip, or a metadata-only rewrite should not advance active_generation. A canonicalized digest (stable field ordering, normalized values, explicit delimiters) decouples the reload decision from inode churn and prevents generation churn from identical content.

Why atomic publication is non-negotiable. Build the candidate off-lock; only one swap (atomic.Pointer.Store or equivalent) flips readers to the new generation. On any validation failure the swap must not occur, active_generation stays at N-1, and a failed-reload signal (status, metric, log, last_reload.rejected) is emitted. Active readers either see the prior generation entirely or the validated new generation entirely — never a half-built candidate.

Required invariant (must hold across every regression): active_generation advances only on successful validation + atomic swap; last_validated_generation tracks the latest successful candidate; last_attempted_generation tracks the latest candidate regardless of outcome. Attempted >= validated >= active.

The defect, in plain terms:

  There are two views of the same queue: the authoritative state (the
  actual pending items) and a telemetry gauge that is supposed to mirror
  that state. Every removal is supposed to decrement the gauge exactly
  once. The defect is that two distinct code paths each take a decrement
  for the same logical removal: the immediate cancellation handler AND a
  later tombstone / sweeper cleanup of the same item. The physical state
  stays correct (it really is empty), but the gauge drifts away from it
  because items get decremented more than once — and, in the observed
  fixture, the drift lands at gauge == 54 with an empty physical queue
  after 100 admitted / 23 canceled / 77 dispatched (terminal accounting
  77 + 23 = 100, correct, but the gauge is lying).

  Root shape, independent of any queue implementation: per-item-ID
  ownership of the gauge decrement is not enforced. Two paths believe
  they own the decrement for the same item ID, and a canceled item that
  is also later swept gets double-counted out of the gauge.

Evidence required before this proceeds.

  1. Queue-occupancy evidence
     - Gauge sampled at every transition of every item: admit, dispatch,
       cancel, tombstone, retry-evict, drain-on-shutdown.
     - For the staging fixture specifically: gauge value vs. physical
       queue size captured at each sample across the full 100-item run.
     - Cancellation observed in every state — a cancellation arriving
       while the item is waiting, while it is mid-dispatch, and after it
       has tombstoned must each be instrumented, not just one path.

  2. Terminal-accounting evidence
     - Invariant: dispatched + canceled + rejected == admitted, with no
       silent drop and no double-count.
     - Per-item-ID reconciliation: every admitted item ID terminates in
       exactly one terminal bucket; no ID appears in two buckets.
     - Separate counters for cancel and dispatch, each itemized, with
       cross-check that no ID is counted by both the cancel path and the
       dispatch path.

  3. Single-decrement ownership evidence
     - For each removal path (cancel handler, tombstone / sweeper,
       dispatch eviction, retry eviction, drain-on-shutdown), assert that
       exactly one decrement fires per item ID.
     - Specifically: tombstone cleanup must be a no-op for IDs already
       removed via the cancel path, and the cancel handler must be a
       no-op for IDs already removed via tombstone. Either direction of
       the race must be demonstrated, not assumed.
     - Trace or counter that proves no item is decremented twice AND no
       item is missed. Per-item-ID ownership invariant: one and only one
       code path is responsible for the final gauge decrement for each
       item ID.

  4. End-state regression evidence
     - After a sustained quiescent window with the physical queue empty,
       assert gauge == 0. Not "approximately zero," exactly zero.
     - Repeated runs (10+ identical fixtures) — no run may end with
       gauge != 0.
     - Mixed workloads: high-cancel-rate runs, high-dispatch-rate runs,
       mid-drain crash + restart, burst-and-cancel, sustained overload.
       Each must converge to gauge == 0 at quiescence.
     - Property-style case: cancel an item, then run the tombstone sweep
       over that same ID — gauge must not move on the second pass.
     - Regression test wired into CI so any future change to the admit,
       cancel, dispatch, or sweep path re-runs the full battery.

Implementation-agnostic framing: the invariant under test is "each item
ID has exactly one decrement owner, and that owner is the path that
performs the final removal." Whether the queue is map-backed,
channel-backed, or sharded, and whether "already removed" is detected
via a status field, a separate tombstone set, or a presence check, is
irrelevant to the evidence above.
