Kibo's current picture (mild pinkness between two toes on one front paw, no cut, swelling, bleeding, lameness, discharge, or behavior change) is consistent with mild salt/chemical irritation between the toes after a salted-walk exposure, especially given how salt residue tends to sit in the webbing. Given Kibo's prior paw pad infection history, it's worth taking this seriously and acting early, even though nothing looks dramatic right now.

1. Immediate cleaning and drying (no medications)

   - Lukewarm plain water rinse of the affected paw, and ideally all four paws. Hold the paw in or under gently running lukewarm water for 20–30 seconds to dissolve salt residue, including between the toes and around the webbing. Plain water is enough; you don't need soap for routine salt removal.
   - Pat dry thoroughly with a clean dry towel. Press between each toe and into the webbing; moisture left between toes is what lets irritation turn into a problem.
   - Recheck all four paws between every toe and on each pad. Note any additional pink/red areas, cracks, broken skin, or moisture so you have a baseline.
   - Discourage licking during and after cleaning. A few licks right after a walk is normal, but persistent licking of an irritated webbing is the most common way this progresses. Options, in order of intrusiveness: redirect with a brief indoor game or treat; wipe the area with a cool damp cloth to interrupt the cycle; if licking continues, use an E-collar/cone (you've used one before with Kibo). Don't apply any cream, ointment, spray, or wipe meant for skin treatment without vet guidance.
   - Keep Kibo on clean, dry indoor flooring for at least an hour after cleaning. Avoid letting him back onto wet, salty, or dirty surfaces immediately.

2. Limiting salt contact on later walks

   - Post-walk paw wipe is the single highest-impact habit. As soon as you're home, wipe each paw with a warm damp washcloth or a silicone paw-cleaning cup, focusing between toes, then pat dry. Doing this every walk removes salt before it sits on the skin.
   - Choose lower-salt routes when possible. Grass, dirt paths, and recently rained-on or freshly plowed streets have less residue than dry, visibly white sidewalks.
   - Timing: walking later in the evening or after a thaw/rain reduces contact with dry crystalline salt.
   - Physical barriers are the most reliable prevention. Dog booties protect against salt and ice; introduce them gradually with positive reinforcement over several sessions before relying on them. If booties aren't an option, a paw wax/balm (e.g., Musher's Secret-style products) is a waxy barrier applied before walks, not a medicated ointment. It's optional; if you'd rather skip it, the wipe-and-dry routine plus route choice is the core of prevention.
   - Keep hair between toes trimmed if it tends to trap moisture and salt debris (do this dry, after the paw is clean).

3. When to call your regular vet

   - Pinkness persists or worsens after 24–48 hours of cleaning and drying.
   - Redness spreads, deepens in color, or develops a defined hot/dark patch.
   - New swelling, heat, moisture between toes that returns after drying, odor, or any discharge (clear, cloudy, or pus-like).
   - Kibo keeps licking the same spot despite wiping/redirection, or starts licking a second paw.
   - Mild favoring of the paw, brief hesitation on steps, or any tenderness when you gently touch between the toes.
   - Cracked pads, broken skin, blister, scab, or a broken/split nail anywhere on the paws.
   - Any change in appetite, energy, or behavior, even subtle — Kibo's prior paw infection started subtly and benefited from early attention, so the threshold for "call" is lower than average.

4. When to seek urgent/same-day evaluation

   - Active bleeding from between the toes or pad that doesn't stop with 2–3 minutes of gentle direct pressure.
   - Rapidly increasing swelling, or the paw becoming markedly warm.
   - Non-weight-bearing lameness or obvious pain on touch.
   - Open wound with discharge, foul smell, or visible tissue damage.
   - Paw(s) very pale, white, or blistered — concerning for frostbite, which salt exposure can worsen in cold weather.
   - Any sign of systemic illness (lethargy plus reduced appetite, vomiting, or fever-like behavior).

5. A practical plan for tonight and the next few days

   - Tonight: rinse the affected paw in lukewarm water, dry thoroughly between toes, do a full four-paw check, and prevent further licking for the next hour or two.
   - Tomorrow and onward: short post-walk wipe-and-dry every walk, route choice to reduce salt contact, and monitor the original spot twice daily for any of the changes in section 3.
   - If anything in section 3 shows up, call your vet; if anything in section 4 shows up, go in same-day. If the area looks identical or improved by 48 hours, you're likely fine to continue prevention and watchfulness.

SECTION — Cross-service failure case (Alex)

Title: Ingest-edge shutdown with accepted work still queued (Jan 28, 2027 quarterly incident practice)
Maintainer: Alex (cross-service failure cases only)
Session: Q1 2027 quarterly incident practice — Thu, Jan 28, 2027, 2:00–3:00 PM ET
Facilitator: Hema (program owner)
Other module owners (unchanged split): Wes — responder path; Nadia — postmortem section. Alex contributes only this cross-service failure case.

SCENARIO (timed)

T+00:00 — Ingest-edge is serving and accepting requests normally. The listener is open, readiness reports true.
T+02:30 — 200 requests have been accepted into tenant queues (i.e., the system has taken responsibility for them: they are past the acceptance boundary, durably enqueued, and visible to dispatch).
T+05:00 — Readiness transitions false. The listener closes; the system is no longer accepting new requests from outside. Existing enqueued work is unaffected at this point.
T+06:00 — Dispatch loop observes readiness false / listener closed and exits the loop instead of draining. No further terminal results are produced.
T+06:01 — At loop exit, 37 of the 200 accepted requests remain queued with no terminal outcome recorded. 163 requests produced terminal outcomes before exit.
State at T+06:01: 163 terminal outcomes + 37 queued-without-result = 200. Reconciliation is possible in principle but requires explicit, non-duplicative handling of the 37.

FACILITATOR PROMPTS (use in order)

1. Refusal vs. responsibility — At T+05:00 the system correctly refused new work. Does closing the listener and stopping the dispatch loop also discharge responsibility for the 200 already accepted? What is the responder's first sentence on the incident bridge?

2. Acceptance boundary — Which subsystem owns the moment of acceptance (listener → queue handoff, vs. queue → dispatch handoff)? Does the answer change whether the 37 are "lost" or "in flight"?

3. Drain vs. result — If re-opening the listener is unsafe under the current readiness condition, what is the responder's obligation to the 37? (Expected answer: every accepted request must reach exactly one terminal result — drain to completion, or apply one explicit terminal result — before the incident is closed.)

4. Reconciliation without duplication — Walk through the math: 163 terminal outcomes + 37 still queued = 200 accepted. If any of the 37 are later given a terminal result, what prevents a duplicate terminal outcome? (Expected answer: idempotency keys at acceptance, queue lease semantics, or an explicit reconcile step keyed on request id.)

5. Dispatch-loop exit decision — At T+06:00, exiting the loop is an autonomous decision by the component. Is that decision consistent with the service's stop conditions, or does it create the very gap being scored? What is the correct exit behavior?

6. Incident clock — The clock starts at the original page (per the established rule). If primary is investigating at minute 0 and isolation has not succeeded by minute 44, what must be in flight before minute 45? (Expected answer: secondary engaged — paging or two-way handoff in flight; acknowledgment latency is scored separately from the pass criterion.)

7. Secondary engagement — If isolation of the readiness transition fails (root cause not narrowed, or remediation cannot be safely applied), does the responder engage the secondary under the established incident-clock rule, and at what minute? Walk through the timing.

8. Postmortem handoff (Nadia's section) — Not scored here. Note for Nadia: the system control under test is the boundary between refusing new work and remaining responsible for already-accepted work; the postmortem must not treat "loop exited" as the root cause, since the loop's exit was a downstream consequence of readiness + listener state.

SCORING

Pass criteria — all four required, no partial credit:

(A) Refusal vs. responsibility separation. The responder explicitly distinguishes "we refuse new work starting at T+05:00" from "we remain responsible for the 200 already accepted." A response that conflates the two (e.g., "listener closed, we're done") is a fail.

(B) Drain-or-result commitment for every accepted request. The responder commits that each of the 200 will reach exactly one terminal result before incident closure, either by draining to completion or by applying one explicit terminal result to the remaining 37.

(C) Reconciliation of all 200 without duplication. The responder's plan reconciles 163 terminal outcomes + 37 still queued = 200, and explicitly prevents duplicate terminal outcomes (idempotency key, queue lease, or explicit reconcile step).

(D) Secondary engaged in flight before the 45-minute boundary under the established incident-clock rule if isolation fails. Engagement (paging or two-way handoff) in flight at minute 45 passes; acknowledgment after minute 45 is a fail for (D) and is scored separately as acknowledgment latency.

Live vs. replay scoring: never combined. Live scores are by observation during the run; replay scores are by postmortem reconstruction. A single attempt is scored in one mode only.

Fit issue first: front paws at 2.4" sit inside both size ranges. Back paws at 2.2" are BELOW both stated minimums (2.25"). That needs resolving before either option works — either re-measure (the "approximately" gives some slack), check if a smaller size exists in either line, or confirm the 2.2" was a soft-tissue measurement at full weight. Fabric (A) stretches slightly more than rubber (B), so A forgives a tight fit more.

Comparing against the vet's protocol (physical barrier + rinse/dry, no topical):

Option A — reusable fabric, set of 4, hook-and-loop, textured sole:
  - Straps hold the boot on during walks; a fallen-off boot defeats the barrier
  - Textured sole = traction on wet pavement and indoor floors
  - Set of 4 = one boot per paw, rotates while drying (matches rinse/dry cadence)
  - Fabric breathes, supporting the drying half of the protocol
  - Reusable = lower ongoing cost, fewer replacements

Option B — disposable rubber, 12-pack, no strap or sole:
  - Rubber is more waterproof as a barrier but traps moisture against the pad — works against the vet's drying emphasis
  - No strap = high slip-off risk on walks; no sole = poor traction on smooth surfaces
  - 12-pack covers longer use but is single-use

Recommendation: A, conditional on the back-paw fit. The straps and sole are decisive for a barrier that actually stays on and stays safe; reusability matches a rinse-and-dry protocol better than occlusive rubber. If the 2.2" back measurement holds and no smaller size exists, ask the seller whether Size 2 runs closer to 2.10–2.40 — that's the only path to A fitting both ends.

Both options cover the same paw-measurement band, but they're built very differently, so the "more plausible" call comes down to construction, not just size.

OPTION-BY-OPTION FOR SHORT WINTER WALKS

Option A — reusable water-resistant fabric, two hook-and-loop straps, textured flexible sole, Size 3 = 2.25–2.50" paws
  - Pros: straps keep the boot on through Kibo's normal gait; textured sole gives real traction on packed snow and lightly iced sidewalks; breathable fabric reduces the moisture-trap risk that's central to your vet's barrier + rinse-and-dry protocol (especially relevant given his 2024 pad-flap history); reusable, so the same pair gets fit-checked once and reused.
  - Cons: takes longer to put on/take off; needs to air-dry between uses; fabric can soak through in deep wet snow if untreated.

Option B — disposable natural-rubber boot, Medium = 2.25–2.75" paws, 12-pack, no rigid sole, no straps
  - Pros: cheap per walk; fast to put on.
  - Cons: no traction on icy pavement — rubber can slip; no straps, so it relies on shape to stay on and tends to walk itself off in snow; rubber + no breathability = traps moisture against the pad, exactly what the vet has warned against since 2024; disposable = each boot is a fresh fit.

WHICH SIZE IS MORE PLAUSIBLE

Kibo's measurements from today: 2.4" front, 2.2" back.
  - Option A, Size 3 (2.25–2.50"): your 2.4" front sits squarely mid-range. Snug and precise.
  - Option B, Medium (2.25–2.75"): your 2.4" front sits at the low end of the range, so a Medium in B will tend to be loose on the front and very loose on the back.
  - Back-paw caveat (applies to both): 2.2" is 0.05" below both options' stated minimums. Neither size is technically correct for the back. Option A's narrower range makes that back-paw looseness easier to see and tighten with a strap; Option B's wider range masks it.

Verdict: Option A, Size 3 is the more plausible pick — but only after a back-paw trial, because the stated 2.25" minimum is a touch too big for Kibo's back paw.

SAFE INDOOR FIT CHECK

Keep this short and supervised, on a non-slip rug, with the boots on briefly only. Kibo's pad-flap history means the goal is "confirm fit, do not test durability."

  1. Put all four boots on while Kibo is calm and sitting. You should be able to slip one finger between the cuff and his leg. Straps snug, not tight.
  2. Stand him up on a non-slip surface (bathmat, yoga mat). Watch his first 10–15 steps.
  3. Walk him on a flat indoor surface for 2–3 minutes only.
  4. Remove immediately. Inspect each paw — webbing, between toes, pad edges, and around the cuff — for any pink/red mark or compressed fur.
  5. Wait at least 10 minutes before the next trial; paws must be fully dry.
  6. Don't repeat more than twice in one day; if the second trial shows the same red marks or any gait change, that boot is the wrong size.

SIGNS THAT MEAN REMOVE THE BOOTS IMMEDIATELY

Behavior:
  - High-stepping, "walking like a horse," or shortened stride.
  - Lifting or favoring a paw; weight-shifting off a leg.
  - Repeated licking, biting, or pawing at a boot.
  - Reluctance to walk on a surface he was fine on a minute ago.
  - Whining, pinned ears, whale eye, or freezing in place.
  - Boot rotates on the paw, slips down off the pad, or comes off entirely.

Physical (check at removal):
  - Boot is wet inside — moisture trapped against the pad, especially important given his pad-flap history.
  - Pink or red skin, hair loss, or a compression line around the cuff.
  - Toes curled, splayed, or peeking out past the sole.
  - Cold or discolored toes (circulation cut off — strap is too tight).
  - Any swelling, discharge, odor, or bleeding.

If you see any physical sign, retire that boot for Kibo — it's the wrong size or material. If you see only mild behavior signs once or twice, he's likely just acclimating; if they repeat, the boot isn't right.

Bottom line: the four-boot set is a confirmed mismatch. Front paws fit; rear paws don't. The 0.05" shortfall combined with strap-snug rotation is a real too-large rear fit, not a borderline measurement.

FIT ASSESSMENT

Front paws (2.4")
  - Sits inside the listed 2.25-2.50" range with margin on both sides.
  - Held orientation through 10 min of walking — no slip, no rotation.
  - Verdict: keep the size-3 reusables on the fronts.

Rear paws (2.2")
  - Falls below the listed minimum by ~0.05", which is enough that the boot is too long relative to paw length and too wide at the metatarsal pad.
  - Rotation with snug straps (two-finger test) means the boot is sliding on the paw, not the straps failing. Straps can't fix a geometry mismatch.
  - No rubbing/redness yet only because it's been 10 min indoors on a dry, flat surface. On snow or uneven ground, that rotation will abrade the interdigital webbing and the pad edges within minutes.

RECOMMENDATION

1. Primary path — seek mixed sizing. Order the next size down for the rears only (many brands sell front/rear split packs or singles). The size-3 fronts are paid for and fit correctly; the rears need a smaller boot. Confirm the rear size against Kibo's measured 2.2" before checkout, not against the listed breed chart.

2. Bridge path if mixed sizing isn't available from this brand — use properly sized disposable barriers on the rear paws, not the size-3 reusables. Critical detail: "medium" disposable booties typically cover roughly 2.0-2.25" paws. Measure the disposable footprint against Kibo's 2.2" rear paw before relying on it. If the disposable is wider than the paw or bunches at the toes, it's the wrong size too — disposables fail more often than reusables when mismatched. The size-3 reusable should NOT be worn on the rear paws outdoors in the meantime.

3. Avoid the four-boot set as a complete kit for outside walks. The rotation evidence is sufficient; you don't need visible injury to call it. Wearing the size-3 on the rear paws outside, even once, on snow is the worst-case combination — abrasion plus moisture plus cold.

IMMEDIATE-REMOVAL SIGNS

Pull the boot the instant you see any of these, even mid-walk:

  - Lameness, head-bob, or shortened stride on the booted leg
  - Paw lifting, shaking, or repeated licking at the boot
  - Boot shifted enough that the central pad or any webbing is exposed to ground or snow
  - Redness, dampness, hair-loss, or any skin change between toes or under strap contact
  - Paw-pad color change — pale, white, blue, or mottled (circulation or cold-injury sign)
  - Swelling of the toes or anywhere above the boot rim
  - Kibo stops, sits down, or refuses to move forward
  - Whining, growling, lip-curl, or guarding when you reach for the boot
  - Wet paw inside the boot — gaiter has failed and snow/water is in
  - Toe-tips feel cold when you palpate just above the boot line

KIBO-SPECIFIC NOTE

Given Kibo's 9/2/24 paw-infection/pad-flap history, treat any behavioral hint (licking, favoring, stopping) as a removal trigger even before you see skin change. The threshold for "take it off and check" should be lower than for a dog without that history. After every outdoor walk in boots for the first two weeks, do a chlorhex wipe on all four paws and a visual check of the webbing and pad edges — same inspection posture as the 9/2/24 incident.

Routine I'd suggest: order the smaller rear size today; in the interim, either skip outdoor boot walks or use correctly sized disposables on the rears only with the size-3 reusables on the fronts. Don't field-test the size-3 on the rear paws outside to "see how it goes" — the indoor rotation already answered that.

The rear-pair exchange is the right call. Each piece points there:

Fit math is clean. Back paws at 2.2" sit in the size-2 window (2.00-2.25). Size 3 (2.25-2.50) gives them roughly 0.05-0.30" of extra internal width to spin in. Front paws at 2.4" are correctly in size 3. So the retailer's rear-only constraint actually matches the fix exactly.

Rotation is a fit symptom, not a defect. A boot that's too wide has internal play; snug fit is what keeps it oriented. The fact that one rotated indoors -- the gentlest possible test -- means it'll be worse on salted sidewalks where Kibo plants, turns, and lifts a paw mid-step.

No harm yet doesn't mean no risk. Rear-paw rotation under load can torque the hock or cause a slip on ice or salt crust. The 2024 pad infection makes you want the barrier to stay intact -- a boot that half-comes off defeats the purpose and exposes the paw to salt anyway.

Vet guidance lines up. Physical barrier plus rinse/dry after salted walks assumes the barrier stays on. Proper sizing supports that.

When the size-2 pair arrives:
- Fit check: one finger max under the strap, paw seated without sliding front-to-back
- Re-run the 10-minute indoor walk before any outdoor use
- Rinse paws (boots off) with cool water after every salted walk, towel dry, air-dry a few minutes before re-booting or settling in
- Watch for the same signs as last September -- licking, redness between toes, any discharge; boots trap moisture, so drying matters more than usual
- Skip balms or topical products unless the vet later okays them

Front size 3 stays as-is.

Quick framing first, because the question depends on what "size" means. "Size 2 in back / size 3 in front" almost certainly refers to binding DIN release values (heel / toe), not boot sizing — boots don't come in mismatched front-back sizes for the same foot. So I'll answer assuming DIN.

Whether 2/3 is "plausible" depends on stats I don't have. DIN is set from a chart (weight + height + ability + age + boot sole length). A few orientation points:
  - DIN 2-3 total corresponds to roughly a child, a very light teen, or a beginner adult skier set conservatively.
  - For a typical adult (~140+ lb / 65+ kg) at recreational ability, 2/3 is on the low end — you'll likely pre-release in chop or when you load the front of the ski. That's a safety problem of its own kind.
  - It is normal for toe (front) to be set ~0.5-1 higher than heel (back), so the front>back pattern itself is fine. The number is the issue, not the asymmetry.

If a shop set 2/3 from the chart using your stats, trust it. If you're setting it yourself, double-check the chart before committing.

Now the part you actually asked for.

INDOOR FIT CHECK (10 min, in the boots with the socks you'll ski in):
  - Shell check: pull the liner out, stand in the shell. Toes should just barely kiss the front; you want ~10-15 mm of heel-space behind. More than that or jammed against the front = wrong shell size.
  - Buckle sequence: toe buckle first, then instep, then cuff, progressively snug. The cuff buckle should close with firm two-hand effort. If any buckle is at max tension and the boot still feels loose, wrong size. If a buckle closes with one finger, too much room.
  - Heel-lift test: flex forward 3-4 times like you're driving into a turn. Your heel should lift less than ~5-10 mm inside the shell. More than that = heel pocket too loose, dangerous on snow.
  - Lateral wobble: stand on a flat floor and roll ankles side to side. The boot should not flop independently of your foot.
  - Stand-still 10 min: any hot spot, tingling, or "I want to take these off" feeling now = it will not get better on snow.

FIRST-WALK TRIAL (carpet or smooth floor, ~5 min total):
  - Min 1: stand still, knees soft, shift weight fore-aft and side-side. Note pressure points.
  - Min 2: walk straight ahead 20 steps, normal stride. The walk should feel mechanical but not painful; expect stiffness, not pinching.
  - Min 3: side-step 10 steps each direction.
  - Min 4: shuffle-walk a small circle both ways (simulates traversing).
  - Min 5: hold a snowplow stance — knees in, ankles flexed, weight forward — for 30 seconds each side. This is the position you'll be in most of the day; if it hurts here, it hurts all day.

REMOVE THE BOOTS IMMEDIATELY (don't "walk it in") IF:
  - Numbness or pins-and-needles in toes/feet within the first 5 min — circulation is compromised; that does not resolve.
  - Sharp, localized pain on one specific spot (especially navicular bone on top of foot, lateral ankle bone, big-toe joint, Achilles). Pressure points become blisters and bruises; they don't soften.
  - Toes jammed against the front with no wiggle room — wrong forward length.
  - Heel lifts more than ~10 mm when you flex forward — no retention on snow, injury risk.
  - Buckles require extreme force to close at the final setting, or won't close at all — wrong shell or wrong last.
  - Cuff digs into the front of the shin when you flex — wrong forward lean or last shape for your anatomy.
  - Any "I should just push through it" voice. That feeling is the signal, not a thing to override.

One more practical note: if a shop fitter is reachable, ask for a standing footbed/joint check. A canting adjustment or a custom footbed fixes more "wrong boot" complaints than re-sizing does, and you can usually iterate on it before you ever click into a binding.

## Why this is observability/serialization, not semantic route-consistency

The defect is an **order-dependent overwrite** between two references that are *both* correct: the owner-map reference and the Cardinality Guardrails reference resolve to distinct canonical identities with distinct source timestamps, and neither one is "wrong" — both must survive. The system, however, observes them through a digest or selection rule that is sensitive to the order the entries happen to be stored in (a Go map serialized in traversal order, or a last-write-wins importer, or a first-matching-storage-row selector).

That's the defining shape of an **observability/serialization defect**:

- The **canonical content** (the two references, their identities, their timestamps, their payload-free fields) is unchanged.
- The **observed artifact** (the canonical byte sequence, the digest, or the surviving row) changes with insertion order.
- The **semantic meaning** — what the routing layer would actually do, which authority controls the 64-pending-batches-per-tenant value, where cost semantics live — is not the thing that broke.

If the routing decisions themselves were inconsistent with the canonical configuration, that would be a **semantic route-consistency failure**: the same input routes to a different service depending on something other than the route content. That isn't what's happening here. The route plan is right; the byte representation of the dual-reference record is not stable.

This is why the existing precedent (metrics-router#506) and the Lantern contract block converge on the same diagnosis: when identical configurations produce different digests, the digest is wrong, not the configuration. The same logic applies — insertion-order sensitivity in a dual-authority record is a digest/serialization defect, not a route inconsistency.

The review-routing consequence matters: this is a **shared-contract / serialization defect**, not a route-owner or authority-interpretation matter. It belongs to the lane that owns canonical byte encoding and reference-record compaction, not to Iris (interpretation), Cyrus (authority interface), or Wes (control inventory).

---

## Review requirements

### 1. Canonical / semantic hashing

- Establish **one canonical byte representation** of a dual-authority record: sort fields by canonical key order, use deterministic separators, serialize to a fixed encoding (UTF-8, LF only, locale-independent), and hash the resulting bytes.
- Two separate, defined digests:
  - **Gate 1 — canonical-archive SHA-256** over the canonical bytes (fails closed on byte divergence).
  - **Gate 2 — schema-aware semantic comparison** over parsed content (fails on missing/added keys, value-type changes, or semantic changes such as casing or units; ignores key order, whitespace, indentation, and equivalent number formatting).
- **Hash mismatch with semantic equality** is classified as **packaging/serialization nondeterminism**, owned by the build/serialization lane. **Semantic mismatch with hash equality** is **real drift**, owned by the canonical-token lane. **Both failing** requires both fixes; neither is a force-flag or regenerate-and-retry bypass.
- For the dual-authority record specifically: the canonical representation must preserve **two independent identities** — `{tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type=owner_map, authority_record_id_om, source_timestamp_om}` and `{tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type=cardinality_guardrails, authority_record_id_cg, source_timestamp_cg}` — under one tenant + canonical service. Compaction must not collapse them; overwriting must not be order-dependent.
- No canonical change without: pinned generator/version, recorded evidence, consumer pins, regenerated outputs, and drift check before rerun.

### 2. Continued fail-closed behavior on real content differences

- **No force flag, no side-channel publish, no regenerate-and-retry bypass.** Both gates are mandatory before any artifact or record is accepted.
- On **real content drift** (a genuine change to one of the references — different `authority_record_id`, a different `source_timestamp`, an added or removed key, a value-type change, a casing/unit/semantic change) the system must **fail closed**: the dual-reference record is rejected, no fallback to "previous good" or alias authority is permitted, and Lantern must render explicit **unknown** rather than silently picking a winner.
- **Hash-only mismatch with semantic equality** also fails closed for the publication path (the build lane owns the fix); it must not be promoted to "passed" by semantic comparison alone. The two gates are *both* required.
- **Stale or missing authority** → explicit unknown, no adapter call, no fallback record.
- **Denied requests** → zero adapter calls; the rejection must precede any adapter access.
- The fail-closed behavior must be regression-tested under **at least these triggering conditions**: a one-field semantic change, a one-byte whitespace change (must NOT trip Gate 2), a key-order-only change (must NOT trip Gate 2), a UID/mode/mtime change on packaging (must NOT trip Gate 2 if semantics match), and an insertion-order change between the two authority references (must NOT trip Gate 1 or Gate 2 if canonical encoding is correct).

### 3. Regressions: different insertion orders and genuine route mutations

These are the two failure classes the contract block is gated on, and each must be covered explicitly.

**A. Insertion-order regressions (the actual defect).** Required cases:

1. owner-map inserted **before** Cardinality Guardrails — verify both references survive with their own identity, `source_timestamp`, and `authority_record_id`; verify one canonical digest; verify one parsed structural identity; verify no adapter call; verify tenant isolation and customer-path isolation.
2. Cardinality Guardrails inserted **before** owner-map — same verification set.
3. **Re-insertion** under the alternate order (write order A→B, reload, write order B→A) — verify the resulting canonical digest is identical to the prior case and the parsed record is identical.
4. **Bulk re-serialization** of an existing on-disk record (no content change) — verify the digest is unchanged.
5. **Cross-tenant re-ordering** — verify tenant isolation holds; verify no cross-tenant behavior, no shared adapter call.
6. **Stale-or-missing in each insertion position** — verify explicit unknown, zero adapter calls, and that "unknown" is not silently replaced by whichever reference happens to be first.

For each: capture digest, parsed structural diff, adapter-call count, customer-path request count, and the explicit-unknown behavior.

**B. Genuine route-mutation regressions.** Required cases (must change digest; must not change fail-closed posture):

1. **Single-target edit** on one route — verify digest changes, semantic comparison passes (the change is real), routing results change accordingly, and the dual-authority reference for the affected canonical service preserves both identities.
2. **Add a route** — verify digest changes, semantic comparison passes, no orphan or merged authority record is created for the new canonical service.
3. **Drop a route** — verify digest changes, semantic comparison passes, reload must not report success if the drop leaves a dangling reference; verify no stale authority survives for the dropped canonical service.
4. **Priority reorder** with identical targets — must produce a digest change proportional to the priority change while preserving both authority references.
5. **Duplicate `payments-primary`-style entry** (or duplicate authority-reference identity) — verify rejection or a deterministic, documented precedence rule with explicit unknown fallback; first-write-wins and last-write-wins are unacceptable because they are insertion-order-sensitive.
6. **A route mutation that coincides with an authority-reference mutation** — verify both changes appear in the digest, the dual reference is preserved, and no merge-and-overwrite collapses the two authorities.
7. **A mutation to one authority reference only** (e.g. `source_timestamp` advances, or `authority_record_id` rotates) — verify the digest changes, the *other* reference is untouched, and the dual identity remains intact.

Across all of (A) and (B):

- **Fail-closed is the default**: any consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, or full-health check leaving baseline is a stop condition. No "self-recovering" override for these.
- **Customer paths are isolated**: zero requests, artifacts, or outputs in Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce across every case.
- **Determinism is structural, not probabilistic**: a single fixture run is not evidence; each case must be run repeatedly (matching the existing 1,000-reload / 120-fixture precedent) and produce identical digests, identical parsed records, and identical routing outcomes.
- **Evidence package** per case: inputs (insertion order or mutation), canonical bytes, digest, parsed structural diff, semantic-diff verdict, adapter-call count, customer-path artifact count, and the explicit-unknown or failure rendering when applicable.

---

**Bottom line for the review:** the insertion-order overwrite is a digest/serialization defect on a dual-authority record, not a route-consistency failure, and the contract block should close on evidence that (i) canonical bytes are deterministic across both insertion orders, (ii) both gates fail closed on real content differences with no bypass path, and (iii) regressions cover both insertion-order variants and genuine route/authority mutations without ever producing an adapter call, a customer-path artifact, or a silently-overwritten authority reference.

Failure-mode read — cross_service_exception_review_total{service_pair, owner_email, pull_request, exception_reason}

Your two flags, plus the rest:

1. pull_request (raw repo + PR number) — unbounded series.
   Every merged PR creates a new time series for every (service_pair, owner_email, exception_reason) tuple. Quiet quarter: 10 services × 5 owners × 200 PRs × 5 reasons ≈ 50k series. That busts Prom's working-set, inflates TSDB on disk and WAL replay cost, and the actual operator query ("show me the PRs that drove this spike") is O(N) over labels instead of a join against the review system. Per-PR debugging belongs in the CodeReview audit store keyed by PR — Prometheus is the wrong system of record for that.
   Bounded fix: drop the label. If you need outcome, use a closed enum (approved_with_exception / changes_requested / overridden) — handful of values, and the dashboard doesn't actually want per-PR detail; it wants counts of overrides.

2. exception_reason — free-text, unbounded and noisy.
   Typos, casing drift, and synonyms ("rate-limit", "rate limit", "RL upstream") make dashboards double-count ServiceA->ServiceB and serviceA->serviceB as different groups — false variance, broken alerts. Free text also smuggles in PII (customer IDs, internal URLs, occasionally secrets) and makes retention/review painful.
   Bounded fix: cluster off-line (reviewer-set enum or tagger), expose only a closed enum (upstream_rate_limit, dependency_deprecated, policy_exception, other). "Other" still bounds cardinality; the long tail goes to logs/audit, not Prom.

3. service_pair — free-form source->target, unbounded if not allowlisted.
   Same drift problem as #2. If it's truly free-form, the dashboard cannot be trusted and alerting on it is a footgun.
   Bounded fix: split into source_service and target_service, each drawn from a service registry enum. Cardinality becomes |services|², bounded by the registry and self-correcting when services are added/retired.

4. owner_email — employee-identifier surface (your second flag).
   Even with cardinality fine, raw email in Prom labels is a PII smell, not just a cardinality one:
   - Identity data sitting in a metrics tier (lower trust than HR/directory). Crosses data-classification boundaries. GDPR/CCPA exposure: deletion/DSAR requests now require Prom relabel history, which most operators don't have a procedure for and Prom itself isn't designed to support cleanly.
   - Deanonymization surface: count by(owner_email, service_pair) builds a live map of who owns which product area. Anyone with Prom query access — broader than HR-read — gets that map.
   - Off-boarding / rotation: historical series keep the old email; you need a re-label job or you accumulate stale attribution. Either way, a process nobody actually owns today.
   - External sharing: screenshots, vendor decks, status-page embeds leak emails in ways that don't show up in postmortems.
   Bounded fix: replace with a stable opaque owner ID assigned at directory sync (UUID), or owner_team if team-level granularity is enough. For per-person attribution, join off-line from the audit store keyed by PR — keep PII out of Prom. If the dashboard needs human-readable names, render them in the dashboard layer via a join, not in the time series itself.

5. Dashboard-specific failure modes (groupby owner + service_pair).
   - sum by(owner_email) over a high-cardinality label is O(N) on the query side, and the dashboard grows with headcount.
   - Can't alert sanely on {owner_email="..."} per owner — you'd write N alert rules. The actual operational signal is count by(owner_team) or count by(service_pair), both bounded.
   - Coupling the dashboard to PII means off-boarding touches the dashboard, not just the metric — quiet PII lifecycle rot.

Below is a synthesized design that fits the post-freeze operating state: evidence is closed (March 15, two-person reconciliation complete, zero audit counters), continuation review is March 25, and no authorization past March 31 is in effect. The metric work below is internal-staff telemetry, not a customer-surface change.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. WHY THIS MATTERS — CARDINALITY AND IDENTIFIER RISKS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The Q1 freeze and the Cardinality Guardrails first-cut decisions (Q4 2023 → still the live scope as of March 22) treat label cardinality and identifier hygiene as a hard, code-review gate, not a soft preference. Six risk classes drive the bounded-design rule:

a. Raw-identifier blow-up. Any label drawn from a per-row, per-request, per-tenant, or per-replay population is effectively unbounded in steady state and grows during backfills or load tests. Documented examples: replay_source_id (rollup-service Nov 14, 2023), tenant_id_hash (rollup-service PR pre-Dec 28, 2023), customer_email (10-minute staging replay produced 38,412 uniques), pod_uid and container_id (open PE proposal on customer_request_errors_total), request_id (Q1 2024 review), raw branch names (otel-collector#239). Each adds one time series per unique value to a high-frequency metric — total series cost grows multiplicatively with the joined label, and storage, index, and query cost follow.

b. Identifier instability and HA churn. Pod UIDs, hostnames, scrape-instance IPs, and request IDs are not stable across restarts or scrape windows. Using them as labels breaks replica dedup, prevents replica tracking across restarts, and confuses HA failover logic. Documented guardrail: replicas must use bounded labels like replica="a"|"b", and cluster federation adds cluster="prod-us-east" — never the underlying instance identity.

c. Identifier collision / authority mixing. The five-field authority contract (tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp) is built so the owner map and Cardinality Guardrails stay in separate authority lanes. A label that mixes the two lanes — or that lets a downstream metric infer "the same" record across them — collapses two authorities into one and reproduces the over-24-hour kept-separate logic into the telemetry layer. The November 17 internal-shadow tally caught this as an order-dependent overwrite risk; the corrective rule is that authority_record_id and source_timestamp must reference the Cardinality Guardrails record end-to-end when authority_type=cardinality_guardrails.

d. Display-name-only or alias inference. The Jan 22 staff-only rehearsal blocked two Cardinality Guardrails records because they identified metrics-router only by display name and omitted canonical_service_id. The contract rule: missing canonical_service_id is an explicit unknown, not a UI alias or fallback inference. A metric label that inherits the same risk — "metric labeled by service display name when canonical_service_id is missing" — reproduces the same failure mode inside the telemetry system and is a Cardinality Guardrails preflight fail.

e. Owner-identifier exposure. cross_service_exception_review_total{service_pair, owner_email, pull_request, exception_reason} was flagged on bounded failure-mode review for unbounded cardinality and unnecessary employee-identifier exposure. Owner identity in metrics must be a bounded role, lane, or team identifier, never a raw person identifier.

f. Source ambiguity and alert coupling. Cardinality Guardrails separates live vs replay vs validation as an alert-source classification invariant. A metric that mixes sources without a bounded source label becomes unusable for both live rollback and validation evidence — replay/mirror panels must not be promoted to live triggers. This is the reason the bounded build_channel="unknown" shape (Nadia's classification) is acceptable: it preserves source separation.

g. Privacy/PII by hash. Hashing customer_email or tenant_id into a label does not bound cardinality — it only addresses privacy. A 50,000-case fuzz run with caller-supplied fixture_name produced 417 distinct values; the bounded alternative was a four-value mismatch_class enum. The same lesson applies to any "pseudonymized identifier" used as a label.

h. Missing operational envelope. A label that ships without an explicit cardinality ceiling, growth-rate estimate, saturation behavior, and alert-source classification cannot be redesigned later — it becomes load-bearing on dashboards and alerts, and removing it is a breaking change. This is the documented reason the September 12 review asked for those four items as a blocking pre-push condition.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. THE DESIGN RECIPE — BOUNDED LABELS, RAW DETAIL IN LOGS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The pattern that has held across Cardinality Guardrails precedents (rollup-service tenant_size_class, rollup-service mismatch_class, route_template rename, replay_source_class, replica labels) is the same in every case:

  Step 1. Pick a stable classification axis that is closed, enumerated, and
          owned. The enum source lives with the service that owns the
          meaning (rollup-service owns tenant_size_class; Lantern owns
          the closed failure class set; Cardinality Guardrails owns
          source_class).

  Step 2. Map every raw identifier to exactly one enum value at the
          ingest / rollup boundary. Raw identifiers never reach the
          metric label set. Mapping is a code path, not a regex.

  Step 3. Carry the raw identifier in structured logs and structured
          trace context only. Debug-level, not info. With a per-tenant
          cap if the raw value could itself become a hot key.

  Step 4. Wire Prometheus exemplars from the bounded metric back to
          the raw-id trace/log when a drill-down is needed. Bounded
          label + bounded exemplar trace = bounded cost + full
          diagnostic power. This is the request_id lesson from Jan 30,
          2024.

  Step 5. Document the ceiling, owner, alert-source classification,
          active-series budget, and a per-tenant cardinality cap at the
          point of label introduction. Hema sign-off for any failed
          checklist item or exception; the rollup-service parity check
          is the hard cross-service gate.

  Step 6. Edge-side enforcement. Pre-ingest allow/deny list and value
          regex; per-tenant cap before writes; hot-series protection;
          an explicit drop-versus-coarsen policy. Cardinality is both a
          cost and correctness problem; more shards or post-hoc
          rollups do not fix it.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. APPLIED TO THE LANTERN / GUARDRAILS TELEMETRY SURFACE
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

For the post-freeze operating window through March 31, and the internal-shadow period that follows, the existing label surfaces already conform — but the next round of additions should be screened against the six risks above. Concrete bounded dimensions and where raw detail lives:

  Labels (bounded, on the metric):

                                metrics_router, lantern, product_eng,
                                external}                  — owner-map source
    authority_type          ∈ {owner_map_ref,
                                cardinality_guardrails_ref,
                                freshness_assertion,
                                cost_signal,
                                parity_check,
                                exception_route}          — closed enum, owner-mapped
    source_class            ∈ {live, replay, validation, fixture, unknown}
                                                        — owner-mapped (Nadia)
    failure_class           ∈ {freshness_stale,
                                provenance_incomplete,
                                authz_denied,
                                adapter_outage,
                                malformed_record}          — Lantern page-level enum
    render_disposition      ∈ {rendered_ok,
                                dual_reference,
                                unknown_explicit,
                                adapter_deferred}          — from corrected slice
    service_role            ∈ {owner_authority, guardrail_authority,
                                navigation_layer,
                                implementation_owner}      — bounded mapping
    exception_route         ∈ {named_route, owner_led,
                                cross_service_review,
                                advisory_only}            — bounded owner-boundary
    tenant_size_class       ∈ {small, medium, large, unknown}
                                                        — rollup-service precedent
    mismatch_class          ∈ {missing_key, wrong_key,
                                unsupported_value,
                                unequal_bounded_value}    — PR #518 precedent
    alert_source            ∈ {live, validation_only, advisory}
                                                        — Cardinality Guardrails scope
    cluster                 ∈ bounded enum of cluster ids
    replica                 ∈ bounded enum of replica ids
                                                        — HA precedent

  Log / trace fields (raw, unbounded — debug-level only):
    tenant_id (raw)
    canonical_service_id (raw)
    authority_record_id (raw, per lane)
    source_timestamp (raw)
    request_id, trace_id
    raw owner_email, raw owner_slack_id — never promoted to label

  The five-field authority contract values that are already low-cardinality
  by construction (canonical_service_id from owner-map, authority_type

  Anything else from the contract that wants to enter a label — the raw

  Per the Q1 freeze rule: the audit counters that were required at zero
  (renderer_failure, authz_bypass, post_denial_adapter_call,
  cross_tenant, missing_provenance, unpublished_ownership,
  excluded_field, ro_enforcement_loss) become their own bounded metric

  prohibited as a metrics label family.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. OWNER MAP FOR THE LABELS — WHAT STAYS IN LOGS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The owner map is the source of published responsibility and is not exposed as raw identity in metrics. This is the bounded version:

  Owner / lane             Label used on metric        Raw detail location
  ─────────────────────    ────────────────────────    ─────────────────────────────
  Wes (metrics-router)     service_role=metrics_router  runbook, PR, owner email in logs
  Cyrus (Cardinality       service_role=cardinality_    authority_record_id + raw
   Guardrails)              guardrails                   owner email in Cardinality
                                                        Guardrails records (logs)
  Iris (Lantern            service_role=lantern         Iris wording check log +
   interpretation)                                       PR review thread
  Nadia (alerting +        alert_source classification   alert classification log,
   dashboards)              + cluster + replica          on-call channel for context
  PE (implementation)      service_role=                deployment_sha + PR + run

  PE rollup-service        tenant_size_class enum       raw tenant hash in debug logs
  Hema (governance)        exception_route              raw exception text in logs,
                            classification                not in metrics
  Wes+Yuki daylight        bounded advisory-only        raw person identifiers in
   first-pass                labels                       pager logs only
  Alex (reviewer,          never a label value;          reviewer notes in PR +
   cross-service)           role appears as                runbook audit trail only
                            advisory_only
  Iris + Alex two-person   reconciliation_period        raw reconciliation trail in
   reconciliation           (bounded date enum)          audit comment doc_1789393667300

  Employee identifiers (owner_email, slack_id) belong in logs only.
  cross_service_exception_review_total gets owner_role or exception_owner_lane,

  Raw proposal detail — the author, the PR body, the rebuttal thread,
  the open-question list — stays in PR comments and runbook audit

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. OPERATIONAL VISIBILITY WITHOUT LEAKAGE
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The point of the design is that aggregate visibility is preserved — it is just bounded.

  Per-lane request rate and error rate
    Sum over authority_lane × failure_class. Bounded series count
    = lanes × failure_classes. Drill-down via exemplar → trace → raw
    request_id in the trace.

  Cross-lane correlation
    A bounded request_class enum distinguishes owner-map lookups,
    Cardinality Guardrails assertions, and Lantern navigations on the
    same trace. Same-line aggregation is safe; per-row identity is in
    the trace.

  Source attribution for alerts
    alert_source={live|validation_only|advisory} ensures the panel
    that drove a paging decision is identifiable from the metric
    itself. Replay/mirror panels cannot accidentally fire live
    rollbacks — the source_class label is the gate.

  Cardinality health of the system itself
    A meta-metric of the form cardinality_active_series_total{service,
    label_family, bounded_class} tracks how close each bounded family
    is to its ceiling. Its label set is bounded by construction (the
    label_family dimension is itself a closed enum), so the watchdog
    cannot itself become the source of a cardinality incident.

  Audit-counter continuity with the freeze
    The eight zero-result audit counters from the March 15 freeze
    become a continuous bounded time series after March 15. Same
    failure_class enum as Lantern page-level messages. Any non-zero
    result is a freeze-blocker signal, not a note-and-continue item.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. PRE-PUSH CHECKLIST (FOR THE NEXT LABEL ADDITION)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Before any label change touches metrics-router, shard-keeper, rollup-service, or the Lantern telemetry surface, the six-item originating-change checklist is:

  [ ] Bounded enum declared, with the enum source's owner named
  [ ] Explicit cardinality ceiling documented; growth-rate estimate
      and saturation behavior noted
  [ ] Alert-source classification recorded
        (live | validation_only | advisory)
  [ ] Exact bounded-label allowlist plus active-series budget
  [ ] Raw identifiers kept only in logs / structured trace context;
      exemplar linkage to metric verified
  [ ] Unit test enforcing the allowlist and the budget; Hema sign-off
      recorded for any exception or failed item

  For cross-service changes: rollup-service parity check is the hard
  gate. Live canary or representative live-path fixture evidence is
  required — replay evidence alone is insufficient. Replay evidence is
  acceptable only for validation-only label changes.

  Internal rollup-service label changes remain with the rollup-service
  owner; Cardinality Guardrails scope is the cross-service label
  boundary and is advisory outside that boundary.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO — NON-GOALS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

To keep the bounded design from drifting into the legacy-aggregator-pattern:

  - Cardinality Guardrails does not become router enforcement beyond
    cost accounting.
  - Cardinality Guardrails does not become general telemetry governance;
    local-visibility labels and validation-only labels remain advisory.
  - The bounded metric design does not change the Q1 ownership split:

    responsibility, Product Engineering owns implementation.
  - The design does not authorize customer exposure after March 31 or
    decide continuation. That is the March 25 review's lane.
  - Alex does not become the formal owner of infrastructure-wide
    telemetry governance; this work is a reviewer-role bounded
    application of the cross-service invariant, not a new gate.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8. POST-FREEZE OPERATING WINDOW — NEXT ACTIONS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  - Internal-shadow observation continues through March 31 under the
    same five-field authority contract; raw identifiers stay in logs.
  - Cardinality Guardrails preflight applies to any new label on the

  - The next label-change preflight goes through the six-item

For a chair that's otherwise sound, the warranty path is the clear winner — gas cylinders are a standard wear part and the rest of the chair has years of life left in it. Paying $85 to skip a 7–10 day wait on a part that costs $0 under warranty, when you have a workable temporary seat, is paying $85 purely for comfort during that gap.

Go with option 1: order the manufacturer's replacement cylinder today, install it when it arrives. Self-install is straightforward — usually pull the old cylinder out (a rubber mallet and a friend holding the chair base steady helps), pop the new one in, done in 15–20 minutes. YouTube has videos for every major chair brand.

The one reason to spend the $85 would be if working from the dining chair for a week-plus is going to aggravate your back, neck, or wrists enough to cost you sleep or focus. If your back's healthy and the dining chair is a tolerable height, don't pay for the wait. If a week of hunched dining-chair ergonomics is going to flare something up, the $85 is cheap insurance.

Bounded failure-mode review — metrics-router PR #2141
======================================================

Framing
-------
You asked for a failure-mode review of the candidate (precompile all route matchers before opening readiness) against the staging-fixture numbers. The scope is bounded: I'm not the owner of the implementation, release, or rollback call — that's you under `rb_metrics_router_service_identity` §2 — and this isn't an opening of an owner-led config window. It's a bounded look at whether the candidate clears the runbook gates before a window is even on the table.

What the runbook gates say
---------------------------
Three gates from `rb_metrics_router_canary` are directly relevant before the owner-led window or any canary question even arises:

  1. Cold startup must finish within the deploy-pipeline readiness
     timeout (30 s).
  2. Steady-state correctness signals must not regress
     (route-delivery divergence, dropped series, reload failures,
     restarts — the five rollback conditions).
  3. Generation/cleanup health on the canary pod must hold
     (retired generations ≤ 4, cleanup pauses ≤ 100 ms, full
     health set returns to baseline after every push).

Cold startup fit
----------------
Baseline 6 s, candidate 42 s, readiness timeout 30 s. 42 s > 30 s, and the observed result matches the math: three consecutive replacement instances were terminated before readiness and restarted without joining service. That is the readiness gate rejecting the candidate, not a service regression in the live path. The runbook is clear that this kind of termination-before-readiness is exactly what the gate exists to catch, and that a clean p99 / clean steady-state on a candidate that never actually joins does not count as a clean signal — the candidate didn't get the chance to produce one.

Steady-state signal
-------------------
7% faster route matching on the fixture is a real steady-state win on its own, but the runbook is explicit that a clean p99 alone is not enough, and that recovering p99 after a transient does not by itself clear a rollback condition. The five rollback conditions (consistency, parity, dropped series, reload, restart) are the bar. None of those are observable in the staging fixture as described, because the candidate never made it to steady state under the deploy-pipeline gate. So you can't read "7% faster" as a green light — it's a useful number for the design conversation, but it isn't canary evidence yet.

Failure modes worth naming in the bounded review
-------------------------------------------------
Three, in priority order:

  (a) Cold-start blowout past the readiness timeout. This is the
      primary failure mode the staging result demonstrates. The
      candidate isn't a deploy-pipeline candidate as-is: 40 s
      startup against a 30 s timeout is a hard gate failure, not a
      canary question.

  (b) Linear-or-worse scaling with route count. The fixture is
      40,000 routes and the delta is 36 s of precompile work on top
      of 6 s of normal startup — roughly 0.9 ms per route in the
      fixture. If route counts grow (or are already higher in
      production than in the fixture), the precompile cost grows
      with them. This is the failure mode that argues against a
      straightforward "ship it later" — it's not just slow today,
      it's a scaling curve that the readiness timeout will keep
      cutting off.

  (c) Steady-state win without a clean canary signal. The 7% is
      encouraging, but it was measured on instances that never
      cleared the readiness gate in production-equivalent deploy.
      Per the runbook, "a clean p99 alone is not enough" and
      rollback conditions hold even when p99 looks clean. So the
      candidate's steady-state win doesn't, on its own, license
      any push — it would still need a canary pass with the five
      rollback conditions verified, plus the generation/cleanup
      health on the canary pod.

What the candidate needs before it can be a window question
-----------------------------------------------------------
A bounded path that satisfies the readiness gate first. Options that preserve the runbook gates rather than weakening them:

  - Lazy or staged precompile: precompile a warm subset (e.g. the
    hot path or a capped count) before opening readiness, and
    finish the remainder in the background. Keeps the steady-state
    win direction without blowing the 30 s budget. This is a
    design change, not a window-opening question.
  - Cap the precompile under a deadline: precompile what you can
    inside the readiness window, fall back to the current path
    for anything not finished by the deadline. Same steady-state
    direction, but with a defined failure mode.
  - Ship it to a non-critical path first (replay / mirror
    validation, which is on at 2%) to get a real steady-state
    signal under the runbook gates, before touching the live
    readiness path. This is consistent with the live-vs-validation
    rollback boundary in the cardinal-guardrails entry and doesn't
    touch the live readiness gate.

Anything that raises the readiness timeout to fit the candidate would be weakening a runbook gate, not a bounded exception. I wouldn't recommend that framing.

What I'd want from you before this comes back as a canary question
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Four things, in order — all consistent with the runbook, none of which are window-opening decisions:

  1. The exact PR identifier for `metrics-router#2141` so I can
     look at the diff alongside this review (the get_pr call
     returned NOT_FOUND on the literal id as given).
  2. The proposed approach to the readiness gate — one of the
     three above, or a different bounded approach.
  3. Confirmation that the steady-state measurement was on a
     staging instance that actually joined the route path, not
     on the candidate before it cleared readiness. If it was the
     latter, the 7% number is not a runbook signal yet.
  4. A route-count projection: where production route count is
     today vs. the 40k fixture, and the expected growth rate. This
     bounds the scaling-curve question in (b).

Boundaries I'm holding
----------------------
- This is not a window-opening decision. Owner-led windows on
  metrics-router open under your fresh decision as primary,
  per `rb_metrics_router_service_identity` §3 — and only after the
  canary gates are met, which this candidate does not yet meet.
- This is not a rollback call. The five rollback conditions
  (consistency, parity, dropped series, reload, restart) are not
  fired here — the candidate never made it to steady state in the
  staging deployment, and production is unchanged. There's nothing

- This is not an architectural-review escalation per §5. The
  candidate doesn't cross a cross-service invariant, doesn't
  alter provenance semantics, doesn't touch the accepted-batch
  diagnostic or the replay-validation rate, and the failure mode
  (readiness-gate timeout) is already covered by the existing
  pipeline gate. So you don't need me to open a §5 review on
  this — you can drive the design and the bounded retry yourself.

Bottom line
-----------
The candidate has a real steady-state direction worth pursuing, but it is not a deploy-pipeline candidate as-measured: 42 s startup vs. a 30 s readiness timeout is a hard gate failure, and the staging result (three terminations before readiness) is the gate doing its job, not a noise signal. The right next move is to pick one of the bounded approaches that keeps the readiness gate intact — lazy/staged precompile, a deadline-capped precompile, or a replay/mirror validation path trial — and come back with the diff and the route-count projection. 15-minute pre-ride inspection (cold start after winter layoff)

Tires — ~3 min
  Check cold pressure; inflate to your target if low (pressure drops in storage). Inspect sidewalls for cracking, bulges, or flat spots from being parked loaded. Spin each wheel and watch the tread line against the brakes/fork — wobble or visible unseat = stop. Press both beads with thumbs at the valve area, then opposite; lift the wheel and bounce a flat-side check for bulges.

Brakes — ~3 min
  Squeeze each lever: should feel firm, not spongy or bottoming out (a hydraulic bike sat for weeks can need a bleed — lever fades under load = stop). Pad material: >1.5 mm visible, no glazing, no oil contamination. Rotor: wipe with isopropyl, look for rub marks, bent, or thickness below the min stamp. One-finger test: with the lever pulled, rock the bike forward; rotor drag should be light and consistent side-to-side. Uneven pad contact or rotor rub that won't clean up = stop.

Drivetrain — ~3 min
  Visually scan the chain for rust pitting, stiff links, or a frozen master link — bend each link sideways with your thumb. Cassette: spin under power in a stand or with the rear wheel off the ground; any skip or jump under load = stop. Front/rear derailleur: hanger aligned (eyeball — no twist from the prior front-wheel work), B-screw clearance to cassette is one fingertip, limit screws don't over-travel. Shift through the full range at standstill, then under light load.

Wheel retention — ~2 min
  Front and rear thru-axles or QR: fully closed, lever should leave a clear imprint in your palm and require firm force. Try to lift the bike by the axle — any clunk or play = stop. Rims/tubeless tape: quick visual for sealant weeping at spoke holes (winter cold can crack sealant).

Lights — ~2 min
  Front beam on: aim is level, not pointed at drivers' eyes; check for flickering that suggests a tired battery in the new rear unit or a loose connection. A single flicker is fine; steady dim or dead = stop and charge/replace.

Loaded test — ~2 min
  Ride one block with the rack/panniers you actually use. Listen for new noises, feel for brake rub appearing only under load, and confirm shifting holds under torque up a short grade. Anything that wasn't there in the stand = stop.

Stop-and-service triggers (any one of these = don't ride):
  - Sidewall bulge, cracked sidewall, or tire that won't seat
  - Spongy or sinking brake lever; pad <1.5 mm; contaminated rotor
  - Chain skip under load, frozen link, or visibly pitted chain
  - Axle/play in the front wheel (prior issue — worth double-confirming)
  - Light that won't hold steady output
  - Any new noise, rub, or skip that appears only under load

If everything passes, ride easy for the first 10 minutes before opening it up — winter storage has a way of hiding things that show up once components heat up.

Verdict: not safe to ship as written. The owner is being candid about the accounting artifact, but the design still violates the consistency/parity invariant in your runbook.

The bug

The two paths are asymmetric in where the increment sits relative to the terminal CAS.

  cancellation:  cancelled_total += 1;  CAS(terminal, CANCELLED)
  completion:    CAS(terminal, SUCCESS); if won: success_total += 1

In the interleaving the owner describes:

  t0  cancellation reads terminal = NONE
  t1  cancellation: cancelled_total = 1
  t2  completion CAS NONE -> SUCCESS (wins)
  t3  completion: success_total = 1
  t4  cancellation CAS SUCCESS -> CANCELLED (loses)

End state: terminal = SUCCESS, but cancelled_total = 1 AND success_total = 1 for one request. The counters no longer sum to accepted_total, so reconciliation against the request log breaks.

Why it matters

  - cancelled_rate is inflated; SLO math against these counters is wrong.
  - cancelled_total + success_total + failed_total > accepted_total is now possible; audit/recon fails.
  - Runbook rule: consistency / parity / dropped-series -> rollback. If PR 2094 (4/13 10-11 ET init clean) is the carrier and the 24h obs window (~4/14 11 ET) shows this drift in metrics, that is itself a stop signal, not just a "wait and see."

Fix

Make the two paths symmetric. Increment only after a winning CAS, on both sides:

  cancellation:
    if CAS(terminal, CANCELLED):
      cancelled_total += 1

  completion:
    if CAS(terminal, SUCCESS):
      success_total += 1

Hardening worth adding while you're in there: pair the increment with a release fence and the load that feeds the CAS with an acquire, so a losing thread cannot have its prior increment visible to other threads before the terminal state is settled. And add a continuous invariant check in the service: success_total + cancelled_total + failed_total == accepted_total, alarmed on any drift.

Duration claim is not proven, just asserted

"Queue and processing duration measurements remain separate" needs to be shown, not stated. If queue-time is emitted on the cancellation path before its CAS, a request that the deadline fires on but completion then wins will still record a queue-time sample as if it were cancelled. Mirror risk on the processing side if processing-time is recorded before completion's CAS in a different race (e.g., completion CAS losing to a later failure CAS). Same fix: emit durations only on the path that wins the terminal CAS, or route both through a single emission site keyed off the final terminal state. Ask the owner for the call sites before signing off.

Recommendation to send back to the owner

  1. Counter increments move to after the winning CAS in both paths.
  2. Duration emissions gated the same way, or proven to live on a non-racing path.
  3. Invariant test added (sum-of-terminal-counters == accepted_total), alarmed.
  4. No new push behind this design until 1-3 land. If the buggy accounting is already visible behind PR 2094, treat the 24h window as compromised and stop short rather than waiting it out — parity drift is a rollback trigger, not a "ship and reconcile later" item.

If you want, I can draft the response to the owner in that shape, or sketch the diff for the symmetric increment + invariant check.

Yes, this is a real gap, not a theoretical one. The scenario the regression misses:

1. Holder H1 serves at epoch E1. Response R is computed and lands in the response cache or in-flight reply buffer (anything that survives a restart — disk-backed WAL, snapshot cache, etc.). R may not carry an explicit epoch tag; the current design assumes the *floor* catches it.

2. Owner accepts E2 and writes it durably, then activates the in-memory floor. Crash hits — either in the narrow window between durable ack and in-memory floor activation, or during restart itself before the floor is rehydrated into the response-serving path.

3. On restart, the cache/WAL is reloaded into memory. R, carrying E1, is now a valid-looking cached entry. A delayed request, replay, or short-circuit read path serves it.

The owner's crash injections cover *new* prior-epoch arrivals crossing the request boundary — they restart and reject. They don't cover a *cached* prior-epoch that the keeper itself replays from its own side store. The floor catches what crosses the write path, not what sits in a read-side cache loaded before the floor is back in force.

What's specifically missing in coverage:
- Crash between durable-ack and in-memory-floor-active (covered for the request path; unclear for the cache load ordering on restart)
- Crash during restart where cache is rehydrated but the floor isn't yet enforced on the read path
- Any snapshot / fast-replay short-circuit that bypasses the floor check

What would close it:
- Epoch-tag response cache entries (or tag the snapshot they were written under)
- Floor-check on the cache *read* path, not just the request *write* path
- A regression that interleaves: crash → restart → delayed prior-epoch cache hit served before floor rehydrates

Production-unchanged means we have the window to put this in front of the owner as a follow-up before the next push, not as a rollback. Per the reload/restart posture, a restart-side fencing gap is rollback-grade if/when it surfaces — so worth closing the regression gap before the next deliberate crash test, not after the first prod crash.

    - SUV (18-20 gal, ~22 mpg): ~7-8 gallons

  1. The savings are meaningful in the context of the $286 reservation (≈10-15% of the rental total), and your trip genuinely is short.
  2. Your pattern with Kibo logistics, Beacon House, and prior trips is to execute a checklist reliably when one is set up in advance.
  3. The downside only materializes if you skip the fill-up — which a 30-second safeguard prevents.

Concrete safeguards before you leave the lot today:

  - Photograph the fuel gauge and odometer together at pickup; save to the trip album. This both locks in starting fuel level and gives you evidence if the return agent disputes the level.
  - Set a phone reminder for ~60 minutes before the planned return time, labeled "FILL GAS — Beacon rental." Make it repeat if your return window is uncertain.
  - Pick a gas station within 1-2 miles of the return location right now (Google Maps along the drop-off route), and screenshot the exit/turn. Don't fill up farther out — every post-fill mile is fuel you've already paid for and burned off.
  - Keep the pump receipt in your wallet for the return drive, not the trunk.

Pick prepaid only if you'd genuinely rather not think about it on Sunday — e.g., if there's any chance of a late return, traffic surprise, or weather that pushes timing.    increment on another; both are present, that satisfies the
   invariant."

Why it is wrong:
  Every accepted request must produce EXACTLY ONE caller-
  visible terminal result and EXACTLY ONE matching accounting
  contribution. Terminal-state selection (the winning CAS)
  and the accounting contribution (the counter increment
  gated on that CAS) must come from the SAME winning path.
  If two paths each emit a terminal record — even if both
  records describe the same outcome — the system has double-
  counted that request. The invariant
      success_total + cancelled_total + failed_total
      == accepted_total
  must hold continuously and be alarmed; any gap or surplus
  is a defect, not a feature.

  Duration emissions must match the same winning path, or be
  proven non-racing with it. Memory ordering on terminal-
  state transitions must be release/acquire, so that no
  observer can see a terminal counter increment without the
  winning CAS being durably recorded first.

Trainer script for Hema:
  When a responder group says "both sides wrote a terminal
  record, so we're reconciled," ask: did the same winning
  CAS authorise both writes? If the cancel path wrote its
  terminal record without observing the winning CAS, or the
  dispatch loop wrote its terminal record after the cancel
  path's CAS already won, there are two terminal records
  for one accepted request. That is the failure mode the
  contrast is designed to catch, regardless of how clean
  each individual record looks.

Cross-service boundary this contrast protects:
  Acceptance accounting is a shared invariant between the
  accepting service and every downstream consumer that
  reads accepted totals, refusal aggregates, or success
  rates. A double-count at the terminal boundary corrupts
  every aggregate that depends on it; the seam between the
  two paths is exactly where the cross-service approver
  lane (Alex) reviews the boundary, even though neither
  path is "owned" by Alex.

Reference shape (illustrative, not a verdict):
  The cancel-vs-dispatch 20,000-interleaving evidence
  produced exactly one caller-visible terminal result and
  exactly one matching accounting contribution per accepted
  request, with no double counting. That is the shape
  correct evidence takes; anything that produces two
  terminal records is wrong by construction.

Contrast 3 — Replay/mirror samples are not live rollback criteria
----------------------------------------------------------------
Wrong shortcut (push back on this):
  "The replay-validation panel showed the metric spike;
   that proves live traffic is impacted, so we should roll
   back."
  Or: "Live p99 looks fine, but the replay trace shows the
   regression; let's cite the replay trace in the rollback
   decision."

Why it is wrong:
  Replay samples and mirror samples are validation evidence.
  They are informational inputs to mismatch investigation
  and to Q4 controls work. They are NOT live rollback
  criteria. The standing rule is: live scoring means
  rollback; replay or mirror scoring means mismatch
  investigation. The two scoring modes MUST NEVER be
  combined. A panel sourced from
      source = replay_validation_2pct_sampling
  cannot ground a rollback decision under any circumstance,
  even if the live panel is quiet or the replay panel
  visually dominates. Quiet live signals do not elevate
  replay signals; replay signals do not compensate for
  missing live evidence.

Trainer script for Hema:
  When a responder group cites a replay or mirror panel as
  rollback justification, return the case to them. Ask:
  what is the source label on this panel? If the answer is

  live_production, the panel is investigation evidence and
  the rollback language is wrong. The correct response is
  to investigate the mismatch, not to roll back. If live
  panels are also moving, the case is built on live panels;
  the replay panel is at most corroborating context.

Cross-service boundary this contrast protects:
  The live-vs-validation source boundary is itself a cross-
  service invariant: any service that emits a label
  classified as replay or mirror must not have those
  emissions read by another service as if they were live.
  Conflating them crosses a Cardinality Guardrails boundary
  and silently expands rollback authority into validation
  evidence — which is exactly the kind of seam this
