FOOT-AND-HIP SEQUENCE — what the slip pattern likely means

You sent 4 clean attempts (no fatigue, controlled grip, same edge, same beat), so the failure is mechanical and repeatable, not fitness-driven. That's the most useful kind of problem to work.

The slip is happening during the HIP SHIFT that precedes the next hand move. On a small edge, that moment is the highest-risk beat in the sequence because:

  - The right foot is the only thing keeping your center of mass from peeling off the wall while your hips translate. As hips shift, the angle between your right leg and the wall opens. If that angle opens without opposition from the opposite hand, the foot unweights passively and pops off.
  - A small edge requires active engagement — heel pulled down so the toe pad presses into the edge. If engagement drops for even a beat during the hip drive, the foot skates.
  - Toe orientation matters. If the right toe is pointing sideways (duck-footed) instead of into the wall, the pulling line through the heel goes past the toe pad and the foot slips off the inside or outside of the edge.

Most common fix candidates, in rough order of how often they actually solve this:

  1. Foot engagement timing — drive the heel down BEFORE the hip shifts, not during. Sequence: set foot, load foot, then drive hips from opposition (left hand pulling, right foot pushing).
  2. Foot position — try moving the right foot up the edge 1-2 inches, or try a different hold entirely (a smear next to the edge, a volume nub, the next edge up).
  3. Opposition — make sure the left hand is fully weighted and pulling before the right hand reaches. A weak opposite-side pull is what most often yanks the foot off.
  4. Hip technique — a drop-knee locks the foot in via rotation; a left-leg flag swings the hips without opening the right ankle. Either can bypass the slip if the straight-on shift is the failure mode.
  5. Static vs. dynamic — if you're moving dynamically to the next hold, the foot can't recover from a slip mid-air. A controlled static shift often reveals whether the foot CAN hold through the position.

BOUNDED PROGRESSION FOR NEXT SESSION

Constraints you're already holding and that match your rehab rule: full warmup, stop before fatigue, no forearm sx during or after — the gate is clear.

Suggested attempt budget: 5 quality attempts, one variable per attempt. Stop after that regardless of send.

  Attempt 1 — Foot timing only. Nothing else changes.
    Focus: set right foot, drive heel, THEN shift hips. Run the move mentally before committing.

  Attempt 2 — Opposition only.
    Focus: left hand pulls HARD, hold that pull through the hip shift, then right hand moves last. Foot timing as in attempt 1.

  Attempt 3 — Foot position variant.
    Focus: try the right foot one edge higher, or a smear adjacent to the small edge. Body position as in attempt 2.

  Attempt 4 — Hip technique variant.
    Focus: drop-knee or left-leg flag instead of straight hip shift. If the straight shift is the failure mode, this often unlocks it.

  Attempt 5 — Full send attempt.
    Focus: pick the working technique from 1-4 and run it clean.

If none of 1-4 feel like progress (foot still slips from the same beat), the move may need a different right-foot hold entirely — at that point, walk the line and look for an alternative foot you haven't tried. That's a 6th-attempt call, not a default.

Brings to next session: a mental note of the exact beat (you have it — "shifting hips for the next hand move"), and one specific cue per attempt. Don't stack cues — single-variable drilling is what makes the next send legible.

Per your own rule: V6-vert still active, no auto-plan — this is a framework, not a schedule. You pick which attempts to run; the budget is the cap.

Two cold-start rollouts of the same service build, contrasted against each other. The contrast trains responders not to treat a restart as acceptance evidence and not to treat "the instance came up eventually" as proof of a healthy cold start.

  Staging candidate (earlier): Instances were admitted to the load-balancer pool before the fixed readiness budget closed. Cold-start compilation time exceeded the budget on first attempt. Instances were terminated, then rejoined the pool only after a retry. The pool saw traffic against the unrouted instances during compilation, and the cold-start path was exercised a second time under retry conditions.

  Production rollout, 2027-05-06 (PR 2141 production evidence): Every instance was kept unroutable until compilation finished. Every cold start stayed within the fixed readiness budget. No instance was terminated. No instance rejoined via retry. No restart occurred.

Failure mode the case trains: confusing "eventually serving" with "served correctly from first contact." A restart is not acceptance evidence. The acceptance criterion is that readiness and serving eligibility remained aligned throughout the cold-start window — instances joined the pool only after readiness closed, and traffic was never sent to an instance whose cold-start work was incomplete. The production rollout passed for that reason; the staging candidate failed for that reason. The distinguishing behavior is alignment between readiness and serving eligibility, not the absence of a crash, not the presence of a successful retry, and not a post-hoc observation that the service was healthy after warmup.

Stop conditions (for the incident-practice framing, not for live use): if any instance is admitted to the pool before readiness closes, if any cold start exceeds the budget, if any instance is terminated and rejoined via retry, or if restart is invoked to recover the cold-start path — treat the rollout as not passing regardless of subsequent health.

Two distinct hazard classes the revised design leaves open, plus three adjacent gaps worth flagging while the owner is in revision mode.

The two flagged gaps, expanded:

1. Race A — read interleaves with promotion. The design specifies that a read after the marker commits but before promotion completes returns explicit unknown. It doesn't specify what a read sees during promotion itself (step 3 in flight). If the index isn't atomically swappable per-record, a concurrent read can land on a half-written entry. A concurrent-read regression test needs to:
   - hammer lookup(key) on N goroutines while publish is in flight
   - assert only three outcomes ever observed: prior value, new value, explicit unknown
   - assert no reader sees a value that later reverts to the prior value
   - assert no reader errors or times out

2. Race B — crash between marker commit and promotion. Recovery semantics aren't specified. Pick one and write the test for it:
   - complete-and-publish (recovery re-runs promotion idempotently from pending)
   - roll-back (recovery deletes the marker; record stays pending until next attempt)
   - fail-closed (marker stays; lookup stays explicit unknown; alert fires)
   Inject at three points: (a) after marker, before promotion; (b) mid-promotion; (c) after promotion, before ack. Each restart must land in a deterministic, documented state. If you pick complete-and-publish, the re-promotion itself needs an idempotency test.

Three adjacent gaps the owner probably wants to know about while they're already in the design:

3. Marker-without-payload. What if the marker commits but the pending payload is corrupt, partial, or never landed? "Signed" needs to be specified — signed over the record hash, or just a version stamp? If signed, hash mismatch is the failure signal. If not, the marker is an authoritative "publish me" with nothing behind it, and recovery has to reject or fail closed. Spec this and add a test.

4. Pending-lookup semantics for callers. Iris's customer-interp lane needs the contract spelled out. When a caller sees explicit unknown, can they distinguish fresh-pending-update-in-flight from genuine miss from negative entry (deleted)? If all three look the same, downstream retry / escalation / "should we tell the customer anything" logic can't be written correctly. Ideally this is enforced at the type level, not just asserted in a test, because Iris's lane consumes whatever this returns.

5. Stale-pending retention. If a writer crashes before the marker commits, pending records accumulate. What's the reaper? A pending key that's been pending for a week — what does lookup return, and what does ops see? Add a test that exercises the retention boundary, not just the happy path.

Concrete test names that would slot into a regression suite:

  TestPublish_ConcurrentReadDuringPromotion
  TestPublish_CrashAfterMarkerBeforePromotion
  TestPublish_CrashMidPromotion
  TestPublish_CrashAfterPromotionBeforeAck
  TestPublish_MarkerWithoutPayloadRecovery
  TestLookup_PendingReturnsExplicitUnknown_AtAllStages
  TestLookup_PendingVsMissVsNegative_DistinguishableToCaller
  TestPending_StaleRetentionBoundary

Result: legitimate Lantern traffic is misclassified as out-of-period, and the 4/1–6/15 evidence base is undercounted. The 30 unknown bucket has a related but distinct cause: records that lack any derivable join key from time alone.

This is a quality problem, not a coverage problem. Two forbidden moves would superficially "fix" the count: (1) substitute processing time for authority time when reconciling split records, which would silently rewrite the evidence window; (2) refresh the authoritative timestamp on the source record to push it back inside the period, which would corrupt the source-of-truth and violate the 4/16 source-time close. Both are out.

The fix is an identity-based join. The retained authority record identity (the stable evt_* identifier assigned at intake) is preserved on every record by design; using it as the join key avoids time entirely.

REQUIREMENT (bounded)

  Title: Deterministic tenant-scoped join via retained authority record identity — Lantern op-evid, Q2

  Scope: Lantern only. Op-evid cycle 4/1–6/15 open and unfrozen. No auth-expand. No renderer change. No customer-path change. No intake correction.

  Identity: The retained authority record identity is the stable record ID assigned at intake (the evt_* identifier from the source-of-truth system). This ID is the join key. It is read-only with respect to the join — not derived, not recomputed, not refreshed.

  Determinism: For a given (tenant, authority_record_id) pair, the join produces exactly one result. Repeated execution over the same inputs produces the same result. The join is a pure function of (tenant, authority_record_id, source records within tenant scope).

  Tenant scoping: Constrained to a single tenant boundary. Cross-tenant (tenant_a, authority_id_from_tenant_b) inputs produce no result — not a synthetic match, not a null-with-warning. Tenant identity is taken from the authority record, not from processing-time context.

  Time semantics:
    - The authoritative timestamp is read by the join; it is never written, never refreshed.
    - Processing time is recorded as join metadata (when the join ran, which bucket the record resolved into). It is not a join key.
    - The split-24h bucket resolves by identity, not by stretching the time window.

  Eligibility (what gets joined):
    - Records carrying a non-null retained authority record identity.
    - Records within the same tenant as that identity.
    - Records whose authoritative timestamp falls within 4/1–6/15.

  Non-eligibility:
    - Records without a retained authority record identity → remain in the "unknown" bucket. This requirement does not invent one.
    - Records across tenant boundaries → remain unjoined. Cross-tenant is not a target.
    - Auth-expand on any record → out of scope.

  Expected effect on Q2 evidence: the 54 split-24h bucket resolves into eligible evidence via identity. The 30 unknown bucket is not reduced by this requirement; that requires a separate intake correction, explicitly out of scope here.

EXCLUSIONS

  - No change to the authoritative timestamp on any record.
  - No substitution of processing time for authority time.
  - No auth-expand.
  - No intake-correction processing.
  - No cross-tenant join.
  - No customer-path change.

OWNER MAP

  - Implementation: Product Engineering.
  - Customer-impact interpretation: Iris.
  - Evidence / measurement interpretation: Anya.
  - Requirement approval: Alex (this gates the bounded shape, not the implementation).
  - Release / rollback: Wes.

  The 4/1–6/15 Lantern op-evid cycle remains open and unfrozen. This requirement operates inside that cycle. It does not close, freeze, or re-open the cycle, and does not pre-empt the post-6/15 closeout decision.

OUT OF BAND

  This is a bounded requirement, not a push-window decision. If implementation lands during an owner-led push window, that is a separate decision per the runbook. The requirement is the bounded shape of the change; the push decision is separate and not implied by approval here.

Pushing back briefly on adding `last_checked_by` to the artifact-canonical report — I think it should stay out of the decision inputs and live in a separate `check_run` record.

The reason is determinism. The report needs to make the same go/no-go call regardless of who happens to be on rotation that day. If `last_checked_by` is a deterministic input, two runs against the same artifact metadata can produce different decisions, and we lose the property that the report is replayable from its inputs alone. It also starts to look like an endorsement field, which is a different thing from a decision field — and conflating them makes it harder later to ask "did the system catch this" vs. "did a person catch this," which are genuinely separate questions.

What I'd keep instead: the four deterministic fields we agreed on (team, release_candidate, canonical_package_version, failure_class). Then a sibling record keyed by run_id with operator_id, timestamp, and report_id, where `last_checked_by` is one field among the operator metadata. That gives you the audit trail without making it part of the decision.

The thing I want to preserve for diagnosing a blocked handoff: we still need enough in the run record that when someone says "handoff X is blocked, why?" we can answer from the deterministic report alone — what the artifact metadata was, what failure_class it landed in, and what the canonical input said. The `check_run` record is then the pointer to "who looked at it and when," which is the right shape for human/operational evidence rather than decision logic. If we ever need to reconstruct why a handoff stalled, the deterministic report tells us the gate; the check_run record tells us the operational context (operator, time, which report version they were looking at). Both pieces survive, but neither contaminates the other.

Concretely, the fields that matter for blocked-handoff diagnosis, all of which stay in the deterministic report:
  - canonical_package_version (did it pin, and to what)
  - failure_class (missing manifest output, missing artifact metadata, version mismatch — the three we already cover)
  - team + release_candidate (so we know whose handoff and which candidate)
  - source_timestamp on the input side, so we can tell stale-input blocks from genuine-mismatch blocks

And in the check_run record: run_id, operator_id, timestamp, report_id. That's it.

Defect analysis (from the live context + memory)

The defect is a deterministic delete-before-promote ordering in the
audit-compaction path:

  1. The live derived index is removed before the rebuilt index is

  2. A crash in that window leaves a partial temporary index on disk

  3. On restart, the process can select the partial temporary file
     and serve historical lookups that omit retained transitions.

This is the same shape as the August 2026 metrics-router#1912 missed-
reload and the prior shard-keeper#188 atomic-replacement findings: the
swap is not actually atomic, and there is no fail-closed posture on
restart. The 2,000-injection run surfaced 37 restart selections of
the partial temporary index (~1.85%) — non-zero, restart-time
visible, and silent to the production/customer surface because the
index is derived, not the source of truth.

Two distinct invariants are being conflated:

  - Source-of-truth safety: signed transition envelopes and the
    observation-derived source_timestamp must remain immutable. The
    recent fix preserves these. Good.
  - Derived-index atomicity: serving must observe either the complete
    old generation or the complete new generation, never a partial.
    This is what the crash run actually broke and what is still
    untested.

The missing artifact is not another design argument. It is
executable evidence that the index swap is atomic across crash and
restart, and that restart cannot select a partial temporary file.

partial temporary index in 37 cases and silently omitting retained
transitions from historical lookup. Production and customer paths
were unaffected because the index is derived, but that is exactly
why a derived-index leak is invisible until a lease or audit claim
crosses it.

What the fix must guarantee

  1. The on-disk swap must be atomic: write + fsync the new index
     under a temp name, then a single rename into the live slot
     (or equivalent that is crash-safe on the target filesystem).
  2. Ordering must be promote-then-delete: the new index is
     published before the old one is unlinked. A crash between the
     two leaves both on disk; restart must pick the published one,
     not whichever happens to sort first.
  3. Restart must be fail-closed with respect to a partial
     temporary index: if a `*.partial` or `*.tmp` file is present
     at startup, restart must treat that as no published index
     (explicit unknown / refuse reads / rebuild from the
     transition log), never as a candidate to serve.
  4. Serving during a swap must observe only the complete old
     index, the complete new index, or explicit unknown — no
     half-written entries, no errors masked as empty results, no
     reads that flip back and forth.

  a. Kill -9 between temp-file write and the atomic rename.

     generation, no `*.partial` is selected, and a forced rebuild

  c. Kill -9 mid-rewrite of the new index (temp file present,

     index is missing or stale-but-present.

In both cases, the failure was genuine, not formatting. Exact-match is doing the job it's supposed to do: refusing to treat two unequal strings as equivalent without proof. Weakening it (or quietly normalizing `v` away) would have allowed those two real drifts to ship.

SOUTH SLOPE BEDROOM AC — PRE-SEASON CHECK (20 min budget)

Assumptions: window unit, manual control, prior drain-channel repair already closed, no active symptoms. If the unit is portable or a through-wall sleeve, skip mounting step and adapt accordingly.

STEP 1 — Setup [1 min]
  Cut power at the unit (or unplug). Note the breaker label. Have a flashlight, damp cloth, vacuum with brush attachment, and a small flat screwdriver ready.

STEP 2 — Filter [3-4 min]
  Remove the front grille/filter per the unit's manual. Hold to light: if you can't see light through it, wash or replace.
    Foam/slatted: warm water + mild dish soap, air-dry fully (do not reinstall damp — promotes mold and restricts airflow).
    Pleated: replace with the exact size printed on the frame (common 16x25x1, but verify).
  Vacuum the evaporator coil face gently while the filter is out. Wipe the grille.

STEP 3 — Exterior drain path [3-4 min]
  This is the closed-repair area — verify it stays closed. With the unit still powered off:
    Look at the rear drain channel/vane and the bottom drain pan from outside (tilt the sash out only if safe; otherwise use a mirror/phone camera). Confirm no standing water, algae mat, insect nest, or debris.
    Confirm the unit is tilted slightly backward (~1/4 in per foot of width) so condensate runs to the rear, not into the room.
    Confirm the drain pan weep holes / outlet are clear — drip a few mL of water into the pan and watch it exit outside, not onto the sill or wall.
    Inspect the sill and interior wall for any staining, swelling, or mineral trail that would suggest a slow leak.

STEP 4 — Cord and receptacle [2-3 min]
  Inspect the full cord length: no cracks, fraying, pinch points, discoloration, melted spots, or missing/bent plug blades. Plug should be a single 3-prong (or unit-specific) molded plug — no adapter, no power strip, no extension cord.
  Inspect the receptacle: fully seated plug, faceplate flush, no warmth, no discoloration, no buzz, no loose fit (plug shouldn't drop out or wobble). Smell for any hot-plastic or ozone odor.
  Confirm the circuit: window ACs want a dedicated or lightly-shared circuit. If anything else on that breaker has been tripping, note it and proceed with caution — that alone is a "stop" sign if you see it during the cooling test.

STEP 5 — Stable mounting [3-4 min]
  Window open only as far as needed; sash supported so it can't drop onto the unit.
  Confirm: angle-iron or L-bracket fastened to the building (not just the sill), sash locked down on the unit's top rail, side accordion panels/foam seals snug against the frame with no daylight gaps, unit not rocking when nudged.
  Confirm nothing is stacked on or draped over the unit, and the outdoor coil (rear) has at least 12-18 in clearance from the wall and isn't packed with leaves or a bird's nest.

STEP 6 — Short cooling test [5-7 min]
  Restore power. Set mode = Cool, fan = High, target temp = 60°F (or lowest setting).
  Within 60-90 seconds you should feel cool air at the supply grille and hear a steady compressor hum — no ticking, scraping, squealing, or metallic rattle.
  Run 5 minutes. Verify:
    Supply air noticeably cooler than return (intuitive hand check at grille vs. intake).
    No dripping from the unit into the room.
    No new smell (musty, sweet/chemical, or burning).
    Receptacle and plug face not warm to the touch.
    Condensate dripping externally (or trickling out the drain path) as expected.
  Return thermostat to a normal setpoint and the fan to Auto.

STOP USING AND CONTACT MANAGEMENT IF YOU OBSERVE ANY OF:
  Water dripping or staining inside the room, sill, or wall (drain path failure — repeat of the prior repair).
  Burning smell, smoke, sparks, or any warmth / discoloration at the plug or receptacle.
  Breaker trips or GFCI resets during the test.
  Compressor short-cycles (clicks on/off rapidly) or fails to start.
  Loud scraping, squealing, knocking, or new persistent rattle.
  Ice forming on the evaporator coil or supply side of the unit.
  Sweet/chemical refrigerant smell.
  Any cord damage, cracked plug, or receptacle that feels loose or warm.
  Mounting loosens, unit rocks, or daylight appears at the seals.
  Musty odor that persists 5+ minutes of run time (possible mold in the air path).

Normal-completion criteria: filter clean, drain path clear and dripping outside, cord and receptacle cool and undamaged, mount solid, cold air within 90 seconds, no drips or smells inside. Anything off the list above → power down and call management before the first heat wave.

Recommendation: keep the async intake, replace the standing weekly meeting with (a) a named-boundary trigger catalog, (b) an async escalation path, and (c) a weekly automated digest that pulls you in only when the digest itself crosses a threshold. This handles the rare real exception quickly without making you a standing gate.

Why the data already answers Hema

The final Q2 numbers — 14 bounded exceptions proceeding, 3 ordinary requests returned before review, and zero requesting routine implementation or release approval — show the intake triage is doing its job. The 3 returned were filtered before they ever reached you. The 14 proceeded within pre-bounded scope under existing team-lead authority. None of them needed your sign-off. A standing meeting is being proposed for a workload the current process already absorbed without you.

Comparison

Standing weekly meeting
  Recreates a queue: every accepted exception waits up to a week for the slot.
  Makes you a standing implementation/release gate — exactly the failure mode you flagged.
  Scheduled regardless of whether anything needs your judgment; most weeks will be no-ops.
  Cost is recurring: your time plus the prep/coordination overhead for whoever brings items.

Async intake + ad hoc on a named trigger
  You engage only when a concrete boundary is crossed.
  No recurring overhead in quiet weeks.
  Response time is bounded by the trigger's severity, not by a calendar slot.
  Real risk: drift if the trigger catalog is vague, or if intake classification gets sloppy.

The risk in the second model is real but solvable — that's what the catalog and digest are for.

Recommended Q3 operating model

1. Self-serve default path. Routine bounded exceptions proceed under existing team-lead sign-off. Intake returns ordinary requests same-day with a reason code (the Q2 pattern). No escalation to you.

2. Named-boundary trigger catalog. You are engaged only when an item hits one of:
   - Cross-team boundary (safety / customer-path internal-reference categories).
   - Auth-expand.
   - Production-state change to a system you own.
   - Any request for routine implementation or release approval.
   - Volume anomaly (intake crosses a threshold you set, e.g., >2σ above the weekly baseline).
   These are the only paths into your queue.

3. Async escalation. Triggered items arrive as a Slack DM with one-paragraph context and a recommendation. You respond within 4 business hours, or delegate. No meeting unless two or more triggered items in the same week need cross-team coordination.

4. Weekly automated digest. Volume, return rate, trigger-category counts, anomaly flags. You read it async. The digest itself triggers an ad hoc 30-minute review only if it surfaces a threshold breach — that's the ad hoc half of Hema's proposal, but driven by signal rather than calendar.

5. Quarterly retrospective. End of Q3: review what triggered, what didn't, refine the catalog. This is the only scheduled touchpoint and it replaces the standing meeting's "visibility" function.

How to respond to Hema

The legitimate concern underneath the standing-meeting proposal is drift and visibility — that without a regular checkpoint, exceptions accumulate unobserved. The digest plus the named triggers address that without the queue. If Hema wants assurance, point her at the digest as the visibility mechanism and the quarterly retrospective as the calibration point. The standing meeting is the wrong tool because the volume doesn't justify it and the cost is making you the gate the Q2 data shows you aren't.

FACILITATOR PREPARATION PACKET — OUTLINE (Draft v1)
Due: July 30

PURPOSE
Two common documentation-integrity scenarios on the wards: (1) late entries where the assessment time differs from the entry time, and (2) corrections or addenda to existing notes. Goal: ensure charting reflects what actually happened, when it happened, and preserves the medical record.

KEY PRINCIPLES (introduce before the examples)
  - The chart must reflect the actual sequence of clinical events.
  - Do not back-date. Do not overwrite or delete prior entries.
  - Late entries, corrections, and addenda must be clearly labeled and dated at the time of writing, while preserving the timestamp of the event they describe.
  - Wording must support — not contradict — the clinical story, the bill, or future readers (covering clinicians, risk, legal).

EXAMPLE 1 — Late entry: actual reassessment time vs. entry time

  What happened
    On night shift, the on-call clinician performed a focused reassessment of a post-operative patient at 02:15 (new dyspnea, lung exam, ABG result reviewed). Documentation was deferred while the patient was stabilized; the note was written at 06:40 during end-of-shift charting.

  Safe wording (drop into the chart as written)
    "Late entry — clinical reassessment performed at 02:15 on [date]. Patient reported new shortness of breath. Lungs with bibasilar crackles. ABG drawn; results reviewed. Plan: [...]. Entry authored at 06:40 by [role/identifier]; event time preserved."

  What the wording must NOT imply
    - That the reassessment occurred at 06:40 (i.e., continuous monitoring that did not happen).
    - That anything is missing or unobserved between 02:15 and 06:40.
    - That the late entry exists to retroactively support a billing level rather than to honestly record the care delivered.

EXAMPLE 2 — Correction / addendum preserving the original record

  What happened
    During morning rounds, the day team noted that the overnight admission note recorded the wrong lesion laterality and omitted a penicillin allergy referenced by the patient and family. The original note is not edited or deleted; an addendum is appended clarifying both points and citing the source of the corrected information.

  Safe wording (drop into the chart as written)
    "Addendum to note dated [date] at [admission time], authored by [original author or 'overnight admitting team'].
     1) Laterality: the lesion of concern is on the [correct side], not [side originally noted]; imaging reviewed at [time] confirms.
     2) Allergy: the patient has a documented penicillin allergy (per patient and family history at [time]); this was not captured in the original HPI and is added here.
     Reason for addendum: factual corrections identified during day-team review."

  What the wording must NOT imply
    - That the original note has been hidden, deleted, or replaced.
    - That the original author was careless or inaccurate where the omission was a documentation gap rather than a clinical error (frame factually, not as fault).
    - That the correction is being made in response to an audit, query, or legal request — unless that is literally true.

ANONYMIZATION NOTES (for the packet itself)
  - Generic descriptors only (age band, clinical setting, post-op day).
  - No names, no MRNs, no specific dates (use [date]/[time] placeholders), no facility or unit names, no attending names.
  - Replace any identifying exam or lab values with neutral equivalents if they could plausibly identify the patient.

OPTIONAL FOLLOW-ON SECTIONS (suggest only; build out if useful)
  - Practice prompts: rewrite a back-dated note as a properly labeled late entry; append an addendum to a note with a clear error.
  - Quick-reference card: "Late entry" / "Addendum" / "Correction" header conventions and the "must not imply" checklist per scenario.

Two things to flag for Devika before she finalizes:
  - Some institutions distinguish "addendum" (new info) from "amendment/correction" (fixing an error); the example above uses an addendum that handles both. If her facility uses separate labels, the second example can be split into two sub-cases.
  - The "must not imply" bullets are the highest-leverage part of the packet — they map directly to common deposition and audit pitfalls, so I'd keep them visible (not buried at the end).

TOP-LINE VERDICT
The fridge crossed the 40°F danger threshold (48°F) and held there 8+ hours — 4× the USDA 2-hour cutoff for perishables. Discard all four items now; relocating them to another fridge or freezer does not undo bacterial growth that already occurred in the danger zone. Raw chicken is the worst case: even thorough cooking won't reliably destroy the heat-stable toxins some bacteria produce above 40°F.

SAFE-CHECK SEQUENCE (no disassembly, minimal door opens)
  1. Time-stamp the current fridge and freezer readings. Do not open the door again until step 2 — every opening buys you nothing and loses cold.
  2. One coordinated open: grab a second thermometer (or a glass of water + thermometer) if available, set it on the middle shelf, close the door, wait 30 min, re-read both compartments.
  3. Exterior visual only: look at the back/bottom grille for heavy dust buildup. A clogged condenser coil is the most common reversible cause, but coil cleaning is technically disassembly — leave it for the tech unless your lease explicitly lets you vacuum the grille.
  4. Door-seal test: close a dollar bill or sheet of paper in the door. Try to slide it out. If it pulls free with no resistance at any point along the gasket, the seal is leaking. Note the location for the tech.
  5. Inside check (same door-open as step 2 if possible): confirm no food is packed against the back wall blocking the cold-air vents — overpacking mimics a broken fridge.
  6. Listen over the next hour: compressor should run 20–40 min, then cycle off 15–30 min. Constant run with no cycling points to a sealed-system / refrigerant fault, which is not user-repairable.
  7. Freezer contents: if items are rock-hard with intact ice crystals, they are safe. Do not open the freezer repeatedly to verify — one peek, then leave it shut.

PER-ITEM GUIDANCE
  Milk (dairy): DISCARD. High risk for Listeria and Staph above 40°F for >2 hr.
  Raw shell eggs: DISCARD. 8 hr at 48°F clears the 2-hr danger-zone window.
  Cooked leftovers: DISCARD. Handling already introduced bacteria; reheat cannot kill all toxins.
  Raw chicken: DISCARD. Highest-risk item; do not cook and serve, do not refreeze.

SHORT ANSWER
  Yes — a 6 mm separation at the toe edge with an intact sole and a sound upper is exactly the case shoe repair shops see all day, and a routine resole (often just a toe-cap resole) is the normal fix. Replacements are usually reserved for shoes whose uppers are also failing.

WHAT THAT SEPARATION ACTUALLY IS
  Most toe-edge separations are a glue-line failure where the rubber toe-cap meets the rand/upper. The rubber itself is fine; the cement has let go. Common causes: repeated toe-hooks and impact loads, heat cycling (car trunks, radiators, dryers), age of the cement, or a small factory void that opened up. Six millimeters is well within the range a tech can clean, re-cement, and clamp back together with no loss of rubber.

WEIGHING RESOLE VS REPLACE

  Strong case for RESOLE when:
    - Upper leather/synthetic is intact: no cracking, no soft spots, no rot smell.
    - Rand is bonded everywhere else; the toe is the only delamination site.
    - Closure (Velcro, laces, straps) still works and the foot still sits where it should.
    - Cost is materially less than a new pair. Typical range is roughly $35–90 depending on shop, mail-in vs local, and whether you also need a rand replacement.
    - You like this model's last/volume and it's still in production.

  Strong case for REPLACE when:
    - Delamination is showing up in multiple places (toe + heel + medial rand) — the glue is failing systemically.
    - The rand rubber itself is torn, crumbling, or pulled away from the leather, not just unglued from the sole.
    - The upper leather is cracking, compressed, or smelling of rot.
    - The fit has drifted and you find yourself wanting a different shoe anyway; a resole won't fix that.
    - The shoe is already two or more resoles deep and the rubber stack is thin everywhere even without a hole.
    - Quoted resole (especially with rand replacement) climbs past roughly half the price of a new pair.

  For your specific pair:
    One localized 6 mm gap, intact rubber, sound upper/rand/closure/fit, no symptoms — that's solidly in the "resole, don't replace" bucket, provided the rest of the rand-to-sole glue line looks intact when you check it.

WHAT A SHOP NEEDS FOR A USEFUL QUOTE

  Photos — phone is fine; use bright, even light, a plain background, and a coin or ruler for scale in at least the close-ups:
    1. Both shoes, full side profile, inside and outside. Lets the shop read the model and see overall shape and wear pattern.
    2. The separation itself, close-up. Gently flex the rand open so the gap depth is visible, and so they can see whether cement residue is on one side (cleaner repair) or both (more prep).
    3. The rand-to-sole glue line running around the rest of the shoe — heel, medial side, lateral side. The shop will decline or up-charge if the bond is failing elsewhere too.
    4. Sole wear pattern — toe, heel, edges. Tells them whether you need a half-sole (toe only) or full resole, and how thin the rubber is overall.
    5. Closure system close-up — Velcro face condition, lace eyelets, any straps or buckles.
    6. Brand and model — tongue label, inside tongue, or any printed text on the rand.

  Written details to include:
    - Brand, model, size, and whether you downsized from street size.
    - Approximate age and rough use (sessions per week; bouldering, sport, trad, or mix).
    - When the separation appeared and whether it was sudden or grew over a few sessions, and whether it followed heat exposure (car, dryer, radiator).
    - Whether the shoe has been resoled before, and if so how many times.
    - Exactly what you want quoted: standard resole, rand replacement, or both. Ask whether they recommend a half-sole given the wear pattern.
    - Your timeline and whether you can drop off in person or need to ship.

  Optional but helpful:
    - A note on storage and any history of heat stress.
    - A second worn pair if you have one, so the tech can see your typical wear pattern in person.

ONE PRACTICAL STEP WHILE YOU DECIDE
  Keep the pair dry, out of sun and heat, and don't keep flexing the toe rand open to look at it — every flex widens the gap and lets dirt into the bond. A loose rubber band or a short strip of tape wrapped around the toe holding the gap lightly closed keeps contamination out and gives the shop a cleaner prep. Don't apply Shoe Goo or similar yourself; a DIY fill contaminates the glue surfaces and some shops will charge a cleanup fee or decline the job if they find it.

Take it in for the in-hand rand inspection and resole if the rand passes.

Reasoning:
- Upper + rand intact means the expensive components survive; $72 is roughly 44% of the $165 replacement, and you keep a shoe whose fit you already know.
- Your time cost is essentially zero: the backup covers ordinary sessions, and there's no urgent climbing on the calendar, so the four-week turnaround is a non-issue.
- The inspection is the right decision point — if the rand turns out to be worse than it looks, you walk out and default to a new pair of the same model (you already know the fit, which is the real win of staying with the same shoe).
- If the rand does fail, the $93 savings evaporates anyway, so the only thing you lose by trying the resole first is a few days of inspection turnaround.

One practical check: confirm with the shop that the inspection itself doesn't lock you into the $72 — you want the inspection to be a free decision point, with the $72 only due once the rand is confirmed and you authorize the work.

Climbing-shoe resole vs. replacement — practical recommendation

Context you already have on file
- Right shoe has a ~6 mm localized toe-edge rand-to-sole separation; upper, rand, closure, fit, rubber, and (importantly) glue line elsewhere are otherwise intact. No foot or forearm symptoms. No injury.
- Same-model new pair: ~$165. Resole at your shop: $72 with ~4-week turnaround. Inspection doesn't obligate you to pay.

Option-by-option

Option A — $72 resole (recommended)
- Keeps a last and volume you already trust, mid-volume last broken in, no break-in period, no fit risk on a new last.
- $93 cheaper than replacement. Roughly 44% of new-pair cost.
- 4-week downtime is manageable because you have a sound older backup pair and no urgent climbing commitment.
- A successful resole typically extends service life by many months; a worn rand plus a fresh sole is generally the most common repair on otherwise-sound uppers.

Option B — $165 replacement
- Useful only if the in-hand inspection fails (rand delaminating from upper, fabric/foam exposed, sour/chemical odor, misshapen toe box, lifting rand, separating heel cup, toe rubber worn through).
- Or if you want a different last/volume, a stiffer or softer shoe, or a closure change. None of those motivations are on file here.
- Cost premium of $93 buys zero functional gain when the upper and rand are intact.

Recommendation
Proceed with Option A — authorize the $72 resole only if the in-hand rand inspection passes. The current shoe is a plausible resole candidate; no replacement motivation is established.

Hidden-rand-damage threshold — when resole stops being economical
Resole stops making sense at the point where the rand itself, not the sole, is the failure mode. Walk away from the $72 repair and replace instead if the shop finds any of:

- Rand delaminating from the upper (lift, peel, or visible gap between rand strip and leather/mesh).
- Exposed fabric, foam, or stitching under the rand.
- Sour/chemical odor, mildew, or trapped moisture in the toe box.
- Misshapen toe box (compression-set, collapsed rand) or separating heel cup.
- Toe rubber worn through to the rand beneath it.
- Glue line failing in multiple places, not just the one ~6 mm spot.

Cost framing for that threshold: a rand rebuild or full rand replacement at a climbing-shoe shop typically runs $45–90 on top of the resole, and rand work frequently approaches or exceeds half the cost of a new pair. Once the rand itself has to be replaced, total repair cost climbs into the $120–$160 range against a $165 new pair, and the failure mode is structural rather than wear — that's the line at which replacement becomes the rational call.

Pre-repair care while the shoe sits
Keep it dry, away from sun and heat; don't flex the open toe rand repeatedly; lightly hold the toe closed with a rubber band or tape. Don't apply Shoe Goo — it can contaminate the glue surfaces and trigger cleanup fees or refusal of service. Don't use cyanoacrylate (superglue) — it cures rigid, can crack with flex, and complicates the resoler's work.

Short answer: skip the outdoor run, and yes on light indoor movement if you hold the frame as movement rather than a session.

On the outdoor call — this isn't really a judgment question once lightning is already reported in the area and the warning window starts before 7:15. Two things to keep in mind:

- "Squeeze between cells" is the pattern that gets people caught. The gap that looks safe on radar is the gap where a cell re-forms or a strike comes out the side.
- The 30/30 clock resets from the last strike, so once lightning is nearby your actual start window keeps sliding right — there's no stable slot to plan around this morning.

Paths being fine and you being uninjured are necessary conditions, not sufficient ones. Lightning overrides them.

On indoor movement — reasonable, with a clear frame:

- Fine: easy walk in place, pacing around the apartment, stationary bike or treadmill at a pace you could hold a sentence at, light mobility. 10–15 minutes, easy breathing.
- Not fine (in the sense of "stops being movement, becomes a replacement session"): intentional duration to 30 min, progressive intensity, anything you'd mentally log as today's training.

The point of doing it is the routine anchor and a bit of blood flow, not preserving the training stimulus. If you keep it short and easy and don't count it, you're fine. If you find yourself extending or pushing, that's the moment to stop — the goal was headspace, not load.

One small optional middle path for later in the day: if the warning lifts and you want to do something, an easy evening walk (not a run) still counts as movement and doesn't collide with the shared weekend time you wanted to protect. No obligation either way.

Nothing in your current state suggests the run matters for anything beyond routine and headspace, which makes "skip and move on" the lowest-regret call here.

Both findings are real admission-control gaps; they sit on axes the 8,000-point rule doesn't cover, so the point-count limit can stay in force unchanged while these get added.

Gap 1 — per-attribute byte cap. The 9 MB single-attribute case is a per-attribute dimension. Today's path bounds decoded-body size (10 MiB ceiling, per the March 2024 413 precedent) and point count, but does not cap any single attribute value. A 9 MB attribute on a 1-point request slips under both because total decoded body stays under 10 MiB. That is a separate axis from points and from total decoded bytes; collapsing it back into the 8k rule or the 10 MiB ceiling would miss it.

Gap 2 — per-pod in-flight decoded budget. The 100-concurrent case is the aggregate dimension. Per-request admission passed on each one, but the pod accumulated ~21 MiB of decoded resident memory per request before enqueue. Per-request ceilings don't bound aggregate in-flight decoded memory; a per-pod budget (or a cap on concurrent decoded-but-not-enqueued work) does. Two follow-up questions worth resolving before any threshold is picked: whether the existing 10 MiB decoded-body ceiling actually fired on the compressed-decode path during this test (the ~21 MiB/request delta is roughly 2× the 10 MiB ceiling, which suggests either the ceiling wasn't enforced on the compressed path or the resident footprint is dominated by decoded protobuf structure rather than raw bytes), and where in the heap the resident memory is actually sitting.

What doesn't change: the 8,000-point rule, the 10 MiB decoded-body ceiling (unless the test shows it wasn't being enforced, in which case the fix is enforcement, not removal), the 64 MiB bounded-decompression guardrail from #229 (separate role — decompression-bomb ceiling, not admission ceiling), and oversized_batch / 413 as the rejection shape.

Routing: both gaps are ingest-edge admission control. Per the owner map impl/release/rollback sit with the ingest-edge owner (alex primary, yuki backup); the recent admission-control track has been yuki-led (PR 2588 and follow-ups), so she's the natural carrier for the next batch unless she's explicitly handing off. Nothing here crosses into metrics-router, shard-keeper, or rollup-service, and it isn't a Lantern question.

Before any threshold lands, the test should bring back: per-request decoded body size on the 100-concurrent run, a heap profile (raw bytes vs. decoded protobuf structure vs. queueing overhead) showing where the ~21 MiB/request is going, and on the 9 MB case the point count, compressed body size, decoded total, and resident footprint of the attribute in isolation. Thresholds picked against those numbers, not against the headline 1.1 → 3.2 GiB delta.

Three options, side by side:

1) Auto-invest OFF
   Cash: $2,420.00   Invested: $0
   - Maximum flexibility: any bill size, any time, no selling.
   - HSA cash at most custodians earns ~0.0-0.5% APY. The whole balance sits
     there earning near-nothing in a vehicle whose value is tax-free compounding.
   - Cost grows every pay period: another $90 biweekly + $225 in Oct all pile
     into low-yield cash instead of investments.

2) Threshold $2,300 (exactly the deductible)
   Cash: $2,300.00   Invested today: $120
   - Cash matches the individual deductible one-for-one, so any single bill up
     to $2,300 is covered without selling.
   - Doesn't cover anything past the deductible: coinsurance on a procedure,
     post-deductible copays, an OOP-max event, or a family-deductible scenario
     would force a sale (or paying from checking and reimbursing).
   - Gets the smallest slice into investments today; future contributions still
     stack above the threshold and get swept.

3) Modest cushion above the deductible (~$2,400-$2,500)
   Cash: $2,400-2,500. Invested today: $20-$0.
   - Small buffer above $2,300 covers typical post-deductible scenarios
     (specialist copays, urgent care with coinsurance, a prescription or two)
     without selling.
   - Today the invested slice is small either way, but as the remaining ~$765
     of 2027 contributions land, they accumulate above the threshold and
     sweep into investments automatically. By year-end, ~$650-$850 would be
     invested depending on which end of the cushion you pick.
   - Still leaves you fully liquid for any bill up to the cushion.

Recommendation: a modest cushion, somewhere in the $2,400-$2,500 range.

Why this fits "practical, liquidity-first":

  - "Liquidity-first" doesn't mean "all cash" -- it means "don't get forced to
    sell at an awkward time to cover a routine bill." A small cushion above
    the deductible handles the routine cases without stranding meaningful
    growth.
  - The HSA's main payoff is decades of tax-free compounding. Every dollar
    that sits in low-yield cash is a dollar not compounding. Even a thin
    invested slice matters more the longer the time horizon.
  - For non-urgent, larger bills you can still pay from checking and reimburse
    yourself later (standard HSA practice), so the cash floor doesn't have to
    cover worst-case OOP-max -- just routine post-deductible expenses.

Tie-break between $2,400 and $2,500 is preference:
  - $2,400 = tighter buffer, slightly more invested over time.
  - $2,500 = a bit more comfort for the occasional pharmacy / copay that
    lands after you've met the deductible, slightly less invested.
  The end-of-year difference is on the order of ~$100 invested either way,
  so this is a feel call, not a financial one.

What would change this:
  - A scheduled procedure, imaging, or any bill you can already see coming ->
    raise the floor above that amount until it's paid and reimbursed.
  - Switching to family coverage (different deductible / OOP structure) ->
    re-anchor the cushion to the new numbers.
  - A year where you expect materially more medical use than 2027 ->
    lean toward the higher end of the cushion, or hold off on auto-invest
    entirely for that year.

South Slope bathroom sink — bounded first-pass:

Before you start — supplies
  Nitrile or latex gloves, old towel, small bucket or plastic bag, flashlight, old toothbrush or a small wire brush, paper towels, a straightened wire coat hanger with a small hook bent in one end (optional but useful).
  No chemical drain cleaner. None. Don't bring any into the bathroom for this task.

Step 1 — Prep (2 min)
  Clear the cabinet under the sink. Put the bucket/bag directly under the pop-up pivot rod assembly. Lay the towel on the cabinet floor. Put on gloves.

Step 2 — Pull the stopper
  Reach under the sink and find the horizontal pivot rod connecting the lift rod to the drain arm. Squeeze the spring clip and slide the pivot rod out of the clevis strap, then unscrew the lift rod knurl nut a few turns. From above, lift the pop-up stopper straight out of the drain. Expect wet hair/soap gunk on the stopper and the pivot rod — drop it straight into the bag.

Step 3 — Clear only what's visible and reachable
  Pull hair and soap off the stopper, the pivot rod, and the pivot ball by hand (gloved).
  Reach into the open drain opening with gloved fingers or the hooked wire and pull out hair that is sitting just below the pop-up — there is almost always a 2–6 inch hair clog right there. Pull it out; do not push it further down.
  Use the toothbrush on the stopper mechanism and the inside lip of the drain opening to scrape soap scum. Wipe everything with paper towels.
  Do not reach past the pop-up cavity. Do not disassemble the P-trap. Do not insert a snake or auger.

Step 4 — Reassemble
  Drop the stopper back in. Re-seat the pivot rod into the clevis strap, replace the spring clip, and snug the knurl nut (hand-tight only — no tools). Lift the lift rod and confirm the stopper rises and falls cleanly. Run water for 30 seconds and look with the flashlight at the pivot rod connection and the trap for any drip. Wipe dry, then look again.

Step 5 — Controlled flow test
  Plug the sink. Fill the basin to normal depth (not to the overflow). Mark the level. Pull the plug and time how long it takes to empty to the marked level.
  Pass = empties in roughly 15–25 seconds, no gurgling, no backup.
  Compare to your earlier ~2-minute baseline.

Stop and contact management (do not keep working) if any of these happen:
  The flow test shows no real improvement (still around a minute or more), or gets worse.
  Water backs up while you run the test, or any other fixture (kitchen sink, toilet, shower) starts to gurgle, rise, or back up — that means the clog is past this sink and needs the building's plumber.
  The pivot rod connection or trap starts dripping after reassembly — don't keep using the sink, call it in while it's a small leak.
  A sewage odor appears at any point.
  You hit resistance with the wire beyond a couple of inches — stop, don't force.

When you contact management, describe it as: "Slow drain isolated to the South Slope bathroom sink; cleared stopper and visible hair/soap at the pop-up; flow test unchanged / showed [X]." That puts you in the queue for their plumber with the snake or camera rather than another round of tenant-side work.

What not to do, in one list:
  No liquid drain cleaners, no gel cleaners, no "enzyme" cleaners as a substitute for clearing — none for this pass.
  No mixing of any products with anything else, including each other and including household cleaners that are already in the cabinet.
  No plunger on this sink unless you first seal the overflow opening with a wet rag and use a flat-bottom sink plunger (not a toilet plunger). If the stopper is removed and you do try a plunger, seal the drain opening around the plunger so you're not just pressurizing the open pipe.
  No hot-water "flush" beyond normal warm tap water — boiling water can loosen the slip-joint gaskets on the trap, and it doesn't dissolve a hair clog anyway.
  No disassembling the P-trap. That's a different procedure with a leak risk if the gaskets aren't reseated, and it's past the scope you set.

If the test passes, you're done — just keep an eye on the cabinet for a day or two and run hot tap water through it for a few seconds after each use for a week to keep soap from re-coagulating on the freshly cleaned surfaces.

Three concerns, plus one clarification I'd want before signing off.

1. Cache fallback partially reverses the 7/13 explicit-failure guarantee. The original bug was a stale-source-of-truth problem (reading retirement inventory). A last-cached active record on lookup error is a milder version of the same shape: alerting from data that may no longer reflect reality. The 7/13 design said "can't read active = signal worth paging on." Replacing that with "show whatever we cached" erodes that signal.

2. `source="active"` will be misleading. If the data is from cache, the label must say so (e.g., `source="active_cache"` plus a `cache_age` field). Otherwise downstream — on-call, dashboards, postmortems — treats a degraded read as authoritative, which is exactly the confusion 7/13 was designed to kill.

3. The proposal collapses two distinct failure modes into one path:
   (a) transient I/O error — cache fallback is defensible, with a staleness bound
   (b) structural failure — active record genuinely missing, auth broken, schema mismatch, or no active bundle after a retirement. Cache fallback here is dangerous: cache says "active=foo, expires 2028-01-01" while the system actually has no active bundle. This is the case that warrants a page. The retired-cannot-page invariant has to keep holding here.
   The proposal needs to split (a) from (b).

4. Prod is healthy and unchanged, which is good — but also: what's driving this? If it's alert fatigue from transient read-path errors, the right fix is upstream (retries, timeout tuning, read-path healthcheck, distinguishing read errors from missing-record), not degrading alert semantics. If it's something else, that rationale should be in the proposal.

Guardrails if this proceeds:
- label cache reads as `source="active_cache"` with a `cache_age`; never `source="active"` on cache hits
- staleness bound: refuse fallback if the last good read is older than N
- classify errors: cache fallback only for transient; structural failures must still fail-explicit
- emit a separate `degraded_read` signal/page so the on-call sees the alert is operating on cache
- "missing active fails explicitly" and "retired cannot page" stay unconditional

Pre-ride no-ride inspection (externally visible only — do not ride at any point during this):

  1. Pad thickness. Sight down the rotor between the pads (or look through the caliper window / between rotor and pad). If friction material is ~1.5 mm or less, or the backing plate is showing, the pads are spent and the pistons have over-extended — that alone gives the long lever pull plus weak bite.
  
  2. Rotor. Check thickness against the minimum stamp (commonly 1.5 mm), and look for bluing/hot spots, deep grooves, or an oily sheen. A contaminated rotor + pads lose bite even with firm lever feel.
  
  3. Hose end-to-end. Trace the line from lever to caliper. Look for bulges, abrasion marks where it passes the head tube or sits under the bar tape, and any wet/oily film at the lever banjo, the caliper banjo bolt, or any inline junction. A micro-seep can self-seal but leave air in the line — that matches your symptoms exactly.
  
  4. Lever body / reservoir area. Look for an oily film around the master piston area or reservoir seal. Do not remove any cap or fitting.
  
  5. Reach / contact adjust dial. Confirm it hasn't been knocked to its closest setting, which shortens effective stroke and feels "mushy."
  
  6. Caliper alignment, visual only. With the wheel in, look across the rotor faces and check the gap is even on both sides in the caliper slot. Mild misalignment reduces pad contact area without necessarily causing rub.
  
  7. Quick checks you already covered: wheel seated in dropouts, rotor bolts present and flush, no visible rub. All consistent with what you reported.

"unknown" at least makes the data legibly unattributed, so downstream filters, chargeback, and per-tenant SLOs can exclude it (or it sits in an explicit orphan bucket). ---

**Boundary — missing or malformed tenant identity**

Reviewing against the 2027-07-16 staging incident: records with missing `tenant_id` were tagged `tenant_id="unknown"` and continued into batching, which let authenticated contexts `alpha` and `beta` share a batch key before export. That is a tenant-isolation defect, not a labeling issue. The follow-up must hold this boundary unambiguously.

The acceptable shapes are exactly two, and both must reject any record that lacks a real tenant identity *before* it is admitted to batching or acceptance:

1. **Fail closed at the admission boundary.** Missing or malformed tenant identity causes the record to be rejected or failed before it is batched, queued, or counted as accepted. No synthetic `tenant_id` is substituted.

2. **Unattributed stream, separated and labeled.** If the owner concludes that records must be retained rather than rejected, they must be routed to a stream that is (a) explicitly labeled as unattributed, (b) excluded from every per-tenant rollup, metric, sampling, retention, or access-control path, and (c) reconciled by a count, not by attribution. A record in this stream carries no `tenant_id` label of any kind — not `"unknown"`, not a hash of authenticated context, not a default.

The proposed hash-of-authenticated-context fallback does not satisfy either shape. It substitutes a deterministic-looking value for a missing `tenant_id`, which still lets distinct authenticated contexts collapse into a single batch key and still looks like a real tenant to downstream metrics, logs, billing, sampling, and alert routing. That is the same failure mode with a different label.

A fallback of *any* kind — string, hash, or default — is acceptable only if a separately authoritative tenant-binding contract exists that (a) names the fallback source, (b) binds it to a real tenant with explicit attribution, (c) is the authoritative input for that binding, and (d) is cited in this PR with its identifier and owner. Until such a contract is named here, the only correct shape is fail-closed at admission.

**What this PR needs to clear the boundary**

- A code path that rejects records with missing or malformed `tenant_id` *before* batching, queueing, or acceptance, with the rejection reason surfaced in structured logs.
- If an unattributed stream is added: a labeled path that is excluded from per-tenant rollups and metric cardinality, reconciled by count, and not given any `tenant_id` label value.
- Regression tests covering at minimum:
  - two distinct authenticated contexts with missing `tenant_id` do not coalesce into a shared batch key;
  - a record whose `tenant_id` is malformed (empty, wrong type, mismatched encoding) is rejected, not retagged;
  - any unattributed stream contributes zero series to per-tenant metrics and zero entries to per-tenant rollups.
- Confirmation that production behavior is unchanged by the fix path (e.g., the path that triggers here is staging-only or already gated off in prod).

**Scope and ownership**

WARMUP (10-15 min — longer than you'd think)
  - 3-4 min easy jog/shuffle to raise body temp
  - Dynamic mobility: lateral lunges, leg swings (front-back + lateral), ankle rolls, groin opener
  - Ball contact ramp: stationary toe taps → partner passes → jogging dribble
  - 3 progressive sprints at 50% / 75% / 90% — never 100% in warmup
  - 1-2 cutting / change-of-direction reps at moderate speed
  Rule: finish warmup breathing hard but not cooked. First game starts at ~70%, not 100%.

SUBSTITUTION (frequent and brief — use them)
  - Don't try to "play through" fatigue just because you can. Rotate.
  - On the bench: light jog or walk + hip swings. Don't sit and cool down — that's how you pull something on the way back in.
  - Hydrate on every sub break (see below).
  - If you can pick the moment, rotate position so one muscle group isn't loaded the whole morning.

HYDRATION (August heat is real)
  - Pre: ~500 ml water in the 1-2 hrs before. A little salt at a meal helps.
  - Bring: water + an electrolyte drink — sodium is the key ingredient, not sugar.
  - On field: small sips every 10-15 min, ~150-200 ml. Don't wait until you're thirsty.
  - Sub break: 200-300 ml plus sips of electrolyte mix. Sip, don't gulp.
  - If you cramp or get a headache mid-morning: it's sodium, not water — sip electrolytes, don't chug plain water.

EFFORT (short repeated games change the math)
  - Treat each short game as a quality interval, not a max effort. There are several more after it.
  - First game: ramp through the first 2-3 min, then settle into honest 80-85%. No sprints in minute one.
  - Last game of the morning: this is when soft-tissue stuff happens — calves, hammies. If you're tightening up, sub off or jog the next rep instead of sprinting.
  - End of every game: 1-2 min easy jog to flush. Don't stop cold.

Two different times, and they serve different purposes. The reassessment time is a clinical fact — when you actually laid eyes on the patient — and it belongs in the body of the note. The entry timestamp is when the EHR captured what you wrote, and the system tracks that on its own. So if you saw them at 14:30 and charted at 16:00, the 16:00 timestamp is already the truth — you just write "reassessed at 14:30" in the text. Never alter the entry timestamp to make it look like you documented in real time. That's backdating, even when the clinical content is accurate.

For errors, use the EHR's correction or amendment function. It strikes the original but keeps it visible in the audit trail, which is what billing, legal, and credentialing reviewers expect. You don't delete and rewrite. For information that wasn't available at the original encounter — a culture that grew out, family history that came in later, a course change overnight — add an addendum dated and timed to when you're appending it, leaving the prior note whole and clearly labeled as supplemented.

Short version for the conversation: clinical time goes in the narrative as the truth you observed; system time stays whatever the EHR recorded; fix mistakes through the correction tool, and use an addendum for late-arriving facts. Never edit the timestamp to hide the gap.

Short answer: do not convert yet, and ask the issuer one specific question before doing anything.

Why this is risky

  Retention offers are almost always tied to the specific product, not just the
  account number. The standard issuer language reserves the right to claw back
  the retention bonus if you product-change, downgrade, or close before the
  commitment ends — even if the underlying account technically stays "open."
  Your $40 statement credit has already posted, which is exactly the kind of
  credit that gets reversed on early downgrade.

  Your 12-month commitment runs from the December 26, 2026 acceptance, so it
  ends around late December 2027 — about four months from now. The renewal fee
  is scheduled for January 2, 2028, after the commitment window. You already
  planned to re-evaluate at that point (your December 27, 2027 calendar
  reminder).

What the offer likely means

  "Immediate conversion to a no-annual-fee version" is a product change, not a
  closure. The account number and history usually survive. But:

    - You almost certainly lose the 2% cash back, the $50 transit credit, and
      any other benefits that justified keeping the card.
    - Whether the $40 statement credit is clawed back depends on the retention
      fine print you accepted in December. Most retention terms treat a
      product change inside the 12-month window as a breach.
    - The $125 fee was charged for the year you committed to; it is typically
      not refunded on mid-year downgrade (though some issuers prorate). Do not
      assume a refund.

The one question that resolves it

  Call the number on the back of the card (not the marketing line that pitched
  the conversion) and ask, in writing if possible:

    "I accepted a retention offer on December 26, 2026 that requires the
    account to remain open for 12 months and has already paid me a $40
    statement credit. If I accept your no-annual-fee product change now,
    does that satisfy or terminate the 12-month retention commitment, and
    will the $40 statement credit be reversed?"

  Get the answer in writing — chat transcript or email confirmation — before
  you accept. If the rep says it satisfies retention with no clawback, save
  that confirmation. If they say it terminates retention, or won't commit in
  writing, treat it as terminates.

The safer path

  Wait until the 12-month commitment ends (around late December 2027). At that
  point you can downgrade with no clawback risk, and you will already be doing
  the annual review you calendared. If your actual 2026 spending came in well
  below $7,000, the original comparison already pointed toward downgrade — you
  just take the no-fee version then instead of now.

  The only reason to convert early is if the issuer confirms in writing that
  the $40 credit is safe and the 2% rewards weren't earning their keep at
  your current spend. Given the four-month runway, that confirmation needs to
  be strong enough to be worth more than the certainty of waiting.

Here's the rule, in two parts: the principle that justifies it, then the formal draft, then a worked example against your Harbor Health / Mosaic Commerce case.

PRINCIPLE

There are two distinct questions a session evidence query can answer, and conflating them produces wrong numbers in both directions:

  - "How many authorized sessions happened?" — a raw occurrence count. Every authorized session happened and counts exactly once. No deduplication.
  - "How many distinct operational items did sessions touch?" — a workload count, grouped by the stable operational identity the session is acting under (release-follow-up ID or incident-handoff ID). Many sessions can act under the same identity; they collapse to one item.

The rule keeps these counts separate. The session record is never edited, merged, or hidden to make the operational count come out smaller. The operational count is derived, not stored, and is derived only when the query is asking about operational workload.

DRAFT

EVIDENCE-QUERY RULE: Authorized Session Counting vs. Operational-Use Counting

Scope. Applies to any evidence query whose result set includes authorized customer sessions in a defined reporting window.

Definitions.

  - Authorized session. A session that completed authentication and was granted access, regardless of duration or subsequent activity.
  - Customer-session count. The total number of authorized sessions in the window. This is the raw occurrence count.
  - Operational-use count. The number of distinct operational items touched by authorized sessions in the window, grouped by stable operational identity.
  - Stable operational identity. One of:
      - Release-follow-up ID — the identifier of the release the session is following up on.
      - Incident-handoff ID — the identifier of the incident the session is being handed off for.
  - Operational-use count (release follow-ups). Count of distinct release-follow-up IDs referenced by at least one authorized session in the window.
  - Operational-use count (incident handoffs). Count of distinct incident-handoff IDs referenced by at least one authorized session in the window.

Counting rules.

  1. Customer-session count = sum of authorized sessions. No deduplication by identity, time, customer, or any other key. If N authorized sessions occurred in the window for a customer, the count increases by N.
  2. Operational-use count (release follow-ups) for the window = count of distinct release-follow-up IDs referenced by authorized sessions in the window. A session contributes one ID (or none).
  3. Operational-use count (incident handoffs) for the window = count of distinct incident-handoff IDs referenced by authorized sessions in the window. A session contributes one ID (or none).
  4. A single authorized session may carry both a release-follow-up ID and an incident-handoff ID. It contributes once to the customer-session count, and (if both IDs are present) once to each operational-use count.
  5. A session with no release-follow-up ID and no incident-handoff ID contributes only to the customer-session count. It contributes to no operational-use count.
  6. The stable identity used for grouping must be present on the session record. Identity must not be inferred from session metadata, customer name, timestamps, or operator notes when no explicit ID is recorded.

Which count to use.

  - Use the customer-session count for: capacity, licensing, audit, access-pattern analyses, and any report where the unit of truth is "this session happened".
  - Use the operational-use count for: workload characterization, on-call load, follow-up queue depth, and any report where the question is "how many distinct operational items", not "how many sessions".

Anti-patterns.

  - Do not subtract or merge sessions from the customer-session count to align it with the operational-use count. The customer-session count is the raw record.
  - Do not count each session as a separate release follow-up or incident handoff when the session carries a stable ID. The ID, not the session, is the grouping key.
  - Do not collapse sessions across different release-follow-up IDs or incident-handoff IDs under the same customer. Two distinct IDs are two distinct operational items, even if both belong to the same customer.
  - Do not report an operational-use count unless the query is asking about operational workload. Reporting it as a session count is a category error.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Window contains:
  - 4 Harbor Health sessions, each tagged with release-follow-up ID R-2027-0312 (no incident-handoff ID).
  - 3 Mosaic Commerce sessions, each tagged with incident-handoff ID I-2027-1107 (no release-follow-up ID).

Customer-session count contribution: 4 + 3 = 7.

Operational-use count (release follow-ups) contribution: 1 (R-2027-0312, from Harbor Health).

Operational-use count (incident handoffs) contribution: 1 (I-2027-1107, from Mosaic Commerce).

If a single Harbor Health session had also been tagged with I-2027-1107 (cross-customer incident handoff), the customer-session count would still be 7, the release-follow-up count would still be 1, and the incident-handoff count would still be 1 — the session contributes once to each, never twice to either.

NOTES ON BOUNDARIES (so this composes with the intake routing rule)

The decision of *whether* to run an evidence query at all, and *which* customer-session records to pull, remains with the mapped implementation/release owner. The operational identity tagging (release-follow-up ID, incident-handoff ID) on each session is treated as provenance: it is recorded at the time of authorization and is not retroactively edited to satisfy a query. If the query would force re-tagging, escalate to the owner of the relevant boundary (provenance for the tagging, ownership for the access to the records).

The 74-vs-83 gap is set vs multiset semantics on the same population, not a data defect.

The nine dual-flagged rows sit in both the delayed set and the retried set. A union over the stable customer-row identity collapses to distinct-set semantics, so each of those nine contributes one row and the result is 74. Summing the two flag columns is multiset-additive: |delayed| + |retried| = |delayed ∪ retried| + |delayed ∩ retried| = 74 + 9 = 83. The 9-row delta is exactly the intersection, and 83 - 74 = 9 confirms it.

Neither number is wrong on its own — they answer different questions. Union = distinct customer rows that had any delayed-or-retried event. Flag-sum = total flag-events fired. Reporting the flag-sum as "delayed-or-retried rows" silently double-counts rows that legitimately carry both audit flags. The fix is to make the union distinct, keep both flags on the deduplicated row, and surface the overlap explicitly so the two numbers reconcile on the page.

Evidence-query rule (concise)

  Requirement: the Q3 delayed-or-retried measure counts each stable
  customer row exactly once in the union, retains both delayed_flag and
  retried_flag on that row, and reports the overlap so the multiset
  flag-sum reconciles to the distinct count.

  Pattern (Postgres-flavor; equivalent for other engines):

    WITH flagged AS (
      SELECT customer_row_id,
             source_timestamp,
             delayed_flag,
             retried_flag
      FROM customer_events
      WHERE source_timestamp >= DATE '2027-07-01'
        AND source_timestamp <  DATE '2027-10-01'
        AND (delayed_flag OR retried_flag)
    )
    SELECT customer_row_id,
           source_timestamp,
           BOOL_OR(delayed_flag) AS delayed,
           BOOL_OR(retried_flag)  AS retried
    FROM flagged
    GROUP BY customer_row_id, source_timestamp;   -- 74 rows

  Reconciliation summary (must accompany the 74):

    distinct_rows      = COUNT(*) from above                      = 74
    delayed_only       = COUNT WHERE delayed AND NOT retried
    retried_only       = COUNT WHERE retried AND NOT delayed
    both               = COUNT WHERE delayed AND retried         =  9
    flag_sum           = (delayed_only + both) + (retried_only + both)
                        = distinct_rows + both                    = 83
    assert: flag_sum == SUM(delayed_flag) + SUM(retried_flag)    -- holds

  Prohibitions baked into the rule:
    - Do not publish 83 as "delayed-or-retried rows." It is a
      flag-event total, not a row count.
    - Do not use UNION ALL over the identity and call the row count
      the measure — it inflates by 9 for the same reason the flag-sum
      does.
    - Do not drop either flag when deduplicating; both audit flags
      must survive the collapse.
    - The overlap count (both = 9) is a first-class field of the
      evidence, not a footnote — it is what reconciles the two
      numbers and explains the 9-row gap to reviewers.

Ordinary failure handling is covered. Activation also needs to be crash-safe, demonstrated by restart evidence, not just claimed.

Required for sign-off:

1. Activation path is crash-safe on its own — not only "the manifest is atomic." Specifically: if the process is killed (SIGKILL), the host crashes, or the service is OOM-killed mid-activation, no half-applied state is left behind, and the next start resolves to a single, well-defined active generation.

Restart evidence: a reproducible test (or trace from a fault-injection run) showing that after a rejected reload *and* after an interrupted reload, the service comes back on the **prior** active generation — not on a partial new one, not on empty/initial state, not on a corrupted route index. The prior gen's routes are served; the new gen is either fully activated or not visible at all.
3. Evidence should distinguish the two failure modes:
   - rejected reload (validation failed / signature bad / checksum mismatch) → prior active gen preserved
   - interrupted reload (process died after fsync of snapshot + route index but before "activated" marker, or died before fsync) → prior active gen preserved; on restart, the prior or the new complete set is chosen, never a half-applied mix
4. Boundary on the test: it has to exercise a real kill/crash, not just an exception return path. A `try/except` that catches and rolls back does not, by itself, prove crash-safety.

  2. Operational-use count = distinct stable release-follow-up IDs (Harbor Health) or incident-handoff IDs (Mosaic Commerce) explicitly referenced by those sessions. Each stable operational ID is counted once regardless of how many sessions reference it.

Mapping rule (per Q3 2027):
  • A session with both ID types → contributes once to each.
  • A session with neither       → contributes only to the customer-session count.
  • A session is NEVER counted as multiple operational items merely because a stable ID exists.
  • Different operational IDs under the same customer are NEVER collapsed.

Identity for operational grouping MUST be a stable identity explicitly present on the session record. Identity is NOT inferred from session metadata, customer name, timestamps, or operator notes.

Do not subtract, merge, edit, hide, or otherwise alter session records to force the two counts to align — they are deliberately distinct axes.
