Contract Ruling — Eligibility Cutoff (September 15, 12:00)

1. Processing time cannot determine eligibility.
   Eligibility is fixed by the authoritative source timestamp — when the event occurred at its source of record. Processing time is incidental: it reflects pipeline latency, queue depth, retries, and ingestion paths that are outside the event's control. Letting processing time gate eligibility lets infrastructure conditions (slow batch, retried job, late ingest) rewrite history — a delayed row gets excluded even though its event is in-scope, and any rule keyed to a business moment (the cutoff) is silently subordinated to whatever happened to the pipeline. Auditability and the cutoff itself both fail.

2. Every row with source timestamp at or before the cutoff must be reconciled, even if it arrives later.
   If the source timestamp is ≤ cutoff, the event is in-scope by the rule that names the cutoff. Excluding such a row because it arrived late redefines eligibility by arrival rather than by the cutoff — i.e., changes the contract without authority to do so. Reconciliation is the operation that confirms presence, attribution, and source match for the row; skipping it for late rows is not a shortcut, it is an unrecorded exclusion that the package cannot absorb.

3. The package cannot freeze until reconciliation is complete.
   Freeze pins the in-scope set. Freezing before reconciliation leaves two symmetric failure modes, both unrecoverable without thawing: (a) a late but in-scope row gets frozen out, so the package ships missing what the cutoff says it must contain; (b) a late row whose source timestamp is actually after cutoff gets frozen in only because reconciliation hadn't yet ruled on it, so the package ships what the cutoff says it must not. Reconciliation must therefore complete for every row with source timestamp ≤ cutoff before freeze can fire.

Scope note: Query implementation stays with Product Engineering. This ruling defines the contract the query must satisfy, not its internal construction.

     * Lump / quarterly means you carry first-month-of-year claims out of taxable cash before reimbursement is available — that's real cash-flow risk on a single big claim.

The Aug 6, 2027 cross-service exception-intake contract requires each request to carry exactly one boundary from {invariant, provenance, failure_mode, ownership, escalation}, plus a mapped owner, an affected component, and a concrete observed failed/at-risk condition. That "exactly one" is the load-bearing piece — it is what lets Nadia's triage lane route by class, what lets the selected boundary owner scope their review, and what keeps the mapped owners' implementation, release, and rollback authority intact. Review-eligibility and the bounded exception counter are both derived from a single, well-formed class field.

"First-token routing" breaks that contract three ways at once:

1. It silently repairs malformed input. A request submitted as `exception_class=ownership,escalation` enters the lane labeled `ownership`. The submitter's intent (and any escalation-class reader, e.g. Alex) is dropped without signal. The Aug 6–30 audit caught two such multi-class requests and returned them; first-token routing would have routed them instead, polluting the counter and shifting ownership.

2. It destroys Nadia's triage distinction. Triage is the boundary that says "return if malformed, route if complete." Two requests about the same incident with the same set of classes could land under different reviewers depending on input ordering — exactly the lane-bypass shape Hema and Nadia closed on Aug 6.

The hole is straightforward: any comparison involving NaN returns false, so `v >= 0 && v <= 1` evaluates to false && false = false, and a short-circuit OR form `v < 0 || v > 1` also evaluates false on both sides. NaN, and likewise +/-Infinity against the unbounded side, slip through whatever range predicate you write if the range predicate is the only thing you write.

Fix order: finiteness first, range second. The finiteness check has to run before the range check or it doesn't help.

  if (!Number.isFinite(v)) reject('not finite');
  if (v < 0 || v > 1)      reject('out of [0,1]');

Use Number.isFinite (not the global isFinite) so non-number inputs like "5" don't coerce past the gate. Use a strict < and > so the endpoints 0 and 1 are accepted; only values strictly outside should be rejected.

Test cases that matter, with the expected outcome:

  NaN            -> reject
  +Infinity      -> reject
  -Infinity      -> reject
  0              -> accept   (lower boundary)
  1              -> accept   (upper boundary)
  -1e-300        -> reject   (just below)
  1 + 1e-12      -> reject   (just above)
  0.5            -> accept   (mid-range)

If the parser accepts string inputs (common for query/path params), add the coerced forms — these are the ones that have actually bitten parsers in the past:

  Number("NaN")       -> reject
  Number("Infinity")  -> reject
  Number("-Infinity") -> reject
  Number("1e1000")    -> reject   (coerces to Infinity)
  Number("0"), Number("1"), Number("0.5") -> accept

The first three groups are the ones that prove the fix; the boundary cases prove you didn't over-correct into an exclusive range.

The defect, briefly: a Prometheus label is part of the time-series identity — every distinct (metric, label-set) tuple is its own series in the TSDB head index, WAL, and on-disk blocks. W3C trace IDs are 128-bit and unique per request by construction, so promoting one to a label makes the label set unbounded: 5,000 distinct values in a 10-minute fixture means 5,000 new series from a single metric, scaling linearly with request rate and amplified by any retry loop, test run, or fanout. Stale series are retained for the lookback window (~5h+), so the index keeps growing long after the source stops. The result is index blow-up, scrape timeouts, dropped samples, retention-driven OOM, and ultimately the metric — and unrelated queries sharing the TSDB — going offline. Production is fine only because nothing is exporting this branch yet; the moment it ships, every request creates a new series. OTel already provides the supported fix: exemplars attach a trace reference to a metric data point without making the trace a label dimension, and trace IDs remain in logs and span attributes for debugging.

Below is the blocking response, ready to paste into the PR.

----

BLOCKING — reject merge. Unbounded-cardinality defect on `debug_trace_id`.

Why this is broken

  Trace IDs are 128-bit and unique per request by design. Promoting one to a Prometheus label makes the (metric, label-set) tuple unbounded: the 5,000 distinct values in a 10-minute staging fixture correspond to 5,000 new time series from a single metric, scaling linearly with request rate and amplified by any retry loop, test run, or fanout.

  Prometheus stores every (metric, label-set) pair as its own series in the TSDB head index, WAL, and on-disk blocks. One high-cardinality label on a hot metric causes index blow-up, scrape timeouts, dropped samples, retention-driven OOM, and ultimately takes this metric — and unrelated queries sharing the TSDB — offline. Stale series stay live for the lookback window (~5h+), so the damage persists well after the source stops emitting.

  This is the textbook high-cardinality-labels anti-pattern the Prometheus project explicitly warns against. OTel already provides the supported mechanism: exemplars link a metric data point to its trace without making the trace a label dimension, and trace IDs remain in logs and span attributes for debugging. The trace never needs to become a metric dimension.

Required before merge

  1. Remove `debug_trace_id` (and any equivalent raw-identifier label) from the metric. Trace correlation belongs in logs and span attributes; trace↔metric linking belongs in exemplar metadata — not in a label.

  2. If a label is genuinely needed for debugging, replace it with a bounded classification — e.g. `trace_class` with a fixed enum (`ok | retry | error | sampled`) — never the raw ID.

  3. Add a CI test for this metric that proves arbitrary IDs do not create new series:
     a. Generate >= 10,000 synthetic trace IDs over a fixture window; assert the metric's label-value set is unchanged after the run.
     b. Assert no new series are created (diff `prometheus_tsdb_head_series` or equivalent before/after the run).
     c. Assert each sampled data point still resolves to its trace via exemplar metadata, so debugging capability is preserved.

  4. Add a static guard (lint or unit test) that rejects any exported label whose values look high-entropy (length >= 16 hex or base64-ish charset) so this regression cannot recur.

Here's the summary for you:

The gap, plainly
- Review binds trust to bundle B0 / digest d0. Restore binds execution to whatever `latest` points at *now*. Between those two moments, a pointer rewrite can substitute a different validly signed bundle B1 ≠ B0. The signatures stay correct; the trust they express was bound to the wrong artifact. This is the publish-atomicity shape (durable record of what was prepared → atomic activate of *that* object) minus the atomic-activate discipline.
- It's also the lease-convergence-readiness error class (rb_1789241064338) one layer up: "pointer ready" / "process ready" ≠ "right thing ready."

Three blocking requirements on shard-keeper#188
1. Pin d0 immutably at review time (signed manifest entry / append-only record / content-addressed key). Not a pointer, tag, alias, or mutable config row.
2. Re-verify at restore: load bytes B* → recompute d* = digest(B*) → assert d* == d0 → verify owner signatures over (B*, d*) → only then mark eligible. On any mismatch: do not load, page the owner, treat as tamper-or-mismatch (no transient retry). Verify-at-sync proves nothing about restore.
3. Pointer rewrites must not silently widen the eligible-bundle set. Either a flipped `latest` to B1 ≠ B0 is rejected because B1 has no matching d0 record, or it's an explicit owner-attested operation that still has to pass the d0→B* equality check. Order non-bypassable: bytes → recompute digest → compare to d0 → verify signatures → eligible.

- Staging repro: B0 pinned, pointer untouched, restore succeeds, audit trail records (bytes loaded, d* computed, d0 compared equal, signature verified) for the *actual restore*, not for sync.

Same-day guidance

Activity
- Normal activity is fine. Keep using the vaccinated arm — gentle movement and normal use reduce stiffness rather than worsen it. You can do your usual work and exercise; just skip anything that sharply aggravates arm pain.

Hydration
- Drink normally. Extra fluids don't boost vaccine response, but staying hydrated helps if a low-grade fever or achiness shows up later today. Moderate caffeine and alcohol are fine; alcohol can amplify fatigue or malaise, so lighter is better if you're unsure how you'll feel.

Local soreness

When to seek urgent care (call 911 or go to ER)
Go right away for any of these — they suggest a serious allergic reaction:
- Trouble breathing, shortness of breath, wheezing, or throat tightness
- Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat
- Widespread hives, rash, or flushing
- Dizziness, fainting, or near-fainting
- Rapid or pounding heartbeat, chest tightness
- Hoarseness or trouble swallowing

Timing: serious allergic reactions almost always begin within minutes to a few hours after vaccination (most within 30 minutes), and rarely past 24 hours. Any new onset of the above in the next 24 hours is the window to watch.

When to contact a clinician (non-urgent)
- Fever above about 102°F (39°C), or any fever lasting more than a day or two
- Arm redness, swelling, or pain that is getting worse rather than better after 24-48 hours, or that spreads well beyond the injection site — can signal a strong local reaction or, rarely, a site infection
- Symptoms persisting beyond ~48 hours without improvement, or anything new that concerns you

The defect, briefly: the storage layer's upsert key is just the (exp_gen, obs_gen) pair. So attempt A1 (mismatch → failure) and attempt A2 (retry, same pair → pass) collide on the key. The second upsert overwrites the first. The review window then queries "what do we know about this pair?" and gets back only the passing record — the mismatch is gone, and the storage layer has no way to detect that it ever happened. Provenance collapses. The closed 2027-09-07 worker-dedup defect is the same shape: an observation keyed on something narrower than attempt identity lets a later attempt launder an earlier failure.

---

Subject: Blocking — parity-fixture storage: retry overwrites prior failure evidence (provenance defect)

Roman —

Bounded provenance review of the parity-fixture storage optimization that upserts by (expected_generation, observed_generation) pair. Blocking. Production unchanged.

**The defect (what I found)**

In staging, attempt A1 against a given (exp_gen, obs_gen) pair surfaced an unexpected downstream key and recorded a failure. A worker retry, A2, with the same generation pair, subsequently passed. Because the storage key is the pair itself, A2 silently overwrote A1. The seven-day review window now returns only the passing observation; the mismatch is no longer queryable, and there is no record that A1 ever ran. The storage layer cannot tell that it has lost provenance — it just looks like the pair was always green.

This is the same shape as the worker-dedup defect we closed earlier this month: an evidence key narrower than attempt identity lets a later attempt erase an earlier mismatch.

**Required to lift the block**

1. **Immutable attempt identity (or equivalent retained failure history).** No two attempts may collide on the storage key. Add an attempt identifier to the composite — e.g., attempt_id = worker + monotonic attempt sequence + timestamp, or any value the layer treats as unique per attempt. The (exp_gen, obs_gen) pair alone must not address an existing record. Acceptable equivalent: storage that retains every prior failure for a pair and refuses to overwrite a failing record with a passing one. Either way, A2 must not be able to launder A1.

2. **Complete signed-generation and key/value evidence for every attempt.** Each attempt record carries, at minimum:
   - attested expected_generation — producer-side attestation of how it was computed, on what input, with a checksum/signature the storage layer can verify
   - attested observed_generation — same, independently
   - exact downstream key observed (raw)
   - exact value observed (raw)
   - worker identity, attempt sequence, attempt timestamp
   - outcome and, on failure, the full mismatch detail

   "Same generation" on a retry must be re-attested, not inherited from the prior attempt. A forged or unsigned generation claim must be rejected at the storage boundary, not accepted as a stealth rewrite.

3. **Regressions proving a later retry cannot erase an earlier mismatch.** Required test set before sign-off:
   - inject A1 = fail with unexpected downstream key, then A2 = pass with the same (exp_gen, obs_gen); assert both records are queryable by pair after A2, and the review-window query returns both
   - inject ≥300 retries against the same pair with mixed outcomes; assert no loss of failure detail and no double-count (mirrors the worker-dedup regression shape)
   - inject concurrent retries against distinct (exp_gen, obs_gen) pairs; assert no cross-pair contamination
   - inject a forged/unsigned generation claim; assert rejection at the storage boundary
   - inject an A2 whose attempt_id collides with A1; assert idempotent rejection, not overwrite

I'm staying scoped to provenance; parity-fixture semantics more broadly are not mine to sign off on. Happy to walk through any of this on the PR.

— Alex

Here's a tight way to frame the rule — split it into the precondition (input must allow normalization) and the postcondition (output must be the result of normalization), with each one explaining *why* it's needed in addition to the other.

  The two-zero-weights case is the canonical example: each weight is
  individually valid (zero is allowed), so a per-weight check passes, but
  the group total is exactly 0 and there is no meaningful denominator. The
  validator has to look at the *group*, not just its members.

  PRE-NORMALIZATION  (fails fast on bad input)
    Require total ∈ ℝ and total > 0.
      - finite  → rejects NaN and ±Infinity from corrupt/garbage weights
      - strictly positive (not >= 0) → rejects the two-zeros case where
        every member is individually valid but the group is unsplittable
    Failing here means "don't try to normalize" — the error can point at
    the offending group, and no NaN/Inf outputs are produced.

  POST-NORMALIZATION  (catches what the precondition can't see)
    Require every wᵢ' ∈ ℝ and Σ wᵢ' = 1 within tolerance.
      - finite per-output → catches floating-point edge cases the
        precondition can't see (e.g. one weight underflows to a denormal
        that becomes 0, single-member groups at float edges, partial
        normalization if a weight was silently dropped)
      - sum-to-1 (within ε) → catches aggregate drift: even when every
        output is finite, weights may have been dropped, double-counted,
        or accumulated rounding error past the tolerance
    Failing here means "the math went sideways despite good input" — a
    different class of bug than a zero total, and worth a distinct error.

  WHY BOTH, IN THIS ORDER
    - Precondition alone: a positive total doesn't guarantee finite
      outputs. You'd silently publish NaN weights to downstream consumers.
    - Postcondition alone: you've already divided through garbage; the
      error you raise talks about output shape, not input cause, and you
      can't always reconstruct which weight was bad.
    - Precondition first tells the owner *why* (input had no denominator).
      Postcondition tells the owner *that* (result isn't a valid
      probability distribution). Reporting cause before symptom makes
      the validator's failures actionable.

  WHAT EACH CHECK REJECTS, CONCRETELY
    total = 0                   → precondition fails (two-zero-weights case)
    total = NaN or Inf          → precondition fails (corrupt config)
    total > 0, one output NaN   → postcondition fails (float edge the
                                  precondition couldn't see)
    total > 0, outputs ≠ 1     → postcondition fails (weights dropped or
                                  rounding past tolerance)

If Wes wants it even more compact, the one-line version is:

  Normalization is defined only when the total is finite and > 0; the
  result is correct only when every output is finite and they sum to 1.
  Both checks are required because each catches failures the other
  structurally cannot.

— What the defect actually is

The Android handoff was marked implementation-ready, but the bytes that would have been published were not the bytes that were validated. The validation verdict, the bytes behind `current`, and the readiness flag are three separate commits, and `current` is mutable. Sequence:

  1. Generated-artifact metadata is validated against the manifest.
  2. Android bytes are fetched through the mutable `current` URL.
  3. `current` is replaced by another writer.
  4. `implementation_ready = true` is published from the *stale* validation result.

Step 4 succeeds because the readiness writer reads its verdict from the validation record, not from the bytes it would actually serve. Result: ready=true, but the bytes the next reader would pull are not the bytes that were checked. This is the same failure class as the canonical-package-version advance you flagged earlier — stale validation re-applied to a moved target — except the target moved inside the process, not across versions. So the canonical_package_version check alone does not catch it; readiness is bound to the validation event, not to the artifact identity.

— What the build/CI side needs to require

Immutable artifact identity, or a content digest, has to be bound through the readiness transition. Specifically:

  • The verdict must be bound to a SHA-256 content digest of the actual bytes, not to a URL, pointer, or manifest version.
  • Validated bytes have to be frozen in an immutable, fsynced location before readiness can be published. The pointer you point at is not the artifact; the bytes are.
  • Advancing `current` to the validated digest and writing `implementation_ready = true` must be one atomic operation under a single lock. A swap between fetch and readiness is exactly the race we just saw.
  • Fail closed on: digest mismatch, any mutation of `current` between digest capture and readiness commit, or any divergence between the readiness record's digest and the bytes the reader would actually load.

The readiness writer should re-check, at commit time, that the digest it is about to certify is still the digest of the bytes behind `current`. If the manifest or the pointer advanced, the verdict is stale and readiness must stay false.

  2. Swap of `current` after digest capture but before readiness commit.
  3. Concurrent swap during the validation-to-commit window (two writers racing the lock).
  4. Crash before the readiness commit lands.

  • A rejected readiness commit must leave ready=false; `current` must not advance; readers must see only the previously validated bytes.
  • A restart after a crash must serve the prior complete validated set with ready=false, never a half-written or absent readiness.
  • active_digest, last_validated_digest, and last_attempted_digest must be observable by run_id so a blocked-handoff diagnosis can tell stale-input blocks from genuine-mismatch blocks.

The theme is that each phrase involves doing something AGAIN — the circled revealer spells out the concept directly.

- DOUBLE TAKE = taking a second look (looking AGAIN, after the surprise makes you glance back)
- SECOND ACT = the act that comes AGAIN, the next iteration / comeback
- LETTERPRESS = pressing letters — and printing is the action of pressing the same letters AGAIN and AGAIN to pull multiple impressions off the press

So the through-line is "repetition / doing it once more": a double take is a look done twice, a second act is a performance done over, and a letterpress run is the same letters struck again and again to print copies.

A tighter way to see it: each phrase ends in a verb that becomes "do it AGAIN" the moment you drop a RE- in front of it — TAKE → RETAKE, ACT → REACT, PRESS → REPRESS. The revealer AGAIN is basically naming the RE- prefix.

Defect

The reconciliation query defines the in-period set with `source_timestamp` (correct — when the event happened upstream) but then layers a `processed_at <= cutoff` predicate on top. That second predicate is operational, not semantic: it describes when our pipeline ingested the row, not when the event occurred. Rows whose `source_timestamp` is in period but whose `processed_at` lands after the cutoff (delayed upstream emission, retry queue, backfill, late-arriving correction) get filtered out before reconciliation runs. Two consequences, both silent:

  1. Delayed and retried in-period rows are dropped from the reconciliation set. They are never attributed to the period they actually belong to, so a "missing" in-period event looks like "period is clean" instead of "we haven't reconciled this yet."
  2. The freeze predicate sees a smaller, prematurely-complete set and fires. The period closes while real in-period `source_timestamp` rows are still unresolved.

`processed_at` is fine as a gate on *actions* taken against already-reconciled rows (e.g., settlement eligibility for rows processed before cutoff). It is not fine as part of the membership predicate that decides which rows the reconciliation owes an answer for. The cutoff is being used in two incompatible roles: defining what counts and deciding what's done.

ONE-PAN PLAN (chicken thighs, sweet potatoes, green beans)

SETUP — 4:15 PM
- Oven to 425°F. Half sheet pan, rimmed.
- FIRST: set KIBO PORTION aside unseasoned in a small foil pouch on a corner of the pan: 1 small chicken thigh + ~1/3 cup sweet potato cubes. Fold loosely. Nothing on it but itself.
- Cube remaining sweets (~1.5 lbs into 1/2" pieces).
- Pat 5 remaining thighs dry, salt + pepper only both sides.
- Trim ~8 oz green beans, smash 4 garlic cloves, halve 1 lemon.

STAGE 1 — ROAST SWEETS, THEN ADD CHICKEN — 4:25 PM
- Toss sweets on the pan with 2 Tbsp olive oil, salt, pepper.
- Roast 425°F, 12 min.
- Push sweets to one side. Add chicken skin-up on the other side; tuck the Kibo pouch on the far corner.
- Drizzle chicken with 1 Tbsp olive oil. Scatter smashed garlic over the sweets.
- Roast 20-25 min more. Pull when chicken hits 158°F internal (carryover will take it to ~163°F during the hold).

PAUSE POINT — 5:05-5:10 PM, when Devika walks in
- Remove the Kibo pouch, portion into his bowl with his normal measured kibble. Set aside — feed him on his usual schedule so the walk isn't rushed.
- Hold the sheet pan at 200°F in the oven, door cracked 1 inch. Chicken rests in its own rendered fat; skin will soften, that's fine — the broil fixes it.
- Green beans stay OFF the pan until the final step so they come out bright and snappy, not limp.

IF COMMUTE RUNS LONG (>45 min hold)
- Transfer chicken only into a small baking dish, add 3 Tbsp water or broth, tent with foil, back into the 200°F oven. Sweets stay on the sheet pan unwrapped. This keeps thighs juicy past 60-75 min without drying.

FINISH — 5 MIN, AFTER THE WALK — ~6:00 PM
- Oven to 475°F or broiler on high.
- Toss green beans with 1 Tbsp olive oil, minced garlic, pinch of salt; spread into the empty space on the pan.
- Broil 4-5 min: beans blister at the tips, chicken skin re-crisps, sweets caramelize at the edges.
- Pull, squeeze half a lemon over everything, rest 2 min, serve.

WHY IT HOLDS WITHOUT DRYING
Thighs have enough fat and connective tissue to coast through 45-90 min at 200°F without tightening, and the brief 5-min broil at the end re-crisps the skin before the interior overcooks. Pulling at 158°F (not 165°F+) is what buys you the long, safe hold.

Total active work: ~10 min. Hold window: 45-90 min safe.

Good — no symptoms, so the rehab gate is clear. On the line itself, the hip drift during the stand is almost always a tension-loss problem in the order of operations, not a strength issue. A few things to focus on:

- Make the sidepull active from the start, not passive. A passive left sidepull is exactly what lets your right hip swing out as you stand. Pull your left shoulder into the wall and keep it loaded the whole move.

- Press through the high left foot *before* you stand. Think of the move as a scissor: left foot pressing down, left hand pulling toward your chest. That pressure is what keeps your hips pulled in.

- Keep the repaired right shoe weighted and engaged on the edge, not flailed. Right leg bent, right hip in — a sloppy right leg is often the real culprit behind the drift.

- Cue "stand onto the left foot," not "stand up." "Stand up" makes you extend vertically and drift; "stand onto the foot" drives through it and locks hips at the wall.

- Pre-set your hips *before* you initiate: flexed, abs on, hips slightly tucked, body compressed close to the wall. Then stand from that compressed position, not from a loose one.

- The crimp is a target, not a throw. Match the rhythm — sidepull pull + foot press + hips-in + reach. It'll be there when you arrive with hips close.

APPLE CRISP — 8x8 pan, not-too-sweet
Serves 4-6. Total hands-on: ~15 min.

FILLING
  6 apples, peeled, cored, sliced 1/4" (~6 cups)
  1 Tbsp lemon juice
  2 Tbsp flour (or 1 Tbsp cornstarch)
  3 Tbsp brown sugar
  1 tsp cinnamon
  1/4 tsp salt
  pinch nutmeg (optional)

Toss in a bowl, scrape into the ungreased 8x8.

TOPPING
  3/4 cup old-fashioned oats
  1/2 cup flour
  1/3 cup brown sugar, packed
  1/2 tsp cinnamon
  1/4 tsp salt
  6 Tbsp cold butter, cubed

Pinch butter into the dry mix with your fingers until you have clumps ranging from pea-size to oat-cluster. Scatter over the filling — don't press down.

SEQUENCE (assemble -> walk -> bake)

  1. Before the walk: prep apples, toss with filling mix, dump in the 8x8. Make topping in the same bowl, scatter on top. Cover the pan with foil or a lid and leave on the counter.
  2. Walk Kibo. 20-30 min rest is fine — apples will darken slightly (cosmetic only), the cold butter will soften a touch but still bakes right. Nothing in this is in any food-safety danger zone for that window.
  3. When you're back: heat oven to 375°F. Uncover the pan.
  4. Bake 35-45 min. Done when the topping is deep golden and the filling bubbles thickly at the edges. If the topping browns before the middle bubbles, tent loosely with foil.
  5. Rest 10-15 min so the filling sets up. Serve warm.

NOTES
  - Slightly soft apples are ideal for crisp — they break down into a jammy filling. Don't toss them.
  - Leave the skins on if you want it more rustic and don't mind the chew.
  - Eat with plain yogurt, cold cream, or a small scoop of ice cream. The recipe is intentionally restrained on sugar, so a topping on the plate helps.
  - One bowl for filling, one for topping (or just the same bowl rinsed), one pan. Minimal cleanup.

Kibo first-salt routine — 10/18/27

  When to boot up
    Any walk on visibly treated pavement, slush, or wet surfaces where deicer may have run off.
    Skip on dry, untreated stretches — boots on for no reason just build nail wear and rub risk.
    Put boots on at the door so treated residue doesn't track back into the apartment.

    Two fingers slide under the cuff when fastened — snug, not compressing fur.
    Toe clearance: paw flat in the boot, no scrunching at the front.
    No fur bunched under the strap; boot sits straight, not twisted around the leg.
    30-second indoor shuffle: no limp, no frantic kicking. If he freezes or back-legs out of them, refit before you leave the hallway.

    Boots off at the door.
    Lukewarm rinse or damp cloth on each paw; get between the toes and around the dewclaw.
    Dry thoroughly, especially between toes — that moisture is exactly what set up the 9/2/24 localized infection.
    Quick pad/crease scan for residue, pinkness, or fresh cracks.

    Redness between toes or on pads.
    Lifting a paw or favoring a leg.
    Licking, chewing, or shaking paws more than usual.
    Limping, gait change, or reluctance to start the walk.
    Any pad crack that's bleeding or not closing within a day.

# Ingest-edge controls — how they compose

The production ingest path applies four independent controls. Each fires on its own condition; none replaces another. Here is how they layer when more than one could apply to the same request.

## 1. Whole-batch hard reject — 8,000 points (permanent)

If the submitted batch exceeds 8,000 data points in total, the request is **rejected as a whole, before any per-item work**. This is a permanent limit, not a retryable condition. The SDK should treat the response as terminal for that batch:

- Do not split the batch client-side and resend the pieces as separate requests in an attempt to slip past the cap. The 8,000-point ceiling is a batch-level invariant, and exceeding it indicates a payload-design or chunking issue the caller needs to fix.
- Do not treat a 4xx response on this path as backoff-eligible. No retry will succeed until the caller reduces the batch.

**Owner:** whole-batch sizing and chunking policy belongs to the mapped batch-ingest owner.

## 2. Decoded-attribute byte cap — 1,048,576 bytes (request-wide, pre-acceptance)

Before the request is accepted and before anything is enqueued, the **total decoded attribute payload across the entire request** is measured against 1,048,576 bytes (1 MiB). If exceeded, the request is **rejected before acceptance and before enqueue** — it never enters the waiting queue, and there is no retry budget consumed.

- This is a request-wide byte measure, not a per-point or per-series measure. A request with many small points can still trip it; a request with few large points can stay under it.
- Because rejection happens pre-acceptance, the tenant's eight-request waiting cap (rule 4) is **not** decremented and no admission slot is held.
- This limit is independent of the 8,000-point cap: a request can be under the point cap and still fail on bytes, or vice versa. A well-formed request satisfies both.

**Owner:** attribute-decoding and byte-budget enforcement belongs to the mapped ingest-decoder owner.

## 3. Pre-acceptance admission gate — 72 decode admissions (retryable)

Once decoded-attribute bytes are within budget, the request enters a **pre-acceptance admission check** with a cap of **72 decode admissions**. If admissions would exceed 72, the result returned to the caller is **retryable** — meaning the SDK can safely retry with backoff, and the request did not occupy an accepted-waiting slot.

- "Retryable" here means the rejection is transient: another request may release an admission slot, after which a retry can succeed.
- This control sits between the byte check (rule 2) and acceptance. It is not a substitute for either the byte cap or the whole-batch cap — it governs how many decoded requests the system is willing to admit simultaneously, independent of their size.

**Owner:** admission-gate sizing and retry/backoff behavior belongs to the mapped ingest-runtime owner.

## 4. Accepted-waiting cap — 8 per tenant (separate)

Once a request clears rules 1–3 and is **accepted**, it occupies one slot in the tenant's waiting queue, which is capped at **8 accepted requests per tenant**. A request that would push a tenant over 8 is held or rejected at acceptance, not pre-admission.

- This is a **tenant-scoped, accepted-state** limit — it only counts requests that have already been admitted.
- It is unrelated to the 72 admission gate (rule 3), which is system-wide and pre-acceptance.
- The byte and admission controls do not reduce or replace this per-tenant cap. A tenant can still hit 8 accepted-and-waiting even when individual requests are small and admissions are well under 72.

**Owner:** tenant queueing and fairness policy belongs to the mapped queue/tenant-isolation owner.

## Composition summary

| Control | Scope | Stage | Outcome if exceeded |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8,000 points | Whole batch | Pre-decode | Permanent whole-batch reject |
| 1,048,576 decoded-attribute bytes | Whole request | Pre-acceptance, pre-enqueue | Permanent reject; no queue slot consumed |
| 72 decode admissions | System-wide | Pre-acceptance | Retryable result |
| 8 accepted waiting requests | Per tenant | Post-acceptance | Acceptance held/rejected |

Key non-replacement points for SDK integration:

- **The byte and admission controls did not replace the whole-batch rule.** The 8,000-point ceiling still applies first, as a permanent reject.
- **The byte and admission controls did not replace the tenant-waiting rule.** The 8-per-tenant cap on accepted requests still applies, independently of byte budget and admission gate.
- A request can fail at any single layer while passing all others. Each layer has its own retry semantics (terminal vs. retryable vs. held) — see the table above.

## What this means for the SDK

- Validate batch point count client-side before sending; treat over-limit responses as terminal.
- Validate expected decoded-attribute size where feasible; do not assume "under the point cap" implies "under the byte cap."
- Treat 72-admission over-limit as retryable with backoff. Do not treat it as permanent.
- Respect the 8-per-tenant accepted-waiting cap by not opening more concurrent accepted requests than the cap allows, even when bytes and admissions are individually fine.

## Open implementation decisions

The following are intentionally **not** decided here and remain with the mapped owners:

- Exact backoff curve and jitter for the retryable admission path — ingest-runtime owner.
- Whether the SDK should pre-flight decoded-attribute size estimates or rely solely on server rejection — ingest-decoder owner.
- Client-side concurrency shaping to stay under the 8-per-tenant accepted-waiting cap — queue/tenant-isolation owner, with SDK-side guidance from the batch-ingest owner.

Bicycle winter routine. Run it before the first salted ride and you'll spot most issues while they're cheap.

1. TIRES (every ride, full check weekly)
   - Pressure: cold drop is real — check weekly, top off before each ride; aim near the upper end of the printed range for winter (firmer tire resists pinch flats on cold pavement).
   - Visual: sidewalls for cuts, cracking, bulges; tread for wear bars; pick out embedded glass/wire.
   - Spin test: true the wheel by eye; any hop or wobble >1–2 mm means a shop visit.
   - If you'll ride on ice/compact snow, swap to a wider tire or dedicated studded tire on the front at least — salt alone doesn't justify studs, black ice does.

2. BRAKES (front + rear, weekly)
   - Lever pull: should feel firm and consistent between front and rear; spongy or lever-to-bar = stop riding, shop.
   - Pads: ≥1.5 mm of material, even wear, no glazing; aligned square to rim/rotor with full contact. Front is your main stopper — keep pads freshest there.
   - Rims: wipe with isopropyl alcohol (not degreaser — it leaves a film that squeals and slips).
   - Cables/housing: any fraying, kinks, frozen sluggishness, or rust bleeding = replace; housing full of salty water is the usual winter failure mode.
   - Quick-disconnect or barrel adjusters: confirm they're seated; a half-loosened adjuster will drift closed and kill lever feel mid-ride.

3. LIGHTS AND REFLECTORS (every ride)
   - Run both lights for 30 sec before leaving the garage — cold cuts rechargeable capacity, so a "full" battery indoors may not be full at 25°F.
   - Lens clean, mount tight, beam aimed level (not up at drivers, not at your front wheel).
   - Reflectors: front white, rear red, side amber on wheels or frame; replace any cracked/missing ones — they're cheap and legally required in most places after dark.

4. CHAIN CARE (after every wet/salty ride, full re-lube weekly)
   - Wipe the chain with a dry rag while pedaling backward — black gunk on the rag is ground-up salt; do this BEFORE any lube goes on.
   - Monthly: degrease the chain fully, scrub cassette and chainrings with a stiff brush, dry, then apply one drop per roller of a wet-condition lube. Let it sit 5 min, wipe off the outside — lube on the outside attracts grit; lube inside the rollers is what you want.
   - Stretch check: lift the chain off the chainring at the front; if it lifts more than ~half a tooth, the chain and likely the cassette are due for replacement.

5. SALT REMOVAL (after every wet/salty ride — non-negotiable)
   - Rinse the whole bike with plain water from a bucket or gentle hose. No pressure washers — they push salt paste into bearings, BB, and hub internals where it kills them quietly.
   - Focus on the chainstay and seatstay undersides, dropouts, fender mounts, and behind the seat tube — salt collects there and eats paint and steel first.
   - Dry everything with a rag, then re-lube the chain.
   - Once a month in salted months, do a more thorough wash with mild dish soap and a soft brush, including the fork lowers and around the brake calipers.

6. SEND IT TO A SHOP (don't ride) when you find any of these:
   - Brake lever pulls to the bar, feels spongy, or one brake is noticeably weaker than the other.
   - Pad material below ~1.5 mm, pads contaminated with oil, or pads not contacting squarely.
   - Wheel hop, wobble, or a broken/spinning spoke.
   - Tire with a visible bulge, a cut you can see casing cord through, or a flat spot.
   - Headset play (rock the bike with front brake held — any clunk), or a creak/tick from the bottom bracket that wasn't there before.
   - Frame, fork, handlebar, or stem with a crack, dent, or paint cracking around a stress point.
   - Chain skipping under load, a stuck link, or visible chain/cassette wear past limits.
   - Cable that moves stiffly or has visible rust bleeding at the housing ends.
   - Lights fail before or during a ride and you have no spare — no lights at dusk in winter is a no-ride condition, full stop.

Quick habit that ties it all together: keep a small kit by the door — rag, soft brush, isopropyl alcohol, wet lube, hand pump with gauge, and a headlamp so you can do the weekly checks in the unlit garage without excuses.

INTERIM PLAN — COLD WORK-ROOM RADIATOR
(Friday 2027-11-20, repair still pending)

PRECONDITION
The failure is one stuck radiator in one room. Other radiators work, so this is not whole-apartment heat loss and not a building emergency. The room is safe to occupy. Goal: stay productive in it without touching the radiator/valve, blocking its access path, buying equipment, or relocating.

CLOTHING (worn inside the work room)
- Base layer: long-sleeve thermal top + thermal leggings
- Mid: wool or fleece sweater
- Optional seated layer: light down vest or shawl over the shoulders
- Feet: wool socks (cotton holds sweat and goes cold). Indoor slippers over the socks help.
- Hands: fingerless gloves, or a USB hand-warmer muff if you already own one. A heated mouse pad is fine.
- Head: a soft beanie. Sounds silly indoors; a lot of heat leaves through the scalp.
- Lap / shoulders: a wool throw. NOT an electric blanket — that counts as a heater.

DOOR POSITION AND ROOM LAYOUT
- Close the work-room door fully while you work. Contain the small heat you and your equipment generate.
- Roll a towel along the bottom of the door to block drafts from the hallway.
- Do NOT move furniture, boxes, or storage against the radiator, the valve, or the supply/return pipes. The access path has to stay visible and reachable for the repair visit.
- Do NOT drape anything over the radiator "to help it warm up." It will not, and it hides the problem from the technician.
- Leave any return-air vent in the room open as the building intended.

SHORT BREAKS
- Every 30–45 minutes, leave the room for 5–10 minutes.
- Step into a warm room (one with a working radiator), close that door too, and let it recover.
- Use the break to refill a hot drink. A warm mug in the hands helps fingers.
- Stand up and walk a short loop. Cold air pools low; circulation matters more than people expect.
- A 1–2 minute stretch keeps blood moving to hands and face.

NON-HEATER COMFORTS YOU ALREADY OWN OR CAN DO
- Hot water bottle, refilled from the kettle. Not a heater.
- Wool throw over the legs while seated.
- Hot drink on rotation so there's always a warm mug in reach.

URGENCY TRIGGERS (escalate from "follow up" to "today/now" on any of these)
1. Indoor temp in the work room drops below ~16°C / 60°F sustained, or below ~13°C / 55°F at any point.
2. The cold spreads to other rooms — the diagnosis is no longer "one stuck radiator," it's a system fault.
3. Pipe-side concerns on that branch: visible condensation, frost, any leak, banging/gurgling, or no movement at all. Frozen-pipe risk once overnight outdoor temps go below freezing.
4. Cold-injury symptoms: persistent finger/toe numbness, blanching that doesn't pink back up after warming.
5. Equipment: laptop battery dying unusually fast, screens dimming, or anything suggesting the room is going below ~10°C / 50°F (lithium-ion capacity collapses in the cold and a dead laptop on a deadline is a real cost).
6. Sustained indoor air below your city's legal minimum heat (commonly ~17–20°C / 62–68°F during heating season when outdoor is below ~13°C / 55°F — look up your specific jurisdiction; NYC, Chicago, Boston, etc. each have written thresholds).
7. No response from management by Monday morning — three business days silent is enough on its own to escalate.

WHAT TO SEND MANAGEMENT (concise, written, dated)
"Work-room radiator still cold as of Fri 2027-11-20 inspection; other radiators in the unit are fine. Indoor temp in the room is reading ~X°C. I have not touched the radiator/valve or blocked access. Please confirm a repair visit by [date]. If not feasible in that window, please advise a temporary solution. — [name, unit, date]"

Attach a photo of the cold radiator next to a working one for contrast. Short messages get answered; long emotional ones get deprioritized.

DECISION POINT
If Monday arrives with no reply, OR any of triggers 1–6 fires before then, move from "wait" to a formal habitability/heat complaint through whatever channel your city or county provides. That is the correct escalation — not buying a heater, not moving out of the room.

Note: I am not storing this as memory — it's a transient apartment issue, and the durable facts (lease, address, etc.) are already in your profile. If the repair drags past mid-December or escalates into a habitability complaint, ping me and I'll capture it then.

    or replayed retry — then drops every in-flight request, fails LB health
    checks, and starts a restart loop. Decode-and-validate is per-request
    input validation; it is not a fatal startup error. The current code is
    effectively a self-DoS: route policies are config that upstream
    pipelines regenerate and retry, so a bad publish from the pipeline
    takes the router down on every attempt.
    Fix: write an HTTP error response (400 with the validation message
    and a stable error code), emit a structured log line, and return.
    Keep the process alive.

MAJOR

2.  ResponseWriter is declared but never used
    The signature takes w but the function never writes to it, including
    on the success path. Callers get an empty 200 with no body and no
    Content-Type. Add a writeResponse(w, policy) (or at minimum set
    Content-Type + 200 + a small ack body) so the client knows the
    publish was accepted.

3.  publish error is dropped
    If publish returns an error it is silently swallowed. On failure the
    client still gets a successful response, the policy state is unclear,
    and we have no signal in metrics/logs to distinguish validation
    failures from publish failures. Capture the error, return 5xx, and
    increment a labeled counter so the two failure modes are visible
    separately.

MINOR

4.  HTTP method not pinned. The handler accepts any verb. If this
    mutates state, gate it to PUT/POST and require an If-Match / version
    so a stray GET (or a curl -X GET from a confused operator) cannot
    trigger a publish.

5.  No body-size or timeout guard. r.Body is decoded inline with no
    MaxBytesReader and no r.Context() deadline. Add both so a slow or
    oversized client cannot stall the goroutine, and so publish
    inherits cancellation when the client disconnects.

6.  Validation error message handling. Whatever decodeAndValidate returns
    is currently logged via Fatal and would likely be written back to
    the client on a 400. Make sure the response body does not echo
    internal field names or stack details; return a stable error code
    and put the verbose reason only in server logs.

QUESTIONS FOR WES

-  Is publish synchronous (handler returns 2xx only after the policy is
   live) or async (202 with propagation later)? Changes whether the
   handler needs to wait on a confirmation and whether an Idempotency-Key
   header matters for retried publishes.

-  Where does decodeAndValidate run today — same process, separate
   worker, or upstream in the config pipeline? If validation already
   happens upstream, this handler is double-paying cost and we should
   just trust a signed payload and verify the signature here instead.

That confirms it: the parser is doing a first-token-wins check, not a chain check. The asymmetry between `gzip, identity` (decoded as gzip) and `identity, gzip` (no-decode path) is the tell — same prefix shape, different paths because the rest of the chain is never inspected.

Shapes that slip past admission under first-token-only:

  - `identity, gzip` — edge skips decode, payload still gzipped. Downstream either rejects loudly or, worse, parses raw gzip bytes as the body. This is the smuggling-shaped one.
  - `gzip, gzip` — one decode on a double-encoded body; downstream sees garbage.
  - `gzip, br` (or any unknown) — edge decodes the first, downstream disagrees on what to expect.
  - `, gzip` / `gzip, ` — empty tokens silently ignored rather than rejected.
  - `gzip; q=0.5, br` — q-values and parameters dropped on the floor.

Risk class is front-end / back-end parser differential on Content-Encoding — same family as CL/TE smuggling. A client that knows the edge does first-token-only can craft a request where the edge decodes N times and an upstream decodes M times, with N ≠ M. The edge and the rest of the path need to agree on what "valid encoding chain" means, and right now the edge's contract is "the first token is the truth, everything else is decoration."

Hi Yuki,

Blocking review on the ingest-edge decoder Content-Encoding allowlist boundary. This is reviewer-level; implementation, canary, release, rollback, and the post-deploy adjustment all stay with you. I am not approving a canary, merge, deploy, or rollback window on this PR — those stay with you, and I will not reopen the close once the test set below is green.

================================================================================
Scope and ownership
================================================================================
- Path: ingest-edge decoder Content-Encoding admission.
- Owner: Yuki (implementation, canary, release, rollback).
- Reviewer role (this note): the Content-Encoding allowlist boundary, the rejection site, and the test set that proves the rejection. Nothing else.
- Adjacent items still open and out of scope here:
  * The 1,048,576-byte decoded-attribute limit and the 72-request decode-admission cap (already in production, already closed at the slot-release boundary).
  * The 10 MiB decoded-body ceiling and the restart-reconstruction retry / same-key replay durability work.
  * Any decision on adding a second encoding to the allowlist in the future — that is a separate PR with its own review.

================================================================================
The framing: one token, one name, one allowlist, before admission
================================================================================
The ambiguous interpretation today is the HTTP Content-Encoding header itself. RFC 9110 allows multiple encodings, multiple header instances, the identity token, the empty string, OWS commas, and quoted-string parameters. None of that ambiguity is load-bearing for ingest-edge. The decoder does not need a parser; it needs a matcher against a single token, and any request whose Content-Encoding is not exactly that one token must be rejected with HTTP 400 before it acquires a decode-admission slot and before any acceptance.

Concretely, the admission rule must be:

  The request's Content-Encoding header, after header-list coalescing per RFC 9110 §5.3, must be exactly the single token <TOKEN> (case-insensitive match, no parameters, no OWS, no other tokens present). Anything else is malformed and is rejected with HTTP 400 on the same code path that emits the response, before the decode-admission slot is acquired and before any acceptance. There is no second token, no fallback, no identity-or-token handling, and no "sniff the body" path.

I will not block on the choice of <TOKEN> itself. If gzip is the only production encoding, the allowlist is {gzip}. If a second encoding is added later, that is a new boundary, a new PR, and a new review.

================================================================================
What the PR must require to admit a request
================================================================================
The PR must demonstrate, at admission time and before the slot is acquired:

1. Exactly one Content-Encoding header is present after header coalescing. The field value is exactly one token. No parameters. No whitespace. Case-insensitive match against the singular allowlist token.
2. Anything that fails the rule in (1) returns HTTP 400 on the rejection path. The 400 is emitted before any decode work, before any decode-admission slot is acquired, and before any acceptance. The rejection is not retried; the caller can resubmit a corrected request.
3. The decode-admission slot is acquired only after the Content-Encoding check passes. A malformed request must not occupy a decode-admission slot for any non-zero duration; it must be rejected at admission.

================================================================================
Test set required before decode admission or acceptance
================================================================================
The proof is the test set, not the assertion. Each of the four cases below must fail at admission (HTTP 400, no slot acquired, no acceptance, no enqueue). The cases are distinct from each other and from the slot-release terminal-path tests already closed.

A. Chained encodings (must fail)
   - Request with Content-Encoding: gzip, gzip — two tokens in one header.
   - Request with two Content-Encoding headers — gzip and gzip separately.
   - Request with Content-Encoding: gzip then a second request on the same connection advertised as a chained encoding — separate admission, separate test.
   - Pass criteria for each: HTTP 400 emitted before slot acquisition; permits_held on the rejected request is zero at the 400-emit timestamp; the slot is re-acquirable immediately by a separate valid request.

B. Duplicated encodings (must fail)
   - Request with Content-Encoding: gzip and a second Content-Encoding: gzip header on the same request (RFC 9110 coalesces, but the boundary here is "exactly one token after coalescing", so a single gzip is allowed only when it is the sole token — duplicate-header pre-coalesce must still reject as malformed if it produces anything other than exactly one token).
   - Request with Content-Encoding: gzip, gzip (single header, duplicated token) — same outcome.
   - Pass criteria: HTTP 400 before admission; no slot acquired; no acceptance.

C. Empty encodings (must fail)
   - Request with Content-Encoding: (header present, empty value).
   - Request with Content-Encoding:   (OWS only).
   - Request with Content-Encoding: "" (quoted empty string).
   - Request with no Content-Encoding header at all (this is the only case whose disposition depends on the singular allowlist rule: if the allowlist requires the header to be present and exactly <TOKEN>, then absent is malformed; if the allowlist accepts absent as "no encoding", that choice must be written down and tested as the singular case, not implied). I will not block on the absent-header choice, but the rule must be singular and the test must pin it.
   - Pass criteria for malformed: HTTP 400 before admission; no slot acquired; no acceptance. Pass criteria for the explicit absent rule (if chosen): behavior is exactly one terminal outcome, exactly once, no slot leak.

D. Unknown encodings (must fail)
   - Request with Content-Encoding: deflate (not on the allowlist).
   - Request with Content-Encoding: zstd (not on the allowlist).
   - Request with Content-Encoding: br (Brotli, not on the allowlist).
   - Request with Content-Encoding: gzip;q=1.0 (parameter on the token — singular match means no parameters).
   - Request with Content-Encoding: gzip ; q=1.0 (OWS + parameter).
   - Request with Content-Encoding: GZIP (case-insensitive match is fine, but verify the implementation does the case-fold and not a partial-string match — pick a casing test that would catch a buggy startsWith).
   - Pass criteria for each: HTTP 400 before admission; no slot acquired; no acceptance; no decoder invocation; no body read for decoding.

================================================================================
The proof matrix
================================================================================
Each of the four cases (A–D) must have:

WALK-IN CHECKLIST — REAR-TIRE SIDEWALL SPLIT

KEEP THE LOAD OFF THE DAMAGED TIRE ON THE WAY THERE
- Walk the bike beside you, upright. Don't lean it toward you or push from the saddle — your weight goes on you, not the bike.
- Steer with one hand on the bars; the other hand is just guiding.
- Take the smoothest line: avoid curbs, potholes, gravel, seams, storm grates, and speed bumps with the rear wheel.
- Empty the rear rack / panniers / backpack off the back. Any load over the rear tire multiplies sidewall stress.
- If you have to cross rough ground, lift the rear by the saddle and roll the wheel over it instead of pushing.
- Go slow. Braking hard loads the rear; coast to a stop instead.

STOP THE TRIP IF YOU NOTICE
- Hissing, ticking, or any sudden air loss.
- The split visibly grows longer or wider, or the casing layers start to separate at the edges.
- A bulge, blister, or soft "give" at or near the split when you squeeze the sidewall.
- The tire goes flat, or it suddenly feels much softer than it did at the door.
- The bead lifts off the rim, or the wheel sits crooked / wobbles where it didn't before.
- Any new rim dent or scratch — could mean the original impact was worse than it looked.

QUESTIONS BEFORE YOU SAY YES TO A REPLACEMENT
- Is the sidewall repairable at all, or is replacement the only safe option? (Almost always replace — confirm.)
- What caused it — underinflation, pinch, curb strike, age, manufacturing? The cause determines whether the new tire is at the same risk.
- Exact size/model match, or is a tougher casing or wider tire a better fit for how I ride? (Rear wears faster — stronger casing is usually worth it.)
- Replace the tube at the same time? (Yes — if the tire's coming off, the tube should too.)
- Does the rim need inspection? (If a curb or pothole caused this, yes — rim damage will kill the next tire too.)
- Tire only, or pair? What's the trade-off in cost and wear mismatch?
- In stock today, or do I need to order? If ordered, how long, and is there a safe walk-home / loaner option in the meantime?
- Full cost broken out: tire, tube, labor, valve, rim tape, any shop supplies.
- Warranty on the new tire, and the shop's guarantee on the install.
- Ask them to show you the old tire's split after removal so you can see how deep it went and judge whether anything else was stressed.

One last thing: tell the tech not to inflate it before you both look at it — they need to see the damage at its current pressure, and you want to confirm the pressure they plan to set on the new tire before they install it.

Yes, retire the whole string. Here's why, and what to check on the replacement.

What's likely happening: a section going dark specifically when you move the cord near the molded plug is the signature of an intermittent break in the cord at a flex point — either fractured conductor strands inside the insulation or a loose/separated connection inside the molded plug body. Two reasons not to keep using it:

- Every make/break under load is a small arc. Low-current arcing won't necessarily trip a breaker, but it carbonizes insulation over time and is one of the more common cord-fire ignition sources. You often can't see or smell it until insulation has already failed.
- The underlying damage (cracked strands, weakened insulation, compromised strain relief) won't heal and worsens with more flexing. UL/ETL listing only covers the product as manufactured; once it's damaged, the listing is no longer in force and the rest of the assembly (sockets, splices, the other end of the cord) can't be trusted either.

It's not field-repairable, so replacement is the right call.

On the replacement, check for:

Certifications (the actual mark, not marketing copy):
- UL or ETL listed mark — on the package AND on a permanent tag attached to the cord, or molded into the plug. Avoid anything that only says "UL style" or "tested to UL standards" without the certification mark itself.
- Marked "indoor" or carrying the indoor-use symbol. (Outdoor strings work fine indoors; the hazard is the reverse.)
- Class 2 listed driver if it's an LED string with a wall-wart transformer — this is the single biggest safety differentiator for LED sets.

Cord specifications (printed on the jacket):
- SPT-2 insulation rather than SPT-1 — same gauge but thicker jacket, more durable.
- Wire gauge, e.g. "SPT-2 18 AWG" or "22 AWG" — heavier (lower AWG number) is sturdier.
- Polarized plug (one blade wider than the other) — required on current listed light strings.
- A replaceable fuse in the plug — usually behind a small slide cover on the plug face; spares included is a plus.
- Real strain relief where the cord enters the plug — the cord should pass through a soft flexible boot before entering the hard plug body, not enter a rigid housing directly.

On the package / instructions:
- Maximum number of connectable strings — don't chain more than listed.
- Lamp rating matches if any are replaceable.

One small longer-term fix worth mentioning: the failure mode (damage near the molded plug) usually traces to pulling on the cord or pinching it at the plug end. Routing the cord so the plug end sits in a stable spot — behind furniture, along a wall corner — and unplugging when Kibo has unsupervised run of the room (which you're already doing) goes a long way toward not repeating this.

POTS DE CREME (3 ramekins)

8 oz heavy cream + 4 oz bittersweet chocolate (60-70%), heated together just to a simmer.

Same-day sequence — minimal water, contaminants kept away from brake surfaces, lube only where it belongs.

  1. Dry-brush first (5 min, indoor or covered area)
     - Stiff nylon brush + old toothbrush on chain, cassette, chainrings,
       derailleur pulleys, dropouts, and around the bottom-bracket shell.
     - Knock loose salt crust off the chainstays/seatstays/down tube before
       any water touches it. Wet salt = paste that hides under paint.

  2. Low-water wash (no hose, no pressure washer)
     - Bucket with diluted mild dish soap OR a rinseless bike wash.
     - Damp sponge/cloth on the frame, top-to-bottom. Wring often.
     - Avoid directing water at the headset, bottom-bracket, hub axles,
       and any cable housing ends — salt wicks in.
     - Second pass with a clean damp cloth to lift residue.

  3. Drivetrain degrease
     - Apply bike-specific degreaser (or citrus/chain cleaner) to chain,
       cassette, chainrings, derailleur cages, both pulleys.
     - Scrub with the toothbrush; rotate cranks backward to work the chain.
     - Wipe chain with a clean rag held against it while backpedaling
       until the rag comes away nearly clean. Repeat once.

  4. Rinse/wipe
     - Light rinse from a low-flow bottle or a fresh damp cloth — never a
       stream aimed at bearings. Follow immediately with a dry towel.

  5. Dry thoroughly (do not skip)
     - Clean dry microfiber on frame.
     - Let the bike sit 10–15 min so trapped moisture exits cable housings
       and bearing seals. Compressed air on the chain and around the
       brakes helps if you have it.

  6. Brake surfaces — SEPARATE step, separate cloth
     - Disc rotors: isopropyl alcohol (90%+) on a lint-free cloth; wipe
       until no residue transfers. Do not touch the braking track with
       bare fingers afterward (skin oil = contamination).
     - Rim-brake surfaces: isopropyl alcohol on a fresh cloth; no grease
       film, no grit embedded in the pads.
     - If you used any spray cleaner anywhere on the bike, mask the
       rotors/rims with a paper towel before spraying.

  7. Lubricate — DRIVETRAIN ONLY, wet-condition lube
     - Salt + wet roads = use a wet lube (not dry). One drop per chain
       roller while backpedaling the whole loop; one drop on each
       derailleur pulley pivot; a thin film on the derailleur pivots and
       the exposed cable segments near the rear derailleur.
     - Wait 5 min, then wipe the chain firmly with a clean rag. The chain
       should look dry on the outside — lube inside the rollers, not on
       the surface. Excess lube is what grinds into a grinding paste.

  8. Post-clean inspection (static + functional)
     - Brakes: squeeze each lever — firm, no sponge. Spin each wheel —
       no rotor rub, no hesitation. Look at pad edges; if glossy or
       contaminated, replace before the next ride.
     - Drivetrain: shift through every gear, both directions. Chain must
       run silent and skip-free under hand pressure on the cranks.
     - Frame: quick visual at dropouts, BB weld, and behind the
       seatpost — salt collects there and hides fresh cracks.
     - Wheels: quick-release/through-axle still tight; spoke tension
       even; no new dents in the (replacement) rear tire; recheck
       pressure since cold/salt rides drop it.
     - Lights: front and rear still firing; salt film wipes off the
       lenses with the same alcohol cloth.
     - Cables/housing: no frayed ends, no rust bleed at ferrules.

Ride-ready the same day; re-lube the chain in ~50 miles or after the next wet/salted ride, whichever comes first.

No EOB file is in the workspace. Before I answer, I need to know: did you mean to attach an EOB, or are you asking me to teach the terms generally so you can read one yourself? Either way I'll explain the four terms — but whether there's anything "to pay or contest now" depends on the specific document, so I can't make that call without seeing it.

## Billed amount

What the provider (doctor, hospital, lab) charged for the service. This is essentially the sticker price — it's what they bill the insurance, not what anyone necessarily pays. It has no direct relationship to what care actually costs or what your plan considers reasonable.

## Allowed amount

What your insurance plan has decided the service is actually worth — also called "negotiated rate," "contracted rate," or "allowed benefit." Two ways it gets set:

- In-network: your insurer has a contract with the provider, so the allowed amount is a pre-negotiated number, usually well below billed.
- Out-of-network: there's no contract, so the allowed amount is set by your plan's fee schedule (often a percentage of Medicare or an "usual and customary" database). This is usually where surprise bills happen, because the provider can balance-bill you for the gap between billed and allowed.

Allowed amount is the number everything else on the EOB flows from.

## Plan payment

What your insurer actually paid the provider. Calculated as:

allowed amount − your cost-share (deductible, copay, coinsurance)

This is what's left after your share is applied. It can be $0 if you haven't met your deductible yet — that's normal, not a sign of a problem.

## Patient responsibility

What you owe the provider. Sum of:

- Deductible — what you pay before insurance starts paying
- Copay — flat fee per visit/service
- Coinsurance — your percentage of the allowed amount after deductible
- Non-covered amount — services your plan doesn't pay for at all (no balance-billing protection for these on most plans)

**Important rule:** for in-network providers, your responsibility is capped at your plan's cost-share. For out-of-network, the provider can bill you for billed minus allowed (balance billing), depending on your state and whether the No Surprises Act applies.

## Whether you need to pay or contest now

That depends on the specific EOB, which I don't have. To answer "pay or contest now" I'd need to see the document. If you share it (drop the PDF/image in the workspace, or paste the four numbers and the denial/adjustment codes if any), I can read it and tell you:

1. Whether the patient responsibility is real or a billing error
2. Whether any of it is balance-billing you shouldn't owe
3. Whether a denial code (CPT/diagnosis mismatch, prior auth, timeliness) means you or your provider should appeal

If you'd rather I just teach the terms generally for now and you'll bring an EOB to read when one arrives, say so and I'll stop here.
